To the bishops of Ariminum, Firmum, and Urbinum. Regarding the destruction of the city and church of Forosimphronium and the expulsion of soldiers and the plundering of goods from the citizens of Fano, an excommunication sentence was issued against the Fanenses once and again by our mandate. Since they persisted contumaciously in this state for a year and more, we, considering that as contumacy increases, punishment should also increase, warned them that according to the statutes of the general council they could be declared heretics and deprived of cathedral dignity, which they had already rendered themselves unworthy of. We ordered the renewal of this sentence by our venerable brother, the bishop of Ancona, and his co-judges to be publicly proclaimed on all Sundays and feast days with bells ringing and candles lit until adequate satisfaction was achieved.

However, our venerable brother, the bishop of Fano, concerned for the salvation of the flock committed to him, lest he be considered a hireling rather than a shepherd by ignoring its destruction, came to our presence and knocked for a long time at the gate of our mercy, having spent no small time at the apostolic see. He earnestly pleaded, though often rejected by us, and eventually overcame us with the appropriate persistence of his supplications, inclining us to have mercy on the aforementioned citizens. Since these citizens, as the bishop conveyed on their behalf, are prepared to make satisfaction according to our mandate, and since it is fitting that subsequent satisfaction should redeem the preceding fault so that the grievance caused by presumption be removed by the humility of satisfaction, we strictly mandate you by apostolic letters and in the virtue of obedience, to personally go to the city of Fano. There, taking into account the previous evasion of the Roman Church by the said citizens, you shall ensure that they take an oath to comply with the mandates of the Church, provide pledges of four thousand Ravennate pounds, and select twenty hostages from the best of the city, whom you shall send to Ariminum along with the aforementioned pledges.

Once these actions are providently and diligently performed with the necessary maturity as required in such an important matter, you shall subsequently inquire into the damages to the church of Forosimphronium, which citizens are said to have inflicted repeatedly with audacious temerity to add affliction to the afflicted, and about the satisfaction they allegedly provided after the initial grievances to the dear son, the elect of that place, as well as the expenses, if any, incurred for the benefit of the church on either side. You shall also ascertain the full truth regarding all circumstances related to this matter from the beginning of the citizens' presumption to the present time and report your findings to us in your letters, so that, informed by you, we may proceed more securely regarding their satisfaction.

You ought to execute the apostolic mandate with such vigilant caution and diligent solicitude that you may increase in fame and merit among people and that we may commend your foresight and circumspection in the Lord. If not all of you can be present, then two of you, etc. Given at the Lateran, on the 16th day before the Kalends of September, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Datum Laterani, XVI Kalendas Septembris, anno septimo pontificatus nostri.

To the bishop of Albano, legate of the Apostolic See. It would be unthinkable that the cause of the Holy Land should not be directed to its desired course, for which, as it pleased the Lord, such a multitude of Christians have perished, and we, from the beginning of our promotion, have endured such heavy labors and expenses, and you have labored beyond all expectations for such a long time, exposing yourself to countless dangers, even as the expenses incurred by others for the promotion of this cause are numerous. However, after kindly receiving and considering your letters, as well as those previously submitted by the other side and those newly offered, the agreement expressed in those letters, when we could have had equally favorable terms long ago, as we heard almost immediately after you reached Egypt, could not please or be acceptable to us.

Indeed, although we have informed you through other letters that our dearest son in Christ, Emperor Frederick of the Romans, ever august, and King of Sicily, had promised a swift journey to that land before and after his coronation and on the day of his coronation, the said emperor asserts that having spent a great deal of money for the princes and others coming with him to that coronation, and having given a large sum of money to those going to Damietta, he was not yet able, as was proper, to cross over with a strong hand, fearing that if he did not come as his magnificence demanded, the matter would more likely be confounded than advanced. The same emperor also firmly promises not only to us but to everyone in general, that in the coming expedition of March, with a strong and powerful arm, he will cross over. Because of this, he has earnestly and persistently requested that we deign to grant him a delay, to which, although it seems he has taken the term for himself until the said crossing, we have never been able to incline, no matter how much he was entreated.

Moreover, we have procured with the venerable brother of ours, the bishop of Ostia, who was sent to Lombardy and Tuscany for the same cause, and with the not insignificant amount of money expended by him from our own, the best aid for the Holy Land, so that if the said emperor, God forbid, does not cross over, you can expect a successful outcome of the matter with the help of Him from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes. And behold, our beloved son, the noble lord, the Marquis of Montferrat, having received the banner of the Prince of the Apostles and the sign of the cross, is preparing himself with a multitude of valiant knights for a swift aid to that land, who, with us granting fifteen thousand marks of silver, has been appointed your and the Roman Church's standard-bearer, and is bound to assist you in the aforementioned matter.

Therefore, as we lay our head in the lap of your discretion, we command you by apostolic writings to diligently consider the aforementioned matters and all the circumstances, having the counsel of the great and prudent men of the army, whom you see fit, whether in this matter or others, to proceed with the maturity that befits you and such a great matter, as you know it should be conducted for the glory of God and the salvation of Christendom. Dated at the Lateran, June 20, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

In the same way, it is written to the Templars, Hospitallers, the master and brothers of the Hospital of St. Mary of the Teutons, and the archbishop of Bordeaux, to each that as the way for the consummation of the matter is manifestly open, and it is hoped that God willing, aid will soon come from across the sea, and as it is said, many from the East are preparing for the aid of the Holy Land, it seems to us more useful to expect the hand of God's mercy than to incline to such agreements.

To the Archbishops of Messina and Reggio. Our beloved son in Christ, Frederick, the ever august Emperor of the Romans and King of Sicily, who was previously asked by us and our brothers, promised in person that he would freely restore our venerable brother, the Bishop of Cefalù, whom he had deprived of the church and other goods. Meanwhile, he was to strictly prohibit any form of alienation by either party under our authority. Therefore, we command your fraternity by apostolic writ, that after the bishop has been fully restored, if you see him as justly suspected of mismanagement, you shall provide him a prudent and honest coadjutor, who will not presume to attempt anything regarding temporal administration without his counsel, until we make other provisions based on verified truth. To the illustrious King Louis of the French. The ineffable depth of divine providence, reaching from end to end, strongly and sweetly arranges all things, and according to the secret design of His disposition, changes the kings of the earth through the succession of passing times. After your father, the illustrious King Philip of the French, had laudably carried out the affairs of his earthly kingdom, as we firmly believe, he was called to better things, and you were happily placed on his throne, so that with you reigning for him, and imitating his piety and justice, it seems that the father lives in the son. Although the death of your said father has saddened us, who loved him with sincere affection, as human beings, yet we have found solace in your elevation, so much so that the joy born from this has tempered the sorrow that occurred from the death of your aforementioned father, your own innate goodness of noble lineage giving us full confidence that you will not forsake the paths of your forebears to be imitated, but will succeed them in the kingdom's seat and in the beauty of virtues, the Lord providing. Therefore, transferring to you the sincere love with which we embraced your often-mentioned father, we are firmly resolved to attend to the honor and advantage of your highness, and to extend to you the apostolic favor in whatever suits. We therefore earnestly request and urge your circumspection, that you may imitate your aforementioned father in commendable deeds, and especially in the true devotion he is known to have had toward the apostolic see and the entire Church of God, so that just as he continually obtained apostolic grace due to his merits, you may also deserve it perpetually. Indeed, we have carefully listened to the letters which your majesty sent us regarding the matter of the noble man Theobald of Ulliaco and his relatives, and have fully understood their content, and have taken care to provide for this matter, considering your person particularly, as honorably as we could, as our letters sent to our venerable brother the bishop of Paris and others will fully declare to you. Therefore, protect your right with such gentleness and moderation that the circumspection of your highness may be rightly commended, and the apostolic favor should not be absent from you but present. Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

Letters to the Lord Pope. To the reverend father and lord Honorius, by the grace of God, the most holy supreme pontiff of the Roman Church and universal pope, Nicholas, by the same grace, the humble patriarch of the Alexandrian see, sends due and prompt reverence. The archbishops, bishops, priests, clerics, and all Christians who are in the land of Egypt implore your paternity and sanctity with sighing and tearful voices. O how great is the tribulation and distress given to us to endure in this life! We believe it is already clear to you, yet we disclose it to you, our lord, as best we can. We do not dare have horses in our homes, nor are we able to carry our dead with a cross through the city. If by any chance a church of the Christians should fall, we are by no means permitted to rebuild it, and every Christian in Egypt over the age of fourteen must pay a tax, known in Latin as "tributum," of one gold bezant and fourteen carubbas, and if he is poor, he is sent to prison and cannot leave until he pays the entire tax. There are so many Christians in the land of Egypt that every year they must pay the court of the Sultan one hundred thousand gold bezants of the Saracens of Babylon. Why should I tell you more, when Christians are sent to all vile and sordid works and even to clean the streets of the city, which is a disgrace to all Christendom? As for Jerusalem, which is built as a city, how it lies destroyed and desolate in the land, it is unnecessary to write to you. It is known throughout the world about the matter of Damietta; how disgracefully it was handled need not be recounted in letters, as it is most shameful to say. Have mercy on us, lord, have mercy on us, come and deliver us, our spiritual father. Just as the saints awaited redemption and liberation from Christ the Savior before His coming, so do we await the coming of your son the Emperor, and not only we await this grace but also more than ten thousand renegades who are dispersed throughout the lands of the Saracens. This must not be omitted, but always held in the heart, as to how, when he comes, the lord Emperor should act. This is the way of salvation and health and without ruin, with the Lord granting: namely, let galleys and ships, as many as there may be, enter through the river Rasceti and dock at the town situated on the island in the river, called Foha, and thus, with the Lord's permission, they will possess the whole land of Egypt without ruin. The river Rascetum is deep and high and wide, and the aforementioned island is full of all goods, as the bearer of these presents, our faithful and familiar, can narrate to you; we have known him to be prudent and discreet concerning this and for this reason, we have sent him to you. Indeed, a most terrible thing was done in the land of Egypt to the disgrace of Christians, namely, concerning the matter of Damietta, where 115 churches were destroyed. By Him who lives forever! I do not lie. May your hand prevail over the enemies of the Cross of Christ. The Saracens, who are called Molene, that is, lords, who held the kingdom of Egypt before Saladin, implore and beseech your sanctity by God to hasten to send the one whom you intend to send, because the whole land of Egypt is yours. Farewell.

Datum ex urbe Roma.

To the noble Duke of Austria. We firmly believe without hesitation that the injury of the Crucified one affects you, and the reproaches hurled against Him fall upon you as a Catholic man, as evidenced by the proof of your deeds. For, having been inspired salutarily by Him from whose gift it comes that He is deservedly and laudably served by His faithful, you once, as if denying yourself, took up the sign of the cross and magnificently crossed the sea to aid the Holy Land. There, representing the cause of Christ with all your spirit, you served both valiantly and usefully for a time. Nevertheless, because the Lord does not forget to show mercy, lest at least His holy name be further blasphemed among the nations, behold, He has resumed the promotion of His own cause by newly renewing the business of the Holy Land. For He has so inspired the heart of our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, the ever-august Emperor of the Romans and King of Sicily, that he, coming to us in Campania, voluntarily took a corporal oath that he would undertake the journey to cross the sea at the feast of St. John the Baptist in two years' time, and to show fuller devotion towards the said land, he publicly betrothed in marriage the daughter of our dearest son in Christ, John, the illustrious King of Jerusalem. Therefore, we have proclaimed a general passage at that same feast, holding firm hope and confidence that the Lord will console His people, restoring to us Jerusalem and the surrounding region, and crown those who lawfully strive for it in that which is foreshadowed by this, which is our mother above.

Thus, in so holy and so arduous a task, we more confidently request of you, the more we know you to have a more eager faith and more devoted affection towards God, and we ask, admonish, and exhort your nobility in the Lord, that understanding more than we can express, you do not cease to assist the Lord Jesus Christ at this opportune time, who, although He does not need our goods, yet repays services freely offered to Him with incomparable rewards. May you, by showing continual services, prove yourself laudably to offer to the Lord a complete holocaust, and by encouraging others to the same by your example, accumulate a greater heap of merits for yourself.

Furthermore, you should be not slightly led by this, that our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious Emperor of the Romans, Frederick, desiring to have you as a companion and chief counsellor in the service of Christ, as we have perceived to be contained in his letters, liberally and willingly offers you ten thousand marks for the aid of your support, nonetheless indicating hope of more substantial help, which indeed you should not hastily spurn, lest, which may the Lord avert, you should seem to slight the cause of Christ. Given at the Lateran, fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa nobili viro duci Austrie scribit, hortatur et monet ut in negotio Terre Sancte assistat, promittendo auxilium ab imperatore Frederico. Dat. Laterani, V Kal. Maii, anno VII.

**Translation to English:**

To F., illustrious emperor of the Romans, ever august, and king of Sicily. We are compelled to send you letters filled with sorrow, for the sword of bitter grief has pierced our soul; we are continually wounded, injury upon injury. For indeed, the lamentable disaster of the Christian army has wounded us with intolerable pain, causing us to mourn not only the labors and expenses which we have borne unceasingly for five years, and which the Christian people have endured in their resources and persons, now utterly lost, but also the disgrace to the Christian name and the injury to Christ Jesus Himself, who, due to our sins, is blasphemed. Behold, we are wounded by a new injury as the entire Christian people cries out against us, blaming us for the collapse of the aforementioned army, and publicly accusing us of causing confusion in the entire Christian world, for not compelling you, as you knew, to cross over to aid the Holy Land, completely ascribing your fault to us, and indeed not without reason, for in truth, while we deferred too much to you, we left the Christian army in peril, a disaster we lament today. To recount our fault from its beginning, you know that for several years we deferred to your will, detaining the crusaders under the hope and appearance of your passage, lest the promotion of your elevation, to which we earnestly aspired, might be delayed by us acting otherwise. Subsequently, at your earnest request, we acted according to your will when you asked us to excommunicate you and all the German crusaders unless you, along with them, crossed over to aid the Holy Land within the term you set for yourself. Yet how many times you requested that this term be extended, and how many times we complied with your will in this matter, both we and your prudence know. Finally, how solemnly and publicly you promised at your coronation that you would cross over to aid the said army is known both here and overseas. Therefore, because of the expectation of your assistance, which you also promised in your letters to the aforementioned army, a settlement, by which the city of Jerusalem was to be restored to Christian worship, was rejected; and in the end, the entire Christian world suffered the shame of a reproach that can be erased by no oblivion. What wonder, then, if the Christian people murmur or even cry out against us and against you, if they believe and declare that we gave you permission to remain, and thus blame us for all the evil that has occurred, ceaselessly assailing us and the Roman Church with unheard-of insults on your behalf? Certainly, if you consider this matter with due reflection, you will recognize the grave danger of your fault and will not rejoice until you do something that seems to make amends to God and men. Awaken, then, awaken, most serene prince, and gird yourself with all your might and heart to avenge the injury of Christ and the Christian name. Consider how great things God has granted you, and strive to repay Him in this matter according to the measure of human ability for all that He has given you. Indeed, if you weigh the debt, you will find no one more obliged to the Lord than you, since He has done more for you than anyone else. If you consider the opportunity to serve Him in this matter, you will find none greater, since with the abundance of necessary resources for this task, you surpass others by His gift, being powerful by land and sea, rich in persons and resources, and more opportune by proximity to pursue the injury

Translation to English:

To the Archbishop and his suffragans. The Lord has looked down from heaven to restore His cause, which appeared to some weak-hearted to be abandoned, by setting aflame the heart of our beloved son in Christ, Frederick, the illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever august, and King of Sicily, with fervor for the aid of the Holy Land. Behold, he girds himself powerfully to exact vengeance on the nations and reprimand the peoples who, by making the glorious tomb of the Lord inglorious, assault Christ with blasphemies and insult the Christian name. Indeed, since the injury is general, affecting each individually and all collectively who serve under Christ the Prince, it would be deemed negligent if we did not urge kings, princes, dukes, counts, city communes, and other Christians through preachers and letters to serve that King, who surpasses the abundance of rewards and exceeds the merit of the servant. And indeed, we do not know with what conscience or security they could appear before the only-begotten Son of God, who have scorned to assist Him, crucified for sinners, in this matter as if it were their own, while they live by His grace, are governed by His grace, and have even been redeemed by His blood. Furthermore, because general aid ought to be rendered to the General Lord, since no one is without His benefits, so no one can excuse themselves from His service, we urge secular princes to decree that in the lands of their dominion, each house should pay at least one Tours coin or equivalent currency each month for three years, since by collecting such contributions faithfully through suitable persons without burdening anyone, a suitable subsidy for the Holy Land can be provided. However, since it is not fitting that we should not move with a finger the burdens we impose on others, nor that those who are sustained from Christ’s patrimony should withdraw their hand from Christ's cause, nor that we should be silent among the clergy about what we preach among the laity, since we ought to lead by example those we wish to invite with words, with the hand preparing the way for the lips: what we have provided in terms of the Tours coin or equivalent currency in lay houses, we wish to be provided for among those clergy who hold lesser benefices, while expecting greater support from others. Therefore, we ask and beseech your community in the Lord, mandating through apostolic writings that you effectively induce the lesser clergy to this end, and take care to solicit each other and other prelates of churches or monasteries, as well as other clergy who have abundant income, in such a way that the result of fuller support may show forth the hand and spirit of liberality. We indeed hope that, since it does not befit you to be sparing with that Lord who became almost prodigal for his subjects, your liberality will provide more for the prosecution of His cause, who pursued our cause at His peril, than the authority of a superior would have decreed. Whatever your prudence does regarding these matters, and about the progress and success of the preachers we send to you, write back to us fully, as opportunity offers. In the same manner... To the Bishops of Modena and Lodi. The Lord has looked down, etc., until: redeemed by His blood. Hence, through preachers sent to various parts of the world, we have decided to entrust to your persons, of whom laudable testimony is given, the office of preaching throughout the province of Milan on this matter, mandating through apostolic writings to you that you give diligent aid and effort to those things contained in other letters to be exhibited to you by the bearer of these presents, and that you faithfully write back to us your progress. Moreover, lest any stain be placed on your glory, or any stumbling block occur in the office committed to you, we strictly command that you extend your hands to no gifts, nor exceed the number of eight attendants, content with only necessary things and the prosecution of preaching. For the cause of the crucified poor does not require a sumptuous or greedy preacher. Given at the Lateran, the sixth day before the Kalends of May, in the seventh year. In the same manner to others appointed for the office of preaching throughout the provinces of the world. Given at the Lateran, etc.

Regesto in Latin:

Gregorius IX papa episcopo archiepiscopo et suffraganeis mandat ut subsidium in Terra Sancta per contributiones fidelium colligatur, et per predicatores sollicitentur principes ad eiusdem regis obsequium. Dat. Lateran. VI Kalendas Maii, anno VII.

**Translation to English:**

To the patriarch of Aquileia, and the archbishops of Mainz, Trier, Cologne, Magdeburg, Salzburg, Bremen, and Besançon, and their suffragans, as well as abbots, priors, provosts, archdeacons, and other ecclesiastical prelates established through their provinces and dioceses. Since He who, according to the omnipotence of His majesty, cannot be contained by place or time, being immeasurable and infinite, and who, while remaining stable, sets all in motion, makes His spirits angels and ministers, and, lowering the height of the heavens, assumed human flesh because His delight is to be with the children of men, and has sent the disciples He had chosen into the whole world to preach the Gospel to every creature, He instructed us by His example to follow in His footsteps. Since we have been taken into the fullness of power and cannot personally attend to every matter, we should, following the advice of Jethro, distribute the burdens among those we have called to share the responsibility, assigning tasks to each according to their own ability as circumstances arise.

Therefore, among the countless and immense concerns that trouble us beyond our strength, we think more urgently and fervently wish that the matter of the Holy Land, which has been gravely disturbed by the sins of the Christian people, be successfully directed by the Lord's aid, especially since our beloved son in Christ, Frederick, the illustrious Roman Emperor, ever august and King of Sicily, has devotedly undertaken to relieve it, inspired by the Lord. We have appointed special preachers throughout the world to those who bear the sign of the true God. But as we expect greater help and support to come from Germany, as has been customary, we desire to send a more honorable person there. Behold, we have provided to send our venerable brother, the bishop of Porto, who, planted by the divine hand like a cedar of Lebanon in the paradise of the Church, rises in the height of contemplation, is sweet with the fragrance of virtues, and is entirely incorruptible in the purity of his reputation, not only working by his strength to support the house of the Lord but also adorning its surface with the splendor of honesty.

We have decided to send him there so that, performing the office of the legation for Christ most fully, he may preach to the people the word of the cross, and strive to rightly govern and direct the indirect, transforming the rough into smooth by uprooting vices and planting virtues. We hold a firm hope and confidence that the Lord, who has given him an eloquent tongue, endowing his voice with the power of His might, will guide his paths in His good pleasure, fertilizing the minds of his listeners by his eloquence. Moreover, although we consider that what is done to one of the least of ours is done to us, as we unworthily represent Him, because, just as one star differs from another in brightness, there is a distinction of merits among them, we wish for the aforementioned bishop to be honored all the more because through him the Apostolic See is more highly honored.

Therefore, we earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort your community, and firmly command you by apostolic letters, that you receive this legate, or rather us through him, cheerfully and devoutly, treating him with due reverence, and strive to obey him effectively in all things, so that you may gain God's favor and ours be favorable and kind to you. Otherwise, we will regard the sentence he properly imposes on the rebellious as firm and, with the Lord's support, will ensure it is observed inviolably.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa patriarchae Aquilegensi et archiepiscopis Maguntino, Treverensi, Coloniensi, Magdeburgensi, Salzburgensi, Bremensi, et Bisuntino, necnon abbatibus et aliis praelatis mandat, ut Portuensem episcopum, legatum suum in Terra Sancta, honorifice recipiant et ei obediant. 1234, Datum apud Lateranum.

**Translation to English:**

To the illustrious King Philip of France. One renders oneself unworthy of the heavenly inheritance and may fear not unjustly being excluded from it, if one is not ignited by zeal for the Christian faith, is not moved by the injury to Jesus Christ, and is not troubled by the pollution of the sanctuary and the insult to the Redeemer, as nations come into His inheritance and defile His temple, leaving Jerusalem like a watchman's hut and the daughter of Zion like a shack in a cucumber field. Isaiah 1:8. Can he be a co-heir with Christ who neglects to provide assistance to Him according to his ability, when He, expelled from the land chosen for the mysteries of our redemption, does not suffer in spirit for those who suffer and will reign with Him? Would not a vassal of any temporal lord be judged as guilty of treason and unworthy of the fief he holds, if he did not resist invading enemies of his lord's land to the best of his ability, and did not strive to expel them? Much more should those who profess Christianity fear being proscribed from the heavenly homeland, dragged to the torments of hell, if they withhold assistance of devotion and compassion from Christ, who complains that His inheritance has been turned over to foreigners and His temple to strangers, and do not place the sword on their thigh, moving from gate to gate in vengeance for those blaspheming His name. Exodus 32:27. Although He needs no goods and can crush enemies with a word, He graciously requires our help so that the fruits of our devotion may increase, with which He may bestow upon us the rewards of eternal life. Thanks be to God, who has placed the concern for this matter in the heart of our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, the illustrious always august Emperor of the Romans and King of Sicily. After receiving our exhortation, he has come to us in Campania and has undertaken this matter personally, promising under oath that, God willing, he will cross over to aid the Holy Land within two years from the present summer. Since it is thus extremely necessary to prepare aid for that land from all sides, that peace be firmly observed among Christian princes and peoples in the meantime, as we have resolved in a meeting with the said emperor, we deem it necessary to ask and admonish your Highness, in remission of your sins, that you strive, if possible, to establish firm peace with our dearest son in Christ, Henry, the illustrious King of the English, or at least extend the truce observed between you thus far, so that the heavenly King's army is not hindered by war and Gaul, which is accustomed to fight the battles of the Lord, is not so occupied with internal conflicts that it withholds the service and devotion owed to the King of kings, and that it may not be excluded from the triumph which the Lord of Hosts will grant to His army. Let the shedding of the blood of Jesus Christ, who reconciled us to the Father, resolving enmity in His flesh and making peace by forming the two into one, move you to this, most serene Prince, who left peace to His disciples when He was about to pass to the Father, and will grant the rewards of eternal peace after the course of this life. Ephesians 2:14. Consider carefully, my son, that whoever does not have peace with his neighbor may hardly or never have peace of mind, without which no one can be rewarded with the prize of eternal peace. Strive, therefore, with a view to heavenly reward, as far as it depends on you, to have peace with your neighbor, so that you may have peace within yourself, and running with unhindered foot, may attain the rewards of eternal peace. Moreover, since we are sending our venerable brother, the Bishop of Norwich, whom we embrace with the arms of sincere affection due to his uprightness, to your presence for this purpose, we again ask your Highness to grant him a gracious hearing out of reverence for the apostolic see and for us, and to comply with the instructions he will propose on our behalf. Given at the Lateran, on the 14th of the Kalends of May, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

**Regesto (in Latin):**

Gregorius IX papa illustri Philippo regi Francorum mandat, ut pacem cum Henrico, Anglo-rum rege, firmet vel treugas proroget, ut subsidium Terrae Sanctae parari possit. Simul eum monet de pace cum proximo habenda. Dat. Laterani, XIV Kal. Maii, anno pontificatus nostri septimo.

**Translation to English:**

To the Abbot of Ehistrebach of the Cistercian Order and Master Gerungus, Scholastic of Bonn in the Diocese of Cologne. Since we have decided to entrust you with the duty of preaching the cross in the province of Trier, so that your words may run unhindered and your labor may bring forth abundant fruit, by the authority of these presents, we grant you permission that when you come to places under interdict, you may open one church once in each place and, excluding the excommunicated and those specifically interdicted, celebrate divine services there, so that you may more effectively propose the word of the cross; furthermore, we allow you to commute the vows of those who have vowed to visit the shrines of Saint James or other saints into the labor of overseas pilgrimage, and to grant, in our stead, the benefit of absolution according to the form of the Church to those who have committed arson or have fallen into canonical penalty for violent assault, provided that the offense is not enormous, that they have made adequate satisfaction to those they injured, and that they have devoutly taken up the sign of the cross for aiding the Holy Land. We also allow you to call upon some honest and suitable men to share the burden of your assigned duty, when you see it is expedient; those who labor in this duty of preaching shall not lose the revenues of their benefices but shall receive them in full as if they were residing in their churches; provided, however, that you do not exceed the number of those to be appointed, and do not appoint more than one from any one church. Furthermore, we take those who have taken up the cross under the protection of Saint Peter and our own, with all their possessions, decreeing that after they have embarked on their pilgrimage journey, all these shall remain under the special protection of the Church until their return or their death is certainly known; also granting to clerics that they may pledge or receive the revenues of their benefices for up to three years as long as they remain absent for this cause, to be delivered without any reduction to those to whom they have pledged them or entrusted them for collection, provided, however, that their parish churches are meanwhile served by an honest vicar, and that no one presumes to undertake this pledge unless he sets out for the journey overseas, and each remains in the service of the land for as many years as he has pledged his revenues. But if he should perhaps return earlier, he shall diligently serve the church whose revenues he pledged, so that the malice of some may be prevented, who, having pledged the fruits of their benefices, are accustomed to visit the shrines of the Holy Land and, returning immediately, defraud both the Holy Land and their churches of their service. And because some are said to have rashly laid down the cross they have assumed, or returned from the ports without completing the journey of the pilgrimage they began, we wish and command that you compel them with canonical censure to take up the cross again and fulfill the vow they made to the Lord. Moreover, so that the devotion of the faithful may be better stirred up for the aid of the Holy Land, you shall ordain solemn processions to be held at least once a month in all places that seem suitable for this, and the psalm "Deus, venerunt gentes" to be chanted in all churches daily in the usual manner. Provided that if you decide to grant any remission of sins to those who come to these processions or other convocations, the remission granted shall not exceed ten days, and if any offerings are made or alms given for the aid of the Holy Land by those who come to such convocations, ensure that they are faithfully preserved so that at the time of passage we may dispose of them as will seem expedient for the support of the Holy Land. Given at the Lateran, the Nones of March, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Abbati de Ehistrebach Cisterciensis ordinis et magistro Gerungo scolastico Bunnensi mandat officium predicationis crucis in provincia Treverensi, concedens facultates ad salutem animarum et subsidium Terre Sancte promovendum. Dat. Lateran. Nonis Martii, anno octavo.

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever August, and King of Sicily. We received with customary kindness our beloved son, L., judge of Bari, who came to our presence, and we diligently listened to what he wished to say to us on your behalf. However, as he mentioned certain persons in our presence, some of whom he requested be provided to the churches of Capua and Aversa, we, due to the absence of some of our brothers, could not make a final decision on this matter, and therefore sent letters to be carried to you according to what seemed appropriate at the time. But the said judge refused to carry them to you, and instead requested an audience with us and our brothers, which we graciously granted. He then presented certain words, as he claimed, instructed by you, which should not have been uttered by your discretion, even if you had suffered a grave injury from us. He claimed that we had given you a protection, which was not a protection but should be called destruction, as it tended, as he suggested, towards the destruction of your person and kingdom. Moreover, he added that, since we were unwilling to receive those you nominated, no others should be sent by us to the aforementioned churches, as you would neither receive them nor allow them to be accepted by those churches. Furthermore, it was later intimated to our ears that you firmly ordered the people of Capua, Salerno, and Aversa that if we sent anyone to their churches not nominated by you, they should not be admitted, and the gates of not only the churches but also the cities should be shut to them. We can scarcely believe these things to be true, and if they are true, consider whether it befits you to do such things, or whether the apostolic see should tolerate them. Indeed, if we may speak frankly, you did not act with sound counsel when you ordered such words to be spoken or actions to be taken against us, because you thereby implied, which we do not believe, that you were prepared and ready to break the bond of charity between us and yourself. We desire, most beloved son, that at all times, and especially in our time, there be firm and sincere love between you and the Roman Church, as we recognize this to be beneficial for the Church itself, for you, and for all of Christendom, nor could anything more bitter easily happen to us than if we were compelled to disturb your state, which we have striven to promote with great care, or to see it disturbed by others, who, if they perceived the apostolic favor lacking for you, would be ready to disturb it, and we should pass by with closed eyes. But if, God forbid, scandals must come, what cause could be imagined to bring more hatred upon you, or more favor to the Church, than if you, through intolerable usurpation, attempt to overturn ecclesiastical liberty, while the apostolic see strives to preserve it according to divine and human sanctions? Surely, you see that those who persuade such things are either blinded by their own ambition or maliciously deceive you, and seek to subvert the paths of your steps with fraudulent counsels and wicked machinations. You can also see with what sincere and paternal affection we are concerned for you, as we not only patiently accept the insult of your words but also, in a way, protect you against ourselves, as we dissuade you from undertaking a cause which could bring upon you a common hatred, while the apostolic see would gain much favor from the same. What then? Shall we not obtain that jurisdiction or power in the kingdom of Sicily which we are known to obtain in the kingdoms of France, England, Spain, and other Christian realms, and even in the empire itself? Shall we have less authority or power in the kingdom of Sicily because we have more right and jurisdiction in it as part of the patrimony of the apostolic see? What are you trying to undertake, what are you planning to begin, misled by false counsels and driven by the heat and strength of your youth? Do you believe it to be prudence or counsel or power against God, and hope to prevail against His Church, with which He has promised to remain until the end of the age, having set aside the fear of Him? If you neglect to heed our admonitions, at least heed the examples of your own household, considering within yourself that the hand of the Lord is not shortened, so that it cannot lift up and cast down, destroy and save. These things we write to you with a kind heart and sincere affection, most illustrious prince, striving to curb the rash impulses of your mind with paternal admonition, rebuke, exhortation, and reproof, and to instruct you in those things which may establish for you an earthly kingdom and prepare an eternal one. Finally, to counsel you regarding the present situation, it is our sincere advice that you immediately send your letters separately to us and separately to the brothers,

**Translation to English:**

To the illustrious King Louis of France. After carefully discussing the petitions your devotion sent to us through our venerable brothers, the Archbishop of Bourges and the Bishops of Langres and Chartres, with us and our brothers with the required diligence due to the magnitude of the matter, and after reaching a final discussion, the aforementioned bishops had already begun their journey back to you with our letters. However, the Archbishop, who remained at the Apostolic See for some of his own affairs and was still present with us, was interrupted by the solemn envoys of our dear son in Christ, Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever august and King of Sicily. These envoys, through their words and the emperor's letters, conveyed his fervent desire, inspired by the Lord, for aid to the Holy Land, and requested urgently that, as he endeavors to encourage Christian kings and princes to this cause with imperial generosity and promises—details of which you will find fully narrated in the letter we have sent to you through our venerable brother, the Bishop of Porto, legate of the Apostolic See—we also strive to exhort all the faithful in Christ to the same cause with apostolic exhortations and indulgences.

Thus, sending the aforementioned legate to you with haste, we ask, urge, and implore your serene devotion and magnificence by the shedding of the blood of Jesus Christ, who for you delivered himself to the cross, that, believing with certainty that the nobleman Raymond, formerly son of Raymond, Count of Toulouse, so fears your might, that if he knows you truly wish to use your full strength against him, he will not dare to resist but will obey the Church's commands, which he offers to follow with true devotion, according to your will. Thus, effectively persuade him with royal admonitions and threats to make true peace with God and His Church, so that the land is cleansed of heretics, the churches and ecclesiastics are suitably compensated for the damages and injuries inflicted until now, the freedom of the Church is secured for the future, and the honor of our beloved son, the nobleman Almeric, Count of Toulouse, who, like his father of blessed memory, risked himself for the service of God and the Apostolic See, is duly considered in this peace as much as possible. Report back to us promptly on what you have achieved in this matter.

For if you accomplish this, without mentioning the loss of resources, you will be the cause of salvation for many souls and bodies, and by removing the impediment of such discord, which can significantly hinder the cause of the Holy Land, you will provide invaluable support to the aid of the same Holy Land. You cannot achieve greater titles of praise and glory than by making the aforementioned nobleman return from the wrong path to the command of the Apostolic See through the mere terror of your power, without the clamor of war and bloodshed. Therefore, we earnestly entreat your serene devotion that, receiving the same legate as our own person with due devotion, you so attend to the aforementioned matters that it may lead to the increase of your temporal and eternal glory. Furthermore, grant full faith to what the same legate will say to you on our behalf concerning the renewal of truces between you and the illustrious King of England. Given at the Lateran, 2nd Nones of April, in the eighth year.

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa Lodoico regi Franciae mandat ut preces ex parte imperatoris Romanorum audiat et nobilem virum Raimundum ad pacem cum ecclesia inducat, simulque eum hortatur ad prorogandas treuguas cum rege Angliae. Datum Laterani, II Nonas Aprilis, anno octavo (1234).

**Translation to English:**

To the Archbishop of Cologne. The enormity of the detestable crime attempted by Henry, Count of Zwerin, against our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King of Denmark, his lord, and his son, undoubtedly incites God and must incite men against him, rendering him odious to all who hate the treachery of perfidy and love the purity of faith. As it has become known to us from the letters of the prelates and princes of the kingdom of Denmark, when the same King had withdrawn to a certain island of his kingdom during the summer for the milder climate with his private family, unsuspecting of any treachery, as he harbored no ill will against anyone, behold, the said count, a violator of the oath of fidelity he had sworn to him, forgetful and ungrateful for the many benefits he had received from him, invaded his tent at night with armed men, attacking the meek while being fierce, armed against the unarmed, a vassal against his lord sleeping in his bed. What we could not hear without pain nor can recite, he wickedly wounded the King and, together with his aforementioned son, led them to a certain forest. Then, transferring himself with them outside the kingdom, he presumes to detain them captive within the limits of the empire. Indeed, such a heinous crime should concern all kings and princes, for it might provide others with an incentive to attempt similar acts against their lords, emboldened by the example of those who hear that the aforesaid count had presumed to do such a deed. Although our apostolic duty makes you all debtors, nevertheless, a special reason, not one but manifold, binds us to the said King, so that we could not fail him without harming our reputation and conscience in such a grave need. Firstly, the kingdom of Denmark particularly pertains to the Roman Church and is known to be tributary to it as a mark of special dominion, and the same King, like his predecessors, has always shown himself faithful and devoted to the Apostolic See. Hence, if the same were to desert him in this case, which Heaven forbid, it would show itself not only ungrateful but also unworthy of such fidelity and devotion. Moreover, there is another valid reason, sufficient by itself to induce us to assist the King, even if the aforementioned reasons were lacking. For the same King, although not publicly bearing the sign of the cross for the aid of the Holy Land, carries it in secret, having taken it at our exhortation, with a certain promise made to us that he or his son will cross the sea in the coming general passage to aid the Holy Land. And if perhaps neither of them can cross personally, he will send a hundred or at least fifty knights there; whence it is clear to anyone willing to see the truth with the eye of reason that we are bound to assist the aforementioned King at least as we are to others who bear the cross. Therefore, rejoicing and commending your charity with worthy praises in the Lord, which has faithfully aimed, as we have heard, at the liberation of the same King and his son, we ask and exhort you earnestly, and by apostolic writings, we firmly enjoin and command you to strive more diligently in the future to do laudably what you have done by yourself until now, invited by the command and prayers of the Apostolic See, to continually intend to free them by whatever means you can, so that your effort may shine through with effect and you, beyond the grace of the Apostolic See which you will fully attain from this, may grow in name among men and in merit with God. Moreover, diligently warn the said count on our behalf, that within a month after the receipt of our letters, which we send to him concerning this, he fully restores the aforementioned King and his son to liberty and permits them to freely depart without any difficulty, and we ourselves will ensure the completion of justice is exhibited if he has any complaint against him.
