**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, the illustrious Roman Emperor, ever august and King of Sicily. Your serenity, as we believe, does not doubt that we love you with sincere affection and aspire to the increase of your honor and name. Hence, when we advise your highness on matters which we know pertain to your honor, you ought to graciously accept our counsel and reverently comply with it. It was indeed the common voice and opinion of all concerning our dearest son in Christ, John, the illustrious King of Jerusalem, who is joined to your highness by marriage, that he would greatly succeed, and that God had magnificently exalted your highness through the alliance with such a prince. It is not surprising if men believed this, considering on one hand, the power of your excellence, which they knew was able not only to maintain the exalted in their sublimity but also to elevate the humble with new honors, and on the other hand, the valor and industry of the said king, deserving not only to retain his honor but to have it increased. Yet behold, the situation seems to have turned contrary, as the king, unless you provide otherwise, is gravely oppressed, contrary to our and others' hopes, where he was expected to be magnificently exalted. All who hear of this are greatly amazed and say: Who is more gracious to the faithful there? Who more terrible to the infidels? Who more useful to the whole cause of the Holy Land? Behold, even if he were not joined to you by any alliance, you should commit the aforementioned kingdom to him because of his valor and industry and the favor he has among men and knowledge of places. Even if he had taken a mere soldier as father-in-law, he should adorn him with royal dignity. Is it more honorable to be the son-in-law of a soldier than of a king? Will it be more honorable for the sons he will have from the daughter of the said king to have a soldier as grandfather rather than a king? Both the humble and the great speak about these and similar issues, marveling at such an act, and, to speak more truthfully, detesting it. We too, and our brothers, are reproached by many because we were the mediators of this alliance, and the king's oppression is somehow blamed on us. Finally, due to the discord between you and the king, the devotion of many towards the aid of the Holy Land has cooled, as it is said, which you will rekindle if you take care to show your favor and good will towards the king as is fitting. Therefore, desiring to remove this cloud from the brightness of your name, and at the same time striving for the aid of the Holy Land, for which your reconciliation with the king is very necessary, we admonish, entreat, and beseech your serenity in the Lord Jesus Christ, asking for a special favor, that you reflect on how absurd it is for such a man to be oppressed because of his alliance with your magnificence, when it is fitting for those joined to your highness to be elevated, and considering the utility of the aforementioned Holy Land, to restore the said king to the fullness of imperial grace, and to reconcile him effectively to yourself, manifesting the serenity of your spirit towards him by the evidence of your actions. For if you diligently consider the bond that joins him to you, you can easily perceive that no one, except your own son, should love you more sincerely than the king, nor can your highness place greater trust in anyone else. To make you fully understand how earnestly we desire this reconciliation, we are sending to you for this reason, more particularly, our beloved son, the abbot of St. Martin of Viterbo, of the Cistercian order, the bearer of this letter, a prudent, religious, and faithful man, earnestly asking your serenity to take care in what pertains to this matter and to kindly hear him. Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico imperatori Romano mandat ut Iohannem regem Ierosolimitanum, ad se affinitate coniunctum, in plenitudinem gratiae imperialis reassumat et sibi reconciliet, ne discordia inter eos subsidium Terrae Sanctae impediat. Datum Laterani, VI Kal. Febr., pontificatus nostri anno XI.

**Translation to English:**

To the prelates and clergy of the city and diocese of Verdun. We invite you all with apostolic letters to undertake the burdens for defending ecclesiastical liberty, as much as we know you are strongly bound to do so, even without our urging, but by your own volition. Indeed, you should know that it has come to our attention that our venerable brother, the Bishop of Verdun, standing as a wall of defense for the protection of ecclesiastical liberty, has endured many burdens, being oppressed heavily by debts, due to the war he has been known to sustain for two years or more. This is because his own citizens, strengthened by the power and favor of Henry, son of the said emperor Frederick, have violently expelled him from his city along with a large part of you, presuming nefariously to destroy his and your houses, plunder goods, break the cloisters of abbeys, and make ditches through their destroyed buildings. Therefore, he humbly requested us to consider the cause for which the said bishop is known to have contracted these debts and to afford a helpful counsel on this matter, also noting his devotion and purity of faith. Since all of you are known to be affected by the business for which this bishop contracted the aforesaid debts, we earnestly beseech, admonish, and exhort your entire community, commanding you by apostolic writings, that you provide the aforementioned bishop with suitable assistance for this purpose, contributing each according to your abilities, so that by sharing the burden among you, you may bear it more lightly and the same bishop may be liberated from the aforementioned debts. Otherwise, as we do not wish this to remain unfinished, lest the aforementioned church be dangerously oppressed under the weight of debts, we have given letters with orders to our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Trier, to compel you to do this by ecclesiastical censure, notwithstanding any appeal. Given at Perugia, on the 3rd of November, in the third year [of our pontificate].

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa prelatis et clero civitatis et diocesis Verdunensis mandat, ut episcopo Verdunensi ad onera debitorum, propter ecclesiastica pericula, liberaliter auxilium impendant, alioquin archiepiscopum Treverensem ad hoc per censuram ecclesiasticam compellere iubeat. Datum Perusii, III Nonas Novembris, anno tertio.

**Translation to English:**

Gregory [IX], etc., to all bishops established throughout Tuscany. We believe it has come to your attention how we have excommunicated Frederick, the so-called emperor, and all those who support him against the Roman Church. Indeed, Raynald and Bertold, sons of the late Duke Conrad, have begun to invade the patrimony of the Church and have thus incurred the sentence of excommunication. Therefore, we strictly enjoin all and each of you not to offer them counsel, assistance, or support, having excommunicated all their counselors, supporters, and allies, and having absolved all from allegiance to the emperor. For if any loss is sustained by them or their possessions on account of this, they can only blame themselves. Moreover, we have decided that none of them should henceforth be assumed to the office of power or any other office of the cities or other places. Their electors, cities, and places should be excommunicated and remain under interdict as long as they hold such offices. Furthermore, they are to be deprived by law of all benefices or fiefs that they hold from the churches, and their sons shall not be admitted to ecclesiastical benefices or dignities without special dispensation from the Apostolic See. Such excommunicated persons cannot obtain the benefit of absolution unless they spend a year in the service of the Holy Land, spending at least as much as they are found to have received from those benefices. Therefore, by the authority of these letters, we strictly command you to proclaim our prohibition and these same sentences, and what we have established as punishment for the aforesaid, on Sundays and feast days, solemnly announcing that Raynald and Bertold, along with their counselors, assistants, and supporters, especially if any are from your cities or districts, are excommunicated by us. Publicly protest that such as these cannot obtain the benefit of absolution otherwise than as stated above. Indeed, since the advancement of the affairs of the Holy Land is the cause for which such things are brought upon us, it is to be feared by all who offer counsel, assistance, or support to Raynald and Bertold lest we be compelled to proceed against them as against enemies of this cause, namely pagans and blasphemers of Christ. Given at Perugia, on the 3rd day before the Nones of December, in the second year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa episcopis per Tusciam constitutis mandat, ut prohibitionem et sententias excommunicationis contra Fridericum imperatorem et Raynaldum et Bertoldum, filios ducis Conradi, necnon eorum consiliarios, auxiliarios et fautores, publice nuntient. Eos ab imperatoris fidelitate absolvit et interdicit ne ad officia civitatum admittantur. Excommunicati ad beneficium absolutionis tantum per annum in servitio Terrae Sanctae obtinendum compellantur. 1237, Perusiae, III Non. Decembris.

**Translation to English:**

To the bishops of Vercelli and Brescia. Since we have decided to send you the form of the oath according to which the men of Lombardy must swear, and our dearest son in Christ, F., the ever august emperor of the Romans and king of Sicily, is sending his beloved son T., the judge of Suessa, his trusted and discreet man, to the regions of Lombardy for this purpose, we strictly command you by apostolic writings in the virtue of obedience to proceed without delay with the said judge in faithfully executing the task entrusted to you, applying diligence and effort so that these oaths are administered according to the same form. You must carefully ensure that you proceed cautiously and circumspectly in this assigned task, so that nothing pertaining to it is omitted and we may rightfully commend your zeal and diligence. If both cannot —, one of you etc. Given at the Lateran, 8th Kalends of April, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa episcopis Vercellensi et Brixiensi mandat ut formam cautionis secundum quam iurare debent homines Lombardie exequantur cum iudice Suessano transmissa a Frederico imperatore, adhibentes sollicitudinem et diligentiam. 1232, Mar. 25. Laterani.

**Translation to English:**

To the abbots of Esternach and Luxembourg and the prior of Luxembourg in the diocese of Trier. Since the case, which is between our beloved sons the chapter of Liège on one side and the commune of Metz on the other concerning the destruction of the village of Maideres, has been brought to us by appeal from the hearing of our beloved sons, the abbot of St. Martin in Trier and his assessors, we decided to entrust it to you, but the said commune has appealed to the Apostolic See. Therefore, Ulric, the procurator of the said commune, coming into our presence and proposing various reasons for grievance, requested that the same case be delegated to others. Lambert, the procurator of the chapter, opposing him, we assigned to both parties our beloved son, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Praxedes, as the auditor, before whom the said Ulric proposed that he, seeing a certain interlocutory sentence pronounced by you contrary to law, namely that you should proceed in the principal matter saving the question of expenses which were being petitioned from you, by which the said commune was aggrieved, appealed to the Apostolic See. He intended to add another reason for grievance, saying that since the citizens of Metz did not dare to leave the city of Metz and feared to approach Trier, both due to wars and other mortal enmities, they requested you to assign them a secure place, but you were unwilling to assign any other than Trier. He furthermore added that when a certain Saturday was assigned to them as a date, and the parties then appeared in your presence, ready to proceed in the cause, you postponed the term to the following Monday, to the detriment and grievance of the said commune, especially because the procurator of the chapter resided in Trier and he was very far from there. He also added that since Master Theodoric, a canon of Trier, was an advocate of the other party, and other canons of Trier are co-canons with the provost of Trier, who is the archdeacon of Liège, you, though the same procurator objected and entirely prohibited, had them as assessors, although he wished you to assume other suitable assessors. He alleged another cause of grievance, namely that since both the said interlocutory sentence and certain other acts of the trial were written in court, when he was transcribing them by your concession, the advocate of the said chapter violently took them from him in your presence, and when he asked you to have them returned to him, you refused to do so. He also added that whenever he asked you to do something or give an interlocutory sentence, whatever the advocate of the other party said, you, holding it almost as law, dared to say or do nothing but what pleased him. He also submitted that the procurator of the commune of Metz who consented to you was reputed, as it is said, to have been corrupted by received money, wherefore he was not bound to litigate under your examination. Finally, he expressed another grievance, namely that when certain testimonies were published and sealed with your seal, son abbot of Luxembourg, you, abbot of Esternach, refused to seal them for this reason only, because the advocate of the chapter objected. Wherefore, asserting his appeal to be just for so many causes of grievances, he requested the case to be delegated to other judges. Lambert, however, procurator of the chapter, contesting the suit, replied that he did not believe such causes of grievance had been proposed on behalf of the commune before you or that for them the other party had appealed, nor did he believe them to be sufficient or true, but if there had been any, it is clear nevertheless that they were withdrawn. Wherefore, the same procurator requested that the said commune be condemned in legitimate expenses, and that your process and that of the prior judges, to whom you decided to remit the parties by interlocutory sentence, be confirmed by apostolic authority, and nonetheless to proceed in the principal matter according to the contents of the prior letters. Therefore, when the said cardinal faithfully reported to us these and other things which were proposed before him, because, although some causes of appeal seemed legitimate, it was established that they were withdrawn, we decided to remit the case to you, by apostolic writings commanding that you proceed in the same cause according to the contents of the prior letters directed to you, setting aside no letters obtained from the Apostolic See except by the consent of the parties. Given at the Lateran, 12th Kalends of March, in the tenth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa abbatibus Esternacensi et Luxeburgensi ac priori Luxeburgensi mandat causam inter capitulum Leodiense et commune Metense super destructione ville de Maideres iuxta priorum litterarum continentiam procedere, appellatione commun

**Translation to English:**

To the citizens of Suessa. The apostolic see, like a loving mother who cannot forget the children of her womb, often brings before itself the groans of many tribulations, the storm of which has grievously weighed upon you and the other people of the kingdom up to now, almost submerging you into the depths. With a motherly affection, it desires that the Lord might deign to end these hardships by removing the yoke of such harsh servitude from their necks. Bringing into effect what it holds in affection, it undertook the matter and shouldered the burden, exposing itself to countless labors and expenses, and did not spare even the persons of its faithful, bearing their weaknesses and carrying the pains of the aforementioned people. Since you have been brought back to the loyalty and dominion of the Roman Church, to which it was undoubted that you belong, adhering as subjects and faithful to the one whose yoke is sweet and whose burden is light, you are thus not of her who generates into servitude, but are rather free sons. It is fitting, therefore, that you should henceforth be rejuvenated by the consolations of the apostolic see, your mother and mistress, rejoicing with gladness after being in sorrow. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, wishing to provide for your welfare, since the Roman Church has the custom of graciously considering the benefits of its subjects, we are inclined by your supplications, with the consent of our brothers, to take you and your city with all the goods you reasonably possess now or will obtain in the future under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves. We decree by the authority of these presents that your city, persisting in the fidelity of the apostolic see, shall be retained in its dominion like Anagni and other cities of Campania, saving the services and revenues owed to the court, perpetually. Furthermore, we grant you the freedom to appoint your own leaders and engage in contracts of sale, purchase, and others, similar to the aforementioned cities of Campania. Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority your laudable and hitherto approved customs, as well as others which our venerable brother, the bishop of Albano, the apostolic see's legate, has prudently granted to you, safeguarding in all things the mandate of the apostolic see. Let no one, therefore, infringe on our protection and concession. If anyone should— (Given at Perugia, on the 14th Kalends of June, in the third year).

**Regesto in Latin:**

Innocentius IV papa civibus Suessanis scribit, eos sub protectione beati Petri et apostolica protectione suscipiens, concedens civitatem cum libertatibus similem Campaniae urbibus, et confirmans consuetudines eorum, mandato sedis apostolicae salvo. Datum Perusii, XIIII Kalendas Iunii, anno tertio.

**Translation to English:**

To the bishop, provost, and dean of Worms. A petition was previously presented to us by our beloved daughter in Christ, the abbess of the monastery of Quedlinburg, which stated that certain vassals and her ministerials, along with some of their accomplices from the Halberstadt diocese, presumed to destroy the walls that fortified the monastery and the ones enclosing its cloister, causing her severe damages and injuries. Moreover, B., the provost of the aforementioned place, who was thrice unlawfully elected to her detriment and burden, intruded as abbess in the same monastery three times and rashly took upon herself the administration, presuming in similar audacity to enfeoff certain goods of the monastery. Therefore, we directed letters in a certain form to our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Magdeburg, and his co-judges, instructing them, among other things, to compel the elected to resign all that she would have from the monastery's goods, and to ensure appropriate reparation was made for the aforesaid damages and injuries. If they found the abbess to be defamed among good and honorable people regarding waste and other matters, concerning which an inquiry had been granted against her to our venerable brother Conrad, then bishop of Halberstadt, and his colleagues, they were to proceed in the matter of the inquiry. Recently, it was reported to us that when the same abbess went to our venerable brother, C., the bishop of Porto, apostolic legate, and begged him to urge the said archbishop and his colleagues to execute the apostolic mandate—which they had been negligent in executing—the legate requested by himself and others that they submit this matter to his arbitration, even though it was not fitting to submit on matters of waste and other excesses disregarded in the inquiry. Since she could not be induced to this, he, unknown to her, had the privileges of the monastery's liberty, which she had in her lodging, and certain apostolic letters brought to him; and when she understood these letters had been cut, greatly fearing, as much as she could, for the diversion of the said privileges, as such fear might fall into the steadfast, she submitted herself to his arbitration, swearing to observe it; thus, neither certain nor concerning certain things, was the arbitration pronounced, causing great harm to the monastery. For by that arbitration, the abbess is bound to renounce all complaints and damages caused by any of the aforementioned, and to pay all debts contracted by the elected and the church in any way, and expenses contracted by the elected after her expulsion, within the assigned terms; the possessions mortgaged by her in any way, whether of the provostship or the monastery, are to remain with those to whom they are known to be mortgaged until the abbess redeems them, and the concessions of fiefs and other matters done by the elected concerning the vassals and ministerials are to remain unshaken. These things, indeed, as were presented to us, should not be upheld, since she would not seem to be distinct from a wasteful abbess if she allowed the wastage of her monastery’s goods and if by the impunity which would arise from such a renunciation, the aforementioned and others were rendered more insolent against the aforesaid monastery, and the intruder, who should have been repelled with rejection, would exist in a better condition than those prelates canonically instituted, who are not bound to the church's debts unless it would be clear they were contracted for their utility, and the alienation of ecclesiastical goods, which is prohibited by law, under which obligation is contained, would find favor, and the ministerials and vassals would seem to exist in such a prerogative that what is not allowed in others would be allowed in them. The abbess is also held by this arbitration to concede the advocacy and all fiefs which Count Hoier holds from the monastery, and which ought to devolve to it upon his death, since he has no offspring, to Count Otto, nephew of the same Count Hoier, so that she is compelled to be generous from the monastery’s goods to its prejudice. It is further contained in the arbitration that the Quedlinburg castle is not to be fortified, and concerning buildings and fortifications, the abbess is not to impede the said Count Hoier and the citizens, since they, through the castle, although many hate it more from fear of punishment than from love of virtue, are feared to raise a heel against the monastery and to withdraw its rights, and they would easily presume to contend equally with the monastery through fortifications and buildings and even to rebel against it. Moreover, since nothing can be done by the arbiter outside the compromise, perpetual overseers for keeping the aforementioned are appointed through the aforementioned arbitration, through whom, if the abbess be found not to have observed any of the aforementioned articles,

**Translation to English:**

Gregory etc., to R., priest and canon of St. Maurice of Hildesheim. We rejoice in the Lord and commend the zeal of your diligence, as if called by the Lord, by the command of our venerable brothers, Conrad, Bishop of Porto, then legate of the Apostolic See, and the Archbishop of Mainz, you have turned to the office of holy preaching and have become a fisher of men. You have drawn out a net full of fish from the sea, as you have rescued those wretched women who, seduced by the suggestion of the enemy of humankind, had fallen into the mire, covered in the filth of lust. You have brought them out of the pit of misery, lest the abyss of despair swallow them. Thus, many of them were given in marriage, others became nuns from being prostitutes, fleeing the brothel, and vowed to keep chastity to the Lord. You, too, can rejoice in the Lord, for the choir of angels rejoices at this deed. But so that no one may take this joy from you, you must vigilantly and tirelessly watch, and bravely pursue that the ancient and cunning enemy might not hinder the conversion and penance of these women with his deceit.

Therefore, we have deemed it right to admonish and exhort your discretion, commanding you through apostolic writings and enjoining for the remission of sins, that you may boldly, with our authority, devote yourself prudently to the noble office of preaching for the conversion of such women, and strengthen and fortify those who have been converted with wholesome admonitions in chastity and religion. To exercise the preaching office committed to you by us more freely and usefully, we grant you the authority by these presents to hear the confessions of such women and to impose salutary penance for their sins. Diligently advise and induce those who support and foster such women for profit, as patrons of impurity, to allow them to come freely to hear your preaching and not hinder their conversion and salvation in any way. As for the women who have left their marital bed and fallen into the sin of the flesh, if their husbands, having been duly admonished by you, refuse to receive them back converted to a better life for God’s sake, you should endeavor to place them in cloisters with the aforesaid converted women so they may do perpetual penance there, yet first enjoining on these husbands for the remission of sins to take back their wives out of divine compassion. Moreover, advise and induce other unmarried men with wholesome exhortations, and if you see it expedient, enjoin upon them for the remission of sins to take some of these women, who cannot keep chastity, as wives, provided they are unmarried. Furthermore, since we have heard that certain clerics and laymen, seeking gain from the price of chastity, do not hesitate to accept the shameful profit of impurity from a certain depraved custom or rather corruption, we grant you leave to prohibit under penalty of excommunication anyone from henceforth demanding or receiving such shameful profit. Therefore, as a prudent man, use the power granted to you with such moderation that, with the favor of divine grace, your works may be acceptable to God and men, confident, indeed, that if you follow the path of our commands, you will obtain the reward of eternal happiness, with the Lord granting it. Given at Anagni, 8th June, year 1.

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa R. presbytero canonico Sancti Mauritii Hildesemensis mandat ut officium praedicationis ad conversionem mulierum exerceat, confessiones audiat, poenitentiam iniungat, et lucrum turpe excommunicatione prohibeat. Anagniae, VI Idus Iunii, anno I.

**Translation to English:**

To the noble man R., son of the late C., Duke of Spoleto, the spirit of wiser counsel. It should have sufficed for your lord that, ungrateful to God and men, he has thus far embittered the Roman Church, his mother, with harsh sorrows, provoked it with severe injuries, and disturbed it with various troubles, if you, his vicar and minister, had not imprudently abused our patience, provoking us boldly with cumulative offenses, as if there were no help to restrain your audacity. But if you are wise, as you are believed to be, we do not need to consider the effort to break your attempts, and the reason we have not yet proceeded to repel injury with injury is due to the virtue of meek patience, by which you and others ought to have been recalled not to insolence but to quicker correction; but from there you are led into impenitence, as we see.

For you are not content with having occupied the castle of Stupizi and invading the Tower of Arnata by siege, burning it to our disgrace, that you destroyed the Castle of Leonis and made our men of Arrone and some from Cassia swear to you, and diverted many others from the loyalty to the Apostolic See, corrupting many with bribes and promises, that you reoccupied Arquata, which your lord, once occupying, spontaneously restored at the admonition of our predecessor, of pious memory, Honorius III; and, as is said, you do not hesitate to mutilate presbyters and other clerics with sacrilegious boldness, afflicting them with various tortures, some nailing to the cross by the service of Saracens, some blinding, the rest afflicted with taxes and collections, and stripping churches in manifest subversion of ecclesiastical liberty. Now having entered the March of Ancona, you exercise deceit and force hostilely to occupy the same, showing yourself manifestly an enemy of the Apostolic See.

However, although it may seem to proceed not so much from the virtue of longsuffering as from the vice of cowardice that we precede warnings when punishment should have already preceded, nevertheless, since it befits us to have greater patience, as the Lord grants us greater power, we attentively admonish your nobility, firmly commanding you through apostolic letters, to resort promptly to salutary counsel to correct yourself, to leave and abandon the March, and within eight days after the receipt of these presents, to restore all occupied and taken, and competently make satisfaction for the given damages and inflicted injuries, or to provide sufficient security concerning these and other matters. Otherwise, we have firmly instructed our beloved son, Cinthius, our subdeacon and chaplain, of whose faith and prudence we have undoubted confidence, to publicly announce you and your supporters, both from the kingdom and others, excommunicated, and to place the lands to which you or yours might come under ecclesiastical interdict, and to our faithful nobleman P. Theodaldus, to manifestly defy you on our behalf; otherwise, we will proceed more severely against your lord and you both spiritually and temporally by the authority of the Lord. Given at Perugia, 7th Ides of November, in the second year of our pontificate.

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa nobili viro R., nato quondam C. ducis Spoletani, mandat ut, Marchiam Anconitanam relinquens, infra octo dies omnia occupata restituat et de iniuriis satisfaciat, alioquin excommunicationem et interdictum contra ipsum et fautores suos minatur. Data Perusii, VII Idus Novembris, anno secundo pontificatus.

**Translation to English:**

To the Rectors of the City. Wishing to abolish the ingrained and presumed corruption in the City against ecclesiastical freedom, we have diligently urged and instructed our beloved son, the noble man A., senator of the City and our seneschal, through our letters, that he should, in reverence to God and to us, no longer send diggers to break down the walls of churches or their houses. We trust that he, as a Catholic man fearing God, will humbly and devoutly obey our commands. However, if it should happen that the divine and apostolic reverence is henceforth scorned, so that such a disgraceful violation of ecclesiastical freedom is no longer overlooked, you shall boldly pronounce the sentence of excommunication both upon those who dare to lay a reckless hand on the walls of churches or their houses for digging, and those who send such people. Given at Rieti, on the 10th day before the Kalends of August, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Rectoribus Urbis mandat ut sententiam excommunicationis in eos, qui muros ecclesiarum seu domorum effodere presumpserint, promulget, ad libertatem ecclesiasticam tuendam. 1229, Jul. 23, Reate.

**Translation to English:**

To the bishop, chapter, and clergy of Gubbio. We believe it has come to your knowledge that we have excommunicated Frederick, the so-called emperor, and all those who support him against the Roman Church. However, Raynald and Bertold, the sons of the late Duke Conrad, have begun to invade the patrimony of the church, and as a result, they have incurred the sentence of excommunication. Therefore, we strictly forbid all and sundry from providing counsel, aid, or favor to them, since we have excommunicated all their advisors, supporters, and allies, and have absolved you from your allegiance to the emperor. If they suffer any loss in their persons or property as a result, they have only themselves to blame. Furthermore, we have decreed that none of them may henceforth be appointed to any position of power or office in cities or other places, and those who elect them shall be excommunicated, and the cities and places where they hold office shall be placed under interdict. Moreover, they shall be deprived by law of all benefices or fiefs they hold from the churches, and their sons shall not be admitted to ecclesiastical benefices or dignities without special dispensation from the Apostolic See, nor shall these excommunicates obtain the benefit of absolution unless they spend a year in the service of the Holy Land and have expended there at least as much as they received from them. Therefore, by the authority of these presents, we strictly command you to publish our prohibition and these sentences, and what we have established as punishment for the foregoing, on Sundays and feast days, announcing solemnly that Raynald and Bertold, as well as their counselors, supporters, and allies, and in particular if there are any from your city or district, are excommunicated by us; moreover, publicly proclaiming that such individuals can obtain the benefit of absolution only as prescribed above. And lo, we have decided to send to you our beloved son, our subdeacon and chaplain, who is esteemed by us and our brothers for his proven merit, whom you should kindly receive out of reverence for the Apostolic See and ourself, and diligently and effectively attend to these matters. Given at Perugia.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa episcopo, capitulo et clero Eugubino mandat, ut excommunicationem in Fridericum dictum imperatorem et Raynaldum et Bertoldum, filios quondam ducis Conradi, necnon eorum fautores publice nuntient, et inhibitiones ne auxilia et consilia praestentur eisdem promulgent; mandat etiam ne tales ad officia assumantur et eos beneficiorum ecclesiasticorum privandos esse decernit, nisi in Terra Sancta per annum deserviant. Data Perusii. 1239.

**Translation to English:**

To the archbishop of Magdeburg, and the bishops of Hildesheim and Merseburg. Our beloved daughter in Christ, S., the abbess of the Quedlinburg monastery, has brought to our attention a grave complaint. Certain vassals and ministeriales of hers, along with some accomplices from the dioceses of Magdeburg and Halberstadt, presumed to destroy not only the walls by which the monastery was fortified but also those enclosing its cloister, under the pretext of a sworn peace, causing her other serious damages and injuries. They further pursued impious actions under the guise of piety, resorting to deeds that can be concealed by no covering. Taking occasion from her use of certain services for the monastery's defense against certain robbers, who were said to be proscribed by the empire, they unlawfully deprived her of her abbacy and influenced the convent of the same monastery to elect another prioress as abbess. The newly elected, or rather intruded, person, without having obtained or sought confirmation from the apostolic see, arrogated the administration to herself, and maliciously presumed to defame and prosecute her before a secular judge. Although it was judged by a secular judgment that she should first be restored before responding to the charges against her, she could not obtain execution of that sentence; because of this, and because she is not only an ecclesiastical person but also directly subject to the apostolic see, she appealed to our hearing. Later, when the aforementioned elected, or rather intruded person, rashly received the abbey and just as rashly resigned it into the hands of a secular judge, committing herself to the judge’s mercy, the same abbess was asked whether she would also commit herself to the judge's mercy; upon her responding that she would make no decision until she was restored as adjudged, she was told by the judge that he held the abbey in his own hands and assigned her a date to respond to her adversaries at Nuremberg. When she presented herself to the judge by her envoys on the appointed date and no accuser appeared against her, the adversary's envoys appeared after the assigned date, upon whose simple assertion the judge declared the abbess contumacious and unlawfully deprived her of the abbey by sentence, despite an appeal having been made against such a sentence and no proof of the charges against her presented. He ordered the convent, vassals, and ministeriales of the aforementioned monastery, absolved from the debt of fidelity and obedience to the abbess, to proceed to the election of another abbess. Thus, the previously intruded person was recklessly elected again and involved herself in administration without seeking apostolic confirmation, presuming to unlawfully enfeoff certain goods of the monastery. Therefore, the repeatedly mentioned abbess urgently pleaded for our aid against such grave injuries according to our office's duty. Consequently, we mandate by apostolic writing that, if the truth supports the aforementioned, notwithstanding any letters possibly obtained from the apostolic see regarding the confirmation or observance of this process within the appointed appeal time, you revoke and nullify whatever the aforementioned bishop and his colleagues rashly attempted after this appeal; remove the elected person entirely from the abbey's governance; restore the abbey with all its rights, both temporal and spiritual, to the aforementioned abbess; and ensure the convent and all subordinates of the said monastery render her the customary and due obedience and reverence, compelling the elected person to resign all possessions of the monastery's goods. Ensure appropriate restitution for damages and injuries inflicted upon the abbess by the aforementioned vassals, ministeriales, and their accomplices. Opponents are to be disregarded, etc. Otherwise, ensure the process of the aforementioned bishop and his colleagues is observed inviolably as it is just. Once S. is restored to the abbey's governance, if found defamed among reputable persons regarding dilapidation and other charges for which an inquiry was obtained against her, proceed first with the inquisition concerning her and then regarding her sisters and others of the monastery, establishing what is canonical and ensuring its enactment, etc. Whichever of them remains abbess, lawfully restore to the monastery’s rights and ownership whatever goods are found unlawfully alienated or disposed of, and obtain a suitable guarantee from her against future alienation, notwithstanding any letters obtained from the apostolic see unbeknownst to this tenor. What if not all, etc.; notwithstanding the claim that you, brother of Hildesheim, are said to have received an indult from the apostolic see not to be compelled to judge causes committed to you by it against your will. Given at the Lateran, the 14th of August, in the ninth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa archiepiscopo Magdeburgensi et episcopis Hildesemensi et Mersburgensi mandat, ut revocent in irritum quae post

**Translation to English:**

To all those who will inspect the present letters. By the providence of the supreme prince, the peculiar people, whom He had preferred over others with the privilege of special grace, was nurtured by the manna of mercy and governed by the rod of rigor, overflowing with the benefits of Hosea, not being lax in punishments. Furthermore, Moses, the friend of the Lord, offered for the same people the sacrifice of lips and did not omit the sacrifice of hands, after offering the holocaust of satisfaction following the host of supplication, he pursued the cause of the people before the Lord with prayers and the cause of God among the people with swords. Truly, the malice of this world, placed in wickedness, while it runs unchecked through the field of license with impunity for excesses, breaks the barriers of law, opens the way to injuries, condemns the law of honesty, promises privilege to error, and while extending hope of impunity to others, invites some to fault, and thus impunity becomes penal when it reserves punishment for greater sins and by the example of unpunished transgression it coaxes others to offense. Hence sometimes tyranny is pardoned in some way and mercy is exercised with severity, when it concerns the public utility that excess is restrained by vengeance and punishment serves as a boundary to offense. Therefore, because of the presumptuous audacity in some against our brethren, lest we seem to neglect the insult to the heavenly King, who is honored and despised in His ministers, and the disgrace to the Christian religion, while the anointed of the Lord, whom the apostolic see assumes for the healthful service of all Christians, are cruelly assailed, we, not as avengers of our own injuries but as zealous defenders of the honor of Christ's spouse and the immunity of the house of the Lord, with the common counsel of our brothers, sanction by this constitution which shall be valid in perpetuity, that if anyone should intrude into this kind of sacrilege, having hostilely pursued or struck or captured a cardinal of the holy Roman Church, or been an accomplice to the deed or commanded it to be done or ratified it or given counsel or favor, or knowingly harbored or defended the same afterwards, he shall be perpetually infamous as guilty of the crime of lese majesty, outlawed and banned, deprived of all legal capacity so that he neither makes a will nor inherits from any testament or intestate succession, and being repelled from all succession, confounded by public repulsion, he shall find fewer successors to his malice. His habitations shall be desolate, and that there may be none to inhabit them, all his buildings shall be given to ruin, and that the perpetual mark of infamy may be witnessed by perpetual ruin, they shall never be restored. No one shall be bound to repay him a debt, nor respond to him in judgment. Whatever may be found among his goods shall be applied to the domain of the treasury or the public, so that nothing of it is passed on to his descendants, but rather with him they are in some way condemned and his belongings. If he holds any fiefs, leases, offices, or spiritual or temporal benefice from any churches, he shall be deprived of them by the law itself; they shall return freely to the churches, with the rectors of the churches disposing thereof at their will. And if he has a son who is a cleric, not a prelate, holding an ecclesiastical benefice, he shall be deprived of it, with no hope of obtaining another. Moreover, to none of the sons and grandsons of such by male descent shall any door of dignity or ecclesiastical or worldly honor be opened. He shall not accede to the governance of any place. He shall be denied the faculty of petitioning, and shall be interdicted from the office of notary, judge, and any other public office or ministry. His testimony shall find no credibility or belief against anyone in judgments, rendering him utterly unworthy as a witness. He shall be prohibited from ascending to orders, denied access to ecclesiastical benefice or office, and that his infamy may be more notorious, no access to legal acts shall be open to him, no gate shall be opened to him, with all hope of dispensation on any of the foregoing removed. To this present sanction, we additionally decree that from such persecution, as from the act of violent hands, one incurs the sentence of excommunication ipso facto, and both the persecutor and the other participants in such a grave evil, as long as they persist in their contumacy, shall be publicly denounced as excommunicated on all Sundays and feast days, with bells rung and candles lit, in all the churches of the place where such a crime has been attempted, as well as in the neighboring cities and dioceses, and they may not obtain the benefit of absolution from anyone other than the Roman Pontiff with the consent of his

**Translation to English:**

To the master of the house of the military order of the Temple of Jerusalem. The wise man so matches times with causes that they do not at all detract from each other, but rather mutually support themselves, when at other times, the matter would not be free from peril, while being exposed not so much to prudence as to fortune. Indeed, our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, the illustrious emperor of the Romans, ever august and king of Sicily, has sent us a grave complaint that you, not considering the various perils that inevitably threaten the Holy Land due to war, strive to violate truces against the form of peace and against the prohibition of his bailiff, repeatedly drawing knights from the kingdom of Jerusalem to stir up war, with some of the pilgrim knights he had led miserably captured by the enemies. Thus, the way seems to be prepared broader for the king of the Persians hastening to the destruction of those parts, so that he may more easily achieve what he intends. Therefore, although by desiring to defeat the enemies of Christ you are deservedly commendable before God and men, because the quality of the time does not require it but rather forbids it, we strictly warn and earnestly exhort you, firmly ordering by apostolic letters, that you do nothing at all by which any danger might threaten the Holy Land or those visiting it, as this would easily result in the confusion of the whole Christian people. Otherwise, if you attempt anything against our command, we could not bear it with equanimity, without duly punishing your excess. Given at the Lateran, on the 4th day before the Kalends of March, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX magistro domus militiae Templi Hierosolymitani mandat ut treuguas non violet neque periculum Terræ Sanctæ aut eam visitantibus inferat, ne confusionem populi Christiani excitet; minatur poenam si mandatum contemnatur. Datum Laterani, IIII Kal. Martii, anno pontificatus nostri quarto.

**Translation to English:**

To the commune of the city of Riga. Those matters which are settled by judgment or agreement, etc., up to "fortified." Therefore, up to "assent," we confirm and strengthen by the authority of the apostolic see the arrangement that was amicably made, with the mediation of our venerable brother G., bishop of Modena and legate of the apostolic see, between you on one side and our venerable brother, the bishop of Livonia, the provost of Riga, and the brothers of the Militia of Christ of the Livonian diocese on the other side regarding the jurisdictions and liberties of your city, as it was prudently made without malice, voluntarily accepted by both parties, and peacefully observed until now, as fully contained in his letters. For greater clarity, we have decided to insert the exact text of those letters into the present document, which is as follows: Before us, W., by divine mercy bishop of Modena, legate of the apostolic see, a question arose between our venerable brother Albert, bishop of Livonia, and our beloved sons Jo., provost of Riga, and Wilcher, master of the Militia of Christ in Livonia on one side, and Albert, syndic of the city of Riga on behalf of the city on the other, regarding the jurisdiction of the city, currency, and certain other articles. The aforementioned syndic claimed that the citizens had the right to appoint a city judge, as they had been granted the Goths' law by the bishop at the founding of the city. Upon inquiry, the aforementioned bishop, present and consenting together with the provost and master, responded that he had granted the citizens the Goths' law in general and specifically freedom from duels, tolls, hot iron trials, and shipwreck from the founding of the city. There was, however, uncertainty among them as to what the Goths' law constituted. With our consent, they agreed to settle all these matters thus: namely, that the citizens may freely elect a city judge and present the elected judge to the bishop, who will invest him. This judge will have jurisdiction over all temporal matters. However, those under the jurisdiction of the bishop or others who hold fiefs from him, like the master, provost, and others, shall not be required to answer before the said judge unless concerning contracts and offenses committed or contracted in the city or within the city’s boundaries. If the bishop, provost, master, or abbot of Dunem are to have houses or fields within the city boundaries, and something is contracted or committed there, it shall be resolved under the one whose house or field it is. If any citizen has possessions in the jurisdiction of the bishop, provost, or master or contracts there or commits an offense, they shall be answerable under the jurisdiction concerned. Clerics or other religious men, such as the master and his brothers or the Hospitallers, like those of Saint Spirit and Saint Lazarus, shall not be required to answer under the city judge in any matter. Currency production in the city, of whatever form, shall be under the power of the lord bishop, provided it is of the same quality and weight as the currency of the Goths or Gotland. The citizens shall be free concerning the aforementioned four articles—namely, iron, tolls, shipwreck, and duels. Moreover, anyone wishing to enter the city for residence shall be allowed to become citizens with the aforesaid liberties. If the citizens can prove within three years that something is of the law of the Teutonic residents in Gotland, the residents of Riga shall enjoy the same, except that, if the Teutons in Gotland institute any priest, the citizens of Riga shall never be able to establish a priest. Done in Riga, in the year of the Lord 1225, in the month of December, in the thirteenth indiction; present were lord Lambert, bishop of Semigallia, lord Guizelin, bishop of Renelensis, master Lambert, canon of Constendalen, count Borgard, Bernard, citizen of Riga, Ludolf of Hanover, canon of Lübeck, merchants, and even pilgrims. Therefore, to none is it allowed—to the confirmation, etc. If anyone—. Given at the Lateran, XIII Kalends of December, in the eleventh year [of our pontificate].

To the Archbishop of Milan and his suffragans. We have delayed informing you about the actions of Frederick, the so-called emperor, in overseas regions because we hope that our venerable brother, the patriarch, the legate of the Apostolic See, along with the masters of the Temple and the Hospital of Jerusalem, and other princes and barons from those parts, will inform us more fully of these matters, and then we will be able to declare them to you more certainly. The pact was such that the Saracens would guard the temple dedicated to Christ and maintain their own rituals, and so Frederick solemnly, or rather vainly, crowned himself in Jerusalem, which was almost completely ruined and deserted. However, the patriarch and the aforementioned masters, as well as many others zealous for God, did not consent to this pact. Instead, the patriarch subjected the city of Jerusalem to ecclesiastical interdict, so that no divine office could be celebrated there. Therefore, it is clearly evident that Frederick, as much as it was in his power, has greatly confused the cause of Christ and the Christian people. It is dreadful to say and shocking to hear that, attempting to combine Christ with Belial, he exposed the sacred to profanation, so that in the temple of the Lord the memory of Muhammad might be celebrated and the detestable law of that most lost person might be preached, who, as much as it was in his power, nullified the law of Christ in the eastern parts. Thus, the enemy of the cross, the foe of faith, the adversary of chastity, condemned to hell, seems to be raised up as if to be worshiped by a judgment contradicted, to the intolerable insult of the Savior and the manifest disgrace of many martyrs of Christ, who valiantly laid down their lives to cleanse the land of Christ, consecrated with blood, from the filth of the Saracens. Therefore, so that your subjects may not be misled by any error concerning these matters, we warn and urge your community earnestly, by apostolic writings, to faithfully explain these things to them, adding whatever you see fit for the honor of the Church according to God. The names of the lands that the aforementioned Frederick left to the Saracens in the pact we have provided to be expressed to you in other letters. Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever august, and King of Jerusalem. By the high counsel of Him who is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, it is ordained that, since His vicars, succeeding each other, are prevented by death from continuing longer, they should sometimes be chosen to the governance of His spouse despite being surrounded by infirmity. This is so that they may understand from their own experience how they should sympathize with the infirm and be able to feel compassion for those who are ignorant and erring, not taking honor for themselves but being divinely called like Aaron, and it may be manifest that His spouse is governed not by man or through man but by Him alone, who is blessed forever.

Now, after our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Honorius, was freed from the debt of the flesh on the fifteenth of the Kalends of April and taken from this present evil world, and after his funeral was celebrated the next day according to custom and his body laid to rest, we gathered with our brothers to elect a successor. After a Mass in honor of the Holy Spirit was devoutly and solemnly celebrated, and after a brief discussion about the substitution of the pontiff, all unanimously, as if divinely inspired, turned their eyes to our weakness. Despite our resistance and reluctance, with much insistence and even violence, they attempted to place this burden upon our shoulders, which we, greatly fearing the weight of it, were most reluctant to bear. However, fearing lest we seem to resist divine inspiration, we finally submitted our shoulders to bear it, hoping in Him who makes His yoke sweet and His burden light through His mercy, with charity as our guide, that He who went before the votes of the brothers with His inspiration will also follow through with His aid. For we have such confidence through Christ towards God, not because we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, who willed us to be His ministers.

Having thus accepted the responsibility of ecclesiastical provision, we are concerned for your honor and well-being, you whom we cherished with the affection of charity while we were in a lesser office, and we have aspired to your advancement. We have deemed it fitting to send the first fruits of our letters to your highness, beseeching, admonishing, and exhorting you earnestly in the Lord, enjoining upon you for the remission of your sins, that you firmly persevere in the devotion to the Apostolic See and humbly and devoutly assist us, as becomes a Christian prince, since we have been chosen by the Lord to its governance. We urge you with diligent and effective zeal to prosecute the business of the Holy Land, and to gird yourself with valor and might for the imminent passage to its aid, with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, to fight the battles of the Lord with a pure heart and unfailing faith, so that you may deserve to obtain from Him the diadem of unfading glory and that we who embrace you with arms of sincerity may be more fervently inflamed to pursue what pertains to your benefit and honor.

Otherwise, no matter how sincerely we love you in the Lord and wish to show you deference as far as we can with God, we will not be able to overlook this in any way, especially since, at your instance, we undertook many concerns and labors for the aforesaid business while we were still in a lesser office. And now we give commands by letters to all our archbishops and bishops that each of them effectively admonish and induce those signed with the cross within their dioceses, and if necessary, compel them by ecclesiastical censure, removing all obstacles of appeal, to gird themselves manfully and mightily for the journey of pilgrimage, to cross over to the aid of the Holy Land in the imminent passage, and thus render their vows to the Lord in a manner pleasing to the eyes of divine majesty and worthy to receive the reward of life from Him in the recompense of the just.

Therefore, dearest son, having due regard with devotion for Him who rules the kingdom of men and who has exalted you by His grace, comply with our prayers and admonitions so that you do not lead us and yourself into such a necessity from which we may not be able to extricate ourselves, even if we were willing. To Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever august, and King of Sicily. We have received with usual kindness your esteemed envoy, G., Judge of Pavia, who came to the Apostolic See with imperial letters, and we have diligently understood both the oral and written messages presented on your behalf. However, upon inspecting the tenor of the letters, which you sent concerning certain guarantors, princes, and others, we noticed that certain matters were omitted, either due to negligence or preoccupation, which might render them seemingly incomplete. Therefore, we have not deemed it suitable to make them public, lest we provide detractors with more material to murmur against us and perhaps against you, as though we were showing you a suspect favor contrary to the sworn and written form. Instead, we confidently send to you enclosed what we have perceived should be added or changed, having admitted for the collation of the letters and some other writings our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Capua, who, as we trust, will fully and plainly impart to you the intent of our decision and the rationale of his judgment. We affectionately encourage and attentively urge your Serenity to diligently attend to our sincerity without any fiction and to securely fulfill them without hesitation, suspecting nothing as though we wish to deceive you in any way, since, with God's grace, all having been pacified, we desire that everything proceeds in the light, leaving no corner in the shadow of deceit, wishing that everything may prosperously proceed according to your desire. However, we strongly believe it is expedient that your envoy, who, we do not know under what spirit, avoiding our presence, has gone to Germany, be swiftly recalled, lest a caution contrary to the prescribed form be offered by the princes. Given at the Lateran, on the 3rd of December, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico, illustri Romanorum imperatori et regi Siciliae, significat se litteras ab eo missas pro fideiussoribus et principibus, ob negligentiam vel occupationem imperfectas, publicandas non duxisse, et monere eum ut sinceritatem apostolicae sedis sine fictione attendat et nuntium suum in Teutoniam profectum celeriter revocet. Datum Laterani, III Nonas Decembris, anno quarto pontificatus.

**Translation to English:**

To O., Cardinal Deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, legate of the apostolic see. Having previously understood that our venerable brother, the Bishop of Metz, was transferred by the apostolic see to the then gravely declining bishopric of Metz from Verdun. Acting as a bulwark for the justice of the Church of Metz, he valiantly resisted the greater and more powerful individuals of the entire empire around the Rhine. After many labors and grave dangers, with divine grace favoring him, he brought peace and tranquility to the aforementioned Church and acquired the county of Metz and with it four noble castles, one of which is equivalent to a city, along with their appurtenances, all of which he bestowed to his church to be possessed perpetually. Because he was compelled by this occasion to incur greater expenses, he had heavily borne the burden of debts. Considering the praiseworthy cause for which the said bishop contracted the aforementioned debts, as well as the integrity of his person and the fervor of his devotion and faith, and also considering that the clergy of the bishopric of Metz were universally affected by the matter promoted by the same bishop, and as they should share both the benefit and the burden, we directed our letters to the prelates and clergy of the city and diocese of Metz to liberally and kindly provide the said bishop with a fitting assistance for this purpose, with each contributing according to their own capacities so that, by sharing the burden among them, they might bear it more lightly, and the said bishop might be freed from these debts. We appointed our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Trier, as executor of this matter, lest the church be oppressed under the burden of these debts. With the counsel of many wise men, he prudently assessed how much each should be bound to contribute for the payment of seven thousand five hundred marks, considering each one's capacities, and pronounced a sentence of excommunication against those who contradicted and rebelled. We, therefore, having accepted and ratified the taxation made by the aforementioned archbishop concerning the above matters, strictly command you by apostolic writings to ensure that the excommunication pronounced by the said archbishop against the contradictors and rebels is observed inviolably, removing the obstacle of appeal until due satisfaction is achieved. Given at Perugia, on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, in the third year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa O. Sancti Nicolai in Carcere Tulliano diacono cardinali mandat ut excommunicationem contra contradictores et rebelles a Treverensi archiepiscopo prolatam inviolabiliter observet. 1229, Oct. 26. Datum Perusii.

**Translation to English:**

To the noble men, barons, knights, citizens of Cologne, ministerials, and all faithful of the Church of Cologne. Although we have deemed it necessary to initiate an inquiry against our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Cologne, we nonetheless wish to provide paternal care for the indemnity of the Church of Cologne. Therefore, we command your community through apostolic letters that you defend the same church against its molesters with all your strength and allow no alienation of its property. Given at Spoleto, on the fourth day before the Ides of July, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa nobilibus viris, baronibus, militibus, civibus Coloniensibus, ministerialibus et universis fidelibus ecclesiae Coloniensis mandat ut ecclesiam Coloniensem contra molestatores defendant et nullam rerum eius alienationem permittant. 1232, Iul. 12. Datum Spoleti.

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans and King of Sicily.

Our letter, as you wrote, reached your senses, but your letter reached ours even more surprisingly. Indeed, if you had weighed the words of our letter with a just examination, if you had not dragged the letter to a rival meaning, setting aside the spouse, you would have found in them, by the judgment of an unbiased interpreter, something that would bind you to your spiritual father and mother.

The tenor of your letter indeed contained that, contrary to the opinion of everyone and the counsel of the princes, as you state, we found you prepared to comply with our wishes, so much so that none of your predecessors is remembered to have been as devoted to the Church in any past times. Yet we shall not inform our mind regarding these princes otherwise than a credible belief established by the trial of fact may support, since the persistence of wrongful suggestion will not change the right judgment of opinion of the Apostolic See, when deeds are to be preferred to words, and certainties should take precedence over suppositions.

Behold, public records from the Church's archives come forth, which, sealed with the seals of almost all the princes, refute the opinion which you seem to have raised against them, because it is not probable that so many and such great men would have given your excellency contrary counsel, as your sealed writings suggest. Regarding your predecessors, if a clearer expression had given anything certain, we would measure in them what we might hope in you, because if the intention of the writer refers to those close in blood, little devotion will be sufficient to surpass them by comparison; if, however, comparison finds a place where the positive barely reaches.

But if you allow your understanding to extend to those predecessors who were illustrious in faith, fervent in charity, sincere in devotion, benefiting themselves and their subjects, who fortified the Church with many privileges of liberty and enriched it with the liberality of many donations, let your magnificence not prefer itself to them in these matters, but rather consider whether in the abundance of such deeds you reach their boundaries.

We beg the ingenuity of a prudent man to consider, whether you rightfully assume the title of much devotion, while you attempt to cast doubt on the benefits of Mother Church, as if what the knowledge of many proclaims could be concealed by the denial of one, and what public knowledge reveals could be made ambiguous by a singular assertion. Moreover, that type of ingratitude, by which received benefits are denied, tends to bring about some disturbance; but that which presumes evil in good and notes hatred in love has sharper stings of greater pain. Concerning the guardianship of you, left to the Apostolic See by the illustrious memory of Empress Constance, Queen of Sicily, you exclude yourself from the grace of benefactions, if the duty of guardianship has been fulfilled, because it was right for it to be done, and it would be wrong if it were found lacking.

However, since no necessity then urged the Church to undertake the not light burden of guardianship for you, who were destitute of all support, the undertaking, which took its beginning from grace, ought to have made you not ungrateful for the duty of prosecution, at least so that you might not try to attach to the guardian the stigma not only of suspected but even fraudulent administration, saying that the Church, under the name of defenders, had sent enemies into Apulia.

Furthermore, the addition of defamation was that whom Mother Church should have promoted, she cast down, raising in the paternal seat a foreign man, who, not content with the empire, nevertheless aspired to the kingdom. And indeed, until now your confession did not hold this, nor did the series of your letters contain until now, which you after God ascribed fully to the zeal of Mother Church, you attributed entirely to the labors of the same nurse whatever you were, and even that you lived.

Whence, therefore, did so contrary, so novel an opinion proceed from these? Whence did so adverse a presumption arise so suddenly? For if the frequent sending of letters had the conscience of the sender, since no cause of new knowledge followed, nor knowledge of new cause, why is it calumniously alleged, what the evidence of fact repudiates? Why is it introduced under a certain cover of duplicity, what the simplicity of truth does not admit? But if the writings previously sent were devoid of the belief of the writer, let your circumspection gather, what conclusion should follow from these.

Is this the assistance you promised to the Church, if necessity should press? Is this the affection of retribution you offered, if grievance should occur? This is not what a mother expected from a son, nor should a guardian have hoped from a ward.

Ah God, what remains of hope for others in such a son, if a mother so diligent is compelled to despair? Ah God, what fragments of favor will others collect from such a ward

**Translation to English:**

To the same. In matters pertaining to God, we confidently invite you to engage in His good works, so that you may become more open to divine grace, which always accompanies glory. Indeed, as we believe, you are aware of the detestable madness of Ezzelino, etc., as is written on the fifth page of this quire concerning this matter… to the podestà, council, and people of Padua. Therefore, we affectionately request and attentively admonish your discretion, by apostolic writings commanding you to cheerfully take up the cause of Christ and pursue it wholeheartedly, to remind the faithful and have them reminded, preaching to them the pre-noted indulgence, so that they may proceed against the said perfidious one and his accomplices in the name of Jesus Christ. And if he does not return to the command of the Church without any pretense within the allotted time, you are to expose his lands and those of his accomplices and supporters to occupiers, so that by thus punishing the wicked one, his followers may be confounded in their wickedness, and others may become more cautious in similar matters. If not all, etc., each of you, etc. Given at Rieti, on the 4th of September, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto**:

Gregorius IX papa potestatem, consilium et populum Paduanum hortatur et mandat ut contra Ezelinum eiusque complices in nomine Christi procedant, et terras eorum occupantibus exponant, nisi mandatum ecclesiae intra terminum impleant. Datum Reate, II Non. Sept., anno quinto pontificatus nostri.

**Translation to English:**

To the Patriarch of Antioch, legate of the apostolic see. Since we have summoned our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Jerusalem, concerning the affairs of that land and with certain brothers of the Temple and the Hospital to our presence, we grant you by special grace the free faculty to absolve the excommunicated and pilgrims after the term has been set for him. Let no one therefore... etc. But if anyone... etc. Given at Rieti, 4th day before the Kalends of August, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa patriarche Antiocheno, apostolice sedis legato mandat, ut patriarcha Ierosolimitanus, ad apostolicam sedem evocatus, post statutum terminum excommunicatos et peregrinos absolvendi facultatem habeat. 1232, Iul. 29. Reate.

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans and King of Sicily. If you truly desire, as is fitting, that the affairs of the Holy Land are not disturbed but rather directed, it is expedient that you do not burden the Hospitallers and Templars, through whom that land has been governed amidst many struggles until now, and without whom it is believed it cannot at all be governed. Instead, you should pursue them with the grace of beneficence, acting in such a way to further your own interests that you acquire incomparable merit with God and a good name among men. Indeed, to remain silent on what is bitterly reproached to us, that their possession seems to be almost fleeting, which was restored to them by us, now we cannot ignore their grievance, full of bitterness, lamenting that they have recently been despoiled by others, as they neither wished nor were able to decline the order of law. Therefore, there is no doubt that from this serious losses could threaten the Holy Land, since those laboring in want do not have the means to defend that land as usual. Therefore, in order to provide for the conscience of yourself and the reputation both ours and yours, we ask, advise, and exhort your imperial majesty in the Lord, that choosing rather to be overcome by the piety of mercy, to which other virtues do not disdain to yield, than to be noted by exacerbated justice, you restore all that was taken from the said Hospitallers and Templars, so that you avoid divine offense and we may justly commend your gentleness, as otherwise you would seem to expose our patience to various accusations. To more fully convey to you our sentiments on this matter, we have entrusted our words to the mouth of the beloved son, the abbot of Casemarie, in whom we would have you trust without hesitation. Given at the Lateran, 26th February, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico Romanorum imperatori mandat ut Hospitalariis et Templariis spoliata restituat universa, ne Terre Sancte negotium detrimentum patiatur, et ut divinam offensam evitet. 1230, Feb. 26. Laterani.

To the beloved daughters in Christ, Sophie, abbess of the Church of the Holy Mother of God, ever Virgin Mary, and of the Holy Apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the holy martyr Cyriacus in Gernrode, and her sisters to be canonically appointed. To prudent virgins, who under the habit of religion, with burning lamps through works of holiness, etc. up to: the sacred religion. Therefore, beloved daughters in Christ, we kindly assent to your just petitions, and the aforementioned monastery in Gernrode, which is known to have been constructed on the land of blessed Peter, which the late Gerol, margrave of blessed memory, offered to the Roman Church with all his property, where you are engaged in divine service, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, John, Leo, and Innocent III, Roman pontiffs, we take under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and we fortify it with the privilege of this present writing. First of all, establishing that the canonical order, which is known to have been instituted in the same monastery according to God, is to be observed there inviolably for all times. Furthermore, whatever possessions, etc. up to: acquire, remain firm and undisturbed for you and those who will succeed you. Among these, etc. up to: with their names: the same place, etc. up to: with its dependencies; the foreign church with chapels, the monastery in Vrose with the village itself and two parishes located in the same, Alsleben major and minor, a chapel with two parishes, Egelen with the abbess's chapel and three other churches, Waledalen with the abbess's chapel and parish, Padeburn with two churches, Heteburn with a parish, four villages called Polege with a church, Nachterstide with a church, Lezere with a church, Strentsen with a church, Drogebul with a church, Burgengerod and Helbelingerod with a church. Indeed, of your novalia (newly cultivated lands), which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, whether from cultivated or uncultivated lands or from the sustenance of your animals or from your gardens, groves, and fisheries, no one may presume to demand or extort tithes from you. Moreover, we prohibit any new and undue exactions by archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches from being made in the same church.
