Furthermore, by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul,

**Translation to English:**

To the noble men, leaders of the Lombard League. If it is wiser to prevent the onset of a flood on a neighbor’s land with suitable barriers, so that one’s own crops are not destroyed by the rapid incursion, and if it is safer to assist a neighbor's burning wall to prevent damage to one's own property, it is clearly and fully evident that, while you render gratuitous, if not necessary, and promised services to the Roman Church, you pursue your own principal interests, as you can more fully perceive than we can explain. Therefore, not by necessity but by will, not by paying a debt but by ensuring your own benefit, you ought to fulfill the promised number of soldiers without reduction and ensure diligently that the time of the soldiers is not continuous but useful to us, as otherwise you would appear to expose both the cause of the Church and your own, and indeed more your own than that of the Church, to unforeseen risk. Further, and not without astonishment and shame, we report that the promised number of soldiers has not yet been completed, and those who have been sent have come so slowly that a large part of the time, which should have been spent in the service of the Church, seems to have passed uselessly. For some cities have sent none, some have sent only a part of the promised number, some have provided insufficient expenses to those who were sent, while others deny reimbursement for horses and arms, as we have heard from others, having extracted an oath from them that nothing more would be required. Furthermore, some soldiers, either unwilling or unable to remain until the appointed time, are already considering returning from the journey. Consequently, the Lombards seem almost inevitably to have incurred blame and infamy, and the effect of multiple benefits expected from the aid to the Church, which the Lord has thus far favored and will, we hope, favor more happily in the future, has been postponed due to the delay. Since, as prudent men you fully know, unless the promised number is fulfilled, when it was believed that the solution would exceed the promise, not only would the promisers rightly become notable, to say the least, but they might also face significant loss for other reasons. We urgently ask and admonish your entire community, by apostolic writings, ordering that, according to the wisdom given you by God, you ensure by all means that the promised number of soldiers is completed, and ensure that the delay made by those coming is not attributed to services to the Church, nor are they compelled to look back due to lack of expenses or deficiency of horses, because it would have been better not to have promised any support to the cause of the Church and yours at all than to withdraw the promised aid when necessity presses, and we could not refrain from being moved should we see ourselves defrauded of the effect of such a solemn promise, since it is not the defrauded but the defrauders who are usually accompanied by guilt and infamy. Therefore, act, act, to vigorously pursue the cause you have undertaken, lest if, God forbid, your magnanimity should be relaxed even a little, you provoke the enemy against you in audacity. Given at Perugia, the Ides of May, in the third year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa nobilibus viris rectoribus societatis Lombardie mandat ut sine dilatione completum sit promissum numerum militum, cum detrimentum ex mora imminere possit, et universitatem eorum monet ut sic promissionem suam servent. 1229, Perusii, Id. Maii.

**Translation to English:**

To the archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and other prelates of churches established throughout the Kingdom of Jerusalem. Since we have summoned our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Jerusalem, to our presence regarding the affairs of that land and other matters, with certain brothers of the Temple and the Hospital, we command you by apostolic writ to kindly receive and honorably treat our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Antioch, the legate of the Apostolic See, who is coming to the said kingdom for the reformation of peace in the discord that has arisen, so that we may justly commend your devotion from that action. Given at Rieti, on the 4th Kalends of August, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa archiepiscopis, episcopis, abbatibus, prioribus et aliis ecclesiarum prelatis per regnum Ierosolimitanum constitutis mandat, ut patriarcham Antiochenum, apostolicae sedis legatum, benigne recipiant et honeste tractent. 1232, Iul. 29. Rieti.

**Translation to English:**

To all the faithful of Christ established through the provinces of Pomezanian and Pozolucense. We give thanks to the giver of all graces, who, bringing you out of the darkness of errors, showed you the light of His truth, mercifully leading you to the recognition of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom, as we trust in Him, you love and will love more perfectly. As we have heard and indeed accept, the beloved sons, the brothers of the Order of Preachers, are preaching healthily to you, and you are receiving them humbly and devoutly, treating them kindly, and paying heed to their teachings and exhortations, for they are thirsty for the salvation of your souls. This is indeed the best sign of your salvation, because being frequently nourished with the food of holy preaching, you can in no way fear the defect of eternal life, since their divinely inspired words are spirit and life. Because as true vicars of Christ, although established with insufficient merits, we embrace His faithful with sincere love, we ask, warn, urge, and beseech you in the Lord Jesus, through apostolic writings, imposing in remission of sins, that as you have laudably begun, you should strive to adhere unshakably to Christ, faithfully endeavoring to keep His flawless law that converts souls. Also, venerating those brothers, the indefatigable workers of the Lord and cooperators of your salvation, with pious love, do not fail to embrace their sound doctrine desirably, effectively obeying their admonitions. That you may more effectively feel our grace towards you, we take your persons and other goods under the special protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves and defend them with the protection of this present writing. Therefore, let no one infringe upon our protection. If anyone does so, etc. Given at Rieti, on the 9th of July, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa universis Christi fidelibus per Pomezaniam et Pozolucensem provincias constitutis gratias agit et hortatur, ut fratres ordinis Predicatorum devote suscipiant et eorum doctrinam sequantur. Sub protectione beati Petri et sua personas eorum et bona suscipit. 1231, Iul. 9, Reate.

**Translation to English:**

To the Rectors of the Lombard Society,

We consistently keep before the eyes of our mind the magnificent services of your devotion, which you have rendered in person and with resources to the Roman Church at an opportune time. We cannot forget these services, but rather, we continually think of providing a suitable and abundant recompense, rightly considering ourselves indebted to all that we can procure for your benefit. Far be it that the Roman Church should be accused of ingratitude, as it is always abundant in grace towards the gracious, accustomed to surpass the merits of supplicants with greater rewards.

Indeed, since our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, the illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever august and King of Sicily, choosing the safer path of peace, so humbled himself that returning reverently at the command of the Church, he deserved to be absolved from the bond of excommunication. The terms of peace between us and him, having been previously negotiated and strengthened by multiple assurances, mediated by the princes of Germany and our venerable brother, the Bishop of Brescia, who stood by you and for you faithfully and prudently, have been sufficiently secured for you and your party, ensuring that he will not harm you in any way; instead, he expressly forgave you if you perhaps offended him. Therefore, you should not at all doubt this, as you could not be lightly harmed without us considering ourselves gravely offended.

Therefore, we earnestly ask, admonish, and encourage your community, commanding through apostolic writings that you remain steadfast in your devotion to the Roman Church, and with faith that works through love, strive to comply with our pleasing commands, being completely certain and secure that, intending to respond to you with a grateful exchange, we would pursue you with worthy rewards of gratitude. And behold, for greater caution, we have deemed it necessary to send you the contents of the letters containing the assurances under our seal. They are as follows: Frederick, etc. The tenor of other letters: In the name of the Lord, amen. Berthold, etc., until: he has made satisfaction. The tenor of other letters: We, I., etc., command the lord emperor, that from the day of absolution, etc., it should be reserved for the lord pope.

Given at Anagni, 10th October, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Rectoribus societatis Lombardie mandat ut devotione erga ecclesiam Romanam persistentes, certi sint de retributionibus gratiarum, et securitatem cautionum sub bulla apostolica mittit. Datum Anagnie, VI Idus Octobris, anno pontificatus nostri quarto.

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever august, and King of Sicily. We have understood that from the letters we recently sent to your imperial highness, you were somewhat moved, because they seemed to contain more bitterness than sweetness. However, since, according to the wise, it is better to correct than to be angry, because discipline's reproof is the way of life, what proceeded from the sincere affection of paternal love was due to the sudden hearing of terrible things, as many were saying, we decided to admonish our son less gently, lest we seem to offer honey in sacrifice. Nor should it be grievous for a son, because a father corrects the son whom he loves, and the Lord rebukes and chastises those whom He loves, since the wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful. And if indeed the reproof was harsh, it was not public but private, not expressed with loud voices but through secret letters, which hardly ever suffice to fully express the writer's feelings. Therefore, so that all matters between us may be conducted in complete purity, we beseech and admonish your serenity in the Lord, that, laying aside all suspicion entirely, you may trust in truth that this proceeded only from the pure spirit of charity, and without hesitation, express your will to us whenever you see fit, we who also willingly tend to your growth unbidden when feasible. Given at Rieti, the 6th day before the Kalends of August, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico, illustri Romanorum imperatori et regi Sicilie, declarat litteras suas ad eum missas fuisse ex sincero affectu paterne dilectionis, eumque hortatur ut omni suspicione deposita, voluntatem suam exponat. 1231, Jul. 27, apud Reate.

**Translation to English:**

To the leaders of the Lombard League. You know, and as we believe, as prudent men, you frequently ponder that we, out of utmost desire and your deliberate counsel, have initiated action against Frederick, the so-called emperor, since he aspires with all his heart to the destruction of Lombardy. Therefore, since you have bound yourselves by certain obligations to provide us assistance against him, as you could never otherwise effectively avert imminent danger nor more prudently ensure the common good, we have hoped and still hope that, keeping truth in its purest form, you will provide us, or rather yourselves, the promised aid and add a prompt willingness to the promise, just as you wish to pursue your own interest irreproachably. 

Indeed, as we have already frequently reminded you, the knights you sent for the service of the Roman Church, below the promised number, delayed by voluntary, lest we say malicious, tardiness, arrived so slowly that now, wanting to calculate a continuous time of coming and going, they have served the church little or not at all. And now, as by His grace the Lord mercifully prospers His church, with many cities and castles already recalled to the church's hand, our dearest son in Christ, John, illustrious King of Jerusalem, and our beloved son, John, Cardinal Priest of the Title of St. Praxedes, propose to proceed against said Frederick, upon hearing but not yet fully knowing that he has returned from overseas, in the name of Jesus Christ, to restrain him and forbid him all power to harm; your said knights, claiming they are not bound to serve further, shamefully threaten to abandon the army, just when they are expected to advance and succeed; in which both we and you would be thoroughly betrayed. 

What perfidy could be more wicked, what treachery more notorious, than withdrawing promised aid at the very moment of necessity from him who is known to have been induced by the confidence of promise? Indeed, grave dangers would inevitably threaten your entire community, but the stain of infamy and the disgrace of confusion would forever follow you and your descendants, as you yourselves can better perceive than can be easily narrated by anyone. Therefore, lest you seem to put your hands under your arms, which now you ought to extend to strength, defending your own heads manfully, we urgently ask, admonish, and exhort your entire community, firmly commanding you by apostolic writing under the obligation of an oath, that you ensure the aforesaid knights persevere faithfully in the service of the church and consequently yours, providing them abundantly with stipends and other necessities, nor should you now be weary of such expenses, which preserve you from many and grave damages and injuries, since money is usefully spent whereby pounds are spared without blame. 

Behold, we send you enclosed under our seal a transcript of the letters of the aforesaid king and cardinal, so that, understanding the urgent necessity from it, you may fulfill more swiftly and freely what we command, adding with eager affection and effect the aid of all kinds of assistance, as you have generously promised, for since by God's grace the Roman Church can provide for itself in many ways, it would by no means be blamed if it did not assist those unwilling to assist it. 

Given at Perugia, on the 6th day before the Kalends of July, in the third year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa rectoribus societatis Lombardie mandat ut milites promissos servitio ecclesie fideliter perseverare faciant et subsidium promissum addant. 1230, Iun. 26. Perusii.

**Translation of the Latin Text:**

To the illustrious King of the French. The Lord, who continually watches over His church with compassion, embraces it with such love, despite its many difficulties, that it can joyfully say, feeling His left hand under its head and His right in embrace: "My beloved will reside between my breasts; I will not let him go until he brings me into the chamber of his mother!" He often allows it to be tested, so that it may not seem harmless, but rather, instructed for salvation, it despises earthly things and longs for heavenly ones, and yearning ardently for the heavenly homeland, laments that its stay among the inhabitants of Kedar has been prolonged. However, lest it be overly disturbed by excessive fear, the Lord does not allow it to be tested beyond what it can bear, but mercifully comforts it, so that it might joyfully sing of the Lord's mercies forever.

Indeed, the church was recently much tempted and troubled when our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, the illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever august, King of Sicily, whom He has exalted above the kings of the earth, seemed, seduced by malicious suggestions of the wicked, to scorn his mother, being wickedly incited by many against her. Thus, various dissensions arose, such that nation rose against nation, and many rumors of wars were spread, from which countless dangers could be feared, with which we could not be unmoved.

But the Lord, magnifying his works with us, inclining to the prayers of many as we trust, humbled the heart of the prince and called him back to his mother's bosom, when, through the mediation of the princes of Germany, both ecclesiastical and secular, a treaty of peace was conducted and mutually accepted by both parties. He, returning humbly and devoutly to the command of the church, deserved to obtain the benefit of absolution, offering himself joyfully for the good pleasure of God and the church. Thus, since serenity is more pleasant after a storm and joy more welcome after pain, Mother Church, justly rejoicing in the reconciliation of such a son, gives thanks to Him, who did not deign to appear in the storm or the fire, but in the gentle whisper of a light breeze, rendering a saving peace to men of good will.

However, since the common good of peace should be a common joy, desired by all, we beseech, admonish, and exhort your royal majesty in the Lord, to magnify the Lord with us wholeheartedly, and humbly ask Him to continue and confirm peace, and do not cease to cooperate in the preservation of peace by all means you can, so that you may more abundantly deserve divine favor from this and we may rightfully commend your sincerity. In the same form of mandate, it is written to the rectors of the fraternity of the City.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa illustri regi Francorum mandat ut, post reconciliationem Friderici imperatoris Romanorum cum ecclesia, pacem continue confirmet et conservet, hortans ad cooperationem in conservatione pacis. 1230, [loco non dato].

**Translation to English:**

To the Archbishop of Mainz. Inclined by your devoted prayers, we grant you the free authority, by the authority of these presents, to compel the archdeacons of the Church of Mainz to maintain proper residence in the same church and to assign them stalls in the choir and places in the chapter, according to their dignities, as pertains to you, as well as to uproot corrupt customs from it and to establish honorable ones therein. Therefore, let no one violate our concession, etc. But if anyone, etc. Given at Anagni, the 30th of October, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa archiepiscopo Maguntino auctoritatem concedit compellendi archidiaconos ad residentiam, assignandi eis loca dignitatis, et extirpandi pravas consuetudines. 1232, Oct. 30, Anagnie.

**Translation to English:**

To the Bishop of Albano, legate of the Apostolic See,

The Lord is great and greatly to be praised, having nourished His Church in the humility of His Son, and marvelously established it with unshakable roots through the sprinkling of His most precious blood. He endowed it with the glorious title of true liberty, so that while its branches spread widely, neither does humility exclude the defense of liberty, nor does the defense of liberty exceed the bounds of humility. In this way, balancing the one with the other, liberty should not become too rigid nor humility too lax. It is therefore appropriately suggested that even if the defender of ecclesiastical liberty sometimes, though rarely, uses the material sword against tyrants and persecutors of the Church—albeit unwillingly—he does so without forgetting customary humility, not seeking bloodshed or desiring to enrich himself at another's expense, but rather to call back the errant to the way of truth, and to preserve them in their liberty with all gentleness.

However, since the defense of liberty depends on Him who triumphs with ineffable providence and incomprehensible disposition in both little and great, saying among other things, "Thou shalt not kill," who, relying on human strength and forgetful of his own safety, more cruel than a wolf in the army of Jesus Christ, presumes to kill, mutilate, or deface the image of the Creator by slaughtering a wandering sheep which he ought to have led back to the fold to ensure there is one fold and one shepherd, as we have learned with bitterness of heart to have happened in recent days?

Come now, brother, come; it is not fitting that we provoke injuries by rejoicing in the shedding of blood, when we call the faithful and sons to the breasts of Mother Church. For no laudable liberty would have any place if bloody servitude were to serve in such a manner. Since the Church, which ought to be liberating and not scourging, defends even those guilty of blood, according to Solomon's word, "Deliver those who are being led to death; and those who are being dragged to destruction, cease not to deliver," and if you say, "We have no strength," He that is the observer of the heart understands, and nothing is hidden from the Savior of your soul, and He will render to every man according to his works; far be it that the Roman Church, which by the Lord's disposition is the mother and teacher of all, should permit the killing or even mutilation of the sons it ought to cherish under the wings of its protection. For thus liberty would yield to servitude, and the purpose of liberty in recalling the errant would be renounced by servitude.

Wherefore, we have deemed it necessary to entreat and exhort your fraternity, firmly commanding through apostolic writings, that those whom the right hand of the exalted Jesus Christ shall bring into the hands of the army from now on, be kept without any killing, mutilation, or dismemberment, which we utterly abhor, so that they may rejoice in having more liberty as captives than serving Pharaoh in the usual manner under the title of servile liberty in Egyptian bondage; strictly prohibiting the ministers and others in charge within the army, under threat of our grace and a pecuniary penalty as you see fit, from daring to attempt anything similar in the army in the future. Thus, we intend to preserve the reputation of the Church and our own unsullied from the slanders of detractors in these matters, so that neither does conscience neglect fame, nor infamy, absorbing the fragrance of life and sweetness, tarnish the title of conscience under the rust of false opinion.

Given at Perugia, the 14th Kalends of June, in the third year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa episcopo Albanensi, apostolicae sedis legato, praecipit ut captivi in exercitu Iesu Christi sine occisione aut mutilatione membrorum custodiantur, et stricte prohibet ministros in exercitu a similibus tentandis, poena pecuniaria imposita. Datum Perusii, XIV Kal. Iunii, anno pontificatus nostri III.

**Translation to English:**

To the rectors of the society of Lombardy, the Marches, and Romagna. Though we are unworthy, we hold the place of Him who made both one, breaking down the wall of separation, and joining the two into one in Himself, the cornerstone. We are obliged to counteract arising discord and diligently attend to matters of concord, unity, and peace. Therefore, when discord recently arose between our beloved son in Christ, Frederick, the ever-august emperor of the Romans and king of Sicily, and yourselves, we observed that the matter seemed likely to escalate unless halted at the beginning and bring further obstacles to the business of the Holy Land, for which there has been long effort. We deemed it fitting to interpose our authority and avert serious dangers by extinguishing such a fire before it gained strength, which might otherwise have arisen unless timely measures were taken.

Therefore, since the emperor and you both submitted all the matter freely and absolutely to our and our brothers' providence and disposition, confirming this by letters and public instruments, and through solemn procurators and envoys sent to our presence by both parties, when it was proposed on behalf of the emperor, among other things, that he was hindered by your society from proceeding against the heretical depravity said to have severely infected those regions, and from restoring ecclesiastical liberty, which was said to be greatly oppressed there, and from securing aid for the Holy Land, for which he had particularly intended to go to those parts, and that captives had been denied to him against the law and honor of the empire: having fully understood these and other matters proposed from both sides, we have deemed it prudent to decide the following from providence: namely, that the emperor, for reverence of Jesus Christ and the business of the Holy Land, in his name and that of his son and the empire, universally and individually remit all rancor, ill-will, injuries, and offenses to all and each who are of the said society, and all bans, constitutions, sentences, and ordinances which he made or imposed through himself or another, or another on his behalf, on the society or any of it, the cities, places, and persons of the said society, and whatever followed from them or because of them, fully revoke, and specifically the constitution made regarding the study and students of Bologna, restoring to full integrity in all things and through everything their state and reputation to all and singular who seem to have been injured by any of the aforesaid, remitting all infamy and punishment which followed from any of the aforesaid, so that what was done by them in the meantime may retain the strength which it might otherwise have obtained.

Moreover, let him receive the cities, places, and persons of the said society into the fullness of his grace and make firm peace with them, especially with the Marquess of Montferrat, Milan, Piacenza, Vercelli, Bologna, Faenza, Alessandria, Turin, Lodi, Bergamo, Brescia, Mantua, Verona, Padua, Vicenza, Treviso, Crema, Ferrara, and the Counts of Blandrata, and any other places and persons whatsoever of the same society. Let him also restore the captives who were taken on account of this discord, with their goods, and other things taken or detained on account of the said discord. Furthermore, let him issue open letters on behalf of his son, declaring that he will hold and keep this peace and concord firm, and remit to those of the society all rancor, ill-will, injuries, and offenses. But those who are of the said society, for the honor of Almighty God and his holy church and the said emperor, shall give to the emperor for the aid of the Holy Land, at the expense of the said society, four hundred knights for two years, and make peace with, and inviolably keep it with, the cities, places, and persons adhering to imperial excellence, both ecclesiastical and secular, remitting to them all rancor, ill-will, injuries, and offenses, and revoking all bans, constitutions, sentences, and ordinances which they made or imposed on the cities, places, and persons adhering to imperial excellence, and whatever followed from them or because of them. Let them restore the captives taken on account of this discord, with their goods, and other things taken or detained on account of the said discord, so that those adhering to the emperor likewise do and observe the same to them. Other captives shall be restored according to imperial law, provided the emperor sends his legate into Lombardy for reforming peace among the discordant.

Moreover, they shall receive and inviolably observe the constitutions, laws, and statutes against heretics, their receivers, defenders, believers, and supporters, promulgated hitherto or to be promulgated in the future by the Roman church and the Roman emperors, and especially by the

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, the illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever august, and King of Sicily. The imperial excellence is not ignorant of the fact that the noble man Raynald, son of the late Conrad, Duke of Spoleto, has provoked us in many ways with intent, inflicting immeasurable damages and the most atrocious injuries upon the Roman Church with audacious pride, and grievously distressing many not without manifest contempt for the Creator. Hence, if we were to repay him according to his iniquities, we would by no means feel compelled to show him any compassion in his distress by interceding for him, but would rather overlook his penalties with a conniving eye. However, since we are, though unworthy, appointed as vicars of Him who taught by word and instructed by example that we should pray for those who persecute and slander us, and since we would in vain ask the Lord to have mercy on us if we did not have mercy on the miseries of the wretched, behold, having put aside resentment toward him, though saving all those things in which he is indebted to the Roman Church, whose rights we must not neglect lest we deserve to be neglected by the Lord, we beseech, admonish and exhort your majesty in the Lord, remembering Matthew 5:7 that the merciful shall obtain mercy, and that the greater a person is, the more placable his wrath should be, that through the merit of Him who prefers mercy to sacrifices, and through our intervention, which desires to prudently consult your honor and his status, you may deign to open the door of clemency to him, so that by sparing and especially by showing mercy you may manifest your power, rendering your gentleness pleasing to God and acceptable to men, and we should be obliged to follow your serenity with worthy acts of thanks. Given at Rieti, on the 7th Ides of June, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico, illustri Romanorum imperatori semper augusto, scribit ut clementiam adhibeat erga Raynaldum, Conradiducis Spoletani filium, qui Romanam ecclesiam damnis et iniuriis infestavit, remittendo rancorem et aperiendo clementiae ianuam. Datum Reate, VII Id. Iunii, anno quinto pontificatus nostri.

**Translation to English:**

To the members of the Lombard League. We offer worthy thanks for the sincerity of your devotion and purity of faith, which you show towards the Roman Church, your mother, through gratuitous acts. We commend your diligence in the Lord, especially because, as our beloved son, the elect of Palestrina, and Otto, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, legates of the Apostolic See, have informed us by their letters that you have entrusted the matter of peace to the hands of the Church. However, since a deadline was fixed for the feast of Saint Michael to send procurators on your behalf to appear before us to happily conclude this matter with the Lord's help, and because it is doubtful whether our brothers will be found together in the curia at that time, we have decided to extend the same deadline to the forthcoming feast of All Saints, in which we wish and command that you present yourselves before our presence through suitable procurators, adequately instructed and having sufficient mandate. Meanwhile, desiring that according to the form of the statute issued concerning the aforementioned matter, which is known to be expressed in the peace treaty, everything should remain inviolate and peaceful, we earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort your prudence through apostolic writings, that you should apply diligent care and effective attention to the observance of peace, humbly and devoutly attending to the wishes of the aforementioned cardinals, so that from this you may more abundantly earn the grace of divine blessing and the favor of the Apostolic See. Given at Spoleto, on the 12th of July, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa societati Lombardie scribit, commendans devotionem et fidem erga ecclesiam Romanam, ac mandat ut procuratores mittant ad curiam pro negotio pacis termino prorogato usque ad festum Omnium Sanctorum, cum diligentia ad pacem observandam. 1229, Iul. 12. Spoleto.

**Translation to English:**

To the noble woman I., Marchioness of Meissen. Inclined by your devotion's requests, we grant you by the authority of these presents that, if the land of the noble man B., your husband, the Burgrave, happens to be placed under ecclesiastical interdict due to his fault, you are permitted during the interdict, while excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, to hear divine services in a low voice through the clerics of the places pertaining to you by right of dowry, provided that you have not caused the interdict. Let no one infringe upon our concession, etc. Given at Anagni, on the 8th of December, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa nobili mulieri I. marchionisse Misnensil concedit, ut tempore interdicti, si terra B. burcravii, viri sui, supponatur interdicto, liceat ei divina audire. 1232, Dec. 8. Anagnie.

**Translation to English:**

To Master Conrad of Marburg, preacher of the word of God in Germany. We, with the most benevolent favor possible before God, support the hospital in Marburg and are diligently intent on its defense so that it may be relieved from the oppression of wrongdoers. We strictly command you, in whom we have full confidence in the Lord, through apostolic writings, to maintain, protect, and defend the said hospital, not allowing it and those residing in it to be unduly disturbed by anyone, suppressing such molesters through ecclesiastical censure, disregarding any appeal. Given at Anagni, 14th October, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa magistro Conrado de Marburc, predicatori verbi Dei in Alamannia, mandat ut hospitale in Marburch manuteneat, protegat et defendat, molestatores per censuram ecclesiasticam compescendo. Datum Anagnie, II Idus Octobris, anno sexto.

**Translation to English:**

Gregory, etc., to the illustrious Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans and King of Sicily. We do not doubt that some wicked-hearted individuals, wickedly instigated by the instigator of all evils, frequently attempt to persuade your gentleness, arrogantly suggesting that you, mercilessly pursuing your own injury, should treat your people of Foggia, Civitate, Casale Nuovo, San Severino, and certain others of Capitanata inhumanely. Thus, these individuals maliciously conspire against your safety and reputation—both of which they feign to cherish—so that, turning your clemency, God forbid, into wrath, you might provoke the merciful Redeemer, who grants mercy to the merciful. They open the mouths of men murmuring and shouting that such a celebrated feast of peace, so fervently sought by the prayers of men, turns so quickly into mourning and lamentation, as many agitate and say, "Did these two great lights come together to envelop many in the darkness of pain and horror? And those who preside over men to assist them, do they consent to the tribulation of their subjects? Why are we pierced with pain in secret and shamed openly unless the subverters of salutary counsels fall from their thoughts, you expelling them according to the multitude of their wickedness, lest they, sitting with the rich in ambush, destroy the innocent in secret? But with the detractors dispersed like clouds by the north wind, the bright light of imperial clemency may shine upon all, in which, as after the dark shadows of night and the narrowness of horrid clamor, men may delight with innermost affections."

Therefore, lest the names of both of us be further blasphemed, we beseech, warn, and exhort your imperial loftiness in the Lord, adjuring you by our Lord Jesus Christ, who prefers mercy and by patience a man's learning is known, to allow yourself to be healthily overcome, for never elsewhere can you triumph more happily. Forgiving your debtors from the heart, may you, who owe everything to Him, justly make Him your debtor, and by considering our shame and your own, make us especially obligated to you. For if you were to act otherwise, which the Lord avert, we could not help but consider ourselves dishonored, as there would not be lacking those who would bitterly reproach us for the confidence we placed in you. Given at Anagni, the Ides of October, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico, Romanorum imperatori et regi Sicilie, suadet ut clementiam servet erga subditos de Fogia, Civitate, Casali Novo, Sancto Severino et Capitaneatu, neque in ira, sed in misericordia agat, monens ne blasphemetur nomen utriusque. 1230, Oct. 15. Anagnie.

**Translation to English:**

To the bishops of Riga and Leal, the brothers of the Knights Templar in Livonia, and all the citizens of Riga. Know that it has come to our attention that a dispute had previously arisen between the Teutons and the Danes over Wironia, Gerve, Maritime, and other provinces. Our venerable brother, the bishop of Modena, then the legate of the Apostolic See, with the consent of the parties, accepted them into our hands, entrusting them on his return to Master I., his chaplain, in our name. Subsequently, the aforementioned master committed them to you under a certain form, as more fully contained in the letters drawn up for this purpose. Therefore, since we have decided to entrust the office of legation in those parts to our venerable brother, the bishop of Semigallia, we command you by the authority of these presents, that removing any obstacle of difficulty and appeal, you restore the same provinces with all their appurtenances and rights to the aforementioned bishop in the name of the Roman Church, notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See or our dearest son in Christ Frederick, the illustrious emperor of the Romans, ever august, king of Jerusalem and Sicily, or his said son to you or others. Otherwise, we give the same bishop letters with our mandate to compel you to do this by our authority, setting aside any appeal. Given at Rieti, January 30th, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Rigensi et Lealensi episcopis, fratribus militiae Templi de Livonia et civibus Rigensibus mandat, ut provincias Wironiae, Gerve et Maritimae cum omnibus pertinentiis restituant episcopo Semigalliensi nomine Romanae ecclesiae tenendas, sublatis difficultatibus et appellationibus. 1232, Jan. 30, Reate.

**Translation to English:**

To Regino, bishop of Modena, and the elected bishop of Mantua. Having understood that our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, the illustrious and ever august Roman Emperor, King of Jerusalem and Sicily, was planning to hold a general meeting with his noble-born son and the princes of the empire, we remind you that we previously instructed you by our letters to diligently engage in discussions with the beloved sons, the leaders of the Lombard society, whom the Roman Church intends to honor in many ways as special sons and to carefully safeguard their welfare. This is so that no cause of scandal arises and the expected benefits from the aforementioned meeting are not hindered, with a transcript of the imperial letters sent to you through you, brother bishop of Modena. 

To remove any doubt from the hearts of the wavering, the Emperor himself is sending a man of proven faith, our beloved son, the master of the house of the Teutonic Knights, whose careful management rightfully makes him gracious, to Lombardy. We hope that through him the matters concerning the foundation of peace will be addressed. Therefore, we command your fraternity through apostolic writings, that in the matters which the same master will present on behalf of the Emperor to the aforementioned leaders, you assist him in such a way that through his and your prudent efforts, the outcome of the aforementioned meeting, to the honor of God and the Church and the same Emperor, as well as the peace and tranquility of the province of Lombardy, achieves its due effect. Moreover, to make clear to you how we have written to the same Emperor on this matter, we have decided to send you a transcript of our letters under our seal. Given as above.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Regino episcopo Mutinensi et electo Mantuano mandat ut cum magistro domus hospitalis sancte Marie Theutonicorum super colloquio generali cum rectoribus societatis Lombardorum assistent, ad honorem Dei et pacem Lombardie. Dat. Laterani, 1235, Mart. 15.

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, ever-august Emperor of the Romans, King of Jerusalem and Sicily. As the matter of peace is being pursued with full diligence by our beloved son, the elected [bishop] of Palestrina and Otto, Cardinal Deacon of St. Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, legates of the Apostolic See, according to our mandate, a meeting was held at Lodi with the leaders and envoys of the Lombards. Although the noble man Gebhard, your legate in Tuscany, did not attend this meeting on your behalf as he should have, even though he excused himself through letters and a messenger, the aforementioned cardinals instructed the said leaders to present themselves before us through suitable and sufficiently instructed procurators on the feast of St. Michael. However, since it is doubtful whether our brothers will be present together at the court at that time, we have decided to extend the deadline to the upcoming feast of All Saints, instructing the aforementioned leaders to appear before us through the previously mentioned procurators with sufficient mandate, as stated above, on the appointed date, and to ensure that the terms established regarding the mentioned matter of peace, which are known to be expressed in the peace treaty, remain intact and undisturbed. Therefore, we wish that you arrange to send prudent men with a sufficient mandate to our presence on the appointed date. Given at Spoleto, on the 12th of July, in the sixth year [of our pontificate].

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico, Romanorum imperatori, mandat ut viros prudentes cum mandato sufficiente ad pacis tractatum in curia ad diem statutum mittat, cuius terminus ad festum Omnium Sanctorum est prorogatus. 1232, Iul. 12. Spoleti.

**Translation to English:**

To the same. Trusting in your faith, etc., up to: inclined, we grant you by the authority of these presents the permission to rebuild the fortress of Circeii, and confidently commit its custody in the name of the Roman Church to you. However, you shall make war and peace by the command of the Roman Church against all men whenever you are requested, and shall surrender the said fortress to the Church without any difficulty, should it desire to retain it in its hands, when it is commanded to you by the Apostolic See. Given as above.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Innocentius IV papa eisdem licentiam reedificandi roccam Circegii concedit eiusque custodiam nomine Romanae ecclesiae committit, ita quod guerram et pacem ad mandatum ecclesiae contra omnes homines faciant et roccam sine difficultate resignent, cum mandatum fuerit ab apostolica sede. Datum ut supra.

**Translation to English:**

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the bishops established in the regions of Marsica, Valva, Theatine, Penne, Aprutium, and others.

In the vast expanse of the sea, the ship of Peter, placed or rather exposed to the whirlwinds of tempests, is constantly tossed by storms and waves, so that its governors and oarsmen scarcely ever find a moment to breathe amid the torrents of downpouring rains. For when the ship sails with full sails towards the harbor with a favorable wind, suddenly a contrary wind, driven by him whose breath ignites coals, sweeps it to the depths of the sea and the turbulent ocean, which, though surrounded by waves, does not sink, because the Lord, residing in it, is eventually awakened by the cries of the disciples. When He drives away the spirits blowing upon it and commands the sea and the winds, there is calm.

Four storms especially shake this ship: the perfidy of the pagans unjustly holds the land consecrated by Christ's blood; the tyranny of rulers seizing temporal things destroys justice and tramples ecclesiastical liberty; the madness of heretics strives to tear Christ's tunic and subvert the foundation of faith; the deceitful perversity of false brothers and sons shakes the entrails and rends the side of their mother church. Thus, there are battles without, fears within; outside, the sword kills, and at home, a similar death is impending. It often happens that the Church of Christ, disturbed by so many distresses, while believing it is nurturing its children, nourishes in its bosom fire, serpents, and basilisks, which strive to ravage everything with breath, bite, and flame. Therefore, to destroy such monsters, to expel the ranks of enemies, and to mitigate the disturbances of tempests, the apostolic see in these times has nurtured with great diligence a certain foster-child, namely Emperor Frederick, whom it received on its knees as if from the womb of his mother, fed at its breasts, carried on its shoulders, frequently snatched from the hands of those seeking his life, studied to educate with many labors and expenses, led to perfect manhood, advanced to the dignity of royalty, and finally raised to the highest pinnacle of imperial eminence, believing him to be the staff of its defense and the rod of its old age.

However, when he moved to Germany to obtain the reins of the empire, he inflicted certain omens that were believed to be joyful but were more truly the darts of his mother’s eyes. For of his own accord, not on advice, and with the apostolic see unaware, he affixed the cross to his shoulders, solemnly vowing to set out to aid the Holy Land. Then he obtained that he and other cross-bearers would be excommunicated unless they departed at a certain time; incidentally, he sought and obtained absolution after first taking an oath to obey the Church's commands on this matter. The Apostolic See, pouring abundant grace upon him to hasten his journey to the aid of the Holy Land, contrary to the custom, invited him to the crown, which usually is not called for this but is invited by multiplied intercessions through magnificent envoys. And so, under the banner of the cross, he more fully and perfectly completed his own affairs up until these times.

Finally, having received the imperial diadem in the basilica of Saint Peter from the hands of our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Honorius, he resumed the cross from our hands, then in a lesser office, publicly renewed his vow, led many to take up the cross from the hope of his support, and received a certain term for crossing over. After conversing with the Roman Church at Veroli, he swore publicly to set out honorably as an emperor at a certain term to be appointed by the Roman Church. Thereafter, at a similar conference at Ferentino, he chose and appointed for himself a term of two years for crossing over, solemnly swearing that he would then cross and take as his wife a noble woman, the daughter of our dearest son in Christ, John, illustrious king of Jerusalem, heir to that kingdom, adding that by this, he bound himself to the service of the Holy Land not as other pilgrims, but as a Hospitaller or Templar forever.

Yet as the aforementioned term approached, he began to propose multiple excuses, claiming to be unprepared for the journey, and offered great services to the Holy Land along with significant obligations, asking for another two-year term. The Apostolic See, lest the whole affair, which primarily rested upon this prince's shoulders after the Roman Church, be dissolved with such labors deflated and exhausted in vain, took counsel with many bishops and other trustworthy men and, omitting nothing of what was pertinent, sent our venerable brother Peter, bishop of Albano, and of blessed memory J

**Translation to English:**

To all archbishops, bishops, etc., established throughout Apulia. The more noble a member in the body of the Church is wounded, the more acutely we, who hold the place of Cephas, are pained, though our merits are insufficient. Truly, because a hidden wound, if left untouched, tends to spread more widely to the scandal of the body, we, having seen that Frederick, the Emperor of the Romans, was neglecting his own salvation while refusing to fulfill the holy vow he had made to God, augmented by oaths, not without detriment to the faith and grave scandal to the whole Christian people, as the wise man declares: "When you heal wounds, pain is the medicine for pain," we wielded the medicinal sword of Peter against him in the spirit of gentleness, by publicly pronouncing the sentence of excommunication, which he had voluntarily had declared against himself, unless he crossed over within a set time to aid the Holy Land and faithfully fulfill other promises, hoping that, being struck in pain, he would return humbly to the one who struck him, seeking the Lord of hosts. But, sadly, we report that, with his heart turned away, he loathes the medicine and abhors the rebuke of discipline, indeed considering the hammer as straw, and not correcting himself with any repentance, he audaciously provokes the Lord against himself by adding sins to sins beyond what we should recount, lest we seem to delight in his reproaches, while we fervently await his conversion. Among other things, disregarding the keys of the Church, by which the Lord granted to blessed Peter and his successors the power to bind and loose, he has divine services celebrated for himself, or rather, to the extent of his power, profaned, to the greater danger of his soul and the weakening of ecclesiastical discipline. Hence, fearing that his wound might become utterly hopeless if we allowed the scar of the neglected wound to seal improperly, we endeavored to apply a healing balm. Would that our effort had achieved the desired effect! Although our predecessor, Pope Honorius of pious memory, through the bishops of Tusculum and Sabina of blessed memory, and our beloved son, master G., our notary, and Roffridus, our chamberlain, and the abbot of St. Martin of Viterbo of the Cistercian order, at different times had caused that emperor to be diligently admonished concerning various articles in which he gravely offended God and the Church, we still, humbling the power of the Church's authority, took care to send our beloved sons, the presbyter of the title of St. Sabina and O., the deacon of St. Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, cardinals, to his presence, to admonish him healthily on our behalf about the foregoing and subsequent matters. To Frederick, illustrious emperor of the Romans, ever august, king of Sicily. We received your letters with customary kindness and diligently noted what was contained within. For, as we gathered from their tenor, you assert, based on reports from certain of your justiciars stationed around the region of Aprutium, that the commune of Ascoli, our faithful subjects, claim to hold certain fiefs of your kingdom and do not permit the services owed to your court to be provided to these justiciars. For they plunder churches, seize clerics, hand the captives over to prisons with sacrilegious audacity, and still detain the cleric Berthold in prison; they despoil men, and commit so many and such great outrages that our faithful can scarcely breathe. And to have an excuse for their sins, since they offend so grievously, they pretend to be offended, so as to provoke you, if possible, to offense. Although we do not believe that our faithful have done these things to you and yours, since it is not our intention to derogate in any way from your rights and honor, through our venerable brother, the bishop of Beauvais, rector of the March of Ancona and the Duchy of Spoleto, we order that whatever has been presumed to your prejudice by them is to be fully rectified. You, dearest son, should similarly ensure that whatever has been presumed by the aforementioned justiciars is rectified, so that you may avoid divine offense, striving both in will and action to please Him who exalts those pleasing to Him unto salvation. Thus, you should be seen to venerate with a sincere spirit His only spouse, the Holy Church, and thereby procure grace in the present and glory for yourself in the future, and we may rightly commend your devotion. Gregory etc. To Frederick, Emperor of the Romans etc., the spirit of sound advice. Would that you had accustomed your imperial majesty to fear of the divine in such a way that, submitting yourself with total devotion to Him who subjected various nations to you, you would not only fear to provoke Him against you, lest you be accused of manifest ingratitude, but also aspire with all desires to serve Him for the benefits received, knowing that He needs nothing from you except for you, and would not leave unrewarded the affection, let alone the effect, of your service. Would that you also humbly recognize the kindness and patience of the Roman Church; which, although you have provoked it in many ways beyond what is expedient to recount, lest it seem we wish to reproach your majesty with accusations, it, always abounding in the bowels of maternal pity towards you, has never proceeded with you except in the spirit of leniency. Therefore, we are accused, and perhaps not undeservedly, that, like cooking a kid in its mother's milk, we seem to indulge you in your harmful desires, to the detriment of many and the scandal of the universal Church. Although, indeed, from the fact that you cast aside the cause of Christ, which you seemed boldly to have undertaken, with almost everyone hoping you would lead it to a glorious end, so feebly, so dangerously, so miserably, immoderate grief, immense amazement, and enormous horror have surrounded both our body and soul on every side, so that we, almost in a state of ecstasy, nearly began to despair completely of the recovery of the Holy Land, weeping most bitterly for so many Christians dead because of you and lamenting their exile, which we wish were not destruction, who, relying on you, undertook the journey to cross over to aid that land, nevertheless we have maintained the measure of gentleness towards you as much as we could, only publishing that sentence which you voluntarily had pronounced against yourself, and delaying those which you agreed should be carried out, unless you fulfilled the other conditions you promised. However, so that no one may suspect that the sincere affection we hold towards you is in any way diminished, as it is said rather, that a father rebukes the son he loves, and conversely, he who spares the rod hates the son, we do not cease to advise your serenity on what we know pertains to the salvation of your soul, which we desire with all our bowels, as well as what leads to the increase of your honor, which we gladly promote where it is fitting. Therefore, we earnestly pray, urge, and exhort your imperial gentleness, beseeching by the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ, that you may not, God forbid, be among those of whom the Lord complains through the prophet saying: "I struck them and they felt no pain; they refused to accept discipline," but rather, corrected in mercy, you receive correction and healing, and earnestly strive to dissolve the various bonds by which you are held bound, and hasten with all speed to the bosom of the mother church that eagerly awaits you, making satisfaction to God, who certainly satisfied you, and rendering justice to men. For, as we believe you know, it is murmured, indeed cried out against us, that we have seemed to pass over in silence the exile of prelates, the plundering of churches, hospitals, orphans, widows, and other religious, and other atrocious injuries. It is also frequently reproached to us, that while the Roman Church bound itself as surety at your insistence, as appears from your letters, concerning the observance of the settlement solemnly made between you and the counts of Celano and Rainald of Aversa, we have deferred to your sublimity in such a way that we seem to have abrogated the justice of those who we never intend to fail in their rights. Nor can we ignore the outcries of those who shout that at the prayers of our predecessor, Pope Honorius of pious memory, you promised to receive our beloved son, the noble man Count Roger, into your grace and favor, promising that you would not harm him but rather increase him, and they conclude reproachfully that we pass over with closed eyes his exile, whom you had taken the cross, and the captivity of his son, when we are especially bound to assist the afflicted and captive. Furthermore, since the kingdom of Sicily pertains to the Roman Church in full right of ownership, we are pierced with compassion for the oppressions of the afflicted, lamenting that we endure impious servitude in them,

Gregorius IX papa consulibus et populo Terracinensi mandat, ut habitationes in monte Spineto aliisque locis extra muros civitatis intra demanium ecclesiae Romanae retineantur, ita quod de temporalibus solum Romano pontifici respondeant. 1232, Jan. 4. Anagnie.

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever august and King of Sicily. Receiving with gratifying affection and treating with due honor the venerable brother, our Archbishop of Capua, who came to us with matters proposed on your behalf, we have carefully understood. Moreover, having held suitable deliberation with our brothers on these matters, although it might seem somewhat difficult for anyone, especially those who do not consider the circumstances, to accept our current response, those who understand the purity of our intent and the nature of the times will find it pleasing, as it is supported by the most evident reason. Indeed, it was established in the general council that lands infected with heretical depravity, unless purged by their lords, should be exposed to crusaders, without prejudice to the rights of the principal lords, provided they offered no obstacle nor any impediment. Although the Roman Church has begun to retain lands in Provence and others, acquired after infinite hardships and countless expenses in the blood of Christians, after defeating the heretics, the One who, understanding the hearts of all men individually, knows that we never intended to derogate from the rights of the empire by this, which we rather plan to preserve inviolate. However, since the conversion of that land is still so recent and delicate, that with a slight change it could easily relapse, which would result in an error worse than the first, it is without doubt to your benefit for your request to be deferred to a more suitable time, when we can consider it with both the honor of the Church and your own, for as a new disturbance has now arisen in that land and the old is not entirely quelled, if anything adverse were to happen, God forbid, many would primarily blame us and you. Therefore, we beseech and admonish your serenity in the Lord not to take offense that we have not taken further action on your request at present, nor be moved by any suspicion that we intend anything other than what we have stated. Furthermore, since you claim to have been despoiled of the City of Castello and demand justice regarding that, let it not be that we deny it to you or others, for we are debtors of justice to all. But you should not be unaware that the Castle of Felicity, now called the City of Castello, rightfully belongs to the Apostolic See, as is evident from many public documents, and the privileges of your predecessors affirm, as do the acknowledgments of the emperors. Hence, listen to what the said archbishop will tell you, as he has heard from us, and if you see it fitting to pursue the justice you intend, you will find us prepared for the fulfillment of justice. Given at the Lateran, 10th December, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

Datum Laterani, IV Idus Decembris, anno pontificatus nostri quarto.

**Translation to English:**

To all the faithful in Christ residing in the provinces of Magdeburg and Bremen, Poland, Pomerania, Moravia, Suravia, Holsatia, and Gotland. As the merciful and compassionate Lord, the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whose mercies are upon all His works, beheld man justly condemned, justice demanding vengeance and mercy suggesting compassion, out of the inestimable abundance of charity, He delivered Himself for him and, by enduring the torment of the cross, redeemed him with the price of His precious blood, whom He created. Knowing that man is exceedingly prone to sin, so that the one whom He made in His own image and likeness would not be lost irrecoverably if there were no means for him to rise again, He established various remedies by which he could earn forgiveness. Therefore, we, though unworthy, who perform His duties on earth, desiring above all things the benefit of souls, gladly lead the faithful people to works of charity, which the same only-begotten Son of God willed to be the cause of salvation, and that they may be more fervently incited to them, we grant indulgence. From the letters of our beloved son, the noble Duke of Masovia, we have understood that the pagan Prussians, who do not know the name of Christ and refuse to come to its knowledge, intend to exterminate it as profane from their lands by destroying the Christians therein, vehemently attacking them, destroying their land, which they cannot defend due to their small numbers, and miserably slaughtering people. Although the same Duke has introduced the order of the brothers of the hospital of Saint Mary of the Teutons into his land for the aid of the Christians, and with the brothers of that order residing there, God mercifully works by miraculously striking down through them the enemies of His name: because, however, they are not able to suffice by themselves for such a great endeavor and need to be assisted by the support of the faithful, we admonish and encourage and beseech your community by Almighty God, imposing on you for the remission of your sins, that having regard to the great charity with which Christ loved and loves you, and repaying Him for all that He has repaid you, as Christians and Catholics should, you might powerfully and manfully gird yourselves, as having zeal for God, to avenge the injury to His name and to free your neighbor from the hands of the pagans, and to act according to the counsel of the aforementioned brothers, so that an eternal reward may be due to you, and the infidels cannot boast that they have impugned the name of Christ with impunity. But because great necessity requires that the support of the faithful be sent there, so that they may proceed more willingly, secure in their reward, we, trusting in the mercy of Almighty God and the authority of His apostles, Saints Peter and Paul, grant indulgence to all who undertake this labor in their own persons and at their own expense, and to those who, not going there at their own expense, will serve there for a period of one year, or to those who will provide aid to the faithful from their own resources, according to the amount of support and their devotion, forgiveness of their sins, such that those who die there in true penance may receive full remission of sins as those journeying in aid of the Holy Land. Given at Anagni, on the Ides of September, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

Datum Anagnie, Idus Septembris, pontificatus nostri anno quarto.

To the Archbishop of Cologne. We had hoped that, elevated by the honor of dignity, you would recognize the weight of the burden, and knowing yourself to be enriched by the Lord’s family, you would feed your subjects with word and example. But, what we report not without much bitterness, you are dishonoring your ministry and rendering yourself unworthy of your dignity, while subjecting spirit to flesh and reason to sensuality, you are indulging in harmful vanities and neglecting the children you were to nurture. We refrain from mentioning the shameful crimes, which are a horror to modesty both in report and hearing, although public rumor, indeed infamy, does not cease to spread them, causing our patience to be reproached by many, as if through lasting tolerance we make ourselves participants in your faults, unless we quell the horrendous scandal arisen from you with due chastisement. Therefore, lest our soul suffer for your soul, and justly be said to you: "What are you doing here, or as if someone here, like... a rooster to be carried away?" we admonish and earnestly exhort your fraternity, giving you counsel in purity of mind, that in caring for your soul's salvation, you preemptively seek a swift remedy through resignation, so that we might more mercifully incline to extend grace to you for more ample provision. Otherwise, unwilling as we ought not to be, to heed such loud complaints concerning you, we direct by our letters to our venerable brother the Bishop of Lausanne and beloved sons Masters W., the Archdeacon of Cambrai, and T., the Dean of St. John of Liège, that they diligently investigate the truth about your excesses and faithfully inform us through their letters what they find, so that, sufficiently instructed by their report, we may proceed in accordance with divine guidance. Gregorius IX papa Coloniensi archiepiscopo ob delicta et turpitudines admoneat et hortetur, ut cessione celeri remedium quaerat, alioquin inquisitionem per episcopum Lausanensem et alios mandet. Datum Reate, II Idus Decembris, anno quinto.

To the Patriarch of Jerusalem. To Frederick, the illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever august, and King of Sicily. Gentleness, piety, and clemency are like three sisters, beautiful, noble, and distinguished, guiding their devotees happily, making them pleasing to God and gracious to men. Indeed, princes ought to follow these virtues more eagerly, embrace them more desirably, and revere them more steadfastly, as the opportunity is more fitting, the means more accessible, and the power more ready to effectively serve these virtues. Hence, the Most High knows that when we invite you to their love through prayers, admonitions, and exhortations, it proceeds from pure faith, a good conscience, and sincere charity, through which we desire you to prosper in the Lord in both your spiritual and temporal endeavors. Now, seeing their tears, groans, and sighs multiply beyond all belief, we are struck with severe pain, astonishment, and horror, as you are said to have so heavily pressed them that, being expelled from the kingdom, they are left with nothing or very little. Since this is neither beneficial to your salvation nor to your honor, as by persecuting the servants of the Crucified you seem to be persecuting Him, and as goods dedicated to divine uses cannot be diverted to other purposes without divine offense, nor can people remain unmoved when they hear their bitter cries, marveling that such things should come from him from whom acts of piety were expected to proceed, we implore, admonish, and beseech your imperial majesty in Christ Jesus, who redeemed sinners with His own blood, that sparing your soul and indulging us, who suffer slanders and mockeries all day because of this, you may restore the masters and brothers to favor and cause all that was taken from them to be restored, so that, appeasing them, you may render yourself pleasing to God, and make us your deserving debtors in the Lord because of this. And so that the addition of a living voice may more fully manifest the affection of our intention to your serenity, behold, we have decided to send to your presence our venerable brother, the Bishop of Modena, a man proven in religion, notable in honesty, and adorned with knowledge, whom we and our brothers sincerely love in the Lord. We ask you to believe without hesitation what he will propose to you on our behalf concerning these and other matters. Given at Rieti, on the Ides of June, in the fifth year.

Letters to Our Lord the Pope. **Translation to English:**

To Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever august, and King of Sicily. One should not dismiss counsel nor doubt at all the intentions behind it when it is preceded by faithful benevolence and accompanied by prudent reason, nor should one less trustfully accept that which is offered voluntarily and not demanded, where the sincere affection of the one advising, foresightedly considering the benefit of the advised or the one to be advised, does not rest but is stirred, excited by the gentle goads of true charity. Nor should you let your longsuffering, which should always rule in the heart of a prince, be misled to exacerbate justice and prejudice equity, proceeding against the Lombards not by the order of law but by might, for it could easily be believed that you might be provoked to this not without our offense from the bitterness of past indignation, thus sharpening the tongues of detractors against you and us. To all the people residing in Amiternum and Furconium, who are steadfast in the faith and devotion to the apostolic see. We, on our part, desiring earnestly to pursue the cause of Christ and likewise attend to your successes, are diligently procuring timely assistance for the defense of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, which principally concerns you, against barbarous nations. However, because the nature of this matter requires general support, behold, we are sending our letters to all prelates of churches, kings, princes, and certain signed with the cross, as we have deemed expedient for this cause, intending to continue our diligent care and commit ourselves to whatever may be appropriate. Moreover, because if you show yourself as courageous in this as is fitting, you will laudably inspire many to the same, we beseech, warn, and exhort your highness in the Lord, adjuring by the blood of the Crucified, that strengthened with fortitude of spirit from on high, mindful that in such matters immeasurability is the best measure, sparing neither persons nor resources, you should earnestly endeavor to send aid thither with both, ensuring the places are fortified so that they may not fear the onslaught of attackers until plentiful aid can be sent there, which, with the Lord as author, will rout the enemies; and further provide anything that you see necessary, so that you may render your magnificent magnanimity commendable to God and men.

Additionally, as you know, the beloved sons, the masters and brothers of the houses of the Hospital and Temple of Jerusalem, have long vigorously and powerfully defended the remnants of those lands with their blood. Now, as they lamentably complain, diminished in their resources within the Kingdom of Sicily and deprived of their accustomed support, they lack the usual power to resist enemies, which indeed could result in great detriment to the universal Church and especially in loss to you. Therefore, we earnestly request and sincerely advise that you restore to them what has been taken and make suitable satisfaction for their losses, favorably pursuing them with the grace of benevolence for the sake of divine recompense, for although they primarily serve the cause of Christ in those parts, they are nonetheless actively pursuing your interest, namely the governance of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, usefully, thus offering a service pleasing to the Lord, so that they may also bring you effective aid.
