In this way, you will serve both the common and your own interest, earning incomparable merit before God and a good name among men. Indeed, to pass over for now what is reproached to us by many, namely that their possession, restored to them by us, was almost fleeting, we have now heard, filled with bitterness, the repeated complaint of the aforesaid, grievously lamenting that scarcely are they restored, they are again and by others despoiled; from which indeed serious losses threaten the aforementioned land, since the same brothers, laboring under want, do not have the means to defend it in the accustomed manner. Since indeed all they have is for the conservation and aid of the said land, the defense of which is known to pertain principally to you, we advise, beseech, and exhort your Imperial Majesty in the Lord, that considering your own conscience and providing wisely for both our reputation and yours, and choosing rather to be surpassed by mercy, to which other virtues do not disdain to yield, than to be noted for severity, you should have all things taken from the said Hospitallers restored to them, so that we may deservedly commend your gentleness, while otherwise you seem to expose our patience to various detractions, for you are not ignorant that men are more prone to evil and often suspect sinister things with slight cause. Moreover, at our advice, the said brothers, so they may obtain your favor, are prepared to place the feudal holdings which they had from others than the court since the time of your late mother of clear memory, into the hands of our beloved son, the Master of the Teutonic Knights, without prejudice to either party concerning possession and ownership, upon obtaining restitution, such that he would hold and preserve their revenues until it is declared by arbitrators what belongs to whom, one to be chosen by you, another by the Hospitallers, and a third by the former two or by us, if they do not agree on this. The aforesaid arbitrators will conclude the matter within a certain term, to be set by the parties or by us if the parties disagree thereon, and the same Master will resign the aforesaid according to their arbitration. Concerning other matters, which are not feudal, they will comply with the law before us or our delegates, whenever you wish to obtain justice regarding them. Therefore, concerning the aforementioned matters, may you convey your will to us through letters. Given at the Lateran, 3rd day before the Kalends of May, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico Romanorum imperatori mandat ut Hospitalariis ablata restitui faciat. Datum Laterani, III Kalendas Maii, pontificatus anno V.

**Translation to English:**

To Reginor and the bishop of Brescia and the elect of Mantua. Since the Lombard League has adhered to us and the Roman Church in a time of need, and in the treaty of peace between us and our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, the illustrious ever-august Roman Emperor, King of Jerusalem and Sicily, the men of this league have been so comprehended that whoever offends them for adhering to us is considered to offend the Roman Church: just as we desire that those things which pertain to the reinforcement of peace be enacted, so we wish to avoid those things which might, God forbid, lead to the violation of peace long deliberated and completed. Indeed, on behalf of the said emperor, it has recently been conveyed to our ears that he intends to hold a general meeting with his noble son and other princes of Germany in the parts of Lombardy, promising to use our counsel and to do nothing that would derogate the peace by offending the Church or the men of the said league, offering a possible and honest guarantee for the security to be provided to the men of the aforementioned league, which we may advise him. Therefore, not wishing to give anyone grounds for malice, we command your discretion, through apostolic writings, that gathering together the beloved sons, the leaders of the said league, you carefully discuss with them the aforementioned guarantee and other matters, and ensure they are admonished and persuaded not to allow any obstacle to the emperor in this regard, but to permit the said noble and others coming to his presence for this reason to pass freely and as peaceful men through Lombardy, both on entry and return, so that they suffer no injury or offense; ensuring that if the meeting with the emperor might be less prudently obstructed by them against our counsel, the business of peace may seem to be deliberately dissolved by them and as far as they are concerned. Since the said emperor proposes to hasten the meeting, you are to ensure our mandate is swiftly carried out, yet cautiously, since we wish all these things to be secret, and write back to us promptly and faithfully whatever you find concerning this among them, so that upon receiving your report, we may provide for the business as shall be fitting. Given at Rieti, 27 September, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Reginori et Brixiensi episcopo ac electo Mantuano mandat, ut rectores societatis Lombardie convenientes super cautione et aliis diligenter tractent, ne impedimentum imperatori opponatur, et transitum pacificum per Lombardiam permittant, iniuriis evitandis; et secretum servandum praecipit. 1231, Sept. 27, Rieti.

**Translation to English:**

To the rectors of the fraternity of the City. Know that it has come to our hearing that certain laymen of the City, having a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, have presumed of their own accord, without the permission of the Apostolic See, to create certain fraternities. By occasion of these fraternities, they hold certain ceremonies around the bodies of the deceased against the general custom hitherto observed in such matters, according to their own will, having appointed their own rectors and treasurers to whom they owe obedience, frequently meeting to observe their statutes, and holding banquets at certain times, to the detriment of the fraternity of the clerics of the City long approved from times past. Indeed, because of such lay fraternities, although they may have a superficial appearance of honesty, it is rightly to be feared that under their pretext, the simple might be led into error, we strictly command and enjoin your community by apostolic writings that you thoroughly prohibit these fraternities from being observed, strictly forbidding the clergy of the City from admitting them in their churches or burying the bodies of the dead with the solemnities introduced on their account. We also decree that no other fraternity, besides the aforementioned fraternity of the clerics, shall be formed in the City henceforth without the special permission of the Apostolic See. You must also place under the sentence of interdiction any clerics who presume otherwise and the churches in which such fraternities of laymen have been celebrated, which may not be lifted without the special mandate of the Apostolic See. Given at Anagni, on the 7th day before the Kalends of November, in the sixth year [of our pontificate].

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa rectoribus fraternitatis Urbis mandat, ne fraternitates laicorum sine licentia apostolica fiant et sepulturae cum sollempnitatibus prohibeantur, sub interdicti poena. 1232, Oct. 26. Anagnie.

**Translation to English:**

To the Bishop of Strasbourg. Although various measures have been issued by the Apostolic See at different times against heretical depravity, because new dangers must be quickly addressed with remedies, as recent threats are more easily lost than old ones, we willingly add measures by which the pestilence of such great peril may be eradicated. We have indeed learned that when some laypersons in parts of Germany are found tainted with the stain of heresy, punishment is immediately administered to them as is due. However, when clerics are convicted of the same, they are reserved for judgment at a later time on account of the solemnity which, according to canonical law, must be observed during their degradation. Thus it happens that some clerics tainted with heretical filth sometimes escape punishment or die in prison, thereby generating grave scandal among laypeople. Considering, therefore, that the offenses of clerics in this matter are to be punished more severely and swiftly, because they ought to be more vigilant in virtues and abstain from vices, and wishing to prevent them from daring to perpetrate evil more securely because judgment is deferred, we have decided to grant you by the authority of these presents that when the prescribed number of bishops cannot be easily assembled according to the canons to degrade one priest or deacon, you, once a cleric in your region has been legitimately proven to be a heretic, may, after summoning the abbots and other prelates and learned and religious persons of your diocese, proceed to degrade said clerics by our authority, leaving them subsequently to be punished with due severity by secular judgment. Given at Anagni, on the 19th of October, in the sixth year [of our pontificate].

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa episcopo Argentinensi concedit facultatem, ut clericos hereticos in sua diocesi legitime convictos, convocatis abbatibus et aliis prelatis, auctoritate apostolica degradet et postmodum iudicio saeculari puniendos relinquat. 1232, Oct. 19. Anagnie.

**Translation to English:**

To the dean of Arras. We have received a complaint from our beloved sons, the dean and chapter of Saint Fursey and the clergy of Péronne, that when they purchase a house in the town of Péronne from laymen, the mayor, sheriffs, and sworn officials of the same town, part of the diocese of Noyon, are hostile and grievous towards them in this matter as much as they can be, and harass the laymen on account of this in multiple ways, subjecting them to their ban and burdening them with undue exactions, seeking frivolous excuses to justify their actions so that they do not appear to be troubling the laymen. Consequently, no one can be found there who, for fear of punishment, would dare to sell them a house for any price, causing significant detriment to them, who in this matter are in a worse condition than laymen. Therefore, they have humbly petitioned us to provide for them with fatherly care in this matter. Not wishing, therefore, to allow the undue grievance of the said dean, chapter, and clergy to continue, we strictly command you by apostolic writings to compel the aforementioned mayor, sheriffs, and sworn officials to completely cease their undue harassment in this matter, by means of ecclesiastical censure, setting aside any appeal, after giving due consideration. Given at Anagni, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa decano Atrebatensi mandat, ut maiorem, scabinos et iuratos ville Peronensis, Noviomensis diocesis, per censuram ecclesiasticam compellat, ne decanum et capitulum Sancti Fursei ac clericos Peronenses indebite molestent, cum domum ab laicis emunt. Datum Anagnie, XVII Kal. Octobris, anno sexto pontificatus nostri.

To the Archbishop of Rouen and the Bishop of Lisieux. On behalf of our venerable brother, the Bishop of Bayeux, it was presented before us that H., the Chancellor of Bayeux, who holds his seal, as he claims to be his right, does not hesitate to wrongfully demand one bezant for each open letter sealed with the same seal, to the great detriment of the bishop's honor and his own spiritual well-being. And although revenues sufficient for the chancellery duties have been assigned to him, he unjustly demands annually the necessary provisions for himself, three men, and four horses, and two sets of clothes for himself and each of the aforementioned men. Therefore, he humbly requested that we order the Chancellor to cease such exactions, especially since chancellors in other cathedrals of the province of Rouen do not presume to do this. Therefore, we command that if it becomes evident to you that such extortion of bezants has occurred, you restrain the said Chancellor from the aforesaid exaction by our authority and under apostolic obedience, and concerning other matters, call those who should be summoned, and once they have been heard, etc. As for witnesses, etc. Given at Anagni, January 6, in the sixth year [of our pontificate].

Regesto in Latin:

Gregorius IX papa, Rothomagensi archiepiscopo et episcopo Lexoviensi mandat, ut si constiterit de extorsione bizantii a cancellario Baiocensi, eum ab exactione compescant sub apostolica obedientia. 1232, Jan. 6, Anagnie.

... to the Master and brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem. Full agreement is to be sought with great eagerness, whose integrity sometimes allows the small to ascend to greatness, and discord is to be avoided with all efforts, whose division often leads to ruin. Indeed, we have heard that the state of the Kingdom of Jerusalem is troubled, and the order is confused, as some, rushing to the aid of our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans and illustrious King of Jerusalem and Sicily, are said to publicly display signs of rebellion. While these do not desist from their undertaken disturbance and others defend the royal rights, the Christian hand is turned against Christians, which ought to be extended against blasphemers of Christ, not wearied by civil wars. Resources meant for the detriment of the enemies are converted to the loss of subjects. Indeed, in such situations, the fate is quite uncertain and the outcome highly suspect, as the scandal of arising discord opens a gate to the enemies' wicked machinations and closes the path of aid to our own. However, since medicine should be prepared before the illness, it is not believed it should be delayed in the illness. Therefore, wishing to promptly remedy the beginning of this evil with swift assistance, lest the delay of care loses the cure's effect, we command you by apostolic writings that, as you hold divine and our grace dear, you prudently and courageously assist our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Antioch, the legate of the apostolic see, in the reformation of the aforesaid kingdom, offering suitable counsel and assistance and effective action to those who pursue the justice of the said Emperor. Given as above. In the same manner, it is written to the Master and brethren of the Temple militia. In the same manner, it is written to the Master and brethren of the House of Saint Mary of the Teutonic Order in Jerusalem. In the same manner, it is written to all the prelates of churches established throughout the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa magistro et fratribus Hospitalis Ierosolimitani mandat ut ad reformationem regni Ierosolimitani cum patriarcha Antiocheno, sedis apostolicae legato, prudenter et viriliter assistant, consulentes et adiuventes eos qui iustitiam imperatoris Friderici prosequuntur. To the prior and brothers of the Order of Preachers established in Austria. Now, as we have sadly heard and regretfully report, due to sins, it is said to be stained in certain parts, especially in Austria, with an unnatural vice so ineffably inimical to God and His faithful that it is regarded as being covered with the disgrace of leprosy. However, because such a horrible filth is to be cleansed by the virtue of your preaching with God as the author, we confidently direct our letters to you, urging and beseeching your entire community in the Lord Jesus Christ, by apostolic letters mandating you to threaten those who, suffering from the stain of such pestilence, openly proclaim their sins like Sodom and do not hide them, as if they do not see the path of life or hear the word of salvation, being enveloped in the darkness of sins. Unless they heed your salutary admonitions and seek to repent, you shall deter them from perpetrating such utterly detestable and wicked acts with severe threats in our name. Speak with a living voice that you will transmit their expressed names to us in writing, by our mandate, so that we may exercise the sword of ecclesiastical vengeance upon them as faithless enemies of the Crucified and contemners of the Christian faith, and make them be avoided by all as heretics. Let your diligence pursue what we have expressed in these and other letters in such a manner that you may obtain the reception of eternal happiness therefrom, and the Apostolic See may continually support your devotion with favor. Given at Anagni, 3rd of September, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa priori et fratribus ordinis Praedicatorum in Austria mandat ut peccatores vitio innaturali laborantes severis comminationibus terreant eorum nomina ad sedem apostolicam transmittere parati. Anagniae, III Non. Sept., anno sexto.

Translation to English:

To Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever august, King of Jerusalem and Sicily. The omission of the middle title among the three distinguished titles with which the Lord has honored you in the letters we sent to your imperial majesty was not due to any lesser affection. It was not intended to detract from your honor, which we rather aim to uphold, but there were reasonable causes for this omission, which our venerable brother, Reginus the archbishop, and our beloved son, the master of the house of the Teutonic Knights in Jerusalem, could have explained to you. However, we trust in Him who rewards virtues and bestows His gifts in crowning men, hoping that the more titles of dignity you bear, the more you strive to become worthy of them. Therefore, we now write the hitherto omitted title of Jerusalem, certainly a clear and honorable one, with joyful novelty. 

We earnestly beseech and admonish your serenity, in the name of Jesus Christ, to recognize that your power and wisdom come from the Lord. Learn to be benevolent, following the works of the indivisible Trinity, to crush the cunning of the wicked through power, subdue barbarian nations, who have thus far savagely ravaged the Holy Land at the instigation of the enemy of mankind, and destroy heretics, who, like venomous creatures, endlessly plot against the souls of the innocent, so that your strength may be commended to God and men. Through wisdom, we wish you to govern the peoples subjected to you prosperously, loving justice without error, which guides those who love it and leads them in salvation.

Furthermore, by benignity, may the Lord grant you to be the comforter of those who merit it, especially the inhabitants of the kingdom of Sicily, who, greatly afflicted for long periods, are almost forced to despair unless they find renewed hope. As Jerusalem is called the vision of peace, we desire you to be a pursuer of peace, so that your faithful may dwell in the beauty of peace and prosperous rest, and the church and ecclesiastical persons may rejoice in full liberty and tranquility.

Moreover, it pleases us that, as you have informed us through your letters, you are sending your noble marshal, Richard Filangerius, across the sea. We send letters to the prelates of the churches and others as you requested. However, we request that you do not refer to him as the legate or viceroy of the empire but rather as your or the emperor's marshal, which we wish you to observe diligently in your letters, as it might otherwise generate prejudice for your heirs, as if the kingdom of Jerusalem were subject to imperial dominion. In addition, we earnestly request that you show propitious clemency towards the houses of the Hospital and the Templars in Jerusalem, restoring to them what has been taken and continuing to pursue them with constant piety, so that it may be pleasing to God and acceptable to us.

Given at Rieti, on the 12th of August, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

Regesto in Latin:

Gregorius IX papa Friderico, Romanorum imperatori, Ierusalem et Sicilie regi, titulum Ierusalem litteris suis inserit et eum hortatur ut potentiam suam ad defensionem Ecclesiae et Terram Sanctam dirigat, necnon etiam ad pacem et iustitiam colendas. Dat. Reate, II Idus Augusti, pontificatus nostri anno quinto.

That persistent enemy of the human race, fabricator of treachery, instigator of despair, promoter of hatred, not content with attacking faith, assailing hope, and undermining charity in each faithful of Christ, strives to uproot virtues so that vices may be sown and ruin follow. **Translation to English:**

To Frederick, illustrious Emperor of the Romans, ever august, King of Jerusalem and Sicily. Having favorably received and advanced your requests through our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Otranto, we are sending the requested letters to you. Meanwhile, since the time has come when the triumphant right hand of your majesty can, by subduing the pride of the arrogant Romans and restraining their furious impulse, with God's favor, continually and steadfastly expand the state of the Church and the Empire, achieving the reward of desired greatness and hoped-for prosperity, we earnestly ask, advise, and urge your highness to rise as a dutiful son of the blessed Church, led by the light of the heavenly illumination, to drive away the hordes of demons and shatter the horns of impious slanderers, so that the rebels may understand and know that you bear the name "invincible and exalted above the kings of the earth," casting down the madness of the arrogant to destruction and raising the grace of the humble to salvation. Thus, even when persecutors of the bride of Christ are overthrown, you may deserve the delights of the bridegroom, and the insignia of your valor may have lasting recognition for posterity. May the favor of the apostolic see, as an assiduous promoter of your devoted supporters, be enhanced by the continuous increase of your renowned name. To effectively and magnificently pursue these objectives and successfully conclude the overseas endeavor, we will apply our mind and effective effort, so that with the Lord as the author, no detriment will come to your rights and the prosperity of your faithful, but rather an increase. Furthermore, since we have decided to send our beloved son, Master I., our notary and your devoted servant, whom we and our brothers hold dear for his merits of loyalty and integrity and whom we consider acceptable to you, to your presence for faithfully narrating these matters, we desire that you grant him full trust in everything regarding the aforementioned and their circumstances, as well as the matter of Gaeta, on our behalf to your highness.

Given at Rieti, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico, Romanorum imperatori, litteras favorabiliter per archiepiscopum Idrontinum transmittit et eum hortatur ad ecclesiae succursum, promittitque nullum detrimentum iuribus eius evenire. 1232, Iul. 24, Reate.

**Translation to English:**

To the bishop and the entire clergy of Tibur. Having understood what you, brother bishop, on behalf of yourself and your clergy, and the noble man Matthew Rubeus, count of Tibur, on behalf of himself and the people of the same city, have proposed in our presence, desiring to put an end to disputes and cut off the cause of scandal, we have decided with the consent of both parties as follows: namely, that all the officials and councilors of the aforementioned city of the past year, as well as the diggers of your houses and churches, should swear to humbly comply with the commands of the Church and yours, brother bishop. Also, one citizen of Tibur will swear on behalf of the aforementioned people to abide by the commands of the Church. You, brother bishop, once all these things have been duly completed, and those things which have been taken from you and the churches have been fully restored, and appropriate satisfaction for the damages has been given to you, shall lift the sentence of interdict you have pronounced upon the aforementioned city on this occasion, absolve the excommunicated according to the form of the Church, and recall the clerics who had left the city on your command. By our grace and special mandate, you, sons of the clergy, will be released from paying one-sixth of those debts only, which were contracted by the priors and vesturaries appointed by you. Once this portion is paid, we desire that you and the churches enjoy in the future the liberty expressed in the statutes of the general council. Therefore, so that what we have provided may achieve the intended effect, we earnestly admonish and exhort your community through apostolic writings, firmly ordering you to unanimously accept all the aforementioned and diligently provide what is to be rendered by you without any difficulty. Furthermore, by virtue of obedience and under penalty of suspension, we strictly prohibit you from presuming to contribute to tallages and collections henceforth without special license from the Apostolic See. Given at Anagni, on the Kalends of September, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa episcopo et universo clero Tiburtino mandat, ut finem litigiis cum Matthaeo Rubeo comite Tiburtino imponant, omnes officiales anni praeteriti iuramentum praestent parendi mandatis ecclesiae et episcopi, damnorum restitutio fiat, interdictum relaxetur, et excommunicati absolvantur; clericis sextam partem debitorum remittit, et prohibet contributionem in talliis sine apostolicae sedis licentia. Datum Anagnie, Kal. Septembris, anno sexto.

Gregorius IX papa neophitis de Bandewe, de Wanneman, et de Winda paciscitur ut episcopum a se instituendum recipiant et iura Christianorum observent, et expeditiones contra paganos pro defensione et fidei propagatione suscipiant. Actum Reate, die 11 Februarii, pontificatus anno quinto, 1234.

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans, King of Jerusalem and Sicily. The sincerity of our inner affection, with which a father's care pursues his beloved son, makes us solicitous and attentive to the increase of your prosperity, so that as you abound in desired successes, the dignity of Mother Church may be expanded by generous increases. Therefore, as your serenity has devoutly requested in your letters, that, as we have sadly heard, the Holy Land, placed in the danger of dissension, may not be overwhelmed by the onslaught of perils but be brought back to the state of desired peace, we send apostolic letters to our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Jerusalem and legate of the apostolic see, to come to our presence, and to the beloved sons, the masters and brothers of the military orders of the Temple and of the Hospital of Jerusalem, that they may not delay to send, if able, in the present passage or in the next, prudent and wise men from their order, through whom we may be usefully informed about the state of the Kingdom of Jerusalem and provide for its peace and progress, commanding them to devoutly comply with your benevolent wishes for the peaceful state of the land and the favor of their order. Therefore, we earnestly ask, advise, and urge your majesty, that, taking up the spirit of piety and tranquility, you may not trouble the aforementioned masters and brothers in any way, but if any disturbance of mind should arise because of them, you should strive to ensure that it is calmed by the force of virtue; prudently recalling them to you through the display of consoling clemency, so that you may establish them as pleasing to you by your favor; adhering to our salutary advice and counsel regarding this and other affairs of your majesty, so that the power of your majesty may be directed to the continuous attainment of happiness with unimpeded progress. To this end, so that the aforementioned patriarch and others summoned to the apostolic see may have free passage and access, may your majesty provide and make the journey expedited by securing conduct through open imperial letters, for it would not happen without our and your support, lest, God forbid, any obstacle hinder their faithful approach. Moreover, concerning the matter of Gaeta, we, lacking no full solicitude, are carrying it forward in affection and effect, so that, with the Lord as author, it may be completed for the honor of the Church and yours, and the salvation of those who adhere to the Church. Given at Spoleto, 12th July, in the sixth year [of our pontificate].

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico, Romanorum imperatori, mandat ut patriarcha Hierosolymitanus aliique vocati ad sedem apostolicam liberum transitum habeant, et necessariam securitatem eis praebere curet. 1229, Iul. 12, Spoleti.

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, the illustrious emperor of the Romans, ever august, and king of Sicily. Since the priesthood and the empire are two lights in the firmament of the Church, by which the world is illuminated in spiritual and temporal matters as by day and night, it is indeed of interest to both of us to remove from detractors any cause for speaking ill of us. These detractors, having darkened hearts, prefer to stain the light with smoke rather than commend it for its brilliance, and they even curse the day by seeking frivolous reasons to obscure our deeds, however clear they may be, as we find more by experience than we can express. Indeed, it is known and widely acknowledged that the noble man Raynald, son of the late Duke C. of Spoleto, inflicted grievous injuries, enormous losses, and manifold troubles upon the Roman Church through his proud wickedness and wicked pride, such that if we were to respond justly according to the wickedness of his deeds, we should not at all be obliged to sympathize with him in his calamity, but rather to deride his downfall. But may the Lord prevent our heart from ever harboring rancor against anyone, and let us sympathize with those who suffer and show due compassion to those who endure hardships. For, as the Gospel truth teaches us that with the same measure that we measure to others, it will be measured to us, we need to show mercy to our neighbor if we wish to find God merciful to us. Therefore, since we are obliged to pray for those who persecute and slander us, we earnestly asked and confidently admonished you in our recent letter to grant pardon to the aforementioned Raynald, safeguarding the right of the Apostolic See, which we could not neglect without peril. However, because people might think that you were primarily moved against him because he provoked us in such a manner, and some might consider that his affliction is pleasing to us, and thus detractors could easily accuse us, first with silent murmurs and then with loud tumult, that we gave cause for his punishment: we now, as if pursuing our own interest, since, if (God forbid) he were to be harmed bodily, a greater reproach would fall upon us than what he inflicted by persecuting the Church, we earnestly beseech and sincerely admonish your imperial majesty, requesting as a special favor, that you no longer be angry with him, but, recalling the mercy of your wrath, spare him for your and our sake, so that from this you may more abundantly merit divine favor, and we may be obliged to follow your gentleness with worthy acts of gratitude. Given at Rieti, on the 5th day before the Ides of July, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico, illustri Romanorum imperatori et regi Sicilie, rogationem facit ut Raynaldo, filio quondam ducis Spoletani, veniam largiatur, iure apostolice sedis salvo, et misericordie recordatus sibi misereatur. 1231, Reate, V Idus Iulii, anno quinto.

**Translation to English:**

To the Patriarch of Jerusalem, the apostolic see's legate. Desiring peace in our days, through which the faithful may reach the eternal peace pleasing to God, albeit transitory, we are touched and grieved by the heart's pain when a discord arises that hinders progress and obstructs the expansion of the faith. Indeed, we have heard, and hearing have conceived great astonishment, that in the Holy Land, the origin of faith, and from which the delightful streams of peace should flow to be spread over the breadth of the world, pernicious dissensions have arisen, which we recount with sorrow. These offend the compassion of the Redeemer, who consecrated that land with His precious blood, and diminish the devotion that should be fostered among the professors of the Christian faith. This is because that royal region, for which countless powerful and noble, rich and poor from all parts of the world, coming, have offered themselves as a living sacrifice to the King of Heaven, is almost recklessly entrusted to destruction, to which diligent care should be given as to the pupil of one's eye. If it is rightly perceived and prudently considered, nothing should be held or deemed dearer than that which offered God visibly to all and directs and leads them by preceding faith to the attainment of His glory.

Therefore, with this consideration of eminent grace, we constantly strive to support the aforementioned land, the homeland of the eternal Father's Son, with due favor of

**Translation to English:**

To the consuls and people of Perugia, regarding the spirit of sound counsel. By the grace of God, with peace reformed between the Church and our beloved son in Christ Frederick, the illustrious Roman Emperor, ever august, King of Jerusalem and Sicily, we must not only abstain from aggression against the lands of the Empire but also defend those lands as far as the duty of our office permits. You, as we have heard, but certainly do not accept—in fact, we find it grave and unworthy—attempt to ally and enter into a society with some who are not of the patrimony, which we can scarcely believe, to the detriment of the said lands and the Empire. You act as though obscured by darkness, not acknowledging that from this you might fall into a difficulty from which you would not easily be able to extricate yourselves. Therefore, that this admonition may pre-warn you and preserve you immune from penalty, we strictly order your community by apostolic writings, under the obligation of fidelity, that you do not presume to enter any society, alliances, or oaths with those who are not of the patrimony or any others to the prejudice of those lands and against the rights and honor of the Empire. All such presumptions, whether they have been presumed until now or in the future, which we do not believe, we decree to be utterly invalid, since it is highly inappropriate that the Empire should be offended by our faithful ones, lest we seem to act contrary to the bonds of peace or invalidate what has proceeded from our lips. Otherwise, we give our venerable brother, the Bishop of Spoleto, a mandate by our letters to restrain you from such presumption by ecclesiastical censure, appeals removed. And if you do not care to obey our orders even then, we will lay our hands upon you spiritually and temporally in such a way that, with the penalty teaching, you will know how rash it is to contravene apostolic mandates. Given at Anagni, 20 November, in the sixth year. Executory for Spoleto against both. Written in the same manner to the Podestà and people of Todi and the Bishop.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa consulibus et populo Perusino mandat ne foedera cum extraneis in detrimentum imperii contrahant, sub poena censurae ecclesiasticae. 1232, Nov. 20. Anagniae.

**Translation to English:**

To the Patriarch of Antioch, legate of the Apostolic See,

We have learned that in the Kingdom of Jerusalem, a territory given with unique privilege to the King, the son of the supreme King, marked with the emblem of Christ under the Christian name, some attempt to divide it. These individuals, in their reckless pursuit of earthly dominion, disrespectfully encroach on celestial matters, as they provoke earthly discord through conspiracies, thus jeopardizing heavenly interests by exposing the land to accidents and uncertain events, which Christians have reclaimed for Christ through arduous efforts and necessary expenditures.

Indeed, the Saracen has not yet failed to turn his hand against the Christian, nor is the adversary's power so diminished that the small flock of the Lord should dissolve itself in internal disputes. Our tents are not so widely expanded there that it should be permissible or desirable to indulge in voluntary strife under the guise of peace. The acquisitions held by many were achieved through many efforts, the seeds sown by many are reaped by these few. Thus, it is neither lawful to offer to peril what has been gained through the shedding of much blood, nor is it expedient to risk what has barely been achieved through Christian diligence.

We are surprised at what could have led the people of that region to, as it is reported, contemplate rebellion against our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans and illustrious King of Jerusalem and Sicily, who, it is said, has shown them no grievance. But even if there were a grievance from the father, what has the son, the legitimate heir of the kingdom—who in his tender youth does not possess the inclination to harm—done wrong? Even if the father’s and son’s efforts were full of distress against them, they could and should have invoked the assistance of the Apostolic See, which has labored more than others for the aid of that land.

Since we are troubled by this scandal and suffer with its infirmities, wishing to swiftly come to the aid of the wounded beginnings lest the medicine be prepared too late, if troubles were to worsen through long delays, we instruct your fraternity by apostolic writings to, after consulting the masters of the Temple and Hospital, as well as others as you deem fit for the matter, not to delay in persuading the nobles of the aforementioned kingdom, the citizens of Acre, and others to return to the loyalty and devotion of the aforementioned Emperor, removing any obstacles of difficulty. Suppress those who might oppose, as follows: We have indeed learned that it is the will of the same Emperor, and we will gladly work to ensure that the people of the region maintain their complete rights. Thus, prudently strive for the peace of that province, so that the reed bruised by the pressure of wars is not broken and the smoking wick of disturbances is not extinguished. Rather, let the homeland rejoice in the silence of peace and the people rest in abundant tranquility.

Given at Rieti, July 26, in the sixth year [of the pontificate].

**Latin Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa Patriarchae Antiocheno, apostolicae sedis legato, mandat ut, consultis magistris Templi et Hospitalis, nobiles regni Ierosolimitani et cives Acconenses ad fidelitatem et devotionem Friderici imperatoris redeant. 1232, Iul. 26, Reate.

**Translation to English:**

To the Bishop of Brescia and Brother Alberic of the Order of Preachers. Previously, our beloved son G., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark, acting at that time in the office of legation in the region of Lombardy, personally went to the city of Bergamo due to internal wars and diligently worked to bring peace to the dissenting factions. The parties humbly and devoutly accepted his exhortations and advice, and under an oath-bound security, committed to comply with his mandates regarding all disputes. Following the terms of this commitment, the cardinal chose the nobleman P. de Turre, a citizen of Milan, to provide governance for the peace of the city. However, with the instigation of an evil-doer and promoter of dissention, the people of Rivola and Suardis, in disregard of the sworn religion, attempted to elect R. de Madello, a Milanese citizen, to power without admitting the aforementioned nobleman, and, more reprehensibly, allowed certain heretics released from the city’s prison to go free, for which the said cardinal pronounced a sentence of excommunication upon them and their supporters and followers, imposing ecclesiastical interdict on the mother church and their parishes. Now, on behalf of the said people, we were humbly petitioned that, as they offer themselves to obey our commands precisely and are ready to satisfy God and the churches adequately, we might mercifully command the relaxation of the aforesaid sentences. Therefore, as the bosom of piety must be opened to those returning to the bosom of the Church, and wishing to imitate Him who came to seek and save the lost sheep, we strictly command you by apostolic writings that if those men make satisfaction to the said nobleman for injuries, just damages, and moderate expenses, and provide sufficient security that they will, to the best of their ability, eradicate heretics and maintain the liberty of the Church, you should, by our authority, care to relax the aforementioned sentences according to the form of the Church. Given at Anagni, November 3rd, in the sixth year.

---

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa episcopo Brixiensi et fratri Alberico de ordine Praedicatorum mandat ut, si homines de Rivola et de Suardis satisfaciant nobili P. de Turre, sententias excommunicationis et interdicti relaxent. Datum Anagnie, III Nonas Novembris, anno sexto.

Translation to English:

To Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans, illustrious King of Jerusalem and Sicily. We ponder thoughts of peace and not of affliction, because a serene sky is considered more beautiful than a cloudy one, prosperity more pleasing than adversity, and joy sweeter than sorrow. Those who stand at the gates of the Church are displeased by discord and division, as our special concern lies with them, even though our affection is generally extended to all the faithful peoples. The danger and suffering that have arisen from the discord between the Romans and the people of Viterbo, and the near-total destruction inflicted upon the Church's patrimony, is known to many and is particularly distressing to us. This is because many are led to destruction, many souls are lost, shining faith is diminished, and heretical perversity is disastrously increased. Some cities have become so infected by the minister of perdition that their inhabitants can be called the cesspool of corruption and the abode of treachery. But since evils grow quickly while good increases slowly, and the former persist all the more firmly the more room they are given to fester: to obtain the peaceful devotion of the Church, and to direct the business of faith and other pressing matters successfully, which thrives best when the matter of dissent is subdued, we desire and hope that through your diligent efforts—through which the untamed may be tamed and the rough made smooth—the cause of such strife may be removed and the pitiable condition of the afflicted restored to a prosperous state. Therefore, we earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort your Highness to persuade and command the authorities and people of Viterbo through imperial letters to obey our beloved sons, T., Cardinal Priest of the title of Saint Sabina, and R., Bishop-elect of Ostia, whom we have decided to send to them for the purpose of negotiating their salvation concerning the matter of peace. This cannot be neglected or postponed without great detriment to themselves and others, which should be avoided eagerly with your effort, as your God-given authority obligates you to bring peace to the nations and, with God's help, to deliver the people of the Savior. Given at Anagni, 12th Kalends of November, in the sixth year.

Regesto:

Gregorius IX papa Friderico Romanorum imperatori mandat ut per litteras imperiales Viterbiensibus suadeat oboedire cardinalibus missis ad pacem tractandam. Anagniae, XII Kal. Novembr., anno VI.

**Translation to English:**

To the bishop of Mantua and the prior of Marcaria in the diocese of Mantua. Our beloved son, the abbot of the monastery of Leno, which pertains directly to us, once made a complaint to us. He informed us that the men of the castle of Leno in the diocese of Brescia presume, to the prejudice and detriment of the said monastery, to elect consuls, a council, and other officials in the same castle by their own authority, to enact their statutes, to convene an assembly, to have bells for the meeting, to exercise temporal jurisdiction, to occupy certain possessions belonging to the monastery in the castle and outside in the name of the community, and to construct mills in the waters and territory of the monastery. Hence, we gave a mandate to our venerable brother, the bishop of Parma, that he should enjoin the same men to appear before us with all their arguments through suitable procurators by the octave of Saint Michael just past, which we assigned to both parties as a peremptory term. This mandate of ours being faithfully executed, the said abbot in person and the convent of the said monastery through a legitimate procurator appeared before our beloved son, S., presbyter cardinal of the title of San Lorenzo in Lucina, whom we appointed as auditor for this matter. Belmos, son of Dominic Sartor, and John Bonus de Foiata appeared for the other side, but not having sufficient mandate, they turned to frivolous exceptions, which the same cardinal, as he ought not to, did not admit; they recklessly departed without obtaining or seeking his permission. Therefore, the aforesaid cardinal pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the same men, consuls, councilors, and their officials. Wherefore, we command you to publish the same sentence, reasonably pronounced by the same cardinal, until suitable satisfaction is made, on every Sunday and feast day, and to have it published throughout the city and diocese of Brescia. Given at Anagni, 17th Kalends of January, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa episcopo Mantuano et priori de Marcaria mandat sententiam excommunicationis, a cardinale Sancti Laurentii in Lucina contra homines castri de Leno pro temerario discessu et occupatione possessionum monasterii de Leno promulgatam, publicare. 1232, Dec. 16. Anagnie.

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans, illustrious King of Jerusalem and Sicily. Wickedness and crimes of the impious displease us everywhere, but those inflict a deeper wound upon us when they occur nearby rather than afar, because of the damage inflicted by flying arrows from close range. Truly, we have received with wonder and distress that the sons of perdition, namely Saracens established in the regions of Apulia, with your favoring consent, which seems unbelievable, have overturned the church of Saint Peter in Bangio Foietano, which rightfully belongs to the monastery of Saint Lawrence of Aversa, turning it into a place for stabling animals, whereas it had been a dwelling place of angels, completely demolishing it, and transporting its stones and timbers to Nocera for constructing their buildings. But because such wicked presumption cannot occur without affront to the Creator, and injury to the Apostolic See, as a noted defamation, we earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort your serenity to prudently consider whether any of the churches, especially those contained within the realm, which ought to rejoice in your protection, since you have been appointed by the Lord as their and others' defender, should be demolished by the sacrilegious hands of infidels, whereas the virtue of the Most High should rather be exalted by the faithful. For the reverence of the divine and the enhancement of your grandeur, we urge that you command the aforementioned church to be restored and its stolen goods returned, which it possessed in its time of integrity. Moreover, because the excess of liberty, which you are said to have granted to these Saracens, is deemed harmful to the Christians nearby and has come to the horror of many who hear it, may it please your eminence to so diminish their presumptions that in no way may they dare to disturb the hearts of your faithful subjects, especially when it would seem an injury to our Redeemer if the sons of Belial, who ought to be oppressed with the chain of perpetual servitude, were to attack the sons of light in our lands or wickedly consider themselves equal in freedom to them. Given at Anagni, on the 3rd day before the Nones of December, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Frederico, Romanorum imperatori, mandat ut ecclesiam Sancti Petri in Bangio Foietano, a Sarracenis deiectam, restituat et rapta restituat, ne Saraceni libertate fruantur, quae Christianae fidei noceat. 1232, Dec. 3. Anagniae.

**Translation to English:**

To the Patriarch of Jerusalem, legate of the Apostolic See. 

The supreme and illustrious King of Jerusalem, Solomon the preacher and true Idida, in Psalm 104:11, the land which is the cord of his inheritance, indeed a singular commercial conquest, comes to us as a peaceful preacher, diligent and beloved at birth, a preacher in life, diligent and beloved in death. For when he was born, the angelic voice brought a hymn of peace, the covenant of reconciliation between God and man. While he lived, he educated the unlearned with doctrine and informed them by example. While he suffered, he sang a song of love, for drawn by the bond of love to the cross, he drew all to himself, when the voluntary death of life overcame the unwelcome life of death. Indeed, in that land as in a special field, God and man, the son of God and man, sowed, and indeed good seed. But an enemy is said to have come and sowed tares among the wheat, discord in place of peace, division in place of reformation, hatred in place of love growing. The head of the family indeed has a prosecution against those whose malice chokes the good seed with tares, and considers what reward to give them in their homeland, when at the time of harvest he will bind bundles to be burned, the wheat being gathered into the barn. We indeed marvel at what is claimed, that for the kingdom of the Lord you did not want to stand as a wall against those rising in opposition, to show yourself as peaceful to the true Solomon against the disturbers of it, to offer yourself as a learned preacher of justice against the injurers, and to show intimate love against the haters. What then will you answer to the Lord of lords, if the land acquired at the price of glorious blood and regained by the blood of many thousands lies open to danger due to your negligence? Is not negligence of this kind comparable to a fault of guilt? Lest we seem to neglect the cause of Christ in such a doubtful case, and conscience reproaches us with delay, we strictly command your fraternity by apostolic writings to present yourself before our sight, without delay, so that through you and some brothers of the Temple and Hospital, as we have sent through other letters, sufficiently instructed about the state of the land, we may both ward off the dangers that seem to threaten, and procure the aids known to be expedient, and thus, with Him who gives calm after the storm and serenity after the cloudy weather causing it, the arising disturbance might provide a remedy for greater peace, and could ensure a more complete diligence in future care for pressing matters. It does not escape our memory that you once requested by special petition for permission to come to us. But what grace did not allow then, necessity now compels. Moreover, to ensure your safe passage to us, we have directed our writings to our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, always august emperor of the Romans, illustrious king of Jerusalem and Sicily, that he may provide for your full security. Given at Rieti, VIII Kalends of August, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Patriarchae Hierosolymitano, apostolicae sedis legato mandat ut se conspectui suo repraesentet, ut de statu Terrae Sanctae sufficienter instruatur et pericula imminentia declinentur. Data Reate, VIII Kalendas Augusti, anno sexto.

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans, King of Jerusalem and Sicily. From the reports presented by the venerable brothers, the Archbishop of Messina and the Bishop of Troia, and our beloved son, Master Peter de Vinea, to us and our brothers, the imperial majesty has filled us with great joy, and we rise in thanksgiving to the King of Heaven. We are grateful that, in the honor of Him who appointed you as an eminent leader among the people, you wish to exercise the greatness of your virtue in those matters which enhance the glory of the Most High, the dignity of the Church, and the sublimity of the Empire, as well as strengthen the Catholic faith and diminish heretical depravity. Indeed, regarding this holy and salutary intention, as well as others that align with the Creator's pleasure, the Mother Church intends to bestow upon you, her beloved son, the fullness of grace and favor. Therefore, we beseech and implore your serenity in the Lord, urging you for the remission of your sins, to act promptly and implement those plans you have conceived laudably with the inspiration of the Lord. Pursue them so powerfully and magnificently that those who abhor the path of righteousness may hasten to the grace of conversion or be led into the pit of confusion, so that the entire family of the Redeemer may experience an increase in prosperity, and both ecclesiastical and imperial dignity may advance and shine with desired honor. Furthermore, other matters through which the aforesaid business may be prosperously carried out, we have entrusted to the aforementioned archbishop and bishop to disclose to your excellency. Grant them favorable faith, and with God’s guidance, do not delay in executing them effectively, especially since we have proposed to offer you counsel, aid, and favor with the advice of our brothers, as you proceed with the advice of the Church in the beginning, middle, and end of the aforementioned matters. Given at Anagni, on the 7th Ides of December, in the sixth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico Romanorum imperatori mandat, ut pro honore ecclesiae et imperii, ac fide catholicae roboranda, consilia et acta laudabiliter concepta magna cum virtute prosequatur, et archiepiscopo Messanensi et episcopo Troiano commissa fideliter exequatur. 1232, Dec. 7. Anagnie.

**Translation to English:**

To the Bishop of Semigallia. Since, even when you were in a lesser office, you brought forth an acceptable fruit from the talent entrusted to you and gathered the sheaves of blessing from your labor, you have deservedly been established as a faithful and prudent servant over the household of the Lord, to whom you must provide sustenance in due time. Advancing from grace to grace and from virtue to virtue, renouncing worldly desires, you have strived to walk in the spirit. Recalling that there is no sacrifice more pleasing to God than to seek the salvation of souls, you were once, inspired by fervor and at the command of our beloved son Otto, cardinal-deacon of St. Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano and then a legate of the apostolic see, crossing the seas with many labors and perils, like Jacob with his staff, for the conversion of peoples. You returned not only with two flocks of sheep but also with various provinces of pagans who believed in Christ, bringing back a green olive branch as a dove to the ark, for the reconciliation of many barbarous nations. Delighted by the grace bestowed upon thee by the Lord, from which more pleasing flowers and fruits have sprung, since the lamp should not be placed under a bushel but on a stand to illuminate the darkness of many, we have decided to consecrate you as the Bishop of Semigallia with our hands. We have an undoubted confidence in you, instructed by evident experiences rather than arguments, that you thirst for the salvation of souls and the growth of the Christian faith. We entrust to you the office of legation in Livonia, Gotland, Vinland, Estonia, Semigallia, Courland, and other provinces and islands of neophytes and pagans surrounding, to extend the boundaries of the faith: we command you by apostolic writings to freely announce Christ in those places, correcting ecclesiastical persons and reforming churches; you should also institute and remove abbots, priors, and other subjects and dignitaries when necessary, promote clerics to orders, confirm the election of bishops, and confer the gift of consecration and blessing to bishops and abbots when needed and deemed appropriate. Clothed with the virtue of the spirit from on high, diligently strive to exercise the care entrusted to you so laudably that through your ministry the Catholic faith may be propagated in those parts, and that you may please Him who advances those who please Him to salvation, ready to compensate for whatever you have done beyond measure. Lest authority of power be lacking to you, to whom the purity of conscience is present and the judgment of reason is believed to be at hand, we grant you by the authority of these presents to strike down contradictors and rebels with the censure of excommunication, suspension, and interdict, for we will hold firm and cause to be inviolably observed, with the Lord as our helper, any sentence you may justly pronounce against them until they provide proper satisfaction. Given at Rieti, the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Episcopo Semigalliensi mandat ut, in provincia sua et aliis regionibus neophytorum, Christum libere annuntiet, personas ecclesiasticas corrigat, ecclesias reformet, abbates et priores instituat et amoveat, electiones episcoporum confirmet, excommunicationis et interdicti censuras in rebelles exerceat. Dat. Reate, V Kal. Febr., anno pontificatus nostri quinto.

**Translation to English:**

To the Bishop of Hildesheim. Since our venerable brother, the Bishop of Nuremberg, has been gravely defamed, as we have learned, due to the document that was publicly read in Würzburg, from which a serious scandal arose against our beloved son O., deacon cardinal of St. Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, then the legate of the Apostolic See in those parts: we, wishing to maintain the rigor of the father and not forsake the leniency of the mother, command your fraternity through apostolic writings to diligently inquire into the truth of these matters. If you do not find him culpable in this regard, instruct him to undergo a public purgation due to the infamy that has arisen against him, taking an oath bodily, and receive the purgation publicly before many, according to the form enclosed with these presents. And because he is said to be suffering from a chronic illness or serious disease, declare that he is not bound by the sentences passed on him by the aforesaid legate, if he could not come to the Apostolic See in the time allotted due to legitimate impediment. But if you find him culpable in the aforementioned matters, or if he cannot undergo the purgation already prescribed for him, ensure that the sentence of suspension which the same cardinal pronounced against the said bishop and certain others on this occasion is inviolably observed, and faithfully inform us by your letters about whatever has been done in this matter, so that we may proceed from there as we see fit according to God. Given at Anagni, on the sixth year, on the 6th of December.

The form of the protestation confirmed by the same oath. I, the Bishop of Nuremberg, protest and assert that I was neither in counsel nor in fact nor in consent regarding the letters that were read in the assembly at Würzburg, where the Lord Archbishop of Magdeburg and I, along with certain bishops and other prelates and clerics, had convened by the command of Lord Otto, deacon cardinal of St. Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, then legate of the Apostolic See, were made or read there, nor did I know anything about them beforehand; and I assert and swear these things to be true. So help me God and these holy Gospels. Regarding the fault, because I did not oppose them afterward, and in all other matters, I implore your mercy and swear to abide by your commands.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa episcopo Ildesemensi mandat ut, de infamia suborta contra episcopum Nuemburgensem propter scripturam lectam Erbipoli, veritatem inquirat et, si innocens invenietur, purgationem coram multis recipiat; si vero culpabilis, suspensionem observet et quid actum sit referat. Dat. Anagnie, VIII Idus Decembr., anno sexto.

To the dean, cantor, and schoolmaster of the greater church of Trier. Tell us, what madness is this that vexes you, that following the deceitful teachings of deception, by acquiescing to the spirits of error you choose not to consent to the truth of the faith?
