The same to the consuls and people of Nepi. The same to all our faithful in Sabina.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa potestati et populo Tuscanensi nuntiat se, consilio fratrum suorum, iuramenta fidelitatis eis per violentiam prestita relaxasse, eosque ab eis absolvisse et ad eorum observantiam non teneri decrevisse. Dat. Perusii, XV Kal. April, anno VIII.

**Translation to English:**

To the Bishop of Regensburg, Chancellor of the Imperial Court. — Since the noble man Henry, son of our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, the Roman Emperor, has been bound under the sentence of excommunication by our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Salzburg, for perjury incurred by rashly opposing his father, we command you by the authority of these presents that, since he has now returned to the grace of the said emperor, you grant him the benefit of absolution according to the form of the Church, after receiving from him sufficient security that he will adequately compensate the Danish knights returning from the service of the Roman Church, as well as the clerics approaching and departing from it, whom he caused to be unjustly despoiled of their goods, not without the injury of the divine and apostolic see. Given at Perugia, on the Kalends of August, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa Ratisponensi episcopo, cancellario imperialis aule, mandat ut Henricum, filium Friderici Romanorum imperatoris, ad gratiam patris reversum, post sufficientem cautionem receptam, absolvat et satisfieri curet militibus Danis et clericis spoliatis. 1235, Aug. 1, Perusii.

**Translation to English:**

The text describes a portion of a document that is not critical to the general history, but the full text can be found in Potthast, Reg. 9933. It is addressed to Beatrice, the illustrious queen of Castile, Toledo, and León. The text celebrates Saint Elizabeth, described as an admirable vessel, a chosen vessel consecrated to the Lord, who was a furnace of charity in works of ardor. It praises her as a vessel of mercy, through which she mercifully offered the wine of true contrition to the tyrants, princes, and magnates of this world. Among those particularly blessed by this vessel's cup was her brother-in-law, Conrad, the former Landgrave, who, though young and dear to the world, was especially graced by this vessel's drink. It led him to forsake worldly dignities and flee from the hands of the impious crucifiers of Jesus Christ to the refuge of the cross. Likewise, Agnes, the virgin handmaid of Christ and daughter of the king of Bohemia, was also inebriated by this vessel's cup. In her tender age, she displayed the celestial signs of heavenly conversation, fleeing from the heights of imperial eminence as if they were venomous reptiles, and, seizing the triumphant banner of the cross, she advanced to meet her bridegroom, accompanied by the chorus of sacred virgins with burning lamps. Given at Perugia, on the seventh day before the Ides of June, in the ninth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Beatrici illustri reginae Castellae, Toleti et Legionis, narrat de sancta Elisabeth, quae vas misericordiae et caritatis eminebat, et de eiusdem virtutibus in Conradum quondam Landgravium et Agnetem regis Boemiae filiam. Dat. Perusii, VII Idus Iunii, anno nono.

**Translation to English:**

To Master P. de Collemedio, provost of Saint Omer in the diocese of Morin, our chaplain. By the authority of these presents, we command your devotion that if our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King of France, cannot be persuaded to retain the land of Venosa any longer, you, in our name, shall receive his resignation of it, and, having sought the counsel of the prelates of the aforementioned land, you shall, according to the wisdom given to you by the Lord, arrange for it as you see best, committing it to one or more suitable persons who should faithfully, in the name of the Roman Church, guard it to the honor of the church and according to our command and will. Furthermore, you shall proceed without delay with the inquiry we have ordered in other letters to be made by you concerning it. Additionally, you shall advise and persuade the king himself and our dearest daughter in Christ, the Queen of France, his illustrious mother, to earnestly strive to make peace between the noble men, the counts of Provence and Toulouse, especially because it is believed that through this the work of peace and faith may be more firmly established. Indeed, sending letters addressed to the king under our seal, you shall only deliver them to him when he cannot be persuaded to keep custody of the said land. Given at Perugia, on the Ides of February, in the eighth year of our pontificate. II. Rescript of the enclosed schedule. Since a marriage contract has already been arranged between the brother of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King of France, and the daughter of the Count of Toulouse, you shall earnestly advise and persuade the same king to have the marriage celebrated between them.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Magistro P. de Collemedio mandat ut, si rex Franciae terram Venusinam retinere non possit, resignationem eius recipiat et de ipsa disponat. Monere debet regem et reginam Francorum ad pacem inter comites Provinciae et Tolosanum promovendam. Perusii, Idib. Febr., pontificatus anno VIII.

**Translation to English:**

To the rector and people of Velletri. The proven constancy of your faith and that of your ancestors shines clearly, like gold tested in fire, making you more pleasing to God and men. By your shining example, you have strengthened the hearts of many who waver, encouraging the faint-hearted to be more ardently loyal to the Apostolic See. Although what you have done reflects the glory and honor of your city, you have made us your debtors by your commendable obligation, so we must provide for your innumerable grievances. Indeed, it would be lengthy to enumerate the various benefits with which the Apostolic See has customarily treated the Romans with usual benevolence, and it would be superfluous to recount their great ingratitude, repaying love with hatred, generous favor with grave injuries, and causing you and other faithful ones unbearable losses and violence. However, the perseverance of your virtue, which knows not to yield to adversity, has shone more clearly when the storm of disturbance raged. For you, unfearing the loss of property nor fearing the danger to persons, kept your minds fixed on the Roman Church, of which you are sons and loyal followers. You stood firm with it in all its trials, not faltering but growing in devotion and faith amidst various pressures, just as the furnace tempers gold, so trial seems to have strengthened your unwavering fortitude. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by your devoted supplications, and knowing that the Lord judges the heart rather than the work, and that bonds of iniquity are also to be loosed, we have decided by the authority of these presents to absolve you from any oaths made to the Romans that prejudice the Apostolic See and the fidelity you owe to it, and we decree that you are not held to observe them. Let no one, therefore, infringe this our constitution etc. If anyone, however, etc. Given as above.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa rectori et populo Velletrensi indulget ut ab obligationibus et iuramentis, quae in praeiudicium apostolicae sedis Romanis praestita sunt, absolvantur. Datum apud Lateranum, anno pontificatus nostri sexto.

**Translation to English:**

To the archdeacon of Novara. From the letters of our venerable brother, the bishop of Piacenza, it has become known to us that Brother Roland of the Order of Preachers went personally to Piacenza to crush the head of the serpent, to capture the little foxes, and to restrain the jaws of the roaring lion with a bridle, so that they might no longer tear the garment of Christ. Having called the people together and delivered the word of God for the edification of souls, he enjoined certain matters upon their leader L. regarding the expulsion of heretics. However, with the connivance and favor of this leader, it is said that the heretics and their supporters violently attacked the bishop of Piacenza, his clergy, Brother Roland, and other religious men. A monk of Saint Savinus was wickedly slain, and Brother Roland and some other religious individuals were wounded with swords and stones. Consequently, the bishop placed the city under ecclesiastical interdict, and the said Dominican brothers promptly left, taking Brother Roland, who was half-dead, with them. The people of Piacenza, moved by grief, humbly begged Brother Roland and the other brothers not to leave, and to accept appropriate satisfaction for the excess committed. Indeed, Brother Roland, who could not be persuaded to return, ordered the capture and detention of the leader and twenty-four others, said to be the perpetrators of this crime, until it would please us to decree otherwise. The people humbly obeyed this command, captured the leader and the others, and handed them over to prison by the intervention of the bishop's diligence. Thus, with the city deprived of leadership and justice consequently silent, the crimes committed there remain unpunished, which, unless swiftly addressed, may result in greater scandal. Therefore, by these our letters, we have commanded them to keep the captives under strict guard and prevent them from escaping until we write to them our decision. Confident in your discretion and desiring to address the issue promptly rather than seeking a remedy after substantial harm, we command you to personally go to the said city, investigate all the aforementioned matters diligently with our venerable brother, the bishop of Piacenza, and report back to us faithfully what you find. Moreover, to prevent division or scandal in the said city or the Lombardy region, ensure that a suitable and faithful governor to the Roman Church is provided for the city, whose diligence and prudence will defend the city from the frauds of heretics and the cunning of the wicked. Upon receiving adequate hostages from the aforementioned leader L., promising obedience to our commands regarding the aforementioned issues, you shall, with the counsel of the aforementioned bishop, arrange for his and his family's release. Given at Anagni, 22nd October, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa archidiacono Novariensi mandat, ut personaliter Placentiam accedens, inquirat super tumultibus a fratre Rollando de Ordine Praedicatorum contra haereticos gestis, et provideat de rectore idoneo civitati Placentinae, captivosque, receptis obsidibus, liberet. 1233, Oct. 22, Anagnie.

**Translation to English:**

To the Patriarch of Antioch, legate of the Apostolic See. We recall having responded to your consultation regarding the proceedings against the people of Cremona, that it should be referred to the imperial authority, especially since we had sent our letters to him so that he might explain to us his will about this matter through his letters. However, since we have learned that you have decided to promulgate the sentences of excommunication against the authority and council and of interdict against the city of Cremona, we instruct you to relax these sentences after the reception of this letter, having received an oath of caution from the said authority and council to comply with the mandates of the church, setting aside all excuses, yet ensuring that you do not impose anything on them under pretext of this caution. Given at Assisi, on the 6th day before the Kalends of October, in the ninth year [of our pontificate].

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Patriarchae Antiocheno, apostolicae sedis legato, mandat, ut sententias excommunicationis contra potestatem et consilium, et interdicti in civitatem Cremonensem, recepta cautione iuratoria, relaxet. 1235, Sept. 26, Assisii.

Translation to English:

To the Bishop of Ascoli. Although we have previously instructed you through our letters to proceed with our authority against the disobedient and rebellious, we now prohibit you from placing any communities under excommunication or interdict without our special mandate. This prohibition should not be extended to the Veronese or Piacentini, or to those who are or will be disturbers of their peace. Given at Viterbo, on the 3rd of the Nones of April, in the tenth year of our pontificate.

Regesto in Latin:

Gregorius IX papa Episcopo Esculano mandat, ne sine mandato speciali communitates excommunicationi vel interdicto supponat, prohibitione non proroganda ad Veronenses aut Placentinos. 1236, Apr. 3. Viterbii.

**Translation to English:**

To the bishop of Merseburg, the provost of Saint Maurice in Halle, and the scholasticus of Saint Mary in Erfurt of the dioceses of Magdeburg and Mainz. We have received a grave complaint from the beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Pegau, that although their monastery has nurtured, supported, and elevated Godfrey and Siegfried, canons of Meissen, Henry, provost of Saint Stephen in Zeitz, and some others, bestowing upon them manifold grace, these same persons, like serpents biting the sides of their mother, unjustly harass the aforementioned monastery, which they are bound to revere and honor, incessantly afflicting and persecuting it concerning revenues, possessions, and other matters.

One of them, namely Godfrey the Younger, did not wish to return certain privileges of the monastery, which had been furtively taken along with some movable goods, until he had extorted a certain sum of money and an annual pension of one mark from them. Furthermore, they incurred serious losses and expenses due to the detention of these privileges, as, during the time when you, brother bishop, raised a question about their subjection, they could not use these privileges to defend the liberty of the monastery.

Therefore, they have humbly requested the fulfillment of justice regarding these matters, and since grace should not remain with the ungrateful, they ask that these individuals be deprived of the benefits they hold from the aforementioned monastery due to the vice of ingratitude, so that, because iniquity proceeds from abundance, they may be less emboldened to harm the monastery if the means to do harm are removed from them. 

Since the aforementioned matters are not yet clear to us, we command you to summon those who should be summoned, and after more diligently examining the truth about the aforementioned matters, if the cause proceeds from the will of the parties, you shall terminate it with due outcome, doing etc.; otherwise, remit it to us sufficiently instructed, setting a deadline etc. up to: you are to receive. If not all etc., two etc. Given at Perugia, the third Ides of January, in the eighth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX episcopo Mersburgensi, preposito Sancti Mauritii in Halle, et scolastico Sancte Marie in Erfodia mandat ut, vocatis evocandis et cognita veritate, causam inter abbatem et conventum Pigaviensis et canonicos Misnenses super privilegiis et rebus mobilibus fine debito terminent aut ad sedem apostolicam remittant. 1235, Jan. 11, Perusii.

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans, illustrious King of Jerusalem and Sicily. To eradicate the heretical depravity from the kingdom of Sicily, so that, with the stains of perfidy, which secretly taint some parts of the same kingdom, wiped away, the purity of the Christian faith may shine forth therein, a letter of gratitude that you sent reported that you have undertaken a new work. Indeed, since above all other works we consider this pleasing to the Lord of graces and also to us, and since we recognize that this will greatly enhance the glory of your name, we conceive great joy from this and justly rejoice with you, ready to provide appropriate support to your highness everywhere, by the virtue of Christ, to abolish the contagion of such a harmful plague. From this indeed, dearest son, it is evident that your greatness delights in the exaltation of the divine name. But because with fervent desire we have long awaited that the beauty of words might be followed by the adornment of deeds, since a tree is considered beautiful more by its fruits than by its leaves, we beseech and implore your excellence in the Lord Jesus Christ, that prudently considering that a honeycomb draws praise from its sweetness and a harvest secures commendation from its yield, you might so conform the words of devotion, which are often set forth in your letters, to works of goodness, that they may bear fruit in action and establish you as preeminent in virtue before the King of Heaven and the princes of the earth and all the faithful, as an exalted prince in power. Otherwise, we think it of little use what the eloquence of a writer labors to convey in letters. Therefore adorn the chamber of your heart with the marks of piety, illuminate the throne with the splendors of good will, so that, with you maintaining severity in private and clemency in the field, the multitude of people subject to you may conceive a cause of joy from you and, with you propitious, may bloom again in the grace of prosperity. For thus, since the love of citizens is an impregnable fortification, the desire which you have conceived against the extermination of heretical depravity may proceed successfully and be completed with God as its author. However, it is expedient that, as you wish to deserve more abundantly the divine grace and favor of the mother church, under the pretext of heretics, some of whom, as you state, were formerly committed to the flames as a bulwark of the faith, no faithful who perhaps by offending your highness were not heretics but erring in some way, found through impatience caused by grievances, should perish in any way, as they did before, to our sorrow and the grief of many, not without offense to the divine majesty, the scandal of the faithful people, and the detriment of your imperial name in your presence, which, if one may propose the word of piety, ought to have been assigned to destroying the faithless rather than destroying the faithful, so that you might be said to be a promoter of the Christian empire rather than a suppressor of the same on account of the afflicted kingdom of Sicily. This we wish to be commended to you henceforth for divine and our reverence, adjuring you through the Son of God, that you might obtain full confidence in our favor, provided that, intent on carrying out the divine good pleasures, you refrain from the grievance of the same kingdom. Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of July, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

---

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico, Romanorum imperatori, mandat ut, heretica pravitate in regno Sicilie extirpanda, operibus fidei Christiane consona agat, cavens ne fideles indebite perimantur. 1233, Id. Iul., Laterani.

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans, illustrious King of Jerusalem and Sicily. We trust that you hold a fervor of sincerity toward our person, and are proven to possess the gift of circumspection, so that even in our silence and that of others, you should take care not to give occasion to malicious individuals eager to speak ill, thereby sharpening and releasing slanderous tongues against us or yourself, who constantly strive to wickedly distort the truth to our and your detriment. Indeed, due to the oppression of the Gaetani and others who adhered to the apostolic see during times of discord, so many murmur against us and even openly curse us, that we have, with shame, become a scandal to many, who ridicule us over the full provision and hope for the concord, which was reformed between you and the church. Although no deceitful suggestions or sly arguments have been able to avert us from the trust we have in your purity, but rather we have remained so immovably steadfast in this regard that we are known to have incurred no light suspicion among the good and wise: nevertheless, considering that several difficulties may emerge which are not expedient to explain in writing, and firmly believing that what is injurious to us, you should consider shameful, we repeatedly implore and beseech your imperial gentleness, adjuring by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and also earnestly advising in good faith, that you should prudently spare both us and yourself in this matter, since there is no further room for dissimulation, and bring this business to an end this time, without attaching any obstacle of further delay, by granting to the Gaetani and others mentioned above, removing from it the clause: "saving the mandate and express in another," namely saving the service due from our dearest son in Christ, your son Conrad, to your court, remitting all offenses against them, restoring them to your favor, granting them security and full liberty to conduct all business throughout the kingdom, empire, and everywhere, by granting them open letters on this matter. Moreover, entrust to our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Messina, and our beloved son, the master of the Teutonic House of St. Mary, until the fifteenth year of your aforementioned son, to whom the above-mentioned will swear fealty, the free administration of the lands, peoples, and all pertaining to them in his name through other letters of yours, so that if both or one of them should die, others or another may be substituted in their place by the counsel of the church, and if your aforementioned son should resign or perish, God forbid, nevertheless the aforesaid shall be maintained until the predetermined term, which you shall promise by your letters not to revoke in any way. Therefore, to expedite these matters with your excellence, we have decided to send to your serenity our beloved son, Master John of Capua, our notary, a prudent and discreet man, of whose faith and diligence we have undoubted confidence and in whom you can fully confide, as he is zealous for and desires the increase of your honor and exaltation. Receiving him with the customary kindness as befits your eminence, and hearing him, on those matters he will propose to you on our behalf, trust in him as you would in us, and do not delay in bringing them to effect, so that you may henceforth close the wicked mouths of speakers, the title of your sincerity may shine, and through filial devotion, you may deliver us from the unrest which we endure continuously for these matters, so that it is rightly considered intolerable by us and others. Given at the Lateran, IX Kalends of April, in the seventh year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico imperatori Romanorum mandat, ut clausula "salvo mandato et expresso in alia" amota, Gaetanos et alios ad gratiam suam restituat et eis plenariam libertatem concedat, administrationem terrarum usque ad annum quintum decimum filii Conradis committendo, et magistrum Iohannem de Capua notarium suum transmittit, ut haec apud imperatorem promoveat. Datum Laterani, VIIII Kal. Aprilis, anno pontificatus nostri septimo.

**Translation to English:**

To the consuls and people of Terracina. Desiring that the form of peace between the Church and the Romans be observed, as much as we love you as special sons of the Church, we can no longer ignore the continuous complaints of the noble man P. Fraiapane, a Roman citizen, who asserts that he was despoiled by us during the time of discord. According to the form of the same peace, those despoiled by the Church due to the aforementioned discord should obtain restitution. Therefore, by the authority of these presents, we command you to respond to him fully regarding his rights as before. Furthermore, we desire that he gains no more rights through such restitution than he previously had, and with his restoration, your rights in all things remain intact. Given at Viterbo, 7th Ides of January, in the ninth year.

---

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa consulibus et populo Terracinensi mandat, ut P. Fraiapane, civis Romanus, restitutionem iustitiarum suarum secundum formam pacis inter ecclesiam et Romanos observatam obtineat, necnon ut nullum novum ius per huiusmodi restitutionem adquirat. 1236, Jan. 7, Viterbii.

**Translation to English:**

I. To the Consuls and people of Gaeta. Desiring with deep zeal the peace and progress of your city, we promote with all possible care what we recognize as beneficial to you. Hence, wishing to procure peace for you, we send you its form enclosed under our seal, which if you decide to accept, notify us through a public instrument, and attend to what our beloved son, Master P., our scribe, the bearer of these presents, will propose to you on our behalf, and send back to us through the same scribe the privilege granted to you by the Apostolic See. Given at the Lateran, June 21, in the seventh year [of our pontificate].

II. Grant of Frederick the Emperor concerning the city of Gaeta to his son Conrad. Frederick, by the grace of God, always august Emperor of the Romans, King of Jerusalem and Sicily. Among the various benefits bestowed on those who are joined or deserving, it is particularly gratifying to the giver when a father grants to his son. Thus, considering the pure affection of love, which binds a father to a son, and acknowledging the bond of nature, we concede, give, and hand over to you, King Conrad, our dearest son, and your heirs in perpetuity, our city of Gaeta with all its appurtenances, rights, and reasons, reserving the service owed to our court. To commemorate and strengthen this our concession and donation to endure perpetually, we have ordered this present privilege to be written by the hand of our notary and faithful servant, and authenticated with the impression of our golden seal. 

III. Pardon for offenses committed by the Gaetans in adhering to the Church. Frederick, etc., to all the people of Gaeta, etc. Let all know that we, at the requests and admonitions of our most holy father in Christ, the Supreme Pontiff, out of honor for him and reverence for the Apostolic See, from innate clemency, which gloriously leads us to spare rather than avenge, have received your community and each of you into our grace, pardoning you all and each for any offense and fault committed against us by adhering to the Church on the occasion of the arisen discord. We further grant you full security everywhere in the empire, our kingdom of Sicily, and all our power, in going, staying, and returning, with your merchandise and goods, in persons and property, and we command that it be observed for you by our open letters.

IV. That no one should harm the Gaetans in persons or goods throughout the empire or kingdom. Frederick, etc., to all established throughout the kingdom of Sicily, to whom these presents shall be shown, his faithful subjects, his grace, and goodwill. Because mercy surpasses judgment, and unless guilt precedes, forgiveness would have no place, we, deeming it more glorious to forgive mercifully than to punish justly, have deemed it proper to inform your community by these presents that, at the prayers and admonitions of the most holy father in Christ, Lord Gregory, the Supreme Pontiff, we have received the community and individuals of Gaeta into our grace, from innate clemency pardoning them all offense and fault committed by adhering to the Church against us on the occasion of the arisen discord. Moreover, we grant them full security everywhere in the empire, kingdom, and all our power, in going, staying, and returning, and in conducting any negotiations and business whatsoever, just as our other faithful subjects. Therefore, we command and instruct your fidelity that you firmly observe peace and security for the same Gaetans who have obtained our grace as for our other faithful subjects, wherever they happen to come, stay, and return with their merchandise and goods, and let no one dare to impede or disturb them in persons or goods. Whoever presumes to do so shall know he incurs the indignation of our majesty as a rash transgressor of our command. Given, etc.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa consulibus et populo Gaietano mandat ut pacem civitatis formam sub bulla mittit, iubens ut eam accipiant et privilegium ab apostolica sede indultum remittant per magistrum P. scriptorem. 1233, Jun. 21. Laterani.

**Translation to English:**

To the noble man, the Count of Marche. The Holy Roman Church, the mother of all faithful Christians, recently found itself in a situation of necessity and confidently requested your assistance, as a devoted son of the same Church. Having understood the situation, you wished to demonstrate the devotion and affection you are known to have towards it, as well as towards us, by effectively providing, as evidenced by the letters we received from him, five hundred pounds of Tours currency through our beloved son, Master Simon, our scribe, in support of the Church. On account of this, we commend your nobility in the Lord and extend to you our sincere thanks. However, with peace restored here and there, thanks to the Father of lights, for the Romans returning at the Church's mandate, we desire, and we command you through apostolic writing, that you ensure the return of the money without any reduction and, upon receiving it, send your letters to us concerning its resignation. Given at Perugia, on the 16th day before the Kalends of July, in the ninth year. In nearly the same manner, for one hundred and fifty pounds of Tours currency to the noble woman. In nearly the same manner concerning "money deposited for this kind of assistance" to the Archbishop of Tours and his suffragans, abbots, priors, and other prelates and canons throughout the province of Tours. In nearly the same manner to the Archbishop of Sens and his suffragans, etc. In nearly the same manner to the Archbishop of Reims, etc. In nearly the same manner to the abbots and convents of exempt monasteries established throughout the kingdom of France. Given at Perugia, on the 17th day before the Kalends of July, in the ninth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa nobili viro, comiti Marchie, mandat ut pecuniam quinquagintas libras Turonensium, ecclesiae Romanae subsidio liberaliter impensam, sine diminutione resignari curet et de resignatione litteras suas mittat. 1235, Iun. 16, Perusii.

**Translation to English:**

To the Bishop of Ascoli. By the authority of these presents, we command your fraternity that, among other tasks that we have enjoined upon you for the peace of the province of Lombardy, you diligently and studiously exert yourself with particular attention for the concord and peace of the people of Verona, attending to this matter with vigilant care and careful vigilance. For although we have directed our writings against the violators of the peace, which had been reformed among them by the authority of the Roman Church, to our venerable brothers, the patriarch of Grado and the bishop of Reggio, we nonetheless desire and command that you also, against them, if their rebellion necessitates it, proceed by our authority, removing the obstacle of appeal. Given at Viterbo, the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa episcopo Esculano mandat ut pro pace Veronensium omnem diligentiam adhibeat et contra violatores pacis auctoritate sua procedat, sublato appellationis obstaculo. 1237, Mart. 27. Viterbii.

**Translation to English:**

To the Countess of Flanders and Hainaut. It is appropriate to pursue the affection of a pious mind with kind favor and to provide support to obtain the desired effect. On your behalf, it was proposed before us that, since you have many lands commonly called "vastinas," which have not been cultivated since time immemorial, you have granted some of them under an annual rent to be perpetually possessed by cultivators. Knights and many other laymen of your land, because these lands lie within the boundaries of their holdings, where by ancient custom, though not by law, they receive and have received greater tithes, demand and extort tithes from these lands brought under cultivation, while the rectors of the churches, to whom by common law the tithes of these new lands are known to belong, either ignore or fear to pursue their rights. Therefore, you have humbly asked us to grant you the authority to bestow these lands on church uses, since you desire to allocate them to ecclesiastical uses and can legally, as you intend, and according to the law of the land, remove them from the hands of laymen. We, therefore, considering your desire in this matter to be pious, grant you by the authority of this present letter the faculty to do so, provided the canonical form is observed and the consent of the diocesan bishop is obtained. Let no one, therefore, etc. But if anyone, etc. Given at Viterbo, on the Nones of November, in the ninth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa comitissae Flandriae et Hanoniae facultatem concedit terras novalium ecclesiis conferendi, servata forma canonica et consensu episcopi diocesani, datis Viterbii, Nonis Novembris, anno nono (1235).

**Translation to English:**

To all archbishops and bishops established throughout the kingdom of France. As we have understood, some, having taken up the sign of the cross and committed themselves to aiding the Holy Land, presume to transfer themselves to that land without waiting for the general passage to be appointed by the Roman Church. By the authority of these presents, we strictly command you to strictly forbid all those signed with the cross in each of your dioceses from daring to embark on the journey to the aforesaid land before the aforementioned passage, setting aside all pretexts. Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to the faithful Christians. Therefore, although they prefer to persist in their stubbornness rather than recognize the words of the prophets and the mysteries of the holy scriptures and come to the knowledge of the Christian faith and salvation, since they seek our defense and help and the gentleness of Christian piety, we, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, Calixtus, Eugene, Alexander, Clement, Celestine, Innocent, and Honorius, Roman pontiffs, admit their petition and grant them the shield of our protection. Furthermore, during the celebration of their festivals, no one should disturb them with sticks or stones, nor should anyone demand services from them other than those they have been accustomed to perform in past times. Moreover, to counter the depravity and greed of evil men, we decree that no one should dare to mutilate or diminish the Jewish cemetery, or exhume buried bodies for the sake of money. If anyone, having known the content of this decree, rashly attempts to contravene it, may he suffer the loss of his honor and office or be punished by the penalty of excommunication, unless he corrects his presumption with worthy satisfaction. Behold, what seemed like hatred contained intimate love, and what appeared bitter eventually brought forth immense sweetness, because after we infused the salutary ointment's prick from us, which enlightened the eyes of a dulled mind, he saw the light walking in darkness and placed in danger, was happily recovered to health. By whose will? By whose diligence making it happen? Moreover, divine virtue willed it and we accomplished it with the Savior's clemency operating, endeavoring to imitate His footsteps, because we believe to nurture sons, not to destroy them, like a father embracing a son coming from afar, we received you returning to the Church's command by Christ's grace with the arms of paternal love, and although many were languishing with pain and indeed some were forming wishes against you so that resistance might oppose your rising to the heights, with diverse sentences of diverse people settled by the power of constancy, we restored you to a healthy state, pursuing your excellency with the grace of not only usual but greater favor. To the archbishops and bishops and other prelates of churches, noble men, dukes, marquises, counts, and barons present at the imperial court. The purity of faith and immense sincerity of devotion, with which you strive, by the grace of the Lord, to shine above other faithful ones in reverence to the Holy Church, offer us full confidence that in those things which we desire according to God, we may find you ready and willing. Therefore, since the time has come that allows no delay in the provision of effective counsel and final aid for the redemption of the Holy Land, which the Son of the Eternal Father is known to have consecrated with His precious blood, we beseech and implore you in the Lord Jesus Christ, and enjoin you for the remission of your sins, so that considering prudently that the cause of the Holy Land cannot be advanced more easily than by having the Christian people established in the serenity of peace and concord, you, setting aside all rancor which you have conceived against the Lombards for whatever reason until now, may induce our beloved son in Christ, Frederick, the Emperor of the Romans, by your earnest exhortations, that he, dispelling any disturbance which the presumption of the Lombards is known to have brought upon him, does not omit to place the business of the Lombard League, the March of Treviso, and Romagna precisely into the hands of the Church, according to the tenor of the imperial authority which we have received from the emperor himself, and sent under our seal enclosed to the rectors of the said league. Thus, with you providing the cause by which the tumult of discord may cease, abundant aid may arise from the province of Lombardy for the goods and people of the Holy Land, and your sincerity may lead to the reward of eternal retribution which the Creator of all has prepared for those who cherish peace. Given at Perugia, 28 July, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

Aug., Perusii.

To the provincial prior of the Order of Preachers in Germany. He who searches the reins and hearts knows how much the matter of the Holy Land presses upon us, as we aspire with all our desires towards its liberation. Therefore, wishing to have many girded by the glory of the cross for the bodily service of the army of Jesus Christ, we command you by the authority of these presents to appoint some brothers of your order, whom you consider suitable, in whose mouth the word of the Lord is not bound, according to the tenor of the letters we have sent you concerning this matter, to the duty of preaching for the cause of the cross. To encourage the faithful people to more willingly and fervently come to hear the word of the Lord, they shall grant, by our authority, a moderate indulgence of several days to all truly penitent and confessed who come to their solemn preaching, as they see fit.

And so that nothing is lacking for the execution of this office, we grant them the power by the authority of these presents to absolve, according to the form of the Church, those who have laid violent hands on clerics and incendiaries, as well as those excommunicated for not paying the tenth or twentieth assigned for the peace and faith and the business of the Holy Land. They may also absolve sacrilegious persons and those who visited the Holy Sepulchre against apostolic prohibition, as well as those who provided aid to the heretics in the regions of the Albigenses against the Catholics, and those who carried iron, arms, wood, and prohibited goods to the Saracens or otherwise gave them counsel, aid, and favor against Christians. They may reconcile penitents, those signed with the cross, and those who wish to take up the sign of the cross, and may convert other vows into a vow of this kind of piety by the authority of these presents; provided that those who are bound by the chain of excommunication for violent laying on of hands shall make adequate satisfaction to those they injured, and the incendiaries to those they harmed by fires, and the withholders of the twentieth and tenth shall render due satisfaction, and also those who carried the aforesaid to the Saracens shall satisfy according to the statute of the general council, unless the excess of the laying on of hands was so grave and enormous that they must be sent to the apostolic see. You shall faithfully inform us by your letters of the quantity of what you order to be deposited and consigned in certain places for the satisfaction of the aforesaid. Given at Perugia, on the Ides of May, in the ninth year.

Gregorius IX papa priori provinciali ordinis fratrum Predicatorum in Teutonia mandat ut fratres idoneos ad officium praedicationis pro negotio crucis deputet et indulgentias moderatas largiantur. Eosdem absolvere et reconciliare potestates praebet, sub conditionibus statutis. Datum Perusii, Idibus Maii, anno nono.

To all our faithful in the patrimony of Saint Peter established in Tuscany. Hearing about the dissensions and wars flourishing among you, the destruction of places, persecutions of churches, oppressions of the poor, captures of men, killings of men, injuries, violence, and robberies being committed in your regions, we are so gravely troubled by these reports that we can scarcely express it in words or explain it in writing. For, as we have learned, the wickedness of the perverse has increased so much in those regions that those, knowing that the cultivation of justice is peace, disturb the peace to inflict injuries, and without distinguishing between the sacred and the profane, they plunder both ecclesiastical and secular goods. Unless this is opposed, as their pride always rises, it will result in nearly irreparable harm to the entire province. Therefore, wishing to apply an appropriate remedy to this mortal plague, we strictly command by apostolic letters to all of you under the obligation of faithfulness, that since it is in the interest of public benefit to curb the audacity of these pestilent ones with due severity, you should gird yourselves powerfully and courageously against the robbers, plunderers, and thieves who are ravaging the province and whom we command to be expelled and excluded entirely from your borders, repressing their insolence in such a way that vengeance controls the excess and punishment deters the sinners from further sin. And because such misdeeds cannot occur without your connivance or assent, for which reason you may not reasonably be excused before God and men, we establish by the authority of these presents that wherever such acts are henceforth committed, the community of the land or the lord of the place where they are committed must in every way amend them from the goods of the community or the same place. Whoever has bought stolen or plundered goods must return them absolutely without any compensation given or to be given, but the buyer shall have his action against the seller, notwithstanding any contrary statute, confirmed oath, or other firm obligation. Moreover, so that all the aforementioned may be observed inviolably, we firmly command by our letters to our beloved son Roland, our subdeacon and chaplain, to compel you to observe them with both spiritual and temporal discipline, removing appeal. Given at Perugia, on the 4th of August, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa universis fidelibus per patrimonium beati Petri in Tuscia constitutis mandat ut contra raptores et fures provinciae pugnare debeant et eorum insolentiam reprimere, statuens ut domini locorum damna restituant et emptores res furtivas restituant. — Rolandum subdiaconum mandat ad observationem huiusmodi compellendum. 1235, Aug. 4, Perusii.

To the provost and chapter of Northhausen. Therefore, following the example of our aforementioned predecessor, we confirm by apostolic authority the process duly and providently held according to the apostolic mandate, and we strengthen it with the page of this present writing. Gregorius IX papa, preposito et capitulo Northlusensilf mandat, ut, secundum mandatum apostolicum predecessoris Honori, instituant prepositum cum collegio secularium canonicorum, sororibus in locis congruentibus collocatis; processus auctoritate apostolica confirmatur. 1235, Dec. 1. Viterbii.

To the Archbishop of Mainz, the Bishop of Hildesheim, and Master Conrad of Marburg, preacher of the word of God. 

A voice was heard in Ramah, a great weeping and lamentation, Rachel weeping, that is, the pious mother Church, for her children whom the devil slays and destroys, and she receives almost no consolation because the children, like vipers tearing at the entrails of their mother, attempt to kill her. For he, who from the beginning did not stand in truth but strives to turn truth into a lie so that he may spread the poison of his fraud more widely, works to lose pregnant souls, lest the offspring of faith, which they conceived from divine love, might come to the birth of a completed work.

Therefore, we, who are charged with caring for her fecundity, are as if cut by the sword of perfidious treachery, while in her entrails we are assailed by the venomous arrows of new error and confusion from the heretics who tear at her womb. To Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans, illustrious King of Jerusalem and Sicily. Having heard the series of letters in which you expressed your will to us regarding the Lombardy matter, we have decided to send certain noble Lombards, originating from Lombardy, through whom it may reach the Lombards that it is very opportune for them to return to your favor, and that they may blame themselves if any peril should befall them. Additionally, we have deemed it appropriate to dispatch our faithful, discreet, and prudent scribe, Master Peter, to our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Antioch, legate of the Apostolic See, and to the leaders of the Society of Lombardy. Gregorius IX papa Friderico, Romanorum imperatori, mandat ut magistrum Hospitalis Sanctae Mariae Teutonicorum ad sedem apostolicam mittat cum mandato sufficiente super quaestione inter ipsum et societatem Lombardiae, ad Kalendas Decembris, ad causam instruendam. To the archbishops and bishops, abbots, and other prelates of churches situated throughout Germany. A voice in Rama, that is, a thunder, recently resounded, which, as a lightning bolt reverberated in the sight of the strong and struck the hearing of the weak like thunder, because although the death of the saints is precious in the sight of the Lord, yet the Catholic mother church is more affected with sorrow by the removal of those sons, from whose battles and triumphs she rejoiced more greatly. It is no wonder if Rachel, the mild sheep seeing the true beginning, mourned over the death of those whom she called the sons of her sorrow, since Egypt, which sits in darkness and suffers from the lack of heavenly bread, wept for Jacob her father for seventy days during the time of her increasing famine. But the Israelite people lamented for Aaron for thirty days and the same for Moses, through whom they knew they were liberated from temporal servitude. The inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead, very brave men, having heard that King Saul and his sons had fallen before the Philistines, took the bodies of the dead from the city of the victors throughout the night and deserved to be blessed and loved by David for a week fasting during the burial rites, who, having torn his garments, likewise mourning over him with all his men, fasting until evening, also urged the sons of Israel to lament, not proposing other causes for tears but that he had provided them with some precious things for delight and ornament. Moreover, it is read that the same thing greatly pleased the people, while Abner followed the bier, weeping at the tomb that he had fallen before the sons of iniquity and lamented that he had not died like cowards do. In the New Testament, indeed, we read that fearsome men, who buried Stephen, did make great lamentation over him, who, although he was appointed for the work of common ministry, yet, being full of strength through the anointing of the spirit, defended the nascent church’s paucity against the multitude of the synagogue. Therefore, O prelates, why is it that as if you do not care for the losses of the flocks committed to you, you do not mourn for Master Conrad of Marburg, the bridegroom of the church, minister of light, cruelly slain by the sons of darkness? Whose tongue, like a dog of the Lord, frightened the grievous wolves? Today, who has shown more zeal for ecclesiastical freedom and the purity of both men, that he would pierce the Israelite with a Midianite woman with a dagger or strike down those sacrificing to idols? Was he not the minister of the true Moses, overthrowing worldly malice as another Jericho with the trumpets of priests, that any wise man, having recognized the menstruations and defects of this moon, would rather seek and have the perpetuity of true justice of the sun? Did he not show us another Mordecai, who turns into bitterness, because he received much bitterness from the contempt of Haman, rejoicing to unite Esther, that is, the church generated by the Gospel of the brother Christ, to Ahasuerus, that is, to blessedness, firmly accusing the eunuchs, the heretics superficially exposed to a long and secure lust for harming, who were also plotting the destruction of the king of glory, whom he had made to be hanged on the gallows, wishing them to perish by solemn torment when openly convicted of depravity, and thus exposed himself for the liberation of his people, Haman, which means iniquity, not even in the moment of crisis did he bend down? Therefore, lest, as the scripture says, men of mercy, for there is none who meditates, be removed from the midst, and since you do not pursue such a crime with all your heart, something similar may be attributed to you, when even Antiochus, otherwise wicked and impious, was moved to tears and anger at the death of Onias, a sober and modest man, removed the murderer from his purple and ordered him to be executed, and you, sons of Israel, priests of the Lord and kings of faithful souls, should have been girded with the swords of Simeon and Levi for the revenge of his death and the raising up of the matter for the extirpation of heresies, strengthening of the Catholic faith, and ecclesiastical sanctions, burst forth with trumpets, proceed with warlike vessels, or with Maccabeus, searching through all the hiding places of their perversity and confidence, and should have condemned the impious by rightful judgment. Because, although we cannot proceed with due severity against the aforementioned men of blood, rebels of light, deserter sons, who, what was horrible to relate and astonishing to hear, dared to seize the aforementioned Master Conrad, a man of consummate virtue and herald of the Christian faith

To all faithful of our Lord Jesus Christ established throughout the kingdom of France, to whom these letters shall come. Rachel, seeing the beginning of her offspring in true faith, the holy Roman Church, a pious mother of sons of the right hand, whose great sorrow is like the sea due to the massacre of her children, has issued and continues to issue a voice of lamentation, weeping, and mourning. We desire this to be heard on high so that through day and night the eyes of the faithful, pouring tears of grief, may not be silent and may not rest until the Lord shows mercy. She laments because the house of the heavenly bread, Mount Zion, from which the law went forth, the city of the great king, has lost the strength and beauty of the kingdom. She weeps because it, once free, has fallen under the yoke of impious tyranny. She mourns because, where the multitude of heavenly soldiers once sang peace, there now the oppression of the most unclean nations has provoked scandals, enmities, and schisms; and, renewing the beginnings of wars, it has sent its hand against the desirable places, casting out the laws of sacred orders and the very laws of nature from the temple of the Lord, introducing various impurities and abominations. Hence, Jerusalem, derided in her sabbaths, has become despised as polluted with menstruation among her enemies.

Although our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans, illustrious King of Jerusalem and Sicily, has restored the same city except for the temple of the Lord, because almighty God did not choose to act more magnificently with the Christian people at that time, the aforementioned emperor entered into a truce with the sultan, the term of which is so near that the intervening time is scarcely believed sufficient for preparation, unless promptness, hope, and fervor of faith hasten to every necessity. Therefore, let no one shrink from journeying to its aid and fighting for the homeland with hope of victory, dying for life, suffering harsh and sad things for him who, despising shame, suffered to be spat upon, beaten with blows, afflicted with scourges, crowned with thorns, presented to Pilate as if guilty of many crimes, and ultimately crucified, offered vinegar, pierced by a lance, he cried out with a loud voice, gave up his spirit for the restoration of human condition, completed the course of present life, satisfied with injuries.

He, to repeat from the beginning, is the one who from the father's throne of glory wondrously inclined the heavens and descended to the depths of our mortality, who did not disdain to become God-man, creator to become creature, lord to take the form of a servant, so that we, who could not hope for pardon through our righteousness, might, by this unheard-of grace, become heirs of God, coheirs of Christ, partake in the consortium of divinity, and share eternal felicity. And although we, adopted through grace, daily accumulate causes of ingratitude, yet he abounds in the riches of goodness, granting different ways of satisfaction for transgressors according to the diversity of wills, powers, and faculties, raising various remedies for the sick, as long as he permits the land, in which he willed to be born, die, and rise again, to be held by infidels for the exercise of the faithful, since the hand of the Lord is not shortened nor his power diminished in any way, that he cannot at once liberate it, as he made all things from nothing. But he seeks from man those causes of compassion and love, by which he first chose to assist fallen and condemned man, showing the end of all perfection and the fullness of the law, who would not have allowed impious hands to be so strengthened against the pious, unless he had foreseen the vindication of his injury from our confusion and the preservation of our discipline from his victory.

Under this occasion, many indeed, unable to satisfy for the measure of their crimes in any other way, as if utterly despaired in the depth of evils, would have perished, had this plank not occurred to them, had they not quickly accomplished by this short path the spaces of many times by the sacrifice of their souls for Christ. Many, also desiring to find the place where the feet of the Lord stood, reached the reward without a course, or later to the crown without a sword, with him rewarding his soldier, who considers only the will in what is offered. But so that the faithful may be effectively and powerfully cleansed for the aforementioned things, we, trusting in the mercy of almighty God and the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, from that power of binding and loosing which God granted to us, though unworthy, grant full pardon of their sins to all those who undertake this labor in their own persons and expenses, of which they have truly repented in heart

To Frederick, Emperor of the Romans, etc. A certain nephew of the king of Tunis, having opened the eyes of his understanding to the recognition of truth with the collyrium of the word of God, was approaching our presence to receive the sacrament of baptism. Regesto:

Gregorius IX papa archiepiscopo Salzburgensi mandat, ut ad subventionem ecclesiae apparatu strenuo se communiat, et Martio proximo cum decenti militia personaliter veniat, vel militiam mittat, quae per tres menses in expensis suis commoretur. 1234, Nov. 25, Perusii.

**Translation to English:**

To the preceptor and brothers of the Hospital of Saint Mary of the Teutons in Jerusalem, in Acre. According to the form of the agreement made concerning the business of the Holy Land, which we are sending to you under our seal, we have decided to provide that our beloved son, the noble man, the Prince of Antioch, appointed as bailiff with the authority of our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, Emperor of the Romans, etc., having taken the oath according to the custom of the kingdom and having been received by the people of the same kingdom, shall hold all the rights and holdings of the Kingdom of Jerusalem pertaining to the king, with the city of Tyre, except for its castle. This castle, by our command and through your beloved master, will be held and preserved by your house for the benefit and honor of the emperor and his son Conrad, and for the preservation of the good state of the said kingdom and the indemnity, as far as possible, of any Christian in the kingdom; which this master not only promised verbally but also through his letters in our presence, and a brother of your order, whom he will place in charge of the castle's custody, will promise to observe these things through his order in word of truth. However, since we desire to add your letters to this as a precaution, we command your entire community to grant them without hindrance, and to diligently strive to fulfill what we have ordered to be done by the aforementioned master, since he cannot personally attend, with attentive effort; our mandate, etc., as above. Given at Viterbo, the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, in the ninth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa preceptori et fratribus hospitalis sancte Marie Teutonicorum in Accon mandat, ut sub bulla formam compositionis super negotio Terre Sancte mittentes, universitas eorum sine difficultate litteras concedat et premissa diligentissime perficiat. 1235, Feb. 19. Viterbii.

**Translation to English:**

To the Rectors of the Lombard League.

The great desire we have long harbored for the peace and tranquility of the Lombards has prompted us to repeatedly send letters to you, concerning a beneficial agreement between them and our dearly beloved son in Christ, Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans, and illustrious King of Jerusalem and Sicily. In our last letters, we recalled that since the Emperor entrusted the affairs of Lombardy, the March of Treviso, and Romagna to the provision, settlement, and regulation of the Church, you were to send trustworthy and honest men, who had full authority on behalf of the Lombard League to negotiate peace and concord with the said Emperor in our presence. Indeed, as devoted sons, you have commendably fulfilled this and the matters entrusted to the envoys have been diligently reported by them in our presence. Among these, it was chiefly requested if the said Emperor would place both the complaints the Lombards propose they have against him and his own grievances in the hands of the Church. Eventually, with the passing of the same envoys as the Lord willed, we have sought to inform ourselves of the Emperor's will concerning this matter. As a Catholic prince and eager to bring about actions that could restore the Church and Empire to the joy of peace, he has entrusted the matter concerning himself and the Lombards—both regarding the detention of royal rights and his own, the past offenses committed by the Lombards against him and the Empire, as well as anything known to have been done by him to the detriment and injury of the Lombards, or generally anything from which discord between them has arisen—to the counsel, provision, settlement, and decree of the Church, with letters patent sealed with a golden bull, promising to uphold and confirm what the Church decides on these matters, or even what will be decided concerning mutual guarantees, as you will be fully informed from the enclosed transcript. Since the province of Lombardy, long embroiled in the storm of discord, with more harm having arisen from it than can be easily documented, must be restored to a state of peace and concord by the Church in these days, especially when we are urged by many cries from the Holy Land to bring swift assistance to its pitiable state, and since this can be more easily procured the more the world is freed from the waves of wars and discord, we have deemed it necessary that everywhere professors of the Christian faith be brought back to a state of peace and concord, compelling them by ecclesiastical censure if necessary. We firmly command by apostolic writings to your discretion that, considering with prudent meditation how fitting and beneficial it is that the right hand of the aforementioned Emperor—whom the wisdom of God has provided as a defender of the Church—be strengthened with victorious might against the oppressors of ecclesiastical liberty, and that the aforementioned land so much more needs to be helped by the aid of Lombardy, as it is seen to be rich in resources and proven to be strengthened by a multitude of the robust, you should induce the hearts of the Lombard League more earnestly toward the love of peace and concord, firmly holding that, as we consider the same Lombards special sons of the Church, we will not suffer that any injury or loss be inflicted upon them by anyone, and we will take effective care to procure for them, with the help of the Lord, the fullness of security from the aforementioned Emperor and our beloved son, the noble man Henry his son, and the princes of Germany. For the diligent and speedy execution of these matters, we have decided to send to you our beloved son I., our chaplain, esteemed by us and our brothers for his evident merit and integrity, whom or rather us in him you should honorably treat, diligently attend to him, and give full faith to what he reports to you on our behalf, taking care and making efforts that if the aforementioned Lombards wish to place all the above matters precisely in the hands of the Church, as the said Emperor has placed himself, you should declare this to us within a month of the receipt of these presents, through letters patent sealed with your seals and those of the cities of the same league, whose tenor should be similar to the aforementioned transcript, sending us the aforementioned letters of the Lombards through the same chaplain. 

Given at Perugia, VI Kalends of November, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa rectoribus societatis Lombardie mandat, ut ad pacem et concordiam cum Friderico II, imperatore Romano et rege Ierusalem et Sicilie, prosequendam, legatos mittant plenis mandatis instructos. 1234, Oct. 27, Perusii.

**Translation to English:**

To the archbishops and bishops, abbots, and other prelates of the churches, and to all the faithful of Christ established in Carneola, Istria, Dalmatia, Bosnia, Croatia, Serbia, and other parts of Slavonia. Deuteronomy 28:35. Reflecting very intently on the miseries and calamities, the anxieties and oppressions, with which the whole body of the Church is miserably shaken and troubled from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, we are affected with great sorrow of heart, and we are more troubled, since we are especially obliged to imitate the footsteps of him who was weak with the weak brothers and burned with others who were scandalized.

For the excesses of an age nearing its end have ensnared the misery of the human condition with so many snares of errors, stained it with so many contagions of adversities, that many, despising the bounds of Zion, ascend the heights of Samaria, lining their walls with the bitumen of the doctrines of heretical depravity, Amos 6:4, not fearing to incur that curse: "Woe to those who despise Zion and trust in the mountain of Samaria," saying, "We have no part in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse." And although the word of God has thundered into all the earth, with the heavens declaring its glory, and it is still poured out by the bishops of places and other workers of the householder, the rain of evangelical truth, yet as the eminent doctor of the Church professes at the rise of the growing Church: "There must be heresies, that those who are approved may be made manifest," at present many are weighed down by the burden of sins and their heart is darkened, Ezekiel 2:5, so that they do not redirect the paths they follow to righteousness, but instead, like a house provoking and transgressing the law of Christ, they foolishly leap forth to the bitterness of doctrine.

As has been reported to our ears, so great has grown the abundance of the faithless in Bosnia and neighboring provinces, that now the whole land mourns and languishes as if deserted and untraveled, filled with thorns, Psalms 80, and nettles, and has become a den of dragons and a pasture of ostriches. Therefore, zeal for souls consumes us, wishing to be weak with the weak and to apply paternal counsel, by which medicine may be provided for wounds, that the swelling wound may receive care as much as is within us: behold, we have decided to send our beloved son, the prior of the monastery of Saint Bartholomew of Trisulti, of the Carthusian order, indeed a man according to our heart, a friend of God, powerful in deed and word, who, imitating the poverty of the impoverished Christ in a despised habit and burning spirit, does not fear to approach to liberate souls deceived by diabolic fraud, to those parts, having fully granted him the office of legation, that with the Lord's help, as a diligent cultivator of the Lord's field, he may uproot and destroy, scatter and disperse, build and plant, as the Lord has given him.

Therefore, we attentively advise and exhort in the Lord, by apostolic writings commanding you to diligently receive the aforementioned prior as a legate of the Apostolic See, indeed as our person in him, treating him kindly and honorably, attending with eager minds to his salutary advices and commands, and firmly holding and observing whatever he decrees among you as sons of devotion, concerning whose prudent discretion we possess that confidence, that with the Lord directing his steps, he will bring back sheaves of eternal fruits with exultation from the scattered seed. Otherwise, we will ratify and, with God's help, inviolably observe the sentence which he rightly pronounces against the rebels; notwithstanding that some of you are exempt. Moreover, so that nothing at all is lacking for pursuing such a holy task, we grant to all Catholics, who, having been admonished by the same prior, take up the character of the cross for the extermination of heretics, the same indulgence and privilege that is granted to those going to the aid of the Holy Land. Given at the Lateran, the Ides of February, in the seventh year.

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa universis Christi fidelibus in Carneola, Istria, Dalmatia, Bosna, Cruacia, Servia et aliis partibus Sclavonie mandat, ut priorem monasterii sancti Bartholomei de Trisulto, legatum ad exterminium hereticorum, recipiant et eius mandatis obediant, concessis crucis privilegia. 1233, Feb. 13. Laterani.

**Translation to English:**

To the podestà and people of Bretenoriont,

The Mediator between God and men, Jesus Christ, who, in order to unite us with our Creator and restore peace between God and man, did not disdain to take on human form within the inviolate womb of a virgin, we are bound, as far as we can, to imitate His footsteps. As His vicars, both in name and deed, we strive with utmost desire to bring discordant people to concord and to uproot dissentions and schisms from the Church of God as much as He permits us, for the celestial granary does not receive any grain that has not purged itself of the tares of hatred. And just as one cannot reach one's destination without a path, so the ascent to the heavenly homeland is not possible without the way that charity provides.

You have indeed heard that the Lord did not regard Cain's offerings, who harbored hatred for his brother. From this, you can conclude that he could not have God appeased, whom the flame of fraternal hatred was internally consuming. It has come to our attention that there is a matter of discord between you, the people of Ravenna, Forlì, Rimini, and Forlimpopoli on one side, and the people of Faenza, Cesena, Urbino, and Cervia on the other, leading to wars and battles among you. You do not consider that, although you intend to pursue the rights of your city, in persecuting your neighbor, you offend God and easily incur the peril of your souls, because it is necessary that fraternal charity is in a way extinguished among those who act contentiously against each other.

However, to prevent the aid to the Holy Land from being delayed or impeded, we recently, with the counsel of our brothers, decided that Christian princes and peoples should observe peace among themselves for at least four years, and that those at discord should be compelled by the prelates of the churches to observe peace or a truce inviolably through sentences of excommunication and interdict. And given that we are bound to procure peace throughout the whole world if it is granted from above: behold, we have decided to send to you our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Antioch, a great member of the Church of God, a man endowed with great honor, duly accepted by us and our brothers for his merit, probity, and devotion. Through apostolic writings, we command you to strive to comply with his mandates and admonitions regarding the re-establishment of peace or the establishment of truces among you and the aforementioned others, or concerning the observance of law in this matter, so that by means of this you may have God propitious and be able to avert the detriment of your souls. Otherwise, the sentence that he shall duly impose on the rebellious for this reason, we will ratify and, with the Lord's help, firmly enforce.

Given at Perugia, VI Nones of March, in the eighth year.

In the same manner to the podestà and people of Cervia and to the podestà and people of Forlimpopoli.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa potestati et populo Bretenoriont mandat ut, per mandata patriarchae Antiocheni, pacem vel treugas cum civitatibus Ravennatibus, Foroliviensibus, Ariminensibus, Foropopuliensibus ex una parte, et Faventinis, Cesenatibus, Urbinatibus, Cerviensibus ex altera parte, reformare studeant. 1234, Mart. 2, Perusii.

Translation to English:

To the noble man R. de Supino, a crusader, rector of the Duchy of Spoleto. When, by the disposition of divine counsel, you not only left your land but also devotedly put your own person at risk and took up the sign of the cross from our hands for the aid of the Holy Land, and later, due to the urgent necessity of the Roman Empire being in great peril, you were advised by us to change this vow in aid of the same empire. And now, as a devoted son of the Church who cannot bear the injuries inflicted by the people of Viterbo upon your mother Church, you have voluntarily offered yourself to crush their arrogance: we commend in the Lord the fervor of your zeal with worthy praises and follow it with acts of gratitude, granting you full remission of your sins, of which you are truly contrite in heart and confessed with your mouth, and granting a similar indulgence to all who, like you, sincerely repent and confess, and who die while collaborating with you in this service to the bride of Christ. Given at the Lateran, on the 17th day before the Kalends of February, in the eleventh year.

Regesto in Latin:

Gregorius IX papa nobili viro R. de Supino, rectori ducatus Spoletani, plenam peccaminum veniam indulget, qui in obsequio sponse Christi adversus Viterbienses se obtulit. 1238, Jan. 16. Laterani.

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans, illustrious King of Jerusalem and Sicily. Having diligently listened to what our beloved sons, the Master of the Hospital of St. Mary of the Teutons and Master P. de Vinea, have conveyed on behalf of your majesty before us and our brothers, we have deemed it appropriate, as we consider you a special son of the Church among the princes of the land and cherish the advancement of your prosperity, to support your and the empire's justice. Therefore, we have decided to send our venerable brother, the Bishop of Ostia, and our beloved son, Th. Cardinal Priest of the title of St. Sabina, to Lombardy with the full office of legation. We carry in our heart that whatever false claims may be whispered into your ears by the tongues of detractors, it should be evident through the effect of their works that the Mother Church does not neglect, at opportune times, to secure your honors according to God. Let your serenity therefore ensure that you conduct yourself towards her as a devoted son, so that you may rightly gain God's favor and receive the desired abundance of graces from the Church. Given at Viterbo, 10th day before the Kalends of June, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico, Romanorum imperatori, mandat ut, ob fidelitatem suam erga ecclesiam, episcopum Ostiensem et Th. tituli Sancte Sabine presbyterum cardinalem in Lombardiam cum plene legationis officio mittat ad fovendam iustitiam imperii. 1237, Mai. 23, Viterbii.

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans, illustrious King of Jerusalem and Sicily. We have kindly received your messenger, the beloved son Master Roger, canon of Salerno, who came to the Apostolic See, and we have diligently understood both what he wished to propose to us in person and what your letters contained. However, when it previously came to our knowledge that your imperial majesty intended to direct your actions toward Lombardy, we, desiring to send someone who seeks only what pleases God and promotes peace and concord without any favoritism, decided, with the counsel of our brothers, to send our venerable brother, the Bishop of Palestrina, to the regions of Lombardy. You can firmly trust him because he has renounced everything for the sake of God and dedicated himself entirely to His service, and he will only proceed with actions that can support the honor of the Church and the empire, as you will be able to clearly see from his deeds. If others suggest otherwise, let your imperial excellence disregard them. Finally, having received your letters, we could not comply with your request to send our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Antioch, to those regions for the aforementioned reasons. Furthermore, as it is believed to be greatly beneficial to your honor that our beloved son, the Master of the Hospital of St. Mary of the Teutons of Jerusalem, precedes your arrival, we earnestly urge and exhort your excellence to instruct the Master to hasten his journey and not delay coming to our presence, so that you may immediately send him to discuss with us matters concerning the honor of the Church and the empire. We believe that if our counsel is followed, with God's help, we can arrange things in such a way that, with the enemies of peace confounded, the concord between the Church and the empire may be restored and maintained indissolubly. Given at Terni, on the 10th of June, in the tenth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Friderico, Romanorum imperatori, mandat ut magistrum Hospitalis sancte Marie Teutonicorum Ierosolimitane ad sedem apostolicam mittat ad tractandum de honore ecclesie et imperii conferenda. 1236, Iun. 10, Interamna.

To the bishops of Minden, Lübeck, and Ratzeburg. Your letters presented to us contained that a long lamentation was heard, that some violent and impious people, called the Scythians, were raised by the devil in the province of Bremen. Having abandoned the light of true illumination and enveloped in the darkness of despicable blindness, neither fearing God nor respecting man, and completely devaluing the teachings of Mother Church, they trample on its freedom. Acting more cruelly than wild beasts, they spare no sex or age, shedding blood like water, wickedly tearing clerics and religious people limb from limb and affixing some to the wall in the manner of a cross in scorn of the Crucified. To ensure that each of their transgressions surpasses their previous transgressions, and that the faithless outdo their perfidy, they abuse the patience of God by handling the food of our salvation, by which life is given to the living, more horrifically than can be expressed. They seek responses from demons, make wax effigies, and consult erroneous witches in their filth, committing many other works of darkness that are not only shocking to those who recount them but also to those who hear them. We, observing that such detestable beginnings must be quickly countered by the powerful right hand, gave you orders in our letters and imposed in remission of sins that, having assumed the office of holy preaching, you diligently and effectively induce the faithful in the dioceses of Paderbo

To Master Conrad of Marburg, preacher of the Word of God. Oh, the judgments and unsearchable ways of God! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been His counselor? As our wounds have now festered before Him, as our iniquities have risen above our heads, as the charity of many has grown cold and iniquity abounds, the misery of the human condition suffers to be ensnared in the snares of so many errors, to be stained by the contagions of so many adversities, many, having despised the borders of Zion, ascend the high places of Samaria, smearing their walls with the bitumen of heretical depravity, not fearing to incur the curse: “Woe to those who despise Zion and trust in the high places of Samaria,” saying: “We have no part in the house of David nor inheritance in the son of Jesse.” However, the author and giver of all good things, knowing that all things work together for good for those who love Him, not to acquire knowledge through experience, since He has known and foreseen all things from eternity, but to make us more certain of our virtue or infirmity and to give a fuller understanding of who are His, predicted that false Christs and false prophets would arise around the evening of the world and the decline of time, as the distinguished teacher professes: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest.” Indeed, upon receiving with our usual kindness the letters of our venerable brothers, the archbishop of Mainz and the bishop of Hildesheim, as well as yours, filled with great grief and not empty of immense sorrow, concerning the abominations of certain heretics exhibited to us, our heart languished with astonishment, our soul was greatly troubled, we were inebriated with bitterness, and our mind was filled with acrimony.
