To the noble man, Count of Toulouse, the spirit of sound counsel. It was previously brought to the attention of the Apostolic See that in the regions of the Albigenses, the vineyard of the Lord was filled with thorns and nettles, and that the King of Babylon, coming into the land of Judah, had despoiled the temple of the Lord of the golden vessels of the Catholic faith. Innocent and Honorius, our predecessors of blessed memory, sent there cultivators who would root out these pestilent weeds with the plow of preaching, and King Louis of France of illustrious memory and others from his kingdom marked with the sign of the cross, who would cleanse the sanctuary of the temple of the filth of contamination with the sword of justice, hoping that there the bunch of the Catholic faith would burst forth to be pressed into the chalice of the Lord, and that once Jerusalem was cleansed, it would rejoice receiving the poor king sitting on a donkey’s colt with palms and flowers. Yet, our said predecessors, laboring much for this, could not succeed, and it was believed that their efforts were voided due to our sins. We, considering that everything is overcome by strenuous labor and that Pharaoh is softened to liberate Israel only after being struck by many plagues, undertook the burden of this task upon our shoulders and decided to send our venerable brother, the Bishop of Porto, then Cardinal Deacon of Saint Angel, to those regions with the office of legation committed to him. He, by the favor of Him who precedes good works by inspiring and follows by helping, restrained the jaws of those who tore the seamless tunic of Christ, intercepted the young foxes that were destroying the Lord’s vineyard, and, in order that the Catholic faith might be fully restored to its former state, having reformed peace between the church and our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King of France on one side and you on the other, he issued several statutes at a council held for this purpose in Toulouse, and arranged for the study of sacred scripture and other arts to be more forcefully organized in Toulouse to confute heresy. But since the unclean spirit is trying again to enter the house from which it had been driven, now swept clean, and Pharaoh is again attempting to subjugate the liberated Hebrews, after his departure, we decided to commit the office of legation to our venerable brothers, first the Bishop of Tournai and then the Archbishop of Vienne, legates of the Apostolic See, so that watching the watches of the night over the flock of the Catholics, they might restrain the wolves from the Lord’s sheepfold. To Frederick, Emperor of the Romans, ever august, illustrious King of Jerusalem and Sicily. The Mediator between God and men, God-man Christ Jesus, humbled heaven to earth so that earth might be elevated to heaven, and in the line of His peculiar inheritance, restored the bonds of peace between both, and being the clasp of concord, united God with man, preserving the rights of both natures. Indeed, since we hold His place on earth, unworthy though we are, for His vicar fulfills His duties, if not as much as he wishes and should, at least as much as he can and is permitted, we must remove scandals from that land, as from the kingdom of the Lord, and sow seeds of peace.

Thus, a certain concord has been achieved in our presence, with our mediation, between the beloved son, the master of the Teutonic Order, on your behalf and that of your son Conrad on one side, and the esteemed sons Henry of Nazareth and Philip of Trecis, knights of Acre, on behalf of the nobles and citizens of Acre and others of the Kingdom of Jerusalem on the other side, occasioned by the discord arisen, namely that they will fully restore you and your son Conrad to all rights of the aforesaid kingdom, both in possession and ownership, to the status before the discord, and they will obey the bailiffs you appoint in your name and that of your son, in arranging fortifications and officials, and in collecting revenues and other rights known to belong to the king by ancient and established custom in that kingdom, saving the assizes and also the ancient and approved customs of the aforesaid kingdom.

Furthermore, they will dissolve the commune, remove the bell, dismiss the consuls and captains appointed after the discord, and nonetheless, they will again swear oaths of fidelity to you and your said son. Moreover, Richard Filangerius, marshal, will be restored to the office of bailiff, provided that to avoid suspicion between him and those of the land, another unsuspected person will manage until the end of September of the coming year, to be appointed by the marshal himself with the counsel of the constable of Acre. After that, the prince of Antioch, appointed as bailiff by your authority, who will swear according to the custom of the kingdom and the men of the kingdom to him, will hold all rights and possessions of the Kingdom of Jerusalem pertaining to the king, with the city of Tyre, except the castle of Tyre, which will be held and preserved by said master and his house for your benefit and honor and that of your aforesaid son, and for the preservation of the good state of the aforesaid kingdom and the indemnity, as far as possible, of every Christian in the kingdom; which the master promised not only verbally but also by his letters in our presence, and his brother of the order, whom the master will appoint for the custody of the castle, will promise by his order in the word of truth to keep these, and we wish to add the letters of the convent for caution. But if the aforesaid prince could not or perhaps would not receive the office of bailiff, or were not in existence, it is provided from now that the aforementioned constable of Acre be appointed bailiff by your authority, as described above concerning the prince. However, if the bailiff is to be removed due to infirmity, bad administration, or some just cause, you will appoint another person, not suspected, from the liegemen of the kingdom, and this will be observed until the legitimate age of the aforementioned Conrad according to the custom of the aforesaid kingdom.

Further, you will recall universally each and every, singularly and collectively, both clerics and laymen, nobles, citizens of Acre and others of the aforesaid kingdom into the fullness of your grace. Specifically, you will provide full security in the kingdom to John of Ibelin, his sons and supporters, and generally to all residing or coming into the aforesaid kingdom, merchants or any others, except that you should not grant any security to said John of Ibelin, his sons and nephews, namely John of Cesarea and the other John of Ibelin, outside the Kingdom of Jerusalem. However, if you have any personal quarrel against said John and his and any others residing in that kingdom, you will demand justice through the judgment of the kingdom, observing the customs and assizes of the land.

To Louis, the illustrious King of France. The King, who rules the eternal dominion of the kingdom, who raised the Church upon the foundation of the Catholic faith, excites the kings of the earth to the service of this Church by His admonitions and invites the princes of the world to its devotion by many examples. He commands that Church to be honored by mortals, for which He, immortal, did not fear to take the form of a servant and endure the cross and the torment of death, exalting him who provides service to His ministers and perpetuating his kingdom by His mercy, who favors the vows of His spouse in due time. 

Indeed, dearly beloved son, you can evidently gather this from your ancestors, and especially from the illustrious memory of Charlemagne, diligently observing how Charlemagne, obedient to the Roman Pontiff, the vicar of Jesus Christ and successor of Saint Peter, to whom the Lord committed the rights of earthly and celestial empire, exposed himself to many labors and hardships for the defense of the Church, and how much honor, praise, and glory he thereby obtained. But perhaps you have not come to know that the same Charlemagne, gathering a great army of warriors against the Church's persecutors, often triumphed magnificently over them; and when the Emperor of Constantinople neglected to defend ecclesiastical liberty, the Church, having received power from the Lord of both spiritual and material swords, so that she might wield one and command the other to be wielded, conferred the empire on Charlemagne, who not only restrained the violators of the Church’s liberties but also those who disturbed ecclesiastical matters by his strength, and adorned him with immense titles of glory, continuing in his person the grace that Pope Zachary had formerly extended to his father Pepin, whom he had exalted to the throne of the Franks. Therefore, Charlemagne, desiring to honor the Church from which he had received all honor, decreed by perpetual law that all subjected to its jurisdiction should inviolably observe the statute promulgated by Emperor Theodosius for the liberty of the Church, namely, that: "whoever has a dispute, whether petitioner or at the beginning of the dispute or during its course, whether when the matter is pleaded or when the judgment is already being pronounced, if he chooses the judgment of the bishop of the Holy See, let him be directed to the judgment of the bishops, without any doubt, even if the other party objects; and all cases which are treated according to civil or even praetorian law shall be settled by the judgment of bishops and obtain the perpetual force of firmness, and a matter settled by their judgment shall not be retried by anyone." From this, you can clearly perceive how unjust and absurd it would seem if the honor of the Church, known to be endowed with such a great privilege of freedom, should be diminished in those immunities which are known to be much less than the aforementioned, in your time. 

Moreover, the other successors of the same Charlemagne, your ancestors, considering the exaltation of churches as their own through similar example, appointed themselves defenders of the Christian faith and of the mother Church, and, diligently observing that they could render nothing similar to God, who had exalted them with the glory of the kingdom, they nevertheless showed themselves free from the vice of ingratitude by endowing the churches with many resources, granting them immense liberties, or rather preserving in due freedom the one from whom they had received all power, deeming it unworthy that the place where the divine name is worshiped, where Christ is immolated on the altar as a host for the redemption of our sins, should be subjected to any burdens of servitude, since it is to be honored beyond human understanding. 

Therefore, if the offspring of the vine preserves the nature of its origin, if the same sap vivifies the branches and the root, it is scarcely believed that you, who are equaled to them in the honor of dominion, should allow yourself to be found contrary to them in morals and inferior in virtuous acts. Indeed, it is hoped that the grace of goodness, which was innate in them, having descended to your person, will permit you to do nothing that could in any way derogate from the liberty and honor of the Roman Church and its members, since the taste of the fountains granted to the origin cannot be denied to the streams derived from it. But lo, we have heard and are grieved that you, dearly beloved son, and the barons of the kingdom, following the counsel of evil men, desire to reduce the Church, which regenerated you from the womb of sanctification into sons and continuously offers the spotless lamb to God the Father for your salvation, into servitude, as if you no longer wish to be called free sons but rather slaves, miserably attempting to enslave the spouse of the eternal King, who has freed you from perpetual servitude. **Translation to English:**

To the patriarchs of Aquileia and Grado, the archbishops of Milan, Ravenna, and Genoa, and their suffragans, as well as to the bishops, abbots, deans, archdeacons, archpriests, and other prelates of churches established throughout Lombardy, the March of Treviso, and Romagna. The Lord Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and men, who, while on earth for the salvation of the human race, revived the multitude of peoples through innumerable acts of mercy, with inexpressible piety provided that, upon His return to the Father's glory, since the prince of darkness was poised to trouble those reborn from the font of baptism with many temptations, He would leave a vicar on earth, endowed with singular power and a wealth of remedies. Through the vigilant care of this vicar and others whom the apostolic dignity elevates, peace would come to the world and full potential for reaching the homeland of heaven would be achieved. Now, sitting at the right hand of majesty, He grants through those appointed by divine disposition to the service of the most excellent bride, namely the Holy Mother Church, that the doctrine of virtues may become amiable to all the faithful, that peace may come to them, and that they may be drawn to desire the rewards of the celestial. Therefore, since the province of Lombardy, to our sorrow, has long been in the peril of discord, and it is known that more dangers have occurred than would be appropriate to explain in writing, we, as we confidently believe through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, who gave the apostles the power to guide the world to the glory of salvation, have duly provided to send to that province two of the Church’s most worthy members, namely our venerable brother, the Bishop of Ostia, and our beloved son Th., cardinal priest of the Title of St. Sabina, whose public commendations we deem superfluous, granting them the full office of legation in Lombardy, the March of Treviso, Romagna, and parts of Venetia. We hope that, as they are known to be abundantly endowed with divine wisdom and virtues, they may more easily and successfully accomplish matters of salvation and grace. We therefore beseech your entire community and exhort you in the Lord Jesus Christ by apostolic writings, to demonstrate by works of gratitude how great is your purity of faith towards God and sincere devotion towards the Apostolic See, to be elevated with continuous honors by the multitude of the faithful. Devotedly and joyfully admit these legates, in whose person we wish to be represented and treated with filial reverence, as angels of peace, and diligently and carefully seek to honor them in every way you know and can. Attend earnestly to matters which contribute to the honor of God and the Church, and to the increase of ecclesiastical liberty, as well as to those by which the state of the empire, and especially the said province, may be healthily reformed by the Lord’s doing, and to the obliteration of the stain of heretical depravity, and the affairs of the Holy Land, which we have entrusted to them with special concern, as we are regarded as more responsible than others for its promotion. Know that through this you acquire the grace of heavenly blessing and obligate us to you not slightly for a worthy reward. Otherwise, the sentence they pass on the rebellious, we will consider valid and, with God's help, ensure it is inviolably observed. Given at Interamna, November 29, in the tenth year. In the same manner to the marquises, counts, podestàs, councils, and communities established throughout Lombardy, the March of Treviso, and Romagna.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa patriarchis Aquilegensi et Gradensit, archiepiscopis Mediolanensi, Ravenatiensi et Ianuensi, eorumque suffraganeis, episcopis, abbatibus, decanis, archidiaconis, archipresbyteris, et aliis ecclesiarum prelatis per Lombardiam, marchiam Tervisinam et Romaniolam constitutis mandat, ut legatos suos, episcopum Ostiensem et cardinalem tituli Sanctae Sabinae, diligenter honorent et eis in omnibus quae pertinent ad honorem Dei, ecclesiae libertatem, et reformationem provinciae salubriter assint. 1236, Nov. 29, Interamna.

To Frederick, Emperor of the Romans, etc. If the memory of the benefits of the eternal creator, which have flowed abundantly through the ministry of His spouse into both the exalted and the humble, were not erased by human ingratitude, if our Lord Jesus Christ, the judge of the living and the dead, about to judge with the books of conscience opened and the works of darkness revealed, so that He may be feared as Lord, the origin of virtues, faith would persist unshaken, the works would be weighed in the balance of justice: then words would be sealed under the sign of truth, and the mouth would not speak against God in heaven, from where thunders issue and God often sends lightning against His persecutors and as the Lord of vengeance. Indeed, from several letters recently sent to us and our brothers by your imperial excellence, we have gathered many things which, if styled more humbly and the bitterness of the page had been sweetened by the feeling of filial reverence, the virtue of discretion under the manna of sweetness would have tempered the irascible spirit, and the image of God, reflected in the mirror of reason, and His likeness, found in the natural powers of the soul through good affection and zeal for righteousness, might not have been deformed perhaps by writing in this way. But among other parts of your letter, which declares the process of our venerable brother the Bishop of Palestrina, the legate of the Apostolic See, as detestable and enormous, and writes that we do not lack the initiative or at least participation in the fault imputed to him, it does not follow the rule of justice and detests truth justified in its works. For as the Apostolic See is bound to reduce the schisms' divisions to the integrity of unity, following the example of the mediator between God and men, who did not disdain to take on human form to restore peace between God and man, our service to God and man compelled us to send a legate to Lombardy to settle the discord between the empire and the Lombards, so that he might bring back those reconciled to the imperial mandate and reform treaties of peace among the discordant peoples. Nor could that holy and salutary purpose of ours be impeded but ought rather to be assisted, which you proclaimed to be coming to Lombardy to root out heretical wickedness, aid the Holy Land, recover the rights of the Church and the empire, and reform peace. For if the reformation of the empire invited you to this, the cause of the empire, whose deformation redounds to the detriment of the Roman Church, the benefit of the churches, suffering long division under the waves of wars, and the danger of souls, for which we are obligated to the possessor of heaven and earth, ought to have stirred us more strongly to procure the goods of concord. Hence, we are believed to have usurped nothing of your right, nor occupied anything of yours, although you assert the contrary, if we, by whose counsel you should have proceeded to this at the beginning, middle, and end, as you have often promised, are found ready to pay our debt to the supreme creditor. Therefore, considering the foregoing more diligently in the manner of an artisan, whose consideration is initially offered those things which ultimately concur in operation, we chose him, in this part, as a minister through whom we might fulfill our ministry, who could be less suspected by you and any dissenters, since his mind, freed from earthly desires, would less infuse his acts with the ferment of hatred or love, who, leaving himself and his own, would have soared into the height of divine love. Who could cast a wrinkle of suspicion on his sincerity, who could obscure his purity by opposing a blemish of duplicity, whom the profession of blessed religion, taken on, has removed from flesh and world, whom the fruit of commendable works and holiness of life has commended to God? Indeed, the place of origin is not rightly introduced against him as an argument of suspicion, since the goodness of man is not deformed by place, but rather the malice of place is reformed by man. This is proven by the fact that neither did the impious world detract from the piety of Christ, nor heaven make a demon holy, nor paradise a man. The lineage is also believed not to suffice for your purpose, nor to profit, since vices of kinship are condemned in vain in one who, by the purity of holy conduct, has become entirely a stranger to his homeland and kin, as if changed into another man. Why more? In vain is something introduced to prove anything, which neither frequently nor inseparably accompanies it. However, the testimony of the beloved son, the master of the Hospital of St. Mary of the Teutons, supports this, and contradicts that which you claim made him, when previously sent with our beloved son Otto, deacon cardinal of St. Nicholas in Carcere

**Translation to English:**

To Frederick, ever august Emperor of the Romans, illustrious King of Jerusalem and Sicily. Considering that the Greek Church, having once separated from the obedience of its mother, the Apostolic See, seemed to lose the life of the Catholic faith because it did not fear being separated from its head, namely the Roman Church, in which the Lord placed the magisterium of faith and the whole ecclesiastical state, because neither does a branch live when it is severed from the root, nor does a member retain life when it is separated from the body. Considering that, since the Church is the unique spouse of Christ, which is undoubtedly founded on blessed Peter, the prince of the apostles, whoever establishes or believes another church can be constituted outside this one, it is certain that he is separated from the life of true faith into the death of heresy: with prudent deliberation, we feared that the said Greeks, whom the flood of schism has transported from the Church of God into the synagogue of Satan, overwhelmed by the torrent of heretical depravity, would be precipitated into the abyss. For which reason, following the example of the supreme shepherd who desires to bring back the lost sheep to the Lord's fold on his own shoulders, we sent to Vatatzes, the so-called patriarch of Nicaea, and the prelates and clergy subject to him, brothers of the Orders of Preachers and Minors, fully learned in divine law, urging them with fatherly admonitions and prayers to rise from the sleep of death, and fleeing from the impending wrath, to reform themselves to Catholic unity with the light of heavenly clarity shining upon them. But, as we learned from the truthful report of these brothers, they proposed various errors against orthodox faith and, closing their ears like the asp, could not be induced by any admonitions to return to the path of ecclesiastical unity. Greatly troubled by vehement grief over this matter, lest the power divinely given to us of plucking up and planting be in vain, we have marked many princes, barons, and knights with the sign of the cross, not so much for the aid of the Constantinopolitan empire as for strengthening and defending the Catholic faith in the eastern parts, following the example of the evangelical cultivator who first digs around the barren fig tree and puts manure, then cuts it down if it does not produce the expected fruit in time. Therefore, by apostolic message and letter, we have asked your serenity to grant free passage to the aforementioned cross-bearers through your land. But since, as we understand, you oppose an obstacle of difficulty to our requests, we have felt it necessary to beseech and admonish your imperial majesty more earnestly, so that, prudently considering that by denying such passage you would incur harm to your soul before God and to your reputation among men, because you would seem to support the said schismatics in their error, grant free and secure passage to those cross-bearers coming to the aid of the city of Constantinople through the aforementioned land and empire. Otherwise, you must know that the Church could not pass over with closed eyes what might be attempted to the subversion of the Catholic faith. To promote this matter more effectively, we have deemed it appropriate to send our beloved son, Master Gregory, our subdeacon and notary, a prudent and experienced man, to your presence, earnestly asking that you regard him with a serene eye, acquiesce to his, or rather our, admonitions, and strive to believe and effectively fulfill what he tells you on our behalf, and in turn, you will write back to us the imperial will's good pleasure on this matter. Given at the Lateran, 16th of the Kalends of April, in the eleventh year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa (Friderico Romanorum imperatori semper augusto) nuntiat se fratres Predicatores et Minores ad Grecos misisse, rogans ut crucesignatis Constantinopolitane civitati succurrentibus transitum liberum concedat, alioquin ecclesia rem non connivet. Dat. Laterani, XVI Kal. Aprilis, anno undecimo.

**Translation to English:**

Gregory, etc., to the illustrious King of France. It has been intimated to our ears on behalf of our dearest son in Christ, James, the illustrious King of Aragon, and the noble Count of Provence, that the city of Marseille, which is known to pertain to the dominion of the said count, rebelliously subjected itself to the noble Count of Toulouse, not without great treachery and audacity, and dared to secede from the jurisdiction of the Count of Provence. The Count of Toulouse, receiving the citizens of Marseille unjustly as his subjects, not only defends them in this iniquity but also, rising against the aforesaid Count of Provence and his territory, presumes to molest him in many ways. This, it is believed, is because of the rancor conceived when the Count of Provence, at the church’s mandate, opposed the Count of Toulouse in the siege of Avignon with your father Louis, of blessed memory, driven by zeal for the faith and the defense of ecclesiastical liberty.

Wherefore, since the said king, having taken up the sign of the cross, has proposed to powerfully attack the Saracens and besiege the city of Valencia, and is bound to defend the Count of Provence for many reasons, he and the aforesaid count have humbly appealed to us to provide assistance. Furthermore, it has come to our attention, as intimated by our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Vienne, apostolic legate, that since the Count of Toulouse has not paid the salary due to the masters of Toulouse, contrary to the oath taken, the university of Toulouse is being irreparably disrupted to the detriment and subversion of the Christian faith, as heretical depravity thereby grows stronger.

His bailiff has also evicted our venerable brother, the Bishop of Vaison, from his house disgracefully, and has taken from him a castle and city belonging to his church, inflicting other grave damages and multiple injuries. The said count, moreover, establishing anew the detestable tolls on salt which his father had once abjured in the land of Venaissin, presumes to vex the church of God and its prelates in many ways, sacrilegiously occupying the goods and revenues of the churches, and often admonished by the said archbishop, he procures no amendment of these.

Because of which, although he is bound by a sentence of excommunication, he nonetheless despises absolution, or rather the keys of the church, presuming to commit many worse things against God and the church, which would be grievous to detail here. We, therefore, considering that if the aforesaid king is unable to proceed against the Saracens due to this hindrance, the benefit that we believe would accrue to the Christian faith from this might perhaps be lost, as the enemies of Christ gain stronger advantages from delay, and that from this, such great dangers of war might arise in the parts of the Albigensians and Provence that, unless countered before they grow stronger, it would hardly or never be possible to remedy thereafter. Moreover, the business of peace and faith, to which the said Count of Toulouse is bound by oath in the hand of our venerable brother, the Bishop of Porto, then apostolic legate, would be put at great risk, because during the turmoil of wars there, heretics might attack our faith more securely. Furthermore, the aid of the Holy Land, to which the count is also bound to proceed, would incur great damage—God forbid—from having to expend in the aforementioned wars and discord what should now be reserved for his passage, and he would always be found unfit to cross if the time granted by us is not devoted to lawful preservation but rather to prohibited consumption. For these reasons, we have deemed it fit to request and urge your royal serenity, etc. Dated at Viterbo, the 13th Kalends of June, in the 11th year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa regi Franciae scribit, ut de rebellione civitatis Massiliae ad comitem Tolosanum et de iniuriis ab eo ipsi comiti Provinciae illatis cognoscat, ne rex ipse ab expeditione contra Saracenos retardetur. — 1237, Maii 20, Viterbii.

**Translation to English:**

To the Archbishop of Milan and his suffragans. The intention we have had and still have in the affairs of our dearest son in Christ, Frederick, and especially in the matter of Lombardy, is fully known to Him who fashioned the hearts of men individually, as noted in Psalm 32:45, though perhaps some with perverse hearts, instigated by the originator of all evils, might assert the contrary.

Indeed, some time ago, letters from the same emperor were presented to us, in which he placed himself entirely in the hands of the Church concerning the affair of Lombardy, in accordance with the solemn advice of the princes and the terms of the compromise we received from him in Tuscany, with the proviso that the matter should be concluded by the recently past feast of the Nativity of the Lord, for his honor and the benefit of the empire. However, a condition was added to these letters which nullified the compromise, and it seemed impossible that the matter could be concluded within the set term. Therefore, through our dear son, the master of the hospital of St. Mary of the Teutons, we admonished the same emperor to place himself unconditionally and precisely in the hands of the Church regarding this matter. This envoy, sent by the aforementioned emperor to our presence, departed with the matter unfinished because the Lombards, although awaited for a long time, did not send their envoys to us within the appointed time.

But shortly after this envoy departed, the ambassadors of the Lombards came to the Apostolic See, asserting firmly that they had been detained by a legitimate impediment and offering to commit themselves unconditionally to us. Desiring to procure peace as is our duty, we accepted the aforementioned commitment and decided to recall the aforementioned master, who returned to the emperor's presence upon being summoned.

Consequently, at the emperor's insistence and with the counsel of our brothers, the three patriarchs, and all the prelates then present at the Apostolic See, we assumed the business of the Holy Land, ensuring that the discordant of the world were compelled to truce or concord, and some of the great princes of the land were already compelled to this. Indeed, the King of Navarre and many noble and powerful men have taken the sign of the cross by God's grace. We have diligently admonished the emperor, both through letters and through our venerable brothers, the archbishops of Mainz and Trier, the bishops of Regensburg and Hildesheim, and the same master, to send the said master to us without delay with full mandate to commit to the aforementioned matters, lest the business of the Holy Land, which has been ordained for the benefit of the Church, the empire, and the whole Christian people, be hindered.

The emperor should know that if he attempts to proceed against the Lombards, especially since they have placed themselves unconditionally in the hands of the Church, it would be indecent for the Church to allow such harm, especially when dealing with a matter that concerns the Redeemer's great glory, and favoritism should not be shown, nor should we suffer anything that could impede the process of the same business.
