[Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers, the archbishop......... and his suffragans, health and apostolic blessing.]

We want to bring to your and others' attention that in the assembly held at Perugia for various ecclesiastical matters, we solemnly freed and declared free all those bound by an oath of fidelity to Emperor Frederick, especially the people of the kingdom, from the oath they owed him. If any voluntarily or under compulsion gave him such or any other oath against the Roman Church, we decree it is not binding because he, having long been ensnared by the chain of excommunication due to his demanding sins, as we have diligently explained to you in other letters, was frequently admonished to stop trampling on ecclesiastical liberty. Not only did he not desist from despoiling religious persons and clerics, but further assaulted them with greater rashness, plundering their goods and those of the churches, and even through the hands of the enemies of the cross of Christ, profaning sacred vessels dedicated to divine uses. He denied water, fire, baking of bread, and other trade to the clerics. Becoming worse than Pharaoh, fearing no divine retribution, he afflicted the clergy with endless torments. Hence, a cry, wail, and horrible lamentation, strong and dreadful, ascended to us from the churches and clerics of the kingdom of Sicily and Apulia, which we could no longer endure with a clear conscience without exercising this ecclesiastical retribution against him, since, according to the canonical sanctions of the holy fathers, fidelity is not to be kept with one who does not keep faith with God and the Church and tramples on divine precepts, especially one separated from the communion of the faithful.

Moreover, we have excommunicated and anathematized all who, against the Roman Church by attacking its patrimony or by unlawfully usurping the spiritual or temporal rights of the Apostolic See, have given aid or favor. We report this not without pain and shame that when the same emperor had sworn with his own hand to cross into the aid of the Holy Land by the term set for him with a multitude of soldiers, ships, and galleys, as the height of imperial majesty required, and incurred upon himself the sentence of excommunication if he did not fulfill this as he had promised, we do not know which improvident counsels or rather diabolical deceit he employed, having taken certain prelates and a few soldiers, with no satisfaction made or absolution received, secretly leaving the port of Brindisi, it is unknown where he went. However, if he crossed to aid the Holy Land so weakly and impotently, it would bring irremediable shame to the entire Christian people, because his power, believed to be the greatest among all Christian princes, would become perilously cheap in the eyes of the Saracens, who would hardly fear anyone henceforth, but rather would audaciously and securely attack and enslave the Christians.

He also published statutes and sent letters to attack and usurp the patrimony of the Apostolic See, causing the city of Benevento, which is a special city of the Roman Church, to be besieged so that no one could enter or leave, and those captured would be subjected to servitude. Also, the suffragans of that city are prohibited from receiving the sacrament of consecration, children from receiving the anointing, and litigants from accessing judgment. Furthermore, causing an army to be gathered, having violently occupied a certain castle of the church, he solicits cities and towns through the patrimony and duchy of Spoleto with letters and gifts in damnable greed, striving to attract the vassals of the church to himself with terrors and blandishments, and to separate them from faith and devotion to the Apostolic See. We announce this briefly to you, lest the truth be overshadowed by lies among you. Therefore, do not believe anyone who by words, writings, or messages suggests anything against the aforementioned truth, because being a shaper of lies, he would be completely alien to the truth.

Therefore, by apostolic writings, we strictly command you in the virtue of

Translation to English:

To the archbishops and bishops, abbots, priors, deans, archdeacons, archpriests, and other prelates of churches, and to the entire clergy, and to noble men, counts, barons, knights, and the people of the cities, castles, and other places established throughout the kingdom of Sicily:

Let the heavens rejoice and the earth exult, for the storm of dreadful lightning, by which the marvelous and fearsome Lord has long allowed you all to be severely afflicted, seems now, through His ineffable mercy, to have been transformed into a gentle breeze, with the removal of him who especially crushed you, the faithful, under the hammer of continuous persecution, and gravely troubled the Church of God in many ways, but most grievously in your case. As can be easily noted by your discretion, we, pouring out deep sighs and many sorrows, have traveled from the Apostolic See to remote places, so that we might bring an end to the afflictions of many, but especially to your distresses. Indeed, what apostolic concern could not accomplish in this, the grace of divine mercy has brought to completion, to be celebrated and remembered for all future times, and has spread over you the mantle of His glory, whom public fame had once revealed as despised and miserable to the world. Therefore, most beloved in Christ, a song of joy must be unanimously undertaken by you, and efforts should be made, through which you may henceforth be fully immersed in all prosperity according to your desires. No obstacles of suggestion, nor delays or impediments of difficulty, should hinder you from recognizing the outpouring of divine sweetness over you through the resulting action, and to return to the most sweet bosom of your mother church, having perpetual tranquility and peace, and that most secure and delightful liberty with which other special sons of the church are happily and firmly endowed, with us devoting every concern to this end, so that, as we rejoice in spirit that a day of joy has come to you after a night of sorrow, whatever we perceive may redound to your benefit and honor, we may accomplish with ready hearts, with the cooperation of divine grace. To make our mind clearer and more fully known to you in these matters, we have decided to visit you through these present letters, and will soon send suitable envoys to you. Meanwhile, arranging that as soon as we are able, we, preparing ourselves for a happy return with the angel of salvation leading the way, may see your desirable land with our own eyes, and with our brothers, take counsel from you on how to remove from you the reproach of oppressive servitude and to add the honor of perpetual liberty with the stable fullness of joy. Given at Lyon, 25 January, in the eighth year.

Regesto in Latin:

Innocentius IV papa universis ecclesiasticis et nobilibus regni Siciliae nuntiat tempestatem persecutionis cessasse, hortans ut ad gremium ecclesiae redeant, pacem et libertatem perpetuam consecuturi. 1249, Jan. 25, Lugduni.

**Translation to English:**

To the Duke of Brunswick,

The faithful Mother Church has long desired that among noble and eminent persons, etc., as stated above in the letter to the Margrave of Meissen up to the point: it could not be done because the former persecutor of the Church, Frederick, feared by you as well as many others, was present. But now, by the providence of God, with him removed from the midst, full freedom arises from every side so that what once lay hidden in the minds of the devout may now manifest to the honor of God and the Church through the effect of works. We earnestly entreat your nobility with all possible affection, imposing upon you the remission of sins, that, with the guiding angel of salvation leading you as an eminent and famous leader, you direct yourself towards those things by which the Holy Mother Church may be filled with the abundance of exultation. We ask you to please, with no delay interposed, from sincere and effective devotion, our dearest son in Christ, W., the illustrious King of the Romans, soon to be elevated to the peak of imperial honor, in whom you have liberally and laudably consented from the beginning of his promotion, and to render the oath of due fidelity to him and assist him openly and powerfully with your support, so that he, supported by the aid of your favor, etc., as in the letter to the Duke of Saxony. In the same manner, to the Margrave of Brandenburg, up to the point: imposing upon you that you direct your mind towards those things by which the Holy Mother Church may be filled with the abundance of joy, etc., as stated above in the previous letter.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa duci de Brunswic mandat, ut W. regi Romanorum, in fastigium imperialis honoris sublimando, fidelitatis iuramentum praestet et assistentiam suam potentem exhibeat. 1235, Mar. 1.

**Translation to English:**

To Brother Stephen of the Order of Preachers, our chaplain and penitentiary. The multitude of responsibilities incumbent upon us distracts us with the countless diversity of profound thoughts, and the more the office of the apostolate imposes duties upon us, the more diligently we must be vigilant concerning emerging matters from all sides. Hence, since we cannot be present in various places simultaneously, to ensure that our vigilance is not lacking where we are not personally present, we prudently designate suitable persons, considering the discrete magnitude of urgent matters to be attended to, fulfilling through them the debt of apostolic service. Indeed, the apostolic see is known to have labored greatly for the cause of peace and faith, particularly in Provence and surrounding areas, expending great effort and undergoing substantial expenses. And because we wholeheartedly desire the sound and peaceful state of those regions, we do not cease to apply appropriate diligence so that, with the Lord's guidance, it may be achieved. Therefore, we command you to personally proceed towards Provence and, with the prudence given to you by God, to engage in diligent discussions concerning the aforementioned matter and all things related to the well-being and tranquil state of the entire land, with the prelates, cities of those parts, the seneschal, and bailiffs, as well as with the procurators of our beloved son, the noble man, the Count of Provence. Establish and ordain with our authority concerning all these matters with the aforementioned prelates, cities, seneschal, and others, whatever you see should be established for the health and peace of the aforesaid land. For we will consider whatever you decide to be done concerning these matters as valid and firm. Given as above.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa fratri Stephano de ordine Praedicatorum mandat ut personaliter in Provinciam accedens super negotio pacis et fidei cum prelatis, civitatibus, senescalco, balivis et procuratoribus comitis Provinciae tractet et statuat. 1236, ut supra.

**Translation to English:**

To the Bishop of Palestrina, Otto, Cardinal Deacon of St. Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, the Archbishops of Auch, Bordeaux, and Rouen, the Bishops of Nîmes, Carcassonne, Agde, Pavia, Asti, and Tortona, the Abbots of Cluny, Cîteaux, Clairvaux, La Charité-sur-Loire, and Fécamp, Gregory of Romania, our subdeacon and chaplain, deans, provosts, and other associates in the Lord. In these days, hardly any prosperity could happen to you that would be pleasing to individuals or acceptable to all, without many speaking variously about it and feeling differently. It follows, therefore, that concerning the recent sorrowful adversity, which is known to have befallen you by divine permission, a matter of multifaceted opinion and discussion arises among some, according to the variety of feelings, over which you should neither be astonished nor troubled in your sincerity or moved in your constancy, for although, as you know, human nature is so arranged that speech is given to all and wisdom of mind is granted to few, it is clear to us and to the minds of the understanding that you, having the honor of God and of the Apostolic See and the salvation of the universal Church, as well as the merit of obedience, under which lies the sum of all virtues, before your eyes, have diligently striven to come quickly with a multitude of the devout to the bosom of the Mother Church, although it could and should rightly be lamented that Gregory of Romania, informed by our letters about the strength of the opposing party, did not have as many galleys as he could have, according to our command, so that your crossing, with Christ leading, might be made safe from all dangers. Therefore, venerable brothers, since your lamp of virtues does not lie hidden under a bushel but shines before all on a candlestick, breathing in Him who is gentle and humble of heart, and continually bears a disposition of mercy towards His afflicted, may you continually hold belief in us and our brothers that though we differ from you in place and in bonds, we are made almost participants in your sufferings, so that we often pour ourselves into sighs and are oftentimes drenched in tears, although our consolation much like yours arises from this: that we hold trust in the ineffable mercy of the Redeemer, that He who planted the Church with His blood and raised it high through the tribulation of His elect, will illuminate it with the face of His kindness across the breadth of the world, with us and the same brothers pursuing you both with affection of compassion and with the help of prayers, so that the Father of mercies and God of all consolation may show Himself gracious in the affluence of His mercy to you, suffering for His name the reproach of captivity, through the merits of the glorious Virgin and the blessed Apostles, and grant us that concerning the tranquility of the Church and peace of the world, as you piously and laudably suggested through your letters, we may be able to provide such that after the storm of sorrow, the serene joy may be able to follow, and the Catholic faith, which, as we have understood from letters and the account of trustworthy ones, is attacked by the incursion of a dreadful people beyond what could be believed, may be inviolably preserved to the glory of the supreme majesty and the salvation of the faithful. Furthermore, since we hold you, dearest to us in Christ, continually in the innermost parts of our love and can scarcely let a day pass without our imaginary vision representing your state to us with tears, do not let admiration take place in you because we have neither sent writing nor message to your sincerity nor has your pain been mitigated by any remedy of our provision, especially since, as the searcher of all knows, it was not postponed under the pretext of occupation or negligence, but mainly because there was a reasonable fear in us that concerning this debt of visitation our desire could not achieve effect. Given at the Lateran, on the 14th of June, in the 15th year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa episcopo Penestrino et aliis prelatis ac religiosis viris ad quos scripserat, de adversitate nuper incursa consolatur, hortans ut fidem et constantiam servent, et promittit se pro tranquillitate ecclesiae et pace orbis provide facturum. Dat. Laterani, XVIII Kalendas Iulii, anno pontificatus XV.

To the Bishop of Mantua. Due to the pressing matter of the general church, we had previously directed that assistance be provided in the amount of one thousand imperial pounds by our venerable brother, the Bishop of Castello, for the needs of the said church, with the execution of our mandate in this matter entrusted to you. However, since the aforementioned bishop has satisfied us in this matter to the extent that we are content, we command you to revoke any sentence you may have issued against the bishop on account of this assistance, and, if the bishop has incurred any irregularity in celebrating the divine office while bound by this sentence, to dispense him by our authority. Given at Vigintimiglia, on the Nones of May, in the eighth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa episcopo Mantuano mandat ut revocet sententiam in episcopum Castellanum propter subventionem mille librarum imperialium latam et, si irregularitatem aliquam contraxit, eundem auctoritate apostolica dispenset. Datum Vigintimiliae, Nonis Maii, anno pontificatus octavo.

**Translation to English:**

To the elected bishop of Arezzo. As we have learned, certain individuals in the cities, castles, and other places of Tuscany are reportedly instituted as powers and governors by a certain F., who was then posing as the emperor, and his natural son, in fact. We, wishing to purge the province from such individuals, so that the progress of peace may not be hindered there by them, command you to ensure that they do not involve themselves in the offices of powers or governors, which they hold to the detriment of their own and others' souls, since they have illegitimately obtained these offices through illegitimate authorities. You are to firmly prohibit the communes and inhabitants of those places from daring to pay or heed them, compelling them to comply with this through ecclesiastical censure, with any appeal set aside. Given at Lyon, on the 7th day before the Kalends of April, in the eighth year [of our pontificate].

Gregorius IX papa electo Aretino mandat, ut nonnullis, qui in Tusciae locis potestates et rectores illegitime se gerunt, officiorum administrationem inhibeat, communibus et incolis ipsorum locorum prohibendo, ne eis salaria conferant. 1235, Mart. 26. Lugduni.

**Translation to English:**

To the council and community of Alexandria. In defense of ecclesiastical liberty and the protection of your rights, you have endured many hardships from your enemies and those of the Apostolic See, and you have also inflicted harm upon them. Therefore, inclined by your supplications, we confirm by apostolic authority all the land that you or any of you have acquired, or will be able to acquire in the future, from those enemies while remaining in devotion to the Apostolic See. We also protect you with the patronage of this present writing. Let no one, therefore, etc. Given at Milan, on the 21st of August, in the ninth year.

Gregorius IX papa consilio et communi Alexandriensi confirmat auctoritate apostolica terram ab hostibus acquisitam. 1235, Aug. 21. Mediolani.

**Translation to English:**

In the name of Christ, amen. Lord Gregory of Romania, legate of the Apostolic See, at the special command of the Lord Pope, requested from the community of Genoa that it grant armed galleys and transports for the expenses of the Lord Pope or other messengers of the Lord Pope, to conduct and return prelates of churches and other persons to the general council to be convened by the Supreme Pontiff. The said Lord Legate, in the name and on behalf of the Supreme Pontiff, on one side, and Henry, son of the late William, syndic of the Genoese community specially appointed for this purpose by the power and counselors of Genoa, who were summoned and assembled to this council by horn and bell as usual, and also these counselors, on the other side, agreed together on the aforementioned galleys and transports and their armaments to be granted to the Lord Pope or his messengers or envoy as follows: namely, that the said syndic promised on behalf of the community to grant and provide ten armed galleys to the said Legate, receiving in the name of the Supreme Pontiff, for carrying the prelates and others to the council and returning them, in such a way that in each galley there will be 108 sailors and 26 subordinates, and 40 supersailors, with the supersailors including 4 sailors, one boatswain, one cook, and 10 crossbowmen, each of whom will have two crossbows, one of horn and the other of wood, and in each galley there will be one rotating crossbow and 30 iron munitions. The community of Genoa will grant and provide these for a fee or price of 275 pounds for each galley per month, with all expenses of the community of Genoa being borne by the Lord Pope or his messengers or the Legate for the Lord Pope, making the payment of the agreed fee or price to the Genoese community for two months, and this one month before the galleys are armed. This is on the condition that if the Lord Legate wishes to reduce the number of supersailors or subordinates required on the galleys, the fee and price should be reduced accordingly, namely 35 Genoese shillings for each supersailor per month and 18 shillings for each subordinate per month, and if by chance the Legate wishes to add more supersailors or subordinates to the galleys or any of them, he is obliged to pay, in addition to the agreed fee and price, 35 shillings for each additional supersailor per month and 18 shillings for each additional subordinate per month, including shillings and provisions.

Moreover, the said syndic promised and agreed on behalf of the community to grant and provide the Lord Pope or his messengers or the Legate for the Lord Pope with ten transports, which will be equipped as follows: there will be 25 men armed with iron in each, who will have two servants, and among them will be two sailors. The Lord Pope or his messengers or the Legate will pay the community for the fee or freight of each transport, including provisions and the hiring of sailors, 86 pounds per month, so that payment is made to the Genoese community for two months, one month before the transports are armed. Furthermore, the Lord Pope or his messenger for him must pay the community for the construction and opening of each transport 26 Genoese pounds only once; provided that if the Lord Legate or messengers of the Lord Pope wish to add more armed men to the transports or any of them, the Lord Legate or the Lord Pope must add for each one 30 Genoese shillings per month, and the community is obliged to provide and must grant as many as they wish to add at the same rate. Additionally, the said syndic promised on behalf of the community to release the galleys and transports to him or the messengers of the Lord Pope beyond two months at the will of the Lord Pope for a similar price and fee, as stated above, and that the galleys and transports should be delivered and conducted to Rome, if it pleases those who will be transported and received at Nice or other places where prelates and others called to the council can safely come.

Furthermore, the said syndic promised on behalf of the community of Genoa to the Legate, receiving on behalf of the Lord Pope, that the community of Genoa will prepare six galleys and six transports beyond the aforementioned ten galleys and ten transports, for which the Lord Pope or the Roman Church must pay nothing unless they wish to take and have them, except for the opening of each transport 26 pounds, specifically agreed that when the Lord Pope or his messengers pay the fee and price of the other ten galleys and ten transports, if they say they do not wish to have or take these six galleys and six transports,

**Translation to English:**

To Roger of Lentini: For the honor and utility of the Apostolic See and the peaceful and healthy state of that land, so that you may be able to execute the business of Sicily, which we have decided to entrust to your providence, more effectively as you will be strengthened by greater authority from us: we have decided, by the authority of these presents, to grant to your nobility that you may freely and wholly receive all the revenues of the cities, castles, and other places of the aforesaid Sicily pertaining to the See, to be expended in promoting the said business in those parts. Given as above.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Innocentius IV papa Rogerio de Lentini concedit, ut redditus civitatum, castrorum et aliorum locorum Siciliae ad Sedem pertinentium libere percipiat ad negotium Sicilie promovendum, et bona rebellium Romanae ecclesiae fidelibus conferat, necnon feudalia militaria in partibus illis concedat. Datum Lugduni, VI Idus Martii, anno VIII.

**Translation to English:**

To the podestà, council, and people of Bologna. While navigating the sea of this world, Peter's little ship is sometimes driven by contrary winds and occasionally struck by the blows of storms, but eventually, with the Lord commanding the winds to cease and the gusts to be still, calm follows the storm, and the ship, plowing the level sea of a tranquil peace, advances, for although it is sometimes battered by unexpected waves, it is not sunk, and though it is shaken by raging waters, it is not shattered. Indeed, the Church, built upon the rock of faith, is frequently attacked and assailed by the enemies of the Christian religion and often by the persecutors of ecclesiastical liberty; but ultimately, when the Most High turns His eyes of mercy upon it and extends His right hand of power as its protector, the detractors of faith are restrained by the bridle of silence, and the hands of persecutors, weakened in their efforts, shrink back from the rights of the Church. Thus, after the cloud of turmoil, the serenity of peace follows, and the sea of this present age is subdued under the Church, with the fury of uprising storms crushed. Therefore, if the faithful of the Church are occasionally troubled by adverse events according to the changeability of time and are sometimes soothed by fortunate outcomes, let them not be cast down by the adversity of misfortune, nor puffed up by the encounter of prosperity, but let all their hope and confidence be placed in Him who opens the bosom of mercy to those who trust in Him and who, after the patience of tribulation, provides remedy in adversity and consolation in prosperity.

For Frederick, the so-called emperor, a persecutor of the Church, once sent letters to our brothers, the prelates of the churches and the princes of the world, requesting a council to be convened, that his deeds might be examined, and we, upon the counsel of the same brothers, determined to summon the prelates and the envoys of kings and princes to the apostolic see. But once he understood this, as the noise of terror is always present in the ears of the impious because a guilty conscience presumes harshly, he subsequently sent other contrary letters, and wickedly, by acting submissive and requesting a council's judgment, he exposed his inner deceit through the variability of his writings. Therefore, as some prelates approached the same seat of power and many others returned to their own places due to fear of the sea, he, upon hearing of the imminent arrival of the rest, laid ambushes for them, capturing them along with the venerable brother, the bishop of Palestrina, and our beloved son, O., cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, legates of the apostolic see, as if it was not enough for him to have harmed the Church in many ways unless he also inflicted an immeasurable offense against it. However, while these things may bring disturbance to the minds of the faithful, the constancy of their hearts should not be changed, nor should their sincere spirits be bent; instead, they ought to support the Church against the same persecutor even more favorably, as they perceive him to have inflicted more grievous injury upon them through these acts. Therefore, we urge, implore, and earnestly command your community to persist most steadfastly in devotion to the Church and, confident in the Lord and in the might of His power, to resist its enemies as the most valiant warriors of Christ, powerfully and manfully. Let not the wickedness of a sudden event strike your hearts with astonishment, but rather let the zeal of God kindle them to the defense of the Church. We, for our part, will so provide for these matters, with God as our helper and hoping that His hand of aid will be present to us, that the designs of the impious will be thwarted, honor will accrue to the Most High, and strength to the Catholic faith and the augmentation of ecclesiastical liberty will follow, as well as benefit to you and other faithful. Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the fifteenth year of our pontificate. In the same manner to the noble duke and people of the Venetians. In the same manner to the podestà, council, and people of Milan, Ferrara, Mantua, Piacenza, Perugia, Todi, Terni, Orvieto, Spoleto, Narni, Anagni, Segni, Alatri, Veroli, Terracina.

To the Bishop of Palestrina, the Archbishops of Rouen, Bordeaux, and Auch, the Bishops of Nîmes, Carcassonne, Agde, Pavia, Asti, and Tortona, and to Oddone of Saint Nicholas in Carcere Tulliano, Cardinal Deacon, to the Abbots of Cluny, Cîteaux, Clairvaux, and to Gregory of Romania, our Subdeacon and Chaplain, to deans, provosts, archdeacons, and others exiled for the liberty of the Church.

The distress of a new case of adversity, emerging with unfortunate events, has recently involved the mourning sons of the womb, which, by considering their actions and the wickedness of the presumed novelty, inflames the breast of the universal Church. It adds to our sorrows, doubles the mournful sighs, and places causes of sorrow. Besides the enormous offense to the Apostolic See and that pestilence of example, which the populace vehemently pursues against the clergy, the injury to the father by his sons wounds the heart, presses a not light burden of sadness, and distresses the vigilant affection of diligence. For it is not tolerable that when the members suffer, the head does not languish, or the husbandman exists without pain when the vine is struck. Who then will give a head of water to the bereaved father, and grant a fountain of tears to his eyes? For Joseph is not, Simeon is held in chains, Benjamin the younger is taken away; the noble sons of Zion, the revered princes of the churches, once clothed in the finest gold, when delivered into hostile hands, are regarded as earthen vessels.

Who can assuage the father's grief or temper the brothers' sorrow with appropriate remedies, while those hastening for the world's peace to the cradle of the mother are snatched by the insidious sons of Satan, and one day unexpectedly took those whom the Apulian region of death received? Egypt, the hostile, the prison of Pharaoh, encloses the senators, and the authors of freedom for others are subjected to the judgment of foreigners, compelled by the laws of necessity to obey the secular judgment, the judges of the world, and the legitimate successors of the apostles.

In the lack of your liberty, there is distress for us, in scarcity, famine, in terror, punishment, and in exacerbation, torment; what we speak is sad, what we feel is lamentable; festive days are turned into mourning; upon the willows, we hang our harps, while you sit by the rivers of Babylon, obedient to the Egyptians, exposed to the judgment of Pharaoh. Would that the hand of Moses might come, by whose service Israel would be returned to his own dominion to offer the usual sacrifices with willing hearts!

Meanwhile, it is worth recalling the beginning of the rising Church, what the constancy of the fathers bore for the ancestral laws, what apostolic toil, what the triumph of martyrs endured. Nor should you pass over the examples of wise women, to whom the softness of nature denied audacity, which can sufficiently strengthen weak knees and render the cup of suffering drinkable, recognized with prudent intellect and inscribed by the finger of the Lord on the tablets of the heart.

Wherefore, we pray and exhort your sincerity in the Lord, that considering with your accustomed devotion the cause of the Church, the injury of the Apostolic See, which against right and duty is vexed by various troubles and attacked by offenses, you may set above the distresses you endure, the affection of the gentle knees of the pious mother who received you at her breasts. That the proof of your faith, which is found much more precious than gold, may have fruitfulness with temptation, and that nothing may be found by the tyrant that is notable by sinister interpretation or deemed worthy of being inserted in his defamations. To Master Jacob, Archdeacon of Laon, our chaplain. Since our venerable brother, the Bishop of Albano, has reported many good and laudable testimonies about you before us and our brothers, and since we have often learned of your diligence through your deeds, we commend your care in this regard. We wish to follow you with special grace and favor, as far as we can with God, for the matters entrusted to you and promoted prudently through your industry. To the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of the churches of the German kingdoms who will inspect the present letters. Since we trust the prudence of our beloved son, Master Jacob, our chaplain and Archdeacon of Laon, the bearer of these presents, and send him to promote the affairs of the church in the kingdom of Germany, we ask, admonish, and earnestly encourage your entire community, commanding that you, honoring him as a special nuncio of the Apostolic See as is fitting, provide him and his retinue with sufficient necessities for himself, his household, and his journeys, so that we may commend your devotion in this matter. Given as above.

Gregorius IX papa Magistro Iacobo, archidiacono Laudunensi et capellano, mandat ut cum Theoderico, magistro domus Theutonicorum Pruscie, ad principes imperii accedat et eos ad devotionem ecclesiae et homagium regi Romanorum inducat; et archiepiscopis, episcopis et prelatis regni Alamanniae mandat ut eidem Iacobo, tanquam speciali nuntio apostolicae sedis, sufficienter necessaria ministrent. **Translation to English:**

To the noble man Stephen, son of the late illustrious King of Hungary. From the customary clemency of the apostolic see in alleviating the grievances of its subjects and especially of the nobility, we apply ourselves more willingly to the study of diligence as we experience the loyalty of our subjects through the pleasing services of devotion. Hence, considering the sincere devotion you are known to have towards us and the Roman Church, and wishing that you may perceive this see as favorable and kind to you, inclined by your petitions, we restore to you and your successors, especially since the kingdom of Sicily currently lacks a king, the counties of Laureto and Combersano, the villages of Terlizzi, San Pietro, and Solito with their appurtenances, as well as a certain land in the diocese of Penne, which you assert belong to you by hereditary right. This is notwithstanding that the late Emperor Frederick is said to have granted them to another according to his will, as long as they do not belong to another or others who remain in devotion to the Church. Let no one therefore infringe upon this restitution of ours. Given at Lyon, on the 5th of the Kalends of March, in the eighth year.

Innocentius IV papa nobili viro Stephano, filio regis Hungarie, comitatus Laureti et Combersani necnon villas Terlitii, Sancti Petri et Soliti cum terris in diocesi Pennensi per hereditarium ius sibi pertinentia restituit, non obstantibus concessis a quondam imperatore Frederico aliis, dummodo non pertineant ad alios in devotione ecclesie persistentes. 1251, Feb. 25, Lugduni.

**Translation to English:**

**Regarding the Money to be Lent to the Roman Church by the Following Prelates:**  
To the Bishop of Palestrina, legate of the apostolic see. Since the Roman Church has received a large sum of money under heavy conditions for the defense of the faith and ecclesiastical liberty, and has not yet satisfied its creditors, even though some payment deadlines have passed, for which said creditors complain loudly to us that they have incurred not insignificant losses: because the resolution of such debts cannot be delayed much longer without serious detriment to the Church due to growing inconveniences, we have decided to attentively ask and admonish dear sons, the abbots and convents of certain monasteries of the orders of St. Benedict, Cluniac, and Premonstratensian, whose names we send you in a certain list under our seal. Similarly, we address this to the commanders and brothers of the Knights Templar and Hospitaller of Jerusalem houses in France. Therefore, we earnestly entreat your nobility with all the affection we can, enjoining upon you for the remission of your sins, that for the honor of Him who has exalted you in many ways and greatly prospered you, directing your spirit to those things by which the said Church may be filled with complete joy, our dearly beloved son in Christ, etc., as above in the next.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa marchioni Misnensi mandat, ut, quia Fridericus de medio sublatus est, plenam et liberam facultatem habeat ad necessitates ecclesiae viriliter adiuvari, non obstante quod filia Friderici in domo sua ad matrimonium cum filio suo sit locata, cum hoc matrimonium propter defectum etatis nec consumari possit. [Anno] 12[29], [Lugduni].

**Translation to English:**

To the Archbishop of Kalocsa. The mother encounters the difficulties of her offspring, and the son is not free from the burdens of the mother; indeed, the bonds of natural affection share in both prosperity and adversity. If, therefore, the tie of love renders one a compassionate participant in the other's suffering, the bond of nature is broken if one does not share in the other's troubles. Thus, the support of a mother should abound for her needy son, and a son should exhaust his utmost resources for the aid of his needy mother. Truly, the Roman Church, which holds primacy among others by divine institution, is compelled to endure various and unbearable burdens of expenses for the defense of faith and ecclesiastical liberty. Unable to bear these alone, it has requested many prelates and other ecclesiastical men to provide assistance. Among these, some, like devoted sons, have so fervently exposed themselves and their possessions for her honor that, due to the expenses they undertook to aid their mother opportunely, they have been burdened with heavy debts. Unless relieved by the mother's providence, they might be entirely consumed by the abyss of usury. Indeed, among other prelates of the world, our venerable brother, the Patriarch of Aquileia, has notably stood by the Church, resisting its enemies who, in hatred of the mother, persecute the daughter, the Aquileian Church, continuously attacking it with war and seeking with all their might to dismantle its fortresses and other defenses. In resisting these malicious attempts, the Patriarch has courageously incurred enormous and unavoidable expenses, contracting large and heavy debts due to the insufficiency of his church's resources. He is so weighed down by these debts that the revenues of the Aquileian Church barely suffice to pay the accumulating usuries. He has humbly beseeched us to provide him with apostolic aid so that he may not, God forbid, be forced to yield to the enemies of the Church due to lack of funds. Although we, who bear the general care of churches, regard the affliction of the Aquileian Church as our own, other churches and ecclesiastical men should also feel the sting of compassion due to this affliction, for this persecution is not to be considered as particularly theirs but common to all, as the Church is one. When afflicted in any part, it surely causes pain in the rest due to the blow suffered, as its members, though many and distant in places, are united in one body by one faith, such that if one is wounded, the others cannot but languish. Therefore, we earnestly admonish, ask, and exhort your fraternity, commanding that you effectively urge and induce all the archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, and other prelates of churches, exempt and non-exempt, in the kingdom of Hungary on our behalf to aid the aforementioned Patriarch with the sum of two thousand marks of silver annually during these times of war so that by their intervention he is not compelled to desist from defending his church and its rights. We may thereby more clearly recognize these prelates as loving ecclesiastical liberty everywhere and fully supporting those who stand as a wall of defense for it. Given at Lyon, August 25, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Innocentius IV papa archiepiscopo Colocensi mandat ut universos archiepiscopos, episcopos, abbates, priores aliosque ecclesiarum prelatos regni Hungariae moneat ad subveniendum patriarche Aquilegensi cum duobus milibus marcarum argenti annuatim pro defensione ecclesie sue. 1251, Aug. 25. Lugduni.

Should they fail to do so, you are to appoint a suitable and devoted person as bishop and pastor to that church by the same authority. We direct you to advise and consent to the chapter regarding our beloved son Hermann, nephew of the noble Duke of Brunswick, whose diligence, industry, and power may beneficially and prosperously govern the same church with God's help. Provide for the mentioned church with him if the said king accepts him. If they fail to appoint him within the term set by you, do not omit to appoint the same H. as bishop to the church with apostolic authority, ensuring he is given due obedience and reverence by the chapter and all subjects of the same church; opposers, etc.—notwithstanding any privilege or indulgence of the Apostolic See. For indeed, because the matter of the Roman Empire is particularly dear to our heart, which is why we diligently aim for its promotion, striving to find ways and paths by which it may be properly directed and receive desired growth, we therefore wish and command that you proceed to promote the same H. only if you first have the consent of the same king in this regard; for we desire those who can and will effectively promote the said matter to be appointed as prelates of the churches. Given at Lyon, on the 19th of February, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Innocentius IV papa .. Caminensi episcopo resignationem suam recipi mandans, et capitulo ecclesie Caminensis iubet, ut de pastore idoneo cum regis Romanorum assensu provideant. Nisi hoc fecerint, mandat ut Hermannum nepotem ducis de Bruneswic in episcopum preficiat, si rex eum acceptaverit. Dat. Lugduni, XI Kal. Martii, anno pontificatus VIII.

Given at Lyon. August 31, in the eighth year [of our pontificate].

**Regesto:**

Innocentius IV papa Henrico cantori Virdunensi mandat ut Ludovicum scholasticum ecclesiae Sancti Salvatoris Metensis in ecclesia Metensi recipiat ac ei de beneficio prebendali cum dignitate vel officio provideat, dignitatibus ad episcopum Metensem spectantibus exceptis. 1251, Aug. 31. Lugduni.

**Translation to English:**

To the abbot of Salem, of the Cistercian order, in the diocese of Constance. Since, as we have heard, a serious war is feared to arise in those parts due to a discord between our venerable brother, the bishop of Constance, and our beloved son, the abbot of Saint Gall, we command you to personally approach both parties. On our behalf, strictly under the penalty of excommunication and suspension, forbid them from initiating any war by themselves or through others, and from inciting any discord on any pretext. Instead, let them work together effectively, as they have done so far, in the business of the general church. If either of them, going against this prohibition, presumes to initiate any war, then strike him with the sword of excommunication and send him suspended to our presence, to receive what he merits. Take care to inform us through your letters, containing the tenor of this mandate, what you have done in this matter. Given at Lyon, on the 2nd day before the Kalends of April, in the eighth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Innocentius IV papa abbati de Saleme Cisterciensis ordinis Constantiensis diocesis mandat ut episcopum Constantiensem et abbatem Sancti Galli a guerris movendis et discordiis suscitandis sub excommunicationis et suspensionis poena inhibeat, et si alter eorum guerram movere praesumpserit, eum excommunicatum et suspensum ad sedem apostolicam mittat. 1251, Mart. 31, Lugduni.

**English Translation:**

To the councilors of the cities, towns, and villages of Germany, to whom these letters are directed, etc. The affection of our heart, which we express to you and the people through special letters, can be easily seen by your industry, if, however, there is a clear understanding in you through the grace of the Lord of virtues. Therefore, we ask you with all the attention we can muster and beseech you in the Lord, commanding and enjoining in remission of sins, that for the honor of the divine name, you take every care and diligence so that the aforementioned people, putting aside all delay, may return to the bosom of the holy mother church and swear the due oath of fidelity to our beloved son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Romans, W., who will soon be elevated to the height of imperial honor, and that they openly favor and powerfully assist him in all things, so that the aforementioned church may owe you and them the rewards of gracious favor for this, and that the same king may be able to hold you in particular benevolence over time. Otherwise, you must gravely fear that God, whose cause is known to be in question here, will avenge with the magnitude of His power for such a fault upon you, and that the church, which desires to exalt devoted sons, will render you, along with the said king, completely alienated from its grace because of your obstinate hardness. Given as above. To the councilors of Speyer. The affection of our heart, which we express to you and the people of Speyer through special letters, etc. as above continues to the end. In the same way to the councilors of Oppenheim. In the same way to the councilors of Frankfurt. In the same way to the councilors of Gelnhausen. In the same way to the councilors of Württemberg.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa consiliariis civitatum, oppidorum et villarum Alamaniae mandat, ut populus ad ecclesiam redeat et regi Romanorum W. fidelitatem iuret, monens de periculo divinae ultionis et gratiae ecclesiae amissione. Datum ut supra.

**Translation to English:**

To the Archbishop of Salerno. Although you may have previously overlooked many issues, like the troubles caused by F., who once acted on behalf of the emperor, in order to avoid conflicts you could not resolve through resistance, we believe, however, that the adversity of that malignity has not uprooted the root of charity and faith you owe to us and the Roman Church from your heart. Therefore, we expect that now, after the cause of rightful fear has ceased with the death of the same F., your faith will work through the promptness of love. Hence, as we are sending our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Bari, to the regions of the Kingdom of Sicily to advance the affairs of the same kingdom and the church, we command that you diligently assist him in these matters, endeavor to bring back both your own and others to the faithfulness of the church with him and through your own efforts, so that it may be evident from this that you have maintained an intact purity of faith towards the same see in your heart, and we, through the praiseworthy testimony of your actions, may not only consider you exonerated but also highly commendable. Given.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa archiepiscopo Salernitano mandat ut, post obitum Friderici, archiepiscopum Barensem adiuvet in regno Sicilie negotiis ecclesiae promovendis atque ad fidelitatem ecclesiae studeat alios revocare. Datum Anagnie.

**Translation to English:**

To all the clergy, dearest sons in Christ of our illustrious King of the Romans, W. Since you are bound to the service of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King of the Romans, W., you ought to enjoy a greater privilege. By the authority of these letters, we grant that you cannot be summoned to judgment, excommunicated, suspended, or interdicted by letters of the Apostolic See or its legates without our special mandate, which makes full and explicit mention of your persons and this indulgence, even if it is stated in such letters that any indulgence of this See does not stand in the way of the petitioners. Let no one, therefore, etc., of our concession etc. Given at Perugia, on the 4th of February, in the ninth year.

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa universis clericis W. regis Romanorum indulget, ne sine speciali mandato suo vocari ad iudicium seu excommunicari, suspendi vel interdici possint. 1235, Feb. 4. Perusii.

Translation to English:

To the podestà, council, and people of Marseille. Your city has been quite devoted to the Roman Church, and we wish that it may always grow in its devotion! Because we wish those whom we love with full affection to flourish in great sincerity; thus, we are very pleased that you are devoted to the Apostolic See, and the more we learn of your affection, the more we will be filled with great joy. However, even if we weigh the merits of individuals on the scale of providence, that we may discern their quality with careful examination and dispense rewards to each according to the demands of their devotion, we nonetheless consider that, by the office of the apostolate we have undertaken, we are debtors to all and must equally provide for the salvation of all, and we are occupied with diligent thoughts for their healthy state, although it is more fitting for us to attend vigilantly to the needs of those whom we know to have deserved more from the same See. Therefore, concerned for your welfare, we often turn to you with all the meditation of our heart, since both your services and the duty of pastoral care, which we are bound to fulfill for all, urgently advise and induce us to do so. Therefore, desiring that you may live under a tranquil and prosperous state and advance in inner and outer peace in the same city, we have decided to specially send to you our beloved son, Brother Stephan, our chaplain and penitentiary, a man learned, honest, and circumspect in counsel, very dear to us and to our brothers by the merit of his proven virtue, that he may hold a diligent discussion with you concerning these matters. Therefore, we command your community to deliberate with him carefully on all matters that concern the peaceful, stable, and healthy state of the same city and the entire region and to fully explain your intentions to him concerning this. Humble yourselves to his advice and counsel, having faith in everything he tells you on our behalf. And so that such a matter may be more effectively executed through him, know that we have given him full power to negotiate and arrange with you concerning this, as he sees fit. Given at Lyon, 14th Kalends of March, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

Regesto in Latin:

Innocentius IV papa potestati, consilio et populo Massiliensibus mandat, ut cum fratre Stephano capellano et penitentiario suo super pacifico et salubri statu civitatis deliberent, plenam ei dantes potestatem tractandi et ordinandi. Datum Lugduni, XIIII Kalendas Martii, anno VIII.

Gregorius IX papa R. comiti Casertano comitatum Caserte, civitatem Caleni, castra Skifati et ad Mare, Caiaciam, Montorum, Roccam Montis Dragonis et alia, quae pacifice possidet, auctoritate apostolica confirmat. 1235, Iun. 15. Genuae.

To the Duke of Bavaria, the spirit of sound counsel. Recently, as above up to: it was not possible, because the former persecutor of the church, F., was especially feared by you more than others who feared him for that reason, which you are believed to often recall with sighs, and many also turn it over in their minds not without a certain horror. Nor should any impediment arise concerning these matters under the pretext of Conrad or another of the offspring of the aforementioned F., since neither they nor any of them have any right, etc., as above up to: is obtained. So that you may more fully and clearly understand the sum of our intention concerning these matters, we send to your presence our beloved son, brother Henry of the Order of Preachers, our penitent, indeed a discreet and provident man, and very much pleasing and acceptable to us for the merits of his devotion, to whom you should give full credence concerning the aforementioned matters, and so accomplish with vigilant mind what we have piously suggested to you in this matter, so that the said king may always rejoice to have special goodwill towards you and yours, and the church, to which special honor in this matter should be bestowed, may hold you in the rewards of gracious favor. Otherwise, both by the same church, as much as by herself and all her devoted followers who can, and by the same king, it will be proceeded against you spiritually and temporally, such that in the end, with the divine right hand triumphing, you will perceive with much anxiety of spirit that it was unwise and dangerous to have fled the most blessed embraces of the exalting mother church, and to have thrown yourself into those darknesses where both temporal ruin and the matter of eternal perdition are known to be contained. Dated as above.

To the podestà and council of Lucca. We cannot show a more effective sign of our affection towards you than by instructing your prudence with necessary admonitions to preserve the goodwill of the Apostolic See for you, ensuring that we remove any matter of dispute that might weaken or dissolve the bond of mutual goodwill, so that, with the root of shared concord firmly established and all pestilence of dissension eradicated, the work of each side may arise as a heavy harvest, expressing the truth of vicarious love. Your community knows for certain and truth compels you to acknowledge that the land of Carfagnana belongs to the rights and property of the Apostolic See, and it never yielded to an external possessor except through the injury of occupation. When the late Emperor Frederick unjustly took it from the Roman Church, we later replaced the detainer, who, usurping the same land under an unjust or null title of possession, holds it in defiance of God, injuring the aforementioned See and endangering your souls. Furthermore, we must not tolerate such grievance from you, nor bear so manifest an offense. Our duty obliges us, demanded of us without fail, not to allow the goods of the aforementioned Church to perish through the silence of dissimulation, which we are specially entrusted to manage. The zeal for your salvation, which warns you of imminent danger from the sacrilegious detention of these goods, also urges us. Therefore, desiring to comply with our conscience and to avert the loss of your souls, we earnestly ask, admonish, and exhort your community and offer you wise counsel, nonetheless strictly commanding through apostolic writings, that, acknowledging the benefit of not exchanging the grace of the Roman Church for the convenience of said detention, since that grace, if you at least strive to preserve it through innocence, can bring greater fruitfulness to you and your city, you release and leave the said land free and unburdened to the legates of the Apostolic See or their or our envoys, and revoke any rectors and officials or others whom you have placed there, and exercise no power in the said land from now on. Do not be encouraged in the detention of the aforementioned land by any trust in the permission of our patience, as we have firmly resolved not to tolerate at all that the rights of the Roman Church be held occupied by anyone, and the more we hold you especially in the bowels of love, the more indignantly it will be borne and the more attentively corrected with the authority of paternal strength, if, God forbid, you persist stubbornly in the unlawful detention of the aforementioned rights. Given as before. II. O. To the Cardinal Deacon of Santa Maria in Via Lata, legate of the Apostolic See. Know that we write to our beloved sons, the podestà and councils of Lucca, Bologna, and Modena in these words: to the podestà and council of Lucca. We cannot show a more effective sign, etc. up to: persist. In the same manner, to the podestà and council of Modena for the land of Carpensis. In the same manner, to the podestà and council of Bologna, as it is written to the Modenese for the land of Carpensis, so to the Bolognese for Medicinat and Argellata.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa potestati et consilio Lucanis mandat ut terram Carfagnanam, iuris sedis apostolicae, legatis liberam dimittant et potestatem ibi non exerceant, ne iniuria ecclesiae Romanae fiat. Datum Laterani.

Therefore, let no one, etc., of our absolution, etc. Given at Perugia, on the 15th day before the Kalends of December, in the ninth year.

Gregorius IX papa potestati et communi Castri Trebarume Spoletane diocesis mandat, ut ab exhibitione iuramenti et pallii Fuliginatibus absolvantur, ob indignitatem illorum propter rebellionem. Dat. Perusii, XV Kal. Decembris, anno nono.

To Master Jacob, Archdeacon of Laon, our chaplain. Our experience teaches us that, driven by the fear of God's name, you diligently and with all your strength strive for the salvation of souls and willingly advance and promote those things that contribute to the strength of ecclesiastical liberty. Since this experience has given us reason to send you to the presence of the noble man, the Duke of Bavaria, and some other nobles and others in Germany, we have decided to entrust to your discretion, by the authority of these presents, that if any of the communities of the cities or castles or villages of those parts, which do not exist in devotion to the apostolic see, should reject, contrary to our salutary admonitions, what we forbid, and should not return reverently to the bosom of holy mother church, and should oppose or rebel against our dearest son in Christ, our illustrious Roman king, who is soon to be elevated to the pinnacle of imperial honor, you are to proceed against them and those who dare to hinder or disturb this pious work, by spiritual and temporal censure, through yourself and also any suitable religious and secular clerics, whom we wish and command to assist you in this matter, as you see fit — notwithstanding any exemption granted to anyone by the apostolic see, stating that they cannot be suspended or interdicted or excommunicated without a special mandate of the same see, making full and explicit mention of such exemption. **Regesto in Latin:**

Innocentius IV papa Magistro Iacobo archidiacono Laudunensi mandat ut, si qua de universitatibus partium Germaniae se contrarias aut rebelles Romanorum regi, sublimando ad imperium, ostendant, procedat contra eos spirituali et temporali censura. Eos autem, qui ad ecclesiae mandatum reverti voluerint, affectu benigno recipiat et absolutionem largiatur. 1251, Febr. 20. Lugduni.

**Translation to English:**

To P. Cardinal Deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil, legate of the apostolic see. Since with the removal of the late F., the Roman emperor, the greatest obstacle that was hindering the affairs of the Kingdom of Sicily has been eliminated, the way has been made more accessible to carry out the same matter. We, recognizing that many and serious responsibilities lie upon you, which you must diligently attend to, have thought it expedient to entrust the guardianship of the March of Ancona, the Duchy of Spoleto, and the Patrimony of St. Peter in Tuscany to certain bishops through our letters, so that you may be more efficiently focused on the aforementioned affair by being relieved in other matters through capable assistants. However, it was never our intention to withdraw those lands from your care; indeed, in the same letters, we instructed the aforementioned bishops to consult you in all things and to ensure their actions align with your guidance. Thus, we are greatly pleased that you have withheld the letters we sent to our venerable brother, the bishop of Fano, regarding the guardianship of the same March, as you wrote to us, not allowing them to be presented to the said bishop, and you may, if you deem it expedient, revoke other letters directed to other bishops regarding the duchy and the Patrimony. Therefore, we command you to pursue the aforementioned matter with strength of spirit so effectively that, with divine grace assisting you, you may bring it to the desired conclusion, always being certain that we are continuously concerned with preserving your honor with all our effort. Given at Lyon, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Innocentius IV papa Petro Sancti Georgii ad Velum Aureum diacono cardinali mandat, ut negotium regni Sicilie fortiter prosequatur, postquam custodia Marchie Anconitane, Ducatus Spoleti et Patrimonii beati Petri in Tuscia episcopis commissa est. 1251, Mar. 21, Lugduni.

**Translation to English:**

To Gebehard of Freiburg, our chaplain, canon of Strasbourg. To the Bishop of Fano. Although we direct the eyes of apostolic solicitude to the state of all kingdoms and provinces of the Christian profession, applying constant diligence so that they may be governed prosperously and healthily, we ought to look more attentively to the March of Ancona, for which, being a special concern of the apostolic see, we are bound to think more vigilantly about it. And although the Roman church has labored incessantly for its preservation, has borne innumerable expenses, tolerated bitter anxieties, and suffered grave detriments, we never neglect its care nor cease to meditate solicitously for its good. Rather, we always turn the gaze of our mind towards it. Like a mother who zealously guards the welfare of her children with tender and intimate love, so the same church with heartfelt affection desires the healthy state of its faithful in the March and does not cease to labor vigilantly for their tranquil governance as a nurse and guardian.

Therefore, not wanting the region to remain without a custodian and overseer, we have deemed it fitting to commit its care to your fraternity, in whom we trust for your prudence and circumspection, by the tenor of these presents. You shall appoint and order bailiffs, judges, and notaries in the counties, communities, and other places, just as we used to do ourselves when we governed it in a lesser office. Furthermore, those from that March who adhered to the church's persecutor, if they wish to return to the church's mandate, you shall receive, and as long as they provide sufficient assurance that they will strictly comply with our mandates, you shall grant them the benefit of absolution according to the church's form.
