It has been delightful for us to love you sincerely in the Lord and to promote eagerly those things which seemed to align with your wishes. This special affection remains strong in you and grows under the influence of trust, as you, who once sought to be a son of light, now desire to be renowned for magnificent and effective devotion to the Church's cause in this serene time, especially since the persecutor of the Church has been removed by the Lord's powerful hand. You seemed previously to be somewhat constrained by necessity because you had contracted a marriage alliance between your daughter and him, although he was cut off from the communion of the Church due to his sins and deserved no affection, being one to be utterly set aside along with your aforementioned daughter. According to the teaching given in evangelical truth, our Creator and Redeemer should be preferred above all, even if father and mother, brothers, sisters, and children are forsaken for the glory of His name. 

Understanding and recognizing openly the obstacles that once prevented Christianity from enjoying the solace of rightful peace and the Holy Roman Church, instituted by divine providence as the mother of the faithful, from attending to those matters that honor God and ensure the salvation of the devout people, we acknowledge that by the grace of God, with darkness now dispersed, the fullness of light has come to the world. It is now easy, especially for you and other Catholic princes, to act as a champion for the Church and to become a magnificent suppressor of the disloyal and rebellious. We have felt compelled to affectionately urge and admonish your nobility, imposing this upon you for the remission of your sins, that you should promptly show yourself fully devoted to our dearly beloved son in Christ, William, the illustrious King of the Romans, who is to be elevated soon to the height of imperial honor. Without any delay, render him the due oath of fidelity and support him clearly and powerfully, so that with your favor and assistance, he may successfully prosper in those matters that honor the Church and ensure the peaceful state of the empire, triumphing with God's help. As a result, he will rejoice to have your special benevolence toward you and yours, and the Church, to which special honor is shown, will be held to reward you with fitting thanks. No obstacle should arise from Conrad or any other offspring of Frederick in this matter, as they have no right to the empire, whose dignity is attained not by succession but by election. To make our full intentions on these matters clearer to you, we are sending our beloved sons, Master Jacob, archdeacon of Laon, our chaplain, and Brother Thierry, preceptor of the Hospital of Saint Mary of the Germans in Prussia, men of discretion and providence, and greatly esteemed and accepted by us for their devotion. You should place full trust in them regarding the above matters and express to us through their prudence what is in your will and contained in your desire, trusting with certainty that in those things we perceive to be desirable to you according to God's will, we will respond liberally and readily with paternal kindness. Given at Lyon, February 19, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa duci Saxoniae nuntiat facultatem, ut carissimo in Christo filio Willelmo regi Romanorum illi fidelitatem iuret et eum sublevet ad fastigium imperialis honoris. Super hiis mandat ut certitudinem intentionis suae per Jacobum archidiaconum Laudunensem et Therricum preceptorem Sanctae Mariae Teutonicorum exprimat. 1234, Feb. 19. Lugduni.

**Translation to English:**

To the noble man Henry Fraiapanes, count of our sacred Lateran palace, prince of Taranto, and lord of the whole land of Otranto. The clear devotion, by which you are known to shine especially towards us and the apostolic see among other nobles, and the magnificent deeds of your ancestors, through which they earned the grace of the same see for themselves and their descendants, earnestly demand from us that we pursue your person with continuous favors and elevate you with multiple honors, imitating the examples of our predecessors, who honored your said ancestors with very many graces and enriched them with the generous granting of grand gifts. Therefore, since we have liberally decided to confirm to you, the heir of the same O. Fraiapane, the concession made by the late Constance, empress of the Romans and queen of Sicily, and also by the late Frederick, emperor of the Romans, then king of Sicily, to O. Fraiapane, your uncle, and his successors concerning the principality of Taranto and the whole land of Otranto, making you subsequently invested with the principality and the aforesaid land, as is more fully contained in other letters of ours, we, rightly accumulating grace upon grace concerning you, also wishing you to enjoy apostolic favor over the aforementioned principality and land, kindly inclined by your supplications, by the authority of these presents, grant you that henceforth you shall be bound to respond concerning the principality and land only to us and our successors, the Roman pontiffs, for which we wish you to be immediately subject to the aforesaid see, strictly forbidding anyone else from henceforth daring to disturb or harass you regarding the mentioned principality and land and all their appurtenances and rights, or to inflict any annoyance on you, or to trouble the said principality and land or you for them with any exactions, collections, or taxes, or any other demands of exactions, nonetheless decreeing that all things pertaining to the right and ownership of the Roman Church shall remain whole, perpetual, and undisturbed to you, to be freely used for your needs and uses. No one, therefore, etc. concerning our concession, prohibition, and constitution, etc. Given at Perugia, on the twelfth Kalends of February, in the ninth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa nobili viro Henrico Fraiapanes, comiti palatii Lateranensis, principi Tarentino et domini terre Ydrontine, concedit ut de principatu et terra predictis nulli alii nisi sedi apostolice respondeat, inhibens quemquam alium perturbare. Dat. Perusii, XII Kalendas Februarii, anno nono.

**Translation to English:**

To the master and brothers of the hospital of Altopassum, diocese of Lucca. We have received from the content of your petition that the former master, Peter de Vinea, who at the time, due to the overwhelming power of the once Emperor Frederick, could not be resisted without grave harm, aspired to your church and house located near the city of Capua and designated for the use of the poor and sick. He frequently and insistently requested that they be granted to him by you, and eventually, he took possession of them along with some of their appurtenances. He then granted a certain hospital of the said diocese with its belongings, which belonged to the bishop of Lucca, to you and your hospital in the name of an exchange for the aforementioned church and house, with the said bishop subsequently reclaiming the hospital to his right as it had been before. Since you have decided to seek the provision of the Apostolic See concerning this matter, we, in our customary kindness, safeguarding your interests, fully restore and grant to you and through you to your said hospital the mentioned church and house with their appurtenances, to be retained by you and your hospital in perpetuity, by our special grace. This is notwithstanding the aforementioned exchange or any conditions, agreements, or contracts made by you with the said Peter, who could and should have known that they held no legal weight, especially since he was presiding over those matters at the time, being a terror not only to humble but also to exalted persons. Nor does it matter if the goods of the same Peter or the aforementioned church and house were occupied by the named Frederick or his officials or supporters, or if they were given by the same Frederick or Peter or anyone else, or even by us to others. Therefore, let none, etc., against our restitution and grant, etc. Given at Perugia, November 29th, in the ninth year [of our pontificate].

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa magistro et fratribus hospitalis de Altopassu Lucane diocesis scribit, eis plenam restitutionem et concessionem faciens ecclesiae et domus prope Capuam, quae ad usum pauperum et infirmorum deputatae sunt, non obstantibus permutatione et contractibus cum Petro de Vinea initis. Datum Perusii, III Kalendas Decembris, anno IX.

**Translation to English:**

Jerusalem. When a request is made to us, etc., up to the effect. Indeed, your presented petition indicated that our beloved in Christ, the noblewoman M., formerly the Countess of Sayn, generously donated and granted all her properties with any rights of ownership then belonging to her in the villages of Rarich and Zaeltanc in the diocese of Trier, for the salvation of her soul and that of her late husband, the Count of Sayn, to you and through you to your hospital, under the condition that you should fully pay the debts of the said count from the fruits of these properties, as it is more fully contained in the public letters made thereof and sealed with the seal of the said countess. We, moved by your supplications, declare this donation and grant, as it was prudently made and does not result in prejudice to anyone, valid and firm, and confirm it by apostolic authority and protect it with the support of this writing. We have had the wording of those letters noted verbatim in these presents; which is as follows: To all present and future, to whose attention this writing may come, the noble woman Mechtild, widow of the late nobleman Heinrich, Count of Sayn, wishes eternal salvation in the Lord. For among other works of piety, it is believed to be more acceptable to God, indeed it is considered the most important, that which is offered to the poor and holy places and to our Creator through them from the abundance of charity. We, considering that the religious men, beloved to us in Christ, the master and brothers of the hospital of Saint Mary of the Germans in Jerusalem, not only devote themselves to hospitality, but also constantly dedicate themselves to the glory of the eternal King, by promoting the faith and valiantly fighting the enemies of the cross, have deemed it worthy to open our hands of generosity to them. Therefore, for the salvation of our souls and that of the good memory of lord Heinrich, Count of Sayn, our husband, we donate and irrevocably grant in perpetuity all properties in Ratich and Zoltano in the diocese of Trier now belonging to us by full right, which the said count, together with us, is known to have purchased from the abbot and convent of Gladembach in the diocese of Cologne, with the consent of the reverend father, lord archbishop of Cologne, with tithes, parish, and any rights of ownership, to the aforesaid master and brothers, or rather to their hospital, with the condition imposed that the same master and brothers fully pay the debts of the said count from the fruits of the tithes and other aforementioned goods not pertaining to the said parish, and these being paid, they shall henceforth possess the said goods freely and discharged from all burdens. The witnesses are the noble lord Heinrich of Arscheit, lord Conrad of Brisich, seneschal Lambert of New Castle, Heinrich of Hysin, and many others. And to ensure full faith is given to these present letters in the future, we have had them strengthened with the safeguard of our seal. Given at New Castle, in the year of the Lord 1250, on the octave of Saint Martin. No one therefore, etc. of our confirmation, etc. Given at Lyons, 5 Kalends of March, in the eighth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa hospitali sanctae Mariae Theutonicorum Ierosolimitanae donationem bonorum in villis Rarich et Zaeltanc a Methilde relicta Henrici comitis Seynensis factam, sub conditione solutionis debitorum, auctoritate apostolica confirmat. 1235, Feb. 25. Lugduni.

**Translation to English:**

To the Doge and the people of Venice. Since the city of Parma, standing like a wall to uphold devotion to the Church and to protect its own liberty and that of its faithful allies against incursions, has suffered countless strikes and scourges, it would indeed seem inappropriate and utterly inhumane if Mother Church were to neglect with feigned kindness the sons of such sincerity, so oppressed, and were to disregard their needs, as if forgetful of maternal care. Certainly, it would be considered reprehensible and detestable if the neighbors, whom the bond of a society to be cherished has linked to them, were to pass over their losses with notable dissimulation and postpone soothing their wounds with their own remedies. Therefore, it is fitting and expedient that the Church and those who are distinguished by the noble title of faith should immediately contemplate and earnestly provide the necessary remedies for restoring their state, which has collapsed under persistent persecution. But since your hand is most required to alleviate their plight and repair the ruin, we have decided to address you specifically from the depths of our hearts on this matter, although we believe without any hesitation that you are diligently considering their relief and carefully planning their support, even without our request. For it is not credible, nor does your usual probity allow us to believe, that you, whose illustrious freedom and noble valor the trumpet of universal acclaim loudly proclaims, and whose magnificent power illustrious deeds continuously attest, would leave the citizens of Parma, your nearest neighbors, indeed brothers, unattended in such distress, as if unknown and unaided as strangers. Therefore, we earnestly admonish, beseech, and exhort your community, mandating that you, with vigilant spirits and diligent efforts, direct your naval assistance to the restoration of the city of Parma, which places special trust in your aid, at the request of the authority and commune of the same city or our beloved son, O., cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Via Lata, legate of the Apostolic See, for the salvation of the whole country. In this way, with your help, the same city, which has been so oppressed, may be restored. Otherwise, we have instructed the aforementioned cardinal by our letters to compel you to this, if necessary, with due severity, the appeal removed, regardless of any privilege or indulgence of the Apostolic See. Given at Lyon, on the 12th Kalends of April, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa duci et populo Venetorum mandat, ut subsidium navale civitati Parmensi oppressae pro ecclesiae devotione praestent, et cardinali O. Sanctae Mariae in Via Lata iniungit, ut eos, si opus fuerit, ad id compellat. Dat. Lugduni, XII Kal. Aprilis, anno VIII.

**Translation to English:**

To the noble man William, Count Palatine of Tuscany, vassal of the Apostolic See, our devoted one. The devotion founded firmly on the rock of the Christian faith of your ancestors always shone forth with the firmness of a conspicuous and lofty building in them, maintaining intact loyalty towards the Holy Church and unwavering strength of perseverance in it, such that it could not be toppled by the impulse of any adverse storm, but continually receives the pleasing increments of beneficial steadfastness. Therefore, due to the clear merits of such great goodness of your ancestors, the Apostolic See justly honored them with distinguished favors so that by this, they and their noble offspring might flourish more and more in the virtuous pursuits of faith and devotion with the same See; and aligning yourself with their pious affections, you are known to have stood firmly in the pursuit of devotion to the Mother Church, and in keeping the integrity of faith and loyalty due to her, overwhelmed by the waves of no storm, though you have endured the harsh inconveniences of exile and the burdens of tribulation. Therefore, inclined by your devoted supplications, we confirm anew to you, with a certain prerogative of apostolic grace, all the fiefs, rights, and other honors that were liberally granted and given by the same See to your predecessors, as it is more fully contained in the privileges and indulgences of the same See, and whatever is known to have been granted by our predecessors, the Roman Pontiffs, to you or the same ancestors and was subsequently held by you peacefully for some time. We hold as pleasing and firm whatever was done by our said predecessors regarding the above. We confirm all these to you, who persist in sincere devotion to the Roman Church and keep the due fidelity to it, by apostolic authority, and we protect them with the support of this present writing. Therefore, let no one etc. violate our concession and confirmation etc. Given at Perugia, on the 9th of January, in the ninth year. The bishop of Chiusi is appointed as conservator regarding this.

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa nobili viro Guillelmo comiti Tuscie palatino mandat et confirmat omnia feuda, iura aliaque honores ab apostolica sede antecessoribus suis concessa et a se pacifice obtenta; eundem in devotione ecclesie persistenti commendans. Datum Perusii, V Idus Ianuarii, anno nono (1235).

**Translation to English:**

To the bishop of Metz. The faith and devotion that our beloved noble son Henry, lord of Licithemberc and advocate of Strasbourg, has towards us and the Roman Church, as well as the requests of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious king of the Romans, W., and of the elect of Mainz, urge us to extend gracious benevolence to our dear son Simon, canon of Strasbourg, son of the late Louis, lord of Licithemberc, advocate of Strasbourg. Therefore, since, as the king and the elect have informed us, we had instructed our venerable brother, the bishop of Strasbourg, by our letters to provide Simon with some prebend or dignity in the city or diocese of Strasbourg, Anselm of Fleckenstein, canon of Speyer, has obtained the provostship of the church of Seltz in the diocese of Strasbourg for Simon, which he rightfully deserves, by means of certain letters subsequently obtained from the apostolic see. However, since the father and brothers of Anselm have openly opposed the business of the Church by adhering to C., the son of the late Fr., former emperor of the Romans, and his supporters, and have occupied and hold occupied the castles and fortifications of the empire, and it is quite unworthy for the sons of persecutors of the Church and ecclesiastical liberty to be promoted to honors and ecclesiastical benefices, which they rather deserve to be deprived of, we, inclined by the prayers of the king and the elect, command that you earnestly admonish and induce the father and brothers of Anselm to return to the devotion of the Church within two months after your admonition, and not delay to restore the said castles and fortifications to the said king. Otherwise, removing Anselm from the mentioned provostship by the advice of our beloved son H., cardinal priest of the title of Santa Sabina, legate of the apostolic see, you shall confer and assign it to the said Simon by our authority; contradictors etc. — notwithstanding that the cause between the aforementioned Anselm and Simon over the said provostship, in which the contestation of the lawsuit has not yet reached, we have decided to recall to the apostolic examination, or that it is said to have been granted to our venerable brother, the bishop of Strasbourg, by the apostolic see, that no one can be provided in his city or diocese without his consent by apostolic letters. Given at Perugia, on the 14th Kalends of February, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa episcopo Metensi mandat, ut patrem et fratres Anselmi de Flekesteim moneat ad castra imperii restituenda, alioquin Anselmum a praepositura amoveat et eam Symoni conferat. Datum Perusii, XIIII Kalendas Februarii, anno nono.

**Translation to English:**

To the chapter and entire clergy of the city and diocese of Lodi. Although the continuous succession of pressing affairs assails our mind, which, by the Lord's appointment, we preside over the universal administration, unworthy as we are, the care of all churches, incumbent upon our shoulders, urges us more intensely with daily meditation, as we are specially, indeed principally, appointed to this by the office of the apostleship entrusted to us. Therefore, when some time ago, our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Gregory, deprived the city of Lodi of episcopal dignity with prudent deliberation, because its community, persistently adhering to Frederick, the former Roman Emperor, bound by the chain of excommunication, committed detestable and utterly unheard-of excesses against clerics and religious persons—let us not speak about the burning of a certain brother of the Order of Friars Minor—we, observing that they have sincerely returned to the bosom of Mother Church, having expelled the perpetrators of their previous misdeeds from the city by a perpetual decree, and noting that the city itself, where the body of St. Bassianus rests, is continuously illuminated with countless and splendid miracles, and wishing, for his honor and the devotion of the community, which we hold dear and acceptable, to reinstate the city almost anew with the title of pontifical dignity, have restored it to episcopal dignity by apostolic authority with the advice of our brothers. We have granted to the beloved son, Bon John, elected of Lodi, with the advice of our said brothers, as pastor of the Church of Lodi, with full administration and care of all the goods, spiritual and temporal, which formerly belonged to the bishopric and the same Church of Lodi, trusting in the prudence of his foresight and the zeal of his diligence and caution, that he will endeavor to show himself vigilant, diligent, and solicitous about the care and advancement of the same, so that it may result to his glory and honor, to your joy, and to the desired benefit and progress of the same church. We therefore earnestly request and urge all of you, commanding that you devoutly and joyfully admit the aforementioned elect, proceeding to the aforementioned church with the grace of our blessing, and treating him honorably, extend to him the obedience and reverence that is due, striving to serve him with vigilant diligence as the father and shepherd of your souls, so that by mutual love, what pertains to prosperity and salvation may come to you and him. Otherwise, the sentence which he legitimately etc. Given at Perugia, 5 Ides of January, in the ninth year.

---

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa capitulo et universo clero civitatis et diocesis Laudensis mandat ut dilectum filium Bonum Iohannem Laudensem electum in pastorem ecclesiae Laudensis admittant et tractent honeste, ei obedientiam et reverentiam impendentes. 1236, Perusii, V Idus Ianuarii.

**Translation to English:**

To the podestà, council, and community of Naples. As the clouds of adverse times have receded and the clear weather of prosperity approaches, your pure devotion, erected as a lamp upon the stand of faith, could not fail to shine upon the inhabitants of the neighboring region. Soon, by extending the rays of its clarity, it illuminated the minds of those obscured by the darkness of prolonged indifference with the infused light of salvation, recalling them from the path of damnable disobedience and directing them onto the path of the Church's salutary commandments. Therefore, extolling your sincerity with great and deserved praise and pursuing the efforts of your diligence with all favor and grace, we earnestly ask and encourage your commendable university and strengthen you in the Lord. We command you, as you fix the anchor of your faith in Him who does not abandon those who hope in Him but comes to them favorably as a strong fighter, and confidently relying on our help and that of the Mother Church, to persist with steadfast spirit in His devotion and love as His freeborn children and nurtured of blessing, such that no fear changes you nor any hostile attack weakens you. And because the beloved sons, the cantor of Brindisi and Brother John of the Order of Preachers, messengers of both your own and the beloved sons, the counts of Caserta and Acerra, who are to be commended for their commendable diligence and industry, have brought certain matters faithfully on your behalf to our attention, and having eagerly understood your devotion through them, with which you fervently strive with equal intent for the exaltation of the Roman Church, we intend to magnify you and your city with many graces and distinguish you with singular privileges. We wish you to know and hold with certainty through the tenor of these presents that, granting you entirely the freedom in appointing podestàs, enacting statutes, and other matters, which our faithful of the Patrimony of Saint Peter are known to possess, by apostolic authority, we shall always be kindly and benevolent towards you as particular sons of the same Church. And upon our forthcoming arrival to those parts, God willing, we shall favorably attend to the virtue of your matters concerning the progress of your city in all respects. Given at Genoa on the 3rd, the 10th day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth year. In the same manner to the podestà, council, and people of Capua.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa potestati, consilio et communi Neapolitanis scribit, laudans devotionem eorum et promittit eos cum privilegiis et libertate distinguere, sicut fideles de Patrimonio beati Petri. Dat. Ianue, 3 Iunii, anno VIII (1235).

**Translation to English:**

To the noble man Marco Ziani, son of the late P. Ziani, Duke of the Venetians. The Apostolic See, guided by the eye of due providence concerning the merits of all its devoted followers, never abandons the balance of justice. According to this balance, with prudent maturity, it measures the actions of each faithful and embraces them with the favorable arms of love and pursues them with the gift of special goodwill, especially those whom clear nobility adorns and whose noble origin embellishes generously. Thus, as we have learned from your own report, the County of Licia belonged to your grandfather of blessed memory, Tancred, and later was occupied and held by others. We, considering that not only the nobility of your lineage but also the sincerity of your clear devotion and entire merits, by which you laudably present yourself as favorable to us and the same See, make an appeal on your behalf, we favorably comply with your requests with kind assent, fully restoring the aforesaid county in our kingdom of Sicily with all its rights and appurtenances to you. And to encourage you to persist more ardently in devotion to the Church, we additionally grant it anew to you as a fief by special grace, unless it pertains to another who persists in devotion to the Church— notwithstanding if the noble man Count Tigritius of Mudignano or his sons claim to have a right in the said county by reason of the noble woman Alberia, your aunt and wife of the same, and daughter of your grandfather, since the same count and his sons adhered to the former Emperor F. of the Romans against the Church and still do not cease to offend, for which they rendered themselves utterly unworthy of grace and benefit of the Church. Furthermore, we wish that once you have possession of the same county, you will be obliged to render homage and swear an oath of fidelity and do other things to the Roman Church or to the king, who for the time being is in the aforesaid kingdom through it, which other vassals of the same kingdom are obliged to do for the counties they hold there. Therefore, let no one—our restitution and concession, etc. Given at Perugia, on the 12th day before the Kalends of March, in the ninth year.

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa nobili viro Marco Ziani, filio quondam P. Ziani ducis Venetorum, comitatum Liciensem in regno Siciliae cum omnibus iuribus et pertinentiis plenarie restituit et in feudum concedit, ob merita et devotionem suam erga ecclesiam. 1236, Feb. 18. Perusii.

**Translation to English:**

To the nobles of Swabia, devoted to the Roman Church. We received with usual kindness the noble man, the Count of Württemberg, your envoy, coming to the Apostolic See, and we fully understood what he proposed before us on your behalf. Indeed, the steadfastness of your faith and sincerity has deserved to find such favor with us that we gladly welcome anyone presenting your desires to us, and we pursue them with due zeal as circumstances demand.

We rejoice in the Lord and have deemed it worthy to extol your nobility with deserved praise because, with the fervor of devotion you have always had towards the Holy Church increasing, you stand and persist with unwavering constancy in the cause of Catholic liberty and your defense against opponents, as we have learned from the faithful account of the aforementioned noble. Therefore, the Apostolic See, congratulating your invincible zeal, is attentively considering your progress and is diligently devising appropriate support for you.

Behold, we are directing our letters to our most beloved son in Christ, W., the illustrious King of the Romans, urging him as is fitting, to hasten with strong hand and exalted arm, with swift deliberation and counsel, to come to the parts of Swabia for your assistance, to crush the opposing sides with the strength of royal power. We also will take care to send a suitable and faithful legate for the king's and the faithful's useful protection, who, filled with the zeal of our spirit, will diligently and effectively pursue the impending business.

However, to ensure we omit nothing that manifest utility demands, we are sending our beloved son, Brother H. of the Order of Preachers, our penitentiary, a man indeed prudent and discreet, to your parts, appointing him to the office of preaching the cross against C., once the son of F., who claims to be emperor, and his supporters, enemies of the Church and yours, and granting him the power to proceed against such supporters under an appropriate form to be given by us, as we will deem expedient for the said business.

But lest your hearts waver with any uncertainty about the success of the adversaries, and thus the persistence of your vigor may be somewhat diminished, we want you to know for certain and to hold that the offspring of the aforementioned F., since she is suspected not only of the hereditary imitation of paternal perfidy but also already a proven emulator of the cruelty of her ancestors and forefathers, will not rise to the honor of the Roman kingdom or empire or the principality of Swabia, which the survivors of that generation have deserved to be excluded from both by paternal and personal offense.

Indeed, let it be far from us that this change could be found in the most just judgment pronounced, or that we should fall into the unjust accusation of apostolic transgression by rebuilding the proud wall of ancient depravity, which divine severity has demolished; therefore be steadfast, beloved sons in the Lord, and in mutual defense, until the hostile adversity collapses before you, hold together with one mind, always to be supported by the timely patronage of the Apostolic See.

Given at Lyons, 2nd Kalends of April, in the 8th year [of our pontificate].

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa nobilibus Suaviae mandat, ut firmiter in defensione catholicae libertatis perseverent, et nuntiat se litteras ad regem Romanorum misisse, ut contra adversarios eorum auxilium ferat. Item, fratrem H. Ordinis Praedicatorum mittit, qui contra fautores C., qui se imperatorem gerit, praedicationem crucis exerceat. Dat. Lugduni, II Kalendas Aprilis, anno VIII.

**Translation to English:**

To the authorities, council, and people of Cremona, may the spirit of wiser counsel be with you. The tender affection of a mother compels her to think even of her errant children, for a mother is never so provoked by the excesses of her offspring that, bound by the union of natural affection, she does not always, with vigilance and concern, meditate upon them. Indeed, it is known to all, both near and far, what reverence and honor you have shown your mother church until now; your evident obstinacy towards her, your notable contempt, and the prolonged obstinacy of your hearts have escaped no one's eyes. For a long time, wandering outside her sweet and wholesome embrace as outsiders and degenerates, you have neglected to return to her and be soothed by her sweetness and be nourished by the honeyed breasts of the same church, and although she has often called out to you to turn from the wrong path to return to her gentle embrace, to be cherished under her wings of goodwill along with other faithful, you would not listen to the voice of her loving recall. It was not enough for you to despise the bosom of your venerable mother, but you also aggravated the offense by adhering to her enemies and her most severe persecutor, who, armed with your weapons, more forcefully lunged at her downfall and committed more harmful acts against her faithful. Yet, although you have been so injurious to her and have acted with the hardness of disobedient children against the clemency of her kindness, she retains no rancor against you nor has she hardened herself against you for all the injuries inflicted, so as to refuse to show mercy. But as a treasury of propitiation, a chamber of compassion, and a home of piety, she conserves mercy within herself, always prepared to forgive more willingly than to punish. Therefore, we, who from the duty of apostleship must look to the salvation of all, because we see you proceeding through deviant paths, call out to you in writing and admonitions to return to the path of salvation, to return to the Lord’s fold and remain in the communion of the faithful there. Indeed, for a long time, which we sorrowfully recount, you have been divided from ecclesiastical unity and separated from your neighbors by grave discord, paying no attention to the dire dangers that have arisen from this division and can occur in the future. For that you may more clearly comprehend the consequence, consider, we ask, as sagacious men not wholly clouded by ignorance, what arises from such dissension. It is evident that much slaughter of men, frequent devastation of lands, the overthrow of ancient liberty, and the crushing of the whole region proceed from it. Why then do you not see this? Why do you not lift your eyes to these things? Do you believe you are raging against enemies when you attack your fellow countrymen? Surely you are not raging against strangers, but against your neighbors, and what is more terrible, against your own kin and allies, indeed, to express it more fully, against yourselves, because you scarcely ever inflict loss on others without soon sharing in the harm yourselves. Behold, therefore, what kind of fruits your discord bears! Behold, what sort of benefit it provides you and what gain it brings to the country! For that noble region, once abundant in good things, used to excel among others, but now, depleted almost to exhaustion due to lack, it is entirely pale; for this reason, we have long ago deemed it right to exhort you through our letters, which we have ordered to be delivered to your community, so that contemplating the forementioned things cautiously, you would take care to return to devotion to the church and reform firm concord with your neighbors. However, because perhaps then the one who, with neck raised against the church, associated with him those he could to offend her, was holding you back from the bond of peace, we, considering that now, with him removed from the midst, the chief obstacle to peace is removed, so that you cannot pretend that you do not have the freedom to proceed to peace, have decided once more to send you our admonitions on this matter. **Translation to English:**

To all archbishops and bishops, abbots, priors, deans, archdeacons, and other prelates of churches, to whom etc. The bright devotion of the citizens of Lyon, shining with full sincerity toward the church, must be so firmly committed to memory that it cannot be obliterated by any forgetfulness over time. Indeed, due to the pressing nature of the times, when a storm of persecution was rising against the church in parts of Italy, we prudently decided to move to other regions, so that we might be able to give greater attention to the defense of the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical liberty. Thus, having avoided the storm of Italy, we arrived in the region of Cismontane, where calm repose and peaceful tranquility prevail, choosing specifically for our stay the city of Lyon, a city distinguished by its title of nobility, flourishing in the purity of faith, united in the bond of peace, rich in the abundance of its resources, and conveniently accessible and suitable for all by its location. In this city, having gathered a universal and celebrated council and diligently presented the cause of the church therein, we proceeded resolutely against its tyrants and persecutors, and, after careful deliberation with the same council, deemed it wise to make provisions concerning the necessary aid for the Holy Land and the Roman Empire, as well as against the imminent incursions of the Tartars and generally concerning the state of the church. This city is, indeed, remarkable for its devotion, having received the universal pastor of the church and the spiritual father of all the faithful with great reverence, and having greatly honored him along with his brethren and other officials and family members. The inhabitants of this city rightly deserve to be called the peculiar sons of the church, as they, tractable in humility, gentle in meekness, benevolent in affection, and composed in modesty, have strived to revere it as a mother and a lady in all things. Hence, the Apostolic See rightly embraces them with greater love, pursues them with more abundant favor, and elevates them with more potent grace, so that their recognized and rewarded goodness may serve others as an effective and operative example for the service of the church. However, because we wish their commendable merits to become known not only to those nearby but also to those afar, and to shine with worthy praise among them, we have resolved to send you our affectionate letters on their behalf, setting forth their devoted services, as we intend to promote both their benefit and honor, not only through ourselves but also through you and others. Therefore, we earnestly beseech and exhort your entire universality, mandating through apostolic writings and strictly commanding in the virtue of obedience, that you at all times receive the same citizens of Lyon, whom we have taken under the protection of Blessed Peter and our own, as particularly commended to you as sons of the Apostolic See, whenever it happens that they come to or pass through lands or places of your jurisdiction. You are to protect them favorably in their persons and goods, providing for their safe conduct if necessary, as they go and return, and not allowing them to be in any way molested or harmed by anyone. And if they seek justice for injuries or any matters, you are to offer it to them fully, without delay and without any hesitation, from your subjects when they request it of you, suppressing objectors with the removal of any hindrance of appeal by both our authority and yours. Furthermore, since it would be difficult for each of them to carry these letters with our seal, we wish and command that if they present to you the tenor or a transcript of these letters, certified with the seal of the archbishop or the official or the dean or the archdeacon of Lyon, who may be at the time, or another person holding dignity in the church of Lyon, you are to place firm faith in such a transcript, and diligently execute the apostolic mandate, as if you had received our letters, fulfilling our command concerning all these things so effectively that you may not be accused of negligence or disobedience, which we could in no way overlook unpunished, but rather be commended for obedience and diligence, which are accustomed to acquire praise and reward. Given at Lyon, on the Ides of February, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa universis ecclesiarum prelatis devotionem et merita civium Lugdunensium exponit et commendat, mandans eos sub protectione sua suscipiendos et iustitiam eis exhibendam. Datum Lugduni, Idibus Februarii, anno octavo.

**Translation to English:**

To Gerard, canon of Mainz, son of the noble Count Silvester, our devoted follower, and to Berthold, his cleric, canon of the church of Saint Peter in Mainz. Your petition presented to us contained that you, some time ago, communicated and gave favor to the late Emperor Frederick and his son Conrad after a sentence of excommunication had been pronounced against them and their supporters by our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Gregory. You received them into their fortifications for a time, and you, son Gerard, once joined the army of the said Conrad and took up arms against the archbishop of Mainz of blessed memory and others who conducted themselves as devoted to the Church and claimed to pursue the business of the general Church. Moreover, due to discord once arising between you and the said archbishop, you plundered certain churches and ecclesiastical persons of his diocese of some revenues and ecclesiastical goods and also caused them to be plundered. Because of this, the said archbishop, by his own authority, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against you, then the cantor of the greater church, and you, son Berthold, then canon of the churches of Saint John of Mainz, and publicly declared you excommunicated. He deprived you of ecclesiastical benefices that you held in his diocese and, as far as it was in his power, made you ineligible to obtain ecclesiastical benefices by a sentence. Later, at the council in Fritzlar of the said diocese, he degraded you from your orders. Furthermore, the same archbishop obtained the confirmation of such sentences by apostolic authority through the bishop of Speyer of happy memory and was allowed that any letters obtained for you from the apostolic see, in which you would be named as clerics, would not be valid unless mention of such deprivation and degradation was made in them. Since, as you claim, you arranged to make amends with the clergy of Mainz for the damages inflicted on them, and the archbishop himself, while he was still alive, received you into grace and absolved you from the aforementioned sentence of excommunication, we, moved by your supplications, considering the sincere devotion by which the beloved noble Count Silvester, your father, son Gerard, is known to have deserved the grace and favor of the apostolic see, by the authority of these presents grant you dispensation, that — notwithstanding the aforementioned sentences of deprivation and degradation, as well as that which rendered you ineligible, as expressed above, their confirmation and such indulgence by no means impeding — you may receive prelatures, dignities, personates, and ecclesiastical benefices with or without care, minister in the orders received and ascend to higher ones, and follow the favors made to you by us regarding your provision, and you, Gerard, may freely retain the aforesaid together with the benefices which you then had and which you subsequently acquired by our letters or otherwise canonically, with or without care. Let no one, therefore, etc., impede our dispensation and concession, etc. Given at Lyon, on the Calends of April, in the eighth year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Innocentius IV papa Gerardo canonico Maguntino et Bertoldo clerico eius canonicis ecclesiae Sancti Petri Maguntinensis concedit dispensationem, ut non obstantibus sententiis deprivationis et degradationis, possint beneficia ecclesiastica recipere et in susceptis ordinibus ministrare. 1251, Apr. 1, Lugduni.

Translation to English:

To the Archbishop of Bari: In order to restore the Kingdom of Sicily to its former state of liberty, which the iniquity of the late Frederick, who claimed himself as emperor, miserably oppressed, we, with pious diligence, have noted that among others, you have fervently supported this cause with us. Therefore, we confidently call upon your brotherhood to cooperate in this concern, knowing that your experience is effective in executing acts of piety. With the removal of the aforementioned Frederick, who had exhausted the strength of the said kingdom, reducing it to extreme misery, the inhabitants of those regions now have the opportunity to rise from the dust, remove from their necks the heavy yoke that oppressed them, and rise to the freedom of the sons of the Church, their mother. We confidently trust in your sincere love and command you to go to those regions. On our behalf, urge and induce the barons, nobles, city communities, and universities of places in said kingdom, promising them the remission of sins, to completely turn away from the sons of the aforementioned Frederick. Encourage them to return to the fidelity of the Apostolic See, to which the kingdom rightfully belongs, as its special and free sons. They should offer mutual aid and counsel against the sons of Frederick, heirs of tyrannical impiety, and their supporters, so that this viperous lineage, inimical to the faithful of the Church through its inherited hatred of the father, may be uprooted from the kingdom. To freely and effectively carry out this apostolic mandate, we grant you the authority to preach, yourself and through others, the word of the cross against the sons of Frederick and their accomplices, according to your God-given prudence. To those who take up the sign of the cross, grant the forgiveness of sins that is given to those signed with the cross for the support of the Holy Land, and to those gathered for the preaching of the cross, grant a forty-day indulgence as often as it seems appropriate for place and time. You may enlist religious men of any order, powerful in deed and word, to whom you can entrust the execution of these tasks in places where you cannot conveniently go. This is notwithstanding any contrary statutes of their orders or any indulgences of any kind granted to them or their orders by the Apostolic See. You have the authority to absolve those excommunicated in those regions for laying violent hands on ecclesiastical persons, provided their offenses are not grave or heinous, and to receive them back into obedience to us and the Church. Grant them the benefit of absolution according to the form of the Church, exempt their places from ecclesiastical interdict, and dispense with religious and clerics who celebrated divine offices with excommunicated persons, except those who closely adhered to the aforementioned Frederick and followed him damnably. You may communicate with the excommunicated in cases expressly forbidden by canon law without fear of canonical penalty or scruple of conscience, and you have the power to restrain contradictors through ecclesiastical censure, dismissing any appeals. You may also celebrate and hear divine offices in places of the kingdom under interdict, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, with closed doors, without ringing bells, and in a quiet voice. We grant you this authority by the present letter.

Regesto in Latin:

Gregorius IX papa archiepiscopo Barensi mandat ut accedat ad partes regni Sicilie et barones, nobiles, civitates communitates, universitates locorum regni inducat ad fidelitatem sedis apostolice reverti et contra filios Friderici consilium et auxilium mutuum largiantur. Conceduntur etiam facultates predicandi, indulgentiam largiendi, excommunicatos absolvendi, et alia necessaria ad exequenda mandata. Datum Anagnie, anno pontificatus eius VIII.

**Translation to English:**

To Thomas of Aquino, Count of Loreto and Acerra:

The sincere devotion you have shown towards us and the Apostolic See has deeply moved our heart, prompting us to consider you as a loyal and devoted son. Recognizing your appropriate request and the worthiness of your cause, we are eager to open the door of our heart to your petition, contemplating earnestly your honor and benefit. The burning devotion you have for your mother church, forsaking her manifest persecutors with whom you were honorably regarded for your many virtues, has persuaded us to show you the grace of the Apostolic See. You steadfastly adhered to her with faith and a firm mind, standing as a defensive wall against those persecutors.

Thus, inclined by your supplications, we confirm and fortify with the protection of this present writing, by apostolic authority, the county of Acerra and the city of Hoienti, as well as the castles of Piedimonte, Alano, and Longano of the Alife diocese, which, as you assert, belong to you by right of succession as the firstborn of the late Adenulf, the first Count of Acerra, your grandfather. We also confirm Sarno, which you now possess, as you propose, the castles of Cucculo, Iohe of the Capua diocese, Montemaranum, and also all goods granted to you by the late Frederick, the Roman Emperor, or his sons, both those you currently hold and those from which Manfred, the son of said Frederick, deprived you, with all their rights, honors, and appurtenances, notwithstanding any letters obtained by your aforementioned grandfather or others from said Frederick or his sons to your and your rights' detriment. Especially given that the kingdom of Sicily is currently without a king, we restore to you by special grace all goods from which Manfred or other persecutors of the church have deprived you at any time, saving the rights of any other party in the aforementioned matters. Let no one, etc., contrary to our restitution and confirmation, etc.

Given at Genoa, 21st June, in the eighth year [of our pontificate].

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Thomasi de Aquino, comiti Loreticensi et Acerrarum, confirmat et restituit comitatum Acerrarum, civitatem Hoientium, castra Pedemontis, Alani et Longani Alifane diocesis, Sarnum, castra Cuculi, Iohe Capuae diocesis, Montemmaranum et omnia bona concessa a quondam Friderico imperatore Romanorum vel filiis suis, tam ea quae nunc tenet quam ea quibus spoliatus est a Manfredo, auctoritate apostolica, cum omnibus iuribus, honoribus et pertinentiis. Ianuae, XI Kalendas Iulii, anno VIII (1234), confirmat.

**Translation to English:**

To the Bishop of Bergamo. We intend, by God's grace, to direct our steps towards Rome for the honor of the Church and the utility of all Italy, and we do not wish to neglect, while passing through Lombardy, to diligently discuss the peace of the Lombards, which has for a long time been disrupted by their prolonged discord. We have decided to send our letters concerning this matter before our arrival as heralds of our desire in this regard, so that in the intervening time, after our Lord God brings us back to Italy by His kindness, no delay will hinder the common peace once deliberation has been had among the Lombards. Thus, when God cooperates, the matter will be accomplished more quickly, since in the meantime, the Lombards, having been forewarned by these letters, will be able to prepare themselves more fully and better for its fulfillment. Our mind especially desires this: that the region, long afflicted by the scourge of wars and torn by constant discord, may be restored with the sweetness of tranquility and solidified with the bond of firm peace. For we cannot think of its prolonged troubles without much sadness of heart, knowing the region has endured much because of its own conflicts, of which it is known to have been both the nurse and supporter. Therefore, with all the affection of our mind, we desire that, with the root of discord extinguished and the seed of peace sown, this region may be refreshed in the fullness of concord, having been exhausted by mutual troubles till now, and that the sincerity of friendship, now seen to be scattered by internal enmities, may be restored.

Therefore, we command your brotherhood strictly in the virtue of obedience by apostolic letters, that you diligently set forth our fervent desire in this matter to the authority, council, and people of Bergamo, announcing on our behalf that we ardently aim at every good for the whole of their region, and that due to the great compassion the Roman Church feels for its great dissipation, we are earnestly laboring to restore concord there. Since hateful dissension has taken such root there, that lovable charity will forever be a stranger unless peace is brought back by support. Moreover, expressly declare to them that since we love and desire a harmonious and peaceful state of the Lombards among other desirable things, and are ready and prepared to provide every help and effort to achieve it, it will indeed be attributed to them and rightly ascribed to their fault if such a great good remains unfinished because of them, and we will justly be excused before God and men. Diligently and earnestly advise and induce them, and furthermore, command them by our authority to send messengers and solemn ambassadors fully empowered in this matter to us when we reach Genoa, with full authority regarding the reformation of peace and concord, so that such a necessary and wholesome matter cannot be impeded or delayed due to any deficiency on their part.

We also wish that both you and the said procurators or ambassadors strive to appear in our presence on the next upcoming feast of the Lord’s Ascension. And to more conveniently handle and complete this matter, ensure with eagerness that they provide full security to all from the other side of Lombardy, so that everyone from both sides can go and return safely everywhere, and ensure that such security is made into open and sufficient letters, to be sent by your special messenger to our beloved son Octavian, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata, or to our beloved son Gregory of Montelongo, legates of the apostolic see, so that they may have them published. For we are sending our letters in a similar form to the other prelates of Lombardy for each of their cities. Given at Lyon, on the Ides of March, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Innocentius IV papa episcopo Pergamensi mandat, ut desiderium suum de pace Lombardorum, diu discordia perturbatum, diligenter exponat Bergamensibus, et eos moneat, ut nuntios ad eum mittant cum pleno mandato de reformatione pacis, ut negotium impediatur. Dat. Lugduni, Idibus Martii, anno VIII.

**Translation to English:**

To the elected Bishop of Bobbio and the Abbot of Mezzano in the diocese of Piacenza. The overwhelming arrogance and insolent pride of the people of Piacenza have risen to such a height that nothing remains for them but to fall into the abyss of disgraceful confusion. For those who seemed to have escaped the persecutor's sword and could enjoy the peace and tranquility in triumph have willingly submitted their necks to the swords of their persecutors. Since this people, driven by a spirit of madness and turning away from the devotion to their mother [church], have shamelessly adhered to its enemies and persecutors, vainly persecuting it, it is fitting that the disloyal should bear loss from their disloyalty. Therefore, we command that you strip all the clerics, both religious and secular, of the city and diocese of Piacenza—who follow this people in such disloyalty and support them in their iniquities—of their dignities, offices, administrations, pensions, and any benefices; and also the laypeople of the fiefs which they hold from the churches. By our authority, you are to revoke any letters those clerics have obtained for acquiring benefices and favors from us or legates of the Apostolic See, and to declare any proceedings taken under those letters null. Furthermore, you are to excommunicate Oberto de Iniquitate—who, as his name suggests, is indeed in agreement with iniquity—and the adherents of said people unless they return to the devotion of the church within a fitting time set publicly by you. You are to publicly announce and have it announced that they are excommunicated in places where you see fit, subjecting the aforementioned city to the strictest interdiction, so that no divine office is celebrated or ecclesiastical sacrament administered there except for baptisms of infants and confessions of the dying. Under the threat of anathema, you are strictly to forbid any city from daring to appoint any of them as a ruler or to allow any of its own citizens to accept the governance of their city while the authority and people persist in such obstinacy. Should anyone dare presume otherwise, those who assume the governance of the city of Piacenza and those who elect the citizens of the same city to govern their own cities shall incur the bond of excommunication by that very act. Meanwhile, no one should presume to engage in commerce, conversation, or contract with the aforementioned authority and people, nor respond to them concerning any debt, making sure that they are expelled as excommunicated persons from places where they are found, and that their possessions may be seized and retained by others without penalty. Opponents, etc. — notwithstanding any indulgence granted by the Apostolic See to any persons or places, preventing them from being interdicted, suspended, or excommunicated by apostolic letters not making full mention of such indulgence, or any other privilege by which your process on this matter might be hindered or delayed and of which special mention should be made in our letters, and the constitution about two days, etc. If not both, etc. Given at Milan, the Ides of July, in the ninth year.

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa electo Bobiensi et abbati de Mezanot Placentine diocesis mandat, ut clericos et laicos populi Placentini, qui ecclesiae devotionem deserentes hostibus eius adhaerent, dignitatibus et beneficiis privent, et ipsos populum ac Obertum de Iniquitate excommunicent, nisi ad ecclesiae devotionem revertantur. 1235, Iulii 15, Mediolani.

**Translation to English:**

To the Archbishop of Cologne and his suffragans. The kingdom of Sicily, a special seat of the Apostolic See, long afflicted by many miseries, has been looked upon with benevolent divine mercy, and has been aided with compassionate consolation. A dark storm of prolonged tribulation had enveloped it, but it has been providentially liberated by the abundance of heavenly mercy to the desired respite of peace. The state of its current affliction has ceased, and the time of calm restoration has arrived. The dense clouds of sorrow that obscured it have disappeared, and the full serenity of joy has appeared, illuminating everything. That gloomy night, that dire night of cruel adversity has passed, and a clear day, a day of gracious propitiation has dawned for it. The renowned kingdom of Sicily has escaped the shackles of harsh servitude to which it had been long bound. It has emerged from the domain of Pharaoh-like subjugation, under which it was oppressed to the utmost depletion. It has passed beyond the most cruel torments of Neronic impiety, which disfigured its entire substance and gnawed at its innermost depths with ulceration, because in the fall of him who was the cause of its collapse and the occasion of the kingdom’s ruin, its burdens were lifted. Its customary freedom, which had long been forced to wander in violent exile, has returned to the kingdom. The free people, who had until now sighed under narrow burdens and burdensome narrowness, now breathe in the vastness of joy. The churches of the kingdom, which for so long were lashed by the hammer of tyrannical persecution, are rising again. They now lift their heads to a state of freedom, which impious hands were pressing into a state of misery, for the woeful voice of the oppressed and afflicted has leapt to the heights of heaven and sounded in the ears of divine majesty: wherefore, upon hearing the wails of so many lamenting, the Lord has shown mercy and, rising on account of their intolerable sufferings, graciously looked down from the highest heaven on the kingdom, to free its oppressed people by loosing the harsh yoke of their captivity. Truly, the mother church, sharing deeply in its bitterness, tasted its tears alongside it. She felt its fierce scourges upon herself and was bruised by its harsh blows; for the torments of that unique son as if pierced the depths of his mother’s heart. Now, however, in its consolation, she herself finds solace and is filled with the abundance of joy in its liberation. But since there are still tears upon its cheeks and the sweat of prolonged suffering appears on its face, the same mother church rises with ardent desire to wipe away those tears with the cloth of her kindness and, with a propitious right hand, to cleanse its sweat, and to fully restore the kingdom to the state of desired salvation, complete freedom, and solid peace, and to preserve it therein with firm stability through God's favor. For our intention is thus: to raise it to greater freedoms and to strengthen it with richer favors, the more it has been trampled by severe oppressions and wearied by harsher vexations. However, since with the removal of Frederick, the former Roman Emperor, some enemies of peace and lovers of discord might cast their eyes of greed upon the kingdom and release their rapacious hands intending to occupy it or to make conspiracies or enter into alliances there or to procure other harmful machinations in hatred or hindrance of the same church, as is recalled to have been attempted by some in times past, we, wishing to wield the sword of ecclesiastical power for the preservation of the kingdom against such persons, decree by apostolic authority that all who might dare to do these things are bound by the bond of excommunication, and that the places they reach, as long as they remain there, are to remain under ecclesiastical interdict. Therefore, we strictly command your community through apostolic letters that you solemnly publish the sentence of this excommunication and interdict in your cities and dioceses through yourself or others, and publicly declare all such presumptuous persons excommunicated, removing every obstacle of contradiction and appeal, and that you publish the said places interdicted as long as they remain there, so that you may fulfill the apostolic command regarding these matters in such a manner that you are seen to effectively execute the business of the Roman Church and we may justly have reason to commend your diligence therein with worthy praises in the Lord. Given at Lyon, on the seventh day before the Ides of February, in the eighth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa archiepiscopo Coloniensi et suffraganeis mandat ut sententiam excommunicationis in eos, qui regnum Sicilie perturbare conentur, publicent et loca ab eis occupata sub interdicto teneant. Dat. Lugduni. VII Idus Februarii

**Translation to English:**

To the consuls and people of Fano. We give abundant thanks to Almighty God, because from the days of Pope Innocent of blessed memory, our predecessor, your city along with the whole diocese, which undoubtedly belongs to the right and property of the Apostolic See, was restored to it after violence was repelled, through which it was unjustly held under foreign power for some time. When your envoy John Rustici came to the presence of that predecessor as your representative with your letters of ratification, he promised on your behalf that both you and all within your jurisdiction would faithfully show allegiance to him, his successors, and the Roman Church, to carry out campaigns and meetings, peace and war at the command of the same predecessor, his legates, and the envoys of the Apostolic See throughout the March, faithfully and at your own expense, to duly respect appeals made to the said predecessor or his legates or envoys, to provide suitable procurements to him, his legates, and envoys, and to pay an annual tribute of fifty pounds of usual currency, half for the city itself and the other half for its district, or if you prefer, nine denarii for each hearth, as is your custom, excepting clerics, soldiers, judges, advocates, notaries, and those known to hold no possessions, who are not accustomed to rendering tribute, which tribute you would deliver to the treasury of the said predecessor and his successors at your expense, humbly requesting and imploring that he would deign to confirm your consulship with its jurisdiction by apostolic authority, with all the domains remaining freely at the disposal of the same predecessor and his successors. Although you were accustomed to offering much greater to others, in order that you might feel and rejoice to have returned to the dominion of the one who can truly say of itself, "My yoke is easy, and my burden is light," the promise and offer made on your behalf by your representative was accepted by that predecessor with the counsel of his brethren. Therefore, in the likeness of that predecessor, we receive you as special sons under the protection of the Apostolic See, whom we wish to be perpetually held under its dominion, confirming to you the consulship with the jurisdiction that belongs to it both in criminal and civil matters, so that all consuls and authorities in office are held to an oath of allegiance to the Roman Pontiff and the Roman Church, and we consider your good customs valid and wish them to be inviolably observed. You and your successors shall perpetually and faithfully fulfill all that has been written and promised to us and our successors, and every ten years renew the oaths of allegiance and observance of the aforementioned, in all things preserving the authority of the Apostolic See. Let no one, therefore, etc., violate our concession and confirmation, etc. Given at Perugia, 15th Kalends of January, in the ninth year of our pontificate.

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa consulibus et populo Fanensibus consulatum cum iurisdictione confirmat, eos sub protectione apostolica suscipit, et promissionem fidelitatis renovare mandat. 1236, Dec. 18. Perusii.

**Translation to English:**

To the master and brothers of the Hospital of St. Mary of the Teutons in Prussia. The matters which are resolved by judgment or agreement, etc., up to: to be strengthened. Indeed, since a dispute had arisen between you on one side and our venerable brother, the Archbishop of Livonia and Prussia, on the other side regarding various articles, a friendly settlement was eventually reached between the parties, mediated by our venerable brothers, P. the Bishop of Albano, W. the Bishop of Sabina, and our beloved son I., the presbyter cardinal of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina, as is more fully contained in the letters drawn up and sealed with the seals of the bishops, the cardinal, and both parties. Therefore, inclined by your supplications, we acknowledge the settlement as properly made and willingly accepted by both parties, and we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it with the protection of the present writing.

We have caused the tenor of these letters to be inserted word by word in these presents; which is as follows: Peter, by the mercy of God, Bishop of Albano, and William, Bishop of Sabina, and John, by the same grace, presbyter cardinal of the title of St. Lawrence in Lucina, to all Christ's faithful who will inspect the present page, health in the name of Jesus Christ. Let your whole community know that, thanks to our mediation, a friendly settlement was reached in this way regarding the various articles of questions and rights between the venerable father Albert, Archbishop of Livonia and Prussia, and our beloved in Christ Theoderic, the master, and the brothers of the Hospital of St. Mary of the Teutons in Prussia and Courland:

1. Firstly, that all injuries and damages caused by the brothers to the archbishop and his household, and vice versa, they fully forgave each other from a pure heart.
2. The archbishop will allow the brothers to freely collect the redemptions of vows, as they have been accustomed to doing, and as it has been granted to them by apostolic letters.
3. The archbishop will diligently and faithfully promote preaching and advising on the business of the cross and faith conducted by the same brothers in those parts, in whatever ways he can.
4. He will not oppose nor will he allow anyone to oppose the privileges and liberties granted to the brothers by the apostolic see, but will allow them to use them freely without contradiction, holding everything as valid that was arranged by the venerable father G., the Bishop of Sabina, formerly of Modena, then the legate of the apostolic see in the aforementioned parts, by interpretation or in any other way.
5. The same archbishop also consents to, expressly ratifies, and will always consider as valid that the aforementioned brothers shall have two-thirds of the lands with tithes in the parts.
6. Similarly, the brothers will do regarding the graces and indulgences granted by the apostolic see to the same archbishop outside of Courland and Prussia, who will freely exercise archiepiscopal jurisdiction throughout his province.
7. The same archbishop will not himself or through others procure any harm to the said brothers.
8. He will never enter into an alliance or friendship with any Christians or pagans against the same brothers.
9. The aforementioned brothers will honor the said archbishop as is proper and just, and will not support those excommunicated and denounced by him unjustly, but will avoid them as is required by law.

Just as our master and lord distinguished a time for enduring from a time for avenging, first patiently bearing sinners' offenses upon His back for a long time, and then sternly questioning the wrongdoers about justice and judgment. Indeed, towards those who have, in recent times, oppressed Christ within the church amidst the storms of persecution stirred by the wickedness of perverse individuals, our patience has benevolently advised, bearing strongly and deferring judgment, offering them place for repentance, so they might earn pardon and the grace of reconciliation. However, among others who have abused the forbearance of apostolic gentleness in arrogance, the nobleman, the Count of Savoy, presents us with just and vehement cause for indignation and astonishment, especially since from the beneficence through which his house experienced the Roman Church as beneficent in many ways, we could have derived a more certain hope that the Count, provoked by a laudable zeal of devotion to the Apostolic See, would be zealous with us in the business of Catholic liberty against all adversaries in certain straits, and would rise and stand with the church, the common faithful mother, against all onslaughts of adversity like a wall. On the contrary, he failed this church, which held such confidence in him, not only in emerging difficulties but also caused harm, when he supported with his forces the once Frederick, who was pretending to rule as Roman Emperor, a man rejected by God so as not to reign treacherously over Christian people, together with his supporters and helpers who were delivered to Satan's judgment by the church and separated from the communion of the faithful, in his rebellion against God, causing much injury and loss to the Apostolic See. Although indeed on all those who presume to capture, detain, or despoil those coming to or departing from the Apostolic See, or hinder them, is annually pronounced the solemn sentence of anathema and excommunication at three major congregations of people by the mouth of the Roman Pontiff, he nevertheless, in favor of said Frederick, weighs down his transgression, and, through various injuries of spoliation and detention, iniquities attempted either by himself or his subjects, whom he aided by neglect or authority, violated the public immunity of those approaching the Vicar of Christ with sacrilegious presumption, a stubborn rejector of the curse by which the punishment of death is inflicted on souls. Indeed, when in the past an army was being sent from the Gallican parts into Italy under the stipends of ecclesiastical provision as support for the Catholic sons of the church, whom the aforementioned Frederick, a subverter of the Christian religion and disturber of evangelical preaching, was crushing with more damnable perfidy than the enmity of unbelief and heathenism, the same Count, to the grave peril of faith and ruin of ecclesiastical liberty, not only impeded the innocent passage of the same army and the legate of the Apostolic See under whom that army of pious collection was advancing to fight the Lord’s battle, in his land, but also around it in neighboring borders, for which the same church uselessly and harmfully suffered many losses. Likewise, disregarding the fidelity by which he was bound to the Church of Turin for considerable benefits which, as it is said, he ought to recognize from it, and thus himself becoming less worthy of the faith of his subjects, he occupied the castle of Ripolium and certain other places and rights, which undoubtedly belong to the same church, either through the fraudulent concession of the aforementioned Frederick, from which a more manifest title of wickedness accrued to him, or through his own ambition’s violence and deceit, by which he strove to attain the illicit detention of another’s property, with reverence for God cast aside; these are held by his authority or favor still occupied, to the enormous injury of the same church and the peril of the Count’s soul. We have awaited until now that he might be pricked by some goad of divine fear concerning all these matters and that he might make worthy fruits of penance for so many sins committed against God and His church, by which restored to the company of the faithful, he might be recalled to the way of life by healthy counsels, from which he has been turned away by wicked suggestions. But since the same Count does not seem to prudently consider from such a plague of guilt which he suffers that a danger of eternal death hangs over him unless it is cured by the remedy of appropriate satisfaction: we, unable to overlook the injuries inflicted on God and the Roman Church and unwilling to foster his sin by any neglect to our peril
