To the community of Castello Matrice in the diocese of Spoleto. Since the beloved sons of the communities of Norcia, Cassia, and Monte San Pietro, as special sons of the Roman Church, continually remain in devotion to the same church, and as we, for this reason, pursue them with apostolic favor, we earnestly ask and exhort your community, strictly ordering you by apostolic writings under penalty of five hundred marks of silver, that you do not offer any counsel, help, or favor to any disloyal individuals of the same church and especially to the citizens of Ascoli, as long as they persist in their disloyalty, against the said communities or any of them, nor should you in any way appoint any of the said citizens to power or as rector in the meantime, fulfilling the apostolic request and command in these matters in such a way that you avoid the same penalty and that we may justly commend the readiness of your devotion. Given at Orvieto, March 13, in the third year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa universitati Castri Matricis Spoletane diocesis mandat ne auxilium vel favorem praebeant civibus Esculanis contra universitates Nursie, Cassie et Montis sancti Petri, sub poena quingentarum marcarum argenti. 1230, Martii 13, apud Urbemveterem.

**Translation to English:**

To the Archbishop of Mainz. The house is indeed firmly established when it is supported by solid columns, and the Church is then fortified with much strength when it is fortified by the virtue and constancy of its prelates. Among these, since you are known to excel in honor and power, it is fitting and proper that you more favorably and ardently support the Church, and that it feels from you stronger support in times of need. For if its status is elevated and progresses with desired increases, you too grow with it through the sharing of its advancements; and if, God forbid, it is troubled by adversities and stung by unfortunate events, its troubles would not pass by you unnoticed, but you would experience its bitterness along with it. Even as you hold a more prominent and exalted position within it, so too would its prosperity bring you greater joy, and its tribulation would disturb you, nor could it rejoice greatly in your advantages without feeling deep sorrow for your adversities.

Indeed, it is clear how much affection the Roman Church has always shown towards you and other prelates of Germany, and how diligently it has strived to magnify and preserve you and your churches with favors, as it never failed in bestowing benefits and graces upon you and your churches, nor were you ever lacking its assistance in your needs, as it indefatigably sought to assist your affairs whenever necessary, as a promotress and diligent assistant in all things. Not without reason, as it found you among others to be ready cooperators and principal helpers in its endeavors; for which reason it is proper and necessary that you diligently watch over its honor, as it does not cease to attend to your benefits.

We have learned that the time for electing a king, to be later promoted to emperor, is at hand; in which case, greater attention and caution should be exercised the more important and difficult the matter, since any negligence or imprudence or laxity in this matter could result in a worse effect and more harmful outcome. Therefore, here one must be exceedingly vigilant, here one must observe keenly, here one must consider prudently, here one must deliberate maturely, here one must provide cautiously, here eyes must be opened, here ears must be attentive, here the mind must not be crude and sluggish but diligent, vigilant, and prudent, where it concerns the advocate of the Church, where its defender is concerned, lest instead of an advocate or defender, an assailant or oppressor is chosen or assumed.

Therefore, the utmost acuteness of thought must be applied from all sides, and a thorough investigation must be conducted everywhere, so that with the Lord's help, someone may be found and chosen who is faithful and devout, who comes from a lineage of devout individuals, and who is deemed fit and sufficient to attain such an honorable position and to exercise the governance of the empire. How the former Frederick, once Emperor of the Romans, and his ancestors and successors conducted themselves towards the mother Church and what recompense they rendered for the benefits received from it, is evident and known to the whole world. For they, exceeding the tyranny of other persecutors, inflicted greater injuries upon it and afflicted it with more severe oppressions, sharpening the bow of fury and the sword of ferocity everywhere, they grievously oppressed it and deeply wounded it, even to its innermost parts.

For in this evil lineage, the malice is derived from fathers to sons with blood, as much by the propagation of flesh as by imitation of deeds, and the descendants succeeded their ancestors. From which it can be clearly discerned and conjectured, if any remnants of this lineage survive, what is to be hoped for in the future from them and what to expect hereafter; for the life and perverse deeds of predecessors proclaim the iniquity of the successor, nor does the horrible and wicked memory of them permit any good to be believed or hoped for from their progeny. Indeed, from a serpent emerges a viper, and a bad tree yields harmful fruit, and a wicked beginning never promises a good outcome.

Therefore, concerning the boy Conrad, son of the aforementioned Frederick, caution must be exercised entirely, so that no intention is directed towards him, nor is he named for this, nor chosen in any way, especially since due to his childhood and extreme lack of age, he is entirely unsuitable and completely unfit for this; nor could he acquire or retain the right that usually arises from election, as due to his childish age, which lacks discretion and does not possess legitimate consent or dissent, he could not give consent to an election if it were made of him, nor would his consent have any efficacy or vigor. Also, the boy should not be elected or named king, because with such an election the Church should be provided with a suitable advocate or defender, and the boy is utterly unfit and useless for executing such a defense office or ministry; the Church would have to remain without the benefit of defense for a long time.

Moreover

**Translation to English:**

To the Archbishop of Cosenza. Since we are sending you, with the advice of our brothers, specially to our beloved son in Christ, Henry, the illustrious King of the English, and to the noble man Edmund, his son, concerning the business of the kingdom of Sicily, which was once negotiated and firmly established between our predecessor of happy memory, Pope Alexander, on one side, and the same King and Edmund on the other, under certain conditions and agreements which have not been fulfilled according to the conditions agreed upon by both sides: we entrust to your fraternity, in whom we place full confidence in the Lord, the task of liberating and absolving, in our name and that of the Roman Church, the aforementioned King and Edmund from all promises, obligations, oaths, and penalties, to which they are bound to us and to the same church on account of the aforesaid business, once the same King and Edmund have likewise freed us and the same church from all such agreements and expressly renounced them, as well as the grant of the aforementioned predecessor and any other grants or collations which they claim have been made by the Apostolic See or its envoys or legates to them or one of them regarding the aforementioned kingdom, and all rights they claim to have in the same kingdom for any reason. We grant you, with the advice and consent of our brothers, the free power by the tenor of these presents; and nonetheless, we appoint you, by apostolic authority, as our and the said church's special procurator and envoy to receive, in our place and that of the church, from the said King and Edmund such absolution, liberation, and renunciation, with the advice and consent of the same brothers, holding firm and valid whatever you decide to do in these matters according to the premises. Given at Orvieto, on the 25th of July, in the second year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa archiepiscopo Cusentino mandat ut Henricum regem Anglorum et Eadmundum filium eius, pro negotio regni Sicilie, a promissionibus et iuramentis absolvat, et eum procuratorem specialem constituit ad recipiendam eorum absolutionem et renuntiationem. Datum apud Urbemveterem, VIII Kalendas Augusti, anno secundo.

**Translation to English:**

To the consuls and all the men of the wool guild from Florence, may the spirit of wiser counsel be with you. We recall that not long ago, we requested through our letters in a certain form, that you, having due compassion for the miserable state of your city and being solicitous for your well-being, should strive to return to the embrace of Holy Mother Church from the region of dissimilarity, through which you are perilously proceeding after the leader of treachery and prince of darkness, namely Manfred, the former prince of Taranto and a manifest persecutor of the Church. However, you, like asps, closing your ears to the apostolic exhortations, not only have you scorned to return to the Church's embrace, but have also presumptuously and damnably attempted many grave offenses against the city of Lucca, which is most devoted to the Apostolic See, against our prohibition, paying no heed to the fact that the powerful arm of the Church customarily advances slowly towards vengeance, and that the delay it applies in punishing excesses it usually compensates later with the severity of the punishment. Since it is now almost evident to us that all the evil suffered these days by the city of Florence, indeed more truly by the Church in the regions of Tuscany, originates from you, and that you alone are the ones who, against us and the said Church, hold the city at this time, we hereby make known to your entirety by the tenor of these presents, that unless by the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary next to come, which we set as a final deadline for you, you care to humbly and precisely return to the mandates of the Church and procure the reformation of the said city, we will from then on firmly prohibit, under the penalty of excommunication, both Venetians and other faithful Christians located throughout Italy from engaging in any trade with you, or from purchasing your cloths or wool from you or others in any way, and we will also expose your persons and all your goods freely for the faithful to seize. Given at Orvieto, on the Ides of July, in the second year [of our pontificate].

**Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa consulibus et universis hominibus artis lane de Florentia mandat ut, nisi infra festum Assumptionis Beatae Virginis, redire ad ecclesiae mandata ac reformationem civitatis procuraverint, Venetis et Christianis per Italiam sub excommunicationis pena prohibebit mercimonia cum eis participare et bona eorum exponet fidelibus. Dat. apud Urbemveterem, Idibus Iulii, anno secundo.

**Translation to English:**

To Master Albert, our notary. You wrote to us about your entire proceedings regarding the affairs of the Kingdom of Sicily with our beloved son in Christ, Louis, the illustrious King of France, and also the response that the said king deemed to make to you on the same matter. In your letters, you added how, while you were on your way to our beloved son, the noble Charles, Count of Anjou and Provence, to have a discussion on the aforementioned matter, the same king recalled you to his presence through royal letters. He secretly told you that, after the response he had made to you on the said matter, he received letters from us through the noble John of Valenciennes, Lord of Caipha. It seemed to him not expedient that you should proceed in the matter with anyone else unless a response first came from us, whom he wished to consult on certain things contained in our letters through his own messenger. However, he did not want to reveal to you what was contained in our letters. You further added that you, being greatly astonished at what the king had newly told you, pondered frequently on what such words might mean, and you took care to propose before the same king that the delay of the said matter could be very damaging. It seemed hard to you, not without reason, that on the very matter which we had committed to your industry so earnestly, and with no mandate from us received to the contrary, you should not proceed with it. The said king replied to you that it pleased him that you should proceed towards Provence to discuss the aforementioned matter with the same count, but in such a way that you should bring nothing to effect unless we first sent you our good pleasure concerning this. Therefore, having received and read your letters, and since nothing concerning the aforementioned had yet reached us from the same king, hoping to receive some messengers from the same king shortly, we had decided to await the arrival of such messengers for a while before sending you our response in this matter. But because we have not yet received any messengers or letters concerning this from the said king, not wanting your mind to remain in suspense any longer, we have decided to send back the bearer of these presents to you, instructing you to inform us by your letters concerning your proceedings, if you have since had any on the same matter with the same count, as well as about the nature of the proceedings and what you have found in it and from the same count. If you have not yet had any discussion with the said count, we wish you to discuss the aforementioned matter discreetly, wisely, and cautiously with him. However, do not proceed to confirm anything with him in any way, as you know you have no authority from us to confirm anything on the said matter, but write back to us everything in detail. For if we happen to receive any messengers or letters from the aforementioned king concerning the premises, we will see to it that you receive a response from us concerning those matters if we deem it necessary. Given at Urbs Vetus, October 25, in the second year.

**Regesto:**

Urbanus IV papa Magistro Alberto notario suo scribit de negotio regni Siciliae cum Ludovico rege Francorum et Carolo comite Andegavie, mandans ut de processu informet et caute agat, sed nihil firmet sine mandato apostolico; si litteras a rege receperit, responsum dabit. Datum apud Urbemveterem, VIII Kalendas Novembris, anno secundo.

**Translation to English:**

To the Bishop of Trento. We have received, which at least due to infamy, if perhaps foolishly, which we do not believe, you do not fear the danger to the soul and honor, you can blush and grieve that you have newly granted certain castles, revenues, and proceeds belonging to the episcopal table to certain nobles in fief, and have pledged some of them under the title of a special mortgage, while enormously wasting and consuming other goods of that table, leading a very dissolute life, and though you hold temporal jurisdiction in the city and diocese of Trento, you do not defend the clerics of the same from the violence and incursions of laymen. Since therefore it is proper for prelates not to diminish but, if they can, to increase the goods and rights of their churches with fairness, not to deform their subjects with examples of depravity but to inform them with the merits of their virtues and to set themselves as a wall of defense for them: we, who are by no means delighted in the misdeeds of these prelates, wishing to show deference to you as much as we are able without offense to the divine and detriment to the clergy and church entrusted to you, admonish and earnestly exhort your fraternity, ordering that if this is so, consulting your honor and safety, you reform your actions, morals, and life for the better, revoke such infeudations and obligations, and completely desist from the waste of your church’s goods, protect and defend those clerics from oppression and injuries like a good shepherd, so that all infamy ceases from you regarding these matters and the scent of praiseworthy reputation follows, and that it may not be necessary to provide otherwise on this matter. Given at Orvieto, V Kalends of February, in the third year.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa episcopum Tridentinum monet et hortatur, ut actus, mores, vitamque reformet, infeudationes et obligationes revocet, et clericos a laicorum violentia defendat. 1229, Jan. 28. Apud Urbemveterem.

**Translation to English:**

To the captain, council, commune, and people of Spoleto, for a spirit of wiser counsel. Recently, after your syndic, having been given special mandate by you for this purpose, swore to comply with our mandates regarding the offenses committed by you against us and the Roman Church during this time, we sent our beloved son, Master Gregory of Naples, our subdeacon and chaplain, to your city for this matter. Among other things entrusted to him, he was given authority to enjoin upon you that you send a syndic with sufficient and full mandate to hear and comply with our mandates in our presence. However, you sent the noble man Bertuld of Babingan, your podestà, and some other fellow citizens to the Apostolic See. But since no syndic appeared before us on your behalf, who could hear and fulfill our mandates, we, although we could have proceeded against you by right due to this contumacy of yours, have deferred in this matter to you for the present with apostolic leniency. We have postponed the expression of these mandates and ordered the same podestà and fellow citizens peremptorily and expressly by word of mouth to send such a syndic to our presence by the next Monday. Moreover, no matter how sufficient this mandate to the same podestà and fellow citizens may seem, we have deemed it necessary to require this from you. Therefore, we command your whole community to send a syndic or suitable procurator with full mandate to hear and receive our mandates, which we will decide to make upon you for the aforesaid reason, and to fully comply with them, to us within the set term, which we assign to you peremptorily, eliminating any obstacle or hindrance of difficulty or occasion. Know that whether you send or not, we will nonetheless proceed in this matter, as justice, with the Lord's guidance, suggests to be expedient. Moreover, we firmly prohibit and enjoin you by the authority of these presents not to presume to inflict any war, molestation, or offense on the noble men, lords of Arrone and Castrolacus, and the people of Interamna, as well as the men of the monastery of Ferentillo and Cascia and Norcia, and other faithful to us and the Roman Church, who have acted against you by our command during this time. Given at Orvieto, 9th July, in the second year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa capitaneo, consilio, communi et populo Spoletanis mandat, ut syndicum seu procuratorem ydoneum cum mandato plenario ad audiendum et recipiendum mandata sua ad sedem apostolicam mittant, et prohibet ne guerram vel offensam inferant fidelibus ecclesiae Romanae. 1230, Iulii 9, apud Urbemveterem.

**Translation to English:**

To the Abbot of Saint Hippolytus of Faenza. The beloved son, the noble man William Azi of Faenza, son of the late Ugolino Azi, presented before us that the former Emperor of the Romans, Frederick, and his supporters inflicted heavy damages on this nobleman and his father when he was alive, because they were devoted to the Church. These damages affected both their homes and other properties. Later, when they waged war against these supporters due to this situation, they caused harm to many people, unlawfully acquiring many goods not only from the supporters but also from others who were not involved in this matter. Therefore, the said nobleman, guided by sound advice, humbly petitioned us that, as he is ready to make restitution for the damages, unjustly taken and acquired, both for himself and his father, who wished this while on his deathbed, and since he does not know those to whom restitution should be made, we might provide him with a wholesome remedy in this matter. Trusting fully in the Lord in your discretion, we command you to publicly announce in these places where such goods were received and damages given, and elsewhere as it seems prudent to you, if after a suitable period, which you shall set as a peremptory deadline, no one appears to whom such restitution should be made, then you shall assign to this nobleman for his and his family's support a portion of these goods, as you deem appropriate after carefully considering all circumstances. The remaining goods should be faithfully distributed with the advice of honest men for the poor and other pious uses, for the souls of those to whom these damages were inflicted, suppressing any opposition, etc. Given at Orvieto, February 2nd, in the third year of our pontificate.

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Abbati Sancti Ypoliti Faventini mandat, ut, si nulli appareant quibus restitutio facienda est, Guillelmo Azi de Favencia partem bonorum assignet pro sua et familiae sustentatione, ceteris in pauperes et pios usus distributis. 1230, Feb. 2, apud Urbemveterem.

Translation to English:

For the perpetual memory of this matter. Once the church of Metz was left without a pastor, and two elections were held in discord there: one for our beloved son Philip, then the treasurer, and the other for the late Theobald, the cantor of the same church. Eventually, this matter was lawfully referred to the Apostolic See through the appeal of the same Philip. While this was pending at our court, the aforementioned Philip, relying on the fact that the same cantor had relinquished his rights, obtained confirmation of his election from the elected Archbishop of Trier, the metropolitan of the place, and received from him the gift of consecration. He also served in the pontifical office for some time. However, although we later deemed this confirmation and whatever followed from it as presumptuous—not only against canonical laws but also to the detriment of the aforementioned See, where this case was being handled—and therefore invalidated it by our letters with the counsel of our brothers, because the same Philip later came into our presence and voluntarily resigned all rights in this matter into our hands, we, to avoid the peril of souls and the scandal of many, decide that whatever was done by him and those who acted on his behalf after his confirmation until the time when he could have learned about this revocation, including absolutions of the excommunicated, the allocation and bestowal of churches and ecclesiastical benefices, judgments and processes of cases by his officials as well as by the Abbot of Saint Vincent of Metz for him, and any other matters pertaining to ecclesiastical jurisdiction, provided all these are otherwise rightly carried out, should by the tenor of these presents remain ratified and firm—notwithstanding the aforementioned revocation of Philip, or if such benefices were later bestowed upon others by our authority—and we decree that all and each of these, by special grace, obtain full firmness. Therefore, let none — our constitution, etc. Given at Orvieto, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the third year.

Regesto:

Gregorii IX papae Philippo electo Metensi, electionem eiusdem confirmavit et concessit ut acta eius post confirmationem, sublata priore revocatione, rata et firma habeantur. Datum apud Urbemveterem, XVI Kalendas Martii, anno tertio.

**Translation to English:**

To Ludwig, Dean of Mainz, our chaplain. Know that it has come to our attention that several prelates of churches, as well as dukes, marquises, counts, nobles, ministerials, knights, and other laypersons in the region of Mainz and the surrounding areas, have dared with sacrilegious audacity to establish and collect new tolls in certain places within their lands and territories, to the offense of the divine name, detriment of the faithful passing through, and scandal of many. However, during three solemn feasts of the year, namely, the Lord's Supper, the Ascension, and the dedication of the basilica of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, each year by the Roman pontiff, who is at the time, all collectors of new tolls or imposts are struck with the sentence of excommunication in front of the multitude of faithful gathered at the Apostolic See, as is customary. We therefore command your discretion to ensure that this sentence is published by you and others wherever and whenever you see fit. Given at Orvieto, the Ides of March, in the third year [of our pontificate].

**Regesto in Latin:**

Gregorius IX papa Ludewico decano Maguntino mandat, ut sententiam excommunicationis contra exactores novorum pedagiorum in provincia Maguntina publicet. 1229, Mart. 15. Apud Urbemveterem.

**Translation to English:**

To the provincial prior of the Dominicans in Lombardy and the guardian of the Minor brothers in Asti. It is more fitting for us to zealously pursue and diligently correct the transgressions in prelates, by which subordinates are more gravely scandalized and such transgressions more perniciously become examples. Indeed, it has come to our attention that our venerable brother, the bishop of Piacenza, seemingly irked by the city of Piacenza's persistence in devotion to the Roman Church, handed it over to Uberto Pelavicino, an openly disloyal son and persecutor of the same church, and introduced Uberto into the said city, escorting him and receiving him in procession, utterly disregarding the seriousness of his episcopal office. Although we do not lend an attentive ear to accusations against prelates, to the extent possible with God, showing deference to them, nevertheless, this is not a fault that can or should be passed over in silence. We command your discretion to diligently inquire into these matters in the aforementioned city, if you can do so safely, or elsewhere in a location near the city where both the bishop and the witnesses to be produced can safely attend, and to faithfully record the truth and transmit it to us enclosed under your seals, having set a peremptory and suitable term for the bishop to appear before us either in person or through an adequate representative — notwithstanding the indulgence of the apostolic see, which is said to have been granted to your orders, that the brothers of those orders cannot be forced to hear cases or involve themselves in matters committed to them by the same see unless the letters of such commission make full and explicit mention verbatim of this indulgence and the orders. Given at Orvieto, 23 February, in the third year (of our pontificate).

**Latin Regesto:**

Gregorius IX papa priori provinciali Predicatorum in Lombardia et guardiano fratrum Minorum Astensium mandat ut de actionibus episcopi Placentini, qui civitatem Placentinam Uberto Pelavicino tradidit, veritatem inquirant et nobis transmittant. 1229, Feb. 23. Apud Urbemveterem.

Translation to English:

To the beloved son in Christ, Ottokar, illustrious King of Bohemia. Since the supreme pontiff, endowed with the keys of the heavenly kingdom in the person of Saint Peter by Him who, with eternal providence, governs both celestial and terrestrial matters, holds the pontifical authority to bind and loose, sometimes dispensing beyond the law from the fullness of his power, and loosens the bond of necessity to which all are bound for the observance of the law. On your behalf, it was presented to us that once the noble woman Margaret, formerly Queen of the Romans, in a provincial chapter of the Friars Preachers convened at Trier, took a solemn vow of chastity, promising to observe the order of the sisters according to the statutes of the aforementioned friars, and pledged obedience in the hands of brother H., then provincial prior of the same Friars Preachers in Germany. She took on the religious habit there and eventually, transferring to the convent of Saint Mark in Würzburg of sisters living according to the aforementioned statutes, under the care and governance of the same prior, she lived for more than a year under the same habit. Afterward, you contracted marriage with her in fact, cohabiting with her for some time as your wife. However, you and the said noble woman, realizing that you could not remain in the aforementioned marriage, which was null, without peril to your salvation, wished to separate, each parting from the other. All these matters are contained in the letters of several bishops of those regions and of the said noble woman, who, on this account, sent a certain messenger to the Apostolic See, and she also freely confessed this while still free. Certain religious men and others from the said regions, present at the said See, affirmed the same to be true. You then wed our beloved daughter in Christ, Kunigunde, illustrious Queen of Bohemia, niece of our dearest son in Christ, the illustrious King of Hungary, in marriage, who is related to you in the fourth degree of consanguinity and third degree of affinity. However, as we have learned, due to the persistence of the marriage contracted between you and the said Kunigunde, peace is preserved in the kingdoms of Hungary and Bohemia and other neighboring provinces, and the faithful of those regions are strengthened to resist the infidelity of the Tartars and other enemies of the Christian faith, and many are liberated who would otherwise be subjected to perpetual servitude, and many other benefits are known to arise. We, having diligently considered these and other preceding matters, declare that, if the aforesaid are indeed true, the marriage which, as mentioned, you and the said noble woman contracted with each other is not valid. Inclining to your supplications and those of the said king imploring apostolic grace on this matter, we dispense with you by apostolic authority so that, notwithstanding the impediment arising from such consanguinity and affinity, you and the said Kunigunde may lawfully remain in the aforementioned marriage contracted between you. Let no one therefore etc. of our declaration and dispensation etc. But if anyone etc. Given at Viterbo, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the first year.

Regesto:

Gregorius IX papa Ottocaro regi Bohemiae declarat matrimonium a rege cum Margareta contractum nullum esse ac dispensationem concedit ut cum Kunigunde remanere possit. 1227, April 20.—Viterbii.

Translation to English:

To Master Albert, our notary. Since we are sending you specifically to our beloved son, the noble man Charles, Count of Anjou and Provence, for the business of the Kingdom of Sicily, we wish to inform you by the tenor of these presents that if it happens that the said business is concluded according to the conditions given to you by us between the Roman Church and the same count, we intend, with the Lord as our guide, to condescend to his wishes regarding the petitions he submitted to us through his messengers in such a way that this business will not be impeded or delayed. These petitions are the following: namely, that we should grant the same count the tithe of all ecclesiastical revenues of the Kingdom of France and the County of Provence, as well as of the provinces of Lyons, Vienne, Embrun, Tarentaise, and Besançon, for the prosecution of this business for three years; and that we should have the word of the cross proclaimed against Manfred, the former Prince of Taranto, and the Saracens of Lucera in all the lands where the tithe is granted to the same count, as well as in Lombardy, Tuscany, the March of Ancona, and other lands adjacent to the said Kingdom of Sicily, where this word can be safely proclaimed, and that we should grant to those who take up the sign of the cross against Manfred and the aforementioned Saracens the same indulgence, privileges, and immunities that were granted to those crossing over in aid of the Holy Land in the general council; and that we should also give to the said count all redemptions of the vows of those persons who take up the sign of the cross in aid of the said business and wish to redeem these vows; finally, that we should receive all the lands of the said count and the lands of those who come with him for this purpose under our and the Apostolic See's protection during the prosecution and promotion of this business, and that we should pronounce a general sentence of excommunication against all those who presume to disturb, harass, or inflict violence upon the count and the others aforesaid in their lands; and that we should never consent that Conrad, a boy born of the late Conrad, son of the late Frederick, formerly Emperor of the Romans, or anyone produced in any way through their line, or even anyone who could claim or might claim to have a right in the aforementioned Kingdom of Sicily or any part of it, should ascend to the throne of the Roman Empire; and that we should take care, if the count himself wishes, to deprive the said Manfred of the same Kingdom of Sicily and all other lands that he holds within the borders of the said Roman Church's lands by definitive sentence, and have all spiritual and temporal sentences already pronounced and to be pronounced against him and all his counselors, supporters, and favorers published everywhere; furthermore, that we, by apostolic authority, should deprive all those who presume to adhere to the same Manfred after the said Kingdom of Sicily has been granted to the aforementioned count of all lands, fiefs, goods, and rights which they hold from the said Roman and any other churches and persons and ecclesiastical places; finally, that we should take care to establish a bond of confederation and peace among all those persons whom the same count will nominate to us, provided that they are such persons whose confederation or unity or unanimity seems expedient to us. Given at the Old City, on the sixth of the Kalends of July, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

Regesto:

Innocentius IV papa, Magistro Alberto notario suo mandat ut ad Karolum Andegavie ac Provincie comitem pro negotio regni Sicilie destinatus, super petitionibus comitis, Ecclesiae Romanae nomine, condescendat. Datum apud Urbem veterem, VI Kalendas Iulii, anno XI.

**Translation to English:**

To the presbyter cardinal of the title of Saint Cecilia, legate of the Apostolic See. We grant to your discretion, in which we have full confidence in the Lord, the full and free authority, by virtue of these presents, to suspend from the upcoming feast of Saint John the Baptist until a year later, the passage of those from the kingdom of France and other lands under your legation, who have taken or will take the sign of the cross for the aid of the Holy Land—despite any contradiction from anyone. Given at Orvieto, on May 8, in the third year [of our pontificate].

**Regesto in Latin:**

Translation to English:

To the authorities, captain, elders, council, and community of Lucca. Intending to procure for you the advantages of peace for the praise and glory of the divine name, we would willingly and diligently wish to remove every obstacle by which such a great good might in any way be hindered. Behold, therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, as our mind, concerned with the honor and exaltation of your city, had vigilantly considered thoughts of peace and concord to be reformed between you and the Pisans by the Lord's will, and as we had sent certain suitable persons to this end to the city of Pisa and to you especially, it suddenly came to our hearing that, through the machinations of the enemy of the human race, who is the author of divisions, an enemy of fraternal peace, and a relentless persecutor of the tranquil state of the faithful, you yourselves, having gathered the forces of your power from all sides, proceeded hostily to attack and besiege the Castle of Aginulfi in the diocese of Luni, which the same Pisans hold, and the said Pisans against you and your city have again gathered and renewed their army. Over this, our hearts are the more troubled the more we fervently desire that the bonds of peace be reformed between you and the same Pisans, so that you, who have been worn down by so many attacks of wars and battles, may breathe from your distresses and vexations. Since we therefore desire with all the affection of our minds that you, who have hitherto drunk the wormwood of discord, may at least in our happy times taste the sweet and beloved fruit of peace by the Lord's will, we have deemed it fit to diligently exhort, entreat, and urge your entire community, commanding that, considering wisely that if you happen to obtain the said castle and have the peace treaty take effect, you would need to restore it entirely, as you hold dear our grace and that of the apostolic see, you immediately, upon receiving the present letters, withdraw from the attack and siege of the said castle, removing any obstacle of difficulty, and return to your own, so that the negotiations already begun on the matter of peace, with God's favor, may have a prosperous progression and a happy outcome. For we have given commands to the community and people of Pisa under certain terms by letters to desist entirely from the gathering of such an army and to cause you and your city no trouble or offense. Therefore, you should strive to fulfill our prayers and commands on this matter in such a way that we may justly commend the promptness of your devotion with worthy praises in the Lord, so that we may consider you lovers and followers of peace and concord. Given as above.

Gregorius IX papa potestati, capitaneo, anzianis, consilio et communi Lucanisi mandat ut impugnationem et obsidionem Castri Aginulfi Lunensis diocesis deserant, ut pax cum Pisanis reformetur; litteris mandavit etiam Pisanis ut ab exercitus congregatione desistant. Datum ut supra.

To the Archbishop of Embrun, legate of the Apostolic See. We have gathered sufficiently from the devoted series of your letters, as well as from our own mind, how entangled and confused, how detestable and harmful the state of Lombardy has been for a long time and still is today. It is particularly evident in this, that it is entangled in costly lawsuits and dangerous discord not without grave offense to God, causing us, as well as some of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, to often sigh deeply and even shed tears. From this arises the fact that concerning your bodily health and the manifold distress of heart, which you are known to have frequently suffered due to the detestable cunning of many from those parts, we sympathize with you with paternal affection, and we also follow you with full acts of thanksgiving to the Lord, for you have strived to pursue the office of legation you have undertaken with all diligence and virtue. To this, because you have earnestly and humbly requested that we set forth our goodwill for you concerning various points contained in your aforementioned letters, we have decided to respond to your fraternity that the benefit of absolution, rashly granted by a certain religious person to Pelavicino and Bosio de Doata, as well as to those Cremonese who were then in the army against the once-treacherous and impious Ezzelino, having no authority over this matter and not keeping the form of the Church in any way, with the Friars Minor and Preachers having been overlooked, through whom such absolution should have proceeded according to your ordinance, you should declare it void by our authority and publicly announce that it holds no weight, provided that if the aforementioned Pelavicino and Bosio wish to return to the mandate of the Church reverently and remain in its devotion with pure faith, and completely renounce the association or confederation they damnably entered with Manfred, the late prince of Taranto, or any other enemies of God and the Church, and also provide fitting satisfaction for those matters for which they are bound by the apostolic see with the chain of excommunication, you may grant them the benefit of absolution according to the form of the Church, having first received suitable security from them for observing these matters, doing the same for the Cremonese and any others or communities even of Lombardy or the March of Treviso as far as relaxing the sentences of excommunication and interdict, provided that they wish to return humbly to the mandate of the Church in the manner stipulated above. Regarding the satisfaction to be given by them, since it is believed that it could scarcely or never be forthcoming, and also concerning obtaining suitable security that they will faithfully observe the mandate of the Church, you should proceed as your discretion sees fit, while taking the utmost care that competent restitution is made to the churches and ecclesiastical persons for immovable goods entirely, and also for movable ones, if any remain, which the aforementioned Pelavicino and Bosio or communities unjustly took from those churches and persons. You should also diligently ensure that if they have imposed any burdens or obligations on those churches and persons or decide to impose them in the future, all such burdens and statutes and all other things that result in their prejudice and detriment to ecclesiastical liberty are removed. Concerning forming a confederation or alliance between any cities in the name of the Roman Church, since it does not befit it to be involved in such matters, you should in no way interfere. Furthermore, because the Lord, the consoler of the deserving, has mercifully heard the groans of His Church and has brought to the desired end the tears of many who were constantly imploring His mercy over such great distresses, by breaking the horns of the aforementioned Ezzelino with His mighty arm, do not preach the cross any longer nor have it preached. Do not demand the redemption of vows nor have them demanded from those who once took the sign of the cross against the same Ezzelino, for we will provide at the appropriate time, as will be expedient. Moreover, we commit to your prudence that you remain in those parts and prudently and commendably execute the office of your legation according to the custom, as long as, considering the appropriate circumstances, you have confidence that, concerning those things affecting the honor of the Church, you can, with God’s favor, prosper. But if your presence there is not fruitful, we grant you permission to return to us whenever you think it advisable.

Given at Anagni, on the Ides of December, in the fifth year [of our pontificate].

The venerable father Albert, former bishop of Ratisbon, prudently considering that the enmities he incurred by opposing, at the mandate of the Roman Church, the former Roman Emperor Frederick, still persisted inexorably against him in those parts, and that because of this he could not obtain peace of body and mind in the governance of the Ratisbon church entrusted to him, nor could he benefit his subjects due to their obstinacy as he ought for their salvation; also considering that on account of the investigation which the most holy father and lord, Pope Alexander, had commanded to be made against him at the instance of the chapter of Ratisbon, the said church of Ratisbon could incur grave harm in spiritual and temporal matters; and for this reason choosing to provide peace and tranquillity for his body and mind, to break the aforementioned enmities, and to protect the church of Ratisbon from such damage, he freely resigned the said governance into the hands of the same lord pope; and the same lord, seeing the praiseworthy intention of the bishop, accepted this resignation, though reserving the episcopal dignity for him, and invalidating the investigation.

Wishing also that the efforts which the bishop is known to have made in promoting the cause of the church against the said Frederick and his followers should be duly compensated with grace, and to provide for the bishop himself lest the excessive poverty should cheapen his episcopal dignity, he ordered us by oral command to ensure provision for him of 300 marks of silver from both the ecclesiastical benefices, even those with the cure of souls, within the city and diocese of Ratisbon, to which the collation pertains to anyone, and from the goods of the Ratisbon see. Although in our previous letters we have earnestly requested your greatness to ensure that the promotion and affairs of the Kingdom of Sicily should not be hindered in any way due to the discord said to have arisen between our dearest daughter in Christ, Margaret, the illustrious Queen of France, your wife, and our beloved son, the noble Charles, Count of Anjou and Provence, your brother, by amicably settling this discord with all effective aid and effort: we, who greatly desire the advancement of the said affair, through which we hope, with the Lord's favor, to liberate the Roman Church from the imminent dangers surrounding it, have decided to earnestly request and exhort your serenity once more, while also advising for the remission of your sins, that you exhort the aforementioned queen to be accommodating, cooperative, and kind in this peace affair with attentive and effective inducements; and if ultimately you find her, heaven forbid, too obstinate and inflexible in this matter, let it please your mildness that the aforementioned affair of the Kingdom of Sicily, so pious, so healthful, so beneficial, initiated with so many labors and discussions and now mostly completed, should not suffer any hindrance or delay due to this, but should proceed freely to the praise and glory of the divine name, the increase of Christian religion, and the peaceful and tranquil state of the aforementioned church. To all Germans residing in Tuscany, Lombardy, the March of Ancona, and other diverse parts of Italy in the service of Manfred, the late Prince of Taranto, and his supporters, may you gain the spirit of wiser counsel. Serving in the camps of damnation and death under the leader of treachery, namely Manfred, the late Prince of Taranto, an open persecutor of the Roman Church, and not realizing that by following his rejected and wicked footsteps, you are hastening towards the ruin of eternal salvation under his precipitate and dangerous leadership: We, moved by paternal compassion for your sorrowful and lamentable state, desiring to draw you back from the final fall with the cord of apostolic exhortation, lest you irreparably collapse, have opened a path to life and shown the way to salvation, by which you may healthily return from the region of dissimilarity to the bosom of Mother Church, having abandoned its persecutors. Behold, now is the acceptable time, behold, now is the day of salvation, in which, if you wish, you can abandon the devil and his minister and serve God and His Church without your detriment. For we intend, for the recovery of the March of Ancona and other rights of the said Roman Church, to retain two hundred of you, decently armed and mounted, for a year, and two hundred more for three months, in the service of the said Church, under the stipends you receive from the said Manfred and his supporters, to be paid to each according to the agreement that will be made between us and you in this matter. We therefore ask and earnestly request your discretion by the tenor of these presents, and we command you by apostolic writings and additionally enjoin it for the remission of sins, that you, concerned for the salvation of your souls and bodies, diligently ensure to return with ready minds to the prepared embrace of maternal acceptance, from the Church not only receiving such monetary but also spiritual stipends, so that the time you have uselessly consumed in the service of the Church's adversaries, you may usefully redeem by serving the same Church. For we will liberally admit those of you who come to us for this purpose to our grace and that of the apostolic see, granting them the benefit of absolution according to the form of the Church from the bond of excommunication, to which they are bound by favoring the said persecutors. And as we find them faithful and prompt in our services, so we will follow them with apostolic favors. Moreover, so that you may more freely withdraw from the aforementioned persecutors, we absolve you all, individually and collectively, from oaths, if you are bound to these persecutors by any such, by apostolic authority and decree you as absolved. Given at Orvieto, 11th of July, in the second year.

Apud Urbemveterem.

To the Bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. Since the noble man Peter, a Roman citizen, who was bound by the chain of excommunication due to the favor once shown to Manfred, the former Prince of Taranto, has urgently requested us to have him absolved from such a bond, we have decided to entrust this matter of absolution to you. We command your fraternity to observe the following form for this absolution and no other: namely, that the same Peter, first of all, swears corporeally to adhere to the commands of the Church and provides a surety in addition, under a penalty you deem appropriate, and that you will command him under the obligation of the sworn oath that henceforth he will neither have nor accept Manfred as senator or lord of the City, nor will he procure or allow him to be chosen or assumed. Instead, he will offer no favor, counsel, or assistance to those wishing to have or assume Manfred, or those procuring his election as senator or lord of the City, either publicly or covertly, nor will he receive or send letters, messengers, or gifts to him, as long as Manfred persists in the excommunication pronounced against him by the Apostolic See, and in the meantime he will provide no help, counsel, or favor. Moreover, he will completely withdraw from all confederations, oaths, promises, or pacts by which he has bound himself to Manfred or others on Manfred’s behalf until now. Regarding these mandates and his acceptance, all of which we wish to be carried out in the Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles in the City, with the rectors of the City personally present with you, you shall have a public instrument drawn up and brought to us. We wish you to proceed with all these while preserving our other mandates, which we see fit for him regarding this matter. Once these are duly carried out as stated, you shall bestow upon Peter the benefit of absolution concerning this sentence of excommunication, according to the form of the Church, further ensuring that this absolution, which you will bestow upon him according to the aforementioned form, is publicly announced by the same rectors as having been conferred in all the major churches of the City in the same form. Given at Orvieto, 14th Kalends of January, the third year of our pontificate.

Gregorius IX papa episcopo Portuensi et Sanctae Rufinae mandat ut Petrum civem Romanum, qui ob favorum Manfredo quondam exhibitum excommunicatus est, sub certis condicionibus absolvat et hanc absolutionem publice in maioribus ecclesiis Urbis nuntiari faciat. Therefore, we desire and command you by the authority of these letters, to diligently and fervently continue the peace negotiations entrusted to you, and to frequently report back to us on the state of the matter and whatever actions you take in this regard. Desiring to reform the bonds of peace and concord between you and the citizens of Lucca to the praise and glory of the divine name, we recently decided to send our beloved sons, Brother Mansuetus of the Order of Friars Minor, our chaplain and penitentiary, and the noble man Sigerius de Sassecta, our marshal, to you as angels of peace specifically for this purpose. However, because we subsequently learned that the said citizens of Lucca, provoked by the things they have reportedly suffered from you in these times, have proceeded with hostility to attack and besiege the Castle of Aginulfi in the diocese of Luni, which you are said to possess, and that you in turn, moved by this, have again gathered an army against the city of Lucca: we, desiring with all our heart that every obstacle be removed which could in any way hinder the good of peace, have sent letters with specific instructions to our beloved sons, the podestà, captain, elders, council, and community of the Lucans, ordering them to immediately, upon receiving these letters, withdraw from the siege and attack of the said castle and return to their homes, as they value our grace and that of the Apostolic See. Therefore, we strongly admonish, ask, and urge all of you, ordering that you also, considering that if the said Lucans, provoked by you, as you know, have done something that perhaps displeased you, you should not recall this too much to mind, but, out of reverence for the Apostolic See and us, desist entirely from such a gathering of forces and inflict no harm or offense upon the said city of Lucca, but, laying aside all resentment, diligently and fervently pursue the peace negotiations which we believe have already been started by the said penitentiary and marshal, lending your ears effectively to their exhortations on this matter so that you may make the King of Peace favorable and kind to you and render us more ready to procure your spiritual and temporal benefits. Given as above.
